On 27,000 future-retrieval trials from household egocentric video, a model must pick the true continuation of a clip among eleven candidates from the same video (chance 0.091), ranked zero-shot by its own training criterion. Each model is paired with a persistence control, an identical copy whose predictor is never invoked, so the paired difference isolates the predictor. Score and contribution dissociate within the native-video V-JEPA family alone: the predictor adds +0.291 top-1 for V-JEPA 2.1 but +0.03 to +0.04 for V-JEPA 2 on the identical trials. Across five models the contribution ranges from +0.291 to negative, and it is negative only for the two action-conditioned models, which we evaluate outside their training regime. Persistence alone recovers the encoder ordering expected from pretraining, a sign that the probe tracks real signal. We suggest reporting each future-prediction score together with its persistence baseline. The gap between them, not the score, is what makes the number interpretable: a necessary check costing one forward pass. Establishing downstream usefulness is a separate matter, for a planning or control evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that future-prediction scores for video world models mix encoder quality with predictor contribution, and proposes reporting each score with a persistence baseline. The predictor adds +0.291 top-1 for V-JEPA 2.1 but only +0.03 to +0.04 for V-JEPA 2.
AI.motivation: Pretrained video world models are chosen for robot learning mainly by future-prediction scores, which cannot be read as evidence of prediction on their own.
AI.method: On 27,000 future-retrieval trials from household egocentric video, each model picks the true continuation among eleven candidates (chance 0.091). Each model is paired with a persistence control whose predictor is never invoked, so the paired difference isolates the predictor.
AI.result: Across five models the predictor's contribution ranges from +0.291 to negative values, and is negative only for the two action-conditioned models, which are evaluated outside their training regime. Persistence alone recovers the expected encoder ordering.
AI.conclusion: The gap between a score and its persistence baseline, not the score alone, makes future-prediction results interpretable, though downstream planning or control evaluation is still needed.

title: Keep Images in Sight: Visual Position Re-Anchoring for Long-Context MLLMs
summary: Long-context multimodal intelligence requires revisiting earlier images as conversations and documents accumulate, yet retaining an image does not guarantee reliable access to its details. By varying context length, redistributing a fixed text passage around the image, and changing positions without adding text, we identify the positional relation between images and questions as a direct influence on visual access. To address this gap, we propose Visual Position Re-Anchoring (VPR), a training-free method that shifts cached visual-key rotary phases toward a short-context reference before question processing. It operates directly on the existing KV cache, preserving standard attention computation without extracting attention maps or adding model forward passes. We develop static and continuous compensation schedules, using the static schedule by default. Across ten checkpoints and ten benchmarks, static VPR improves 97 of 100 model--task scores. Further analysis shows greater attention to regions containing answer evidence across six checkpoints, with minimal runtime overhead under fixed rotary frequencies. These findings demonstrate an efficient way to sustain visual access through positional adjustment within the cache.

AI.tldr: VPR is a training-free method for long-context multimodal LLMs that shifts cached visual-key rotary phases toward a short-context reference before question processing. Static VPR improves 97 of 100 model-task scores across ten checkpoints and ten benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Retaining an image in context does not guarantee reliable access to its details, and the positional relation between images and questions affects visual access.
AI.method: VPR operates directly on the existing KV cache, adjusting rotary phases of visual keys without extracting attention maps or adding forward passes. Static and continuous compensation schedules are developed, with the static schedule used by default.
AI.result: Static VPR improves 97 of 100 model-task scores across ten checkpoints and ten benchmarks. Attention to regions with answer evidence increases across six checkpoints, with minimal runtime overhead under fixed rotary frequencies.
AI.conclusion: Positional re-anchoring within the cache is an efficient way to sustain visual access in long-context MLLMs.

title: From Seeing to Remembering: Brain-Informed Agentic Text-to-Video Generation for Enhancing Memorability
summary: Generating videos that faithfully convey intended semantics while remaining memorable to viewers is valuable for applications such as advertising, education, and storytelling. However, memorability-oriented text-to-video generation remains underexplored, as human memory involves complex neural processes that are difficult to model and translate into generation guidance. In this paper, we propose MemCrafter, brain-informed approach that enhances video memorability through iteratively agentic prompt refinement. The agentic framework contains two key components. First, we construct a cortical region-based neuro-memorability signal that predicts video memorability from estimated neural responses, providing both an optimization objective and interpretable region-level information. Second, we develop a sensitivity-aware feedback module, motivated by a conceptual sensitivity analysis of the optimization objective, to derive actionable guidance for prompt refinement while preserving semantic fidelity. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MemCrafter consistently improves predicted video memorability while maintaining semantic alignment and perceptual quality.

AI.tldr: MemCrafter is a brain-informed agentic text-to-video framework that refines prompts iteratively to improve predicted video memorability. It uses a cortical region-based neuro-memorability signal and a sensitivity-aware feedback module, while keeping semantic alignment and perceptual quality.
AI.motivation: Memorability-oriented text-to-video generation is underexplored, and the neural processes of human memory are hard to translate into generation guidance.
AI.method: A cortical region-based neuro-memorability signal predicts memorability from estimated neural responses and serves as the optimization objective. A sensitivity-aware feedback module, based on a conceptual sensitivity analysis, produces guidance for prompt refinement.
AI.result: Experiments show that MemCrafter consistently improves predicted video memorability while maintaining semantic alignment and perceptual quality.
AI.conclusion: Brain-derived memorability signals can guide agentic prompt refinement for more memorable generated videos without losing semantic fidelity.

title: Toward Cross-Rubric Surgical Skill Assessment via Joint Embedding Prediction
summary: Expert review of surgical videos is essential for surgical training but labor-intensive, motivating AI-assisted skill assessment to provide feedback at scale. Although surgical assessment rubrics may use different language to describe similar skills, existing automated methods commonly predict predefined skill levels or numerical scores tied to fixed rubrics, limiting their ability to transfer across semantically equivalent assessment criteria. We propose Predictive Rubric Alignment (PRA), a joint embedding prediction approach that scores surgical videos using natural-language descriptions of skill levels. Rather than matching level probabilities, PRA predicts a rater-weighted combination of skill-level description embeddings. Adjacent description features define a score-parameterized path, and the predicted embedding is projected onto this path to read the score. We introduce two variants: \textit{PRA-item}, which uses learned queries for predefined assessment items, and \textit{PRA-cond}, which generates queries from textual item names to enable assessment of unseen items without retraining. On AIxSuture, a dataset of expert-rated suturing videos, PRA outperforms published baselines in skill classification. We further evaluate zero-shot transfer to the smaller surgical skill assessment benchmark JIGSAWS. Trained on only two AIxSuture rubric items, PRA-cond assesses unseen JIGSAWS items without further training, yielding positive score correlations and greater Grad-CAM overlap with instruments and suture than a description-matching baseline. These results support predictive rubric alignment as a promising direction for flexible and explainable automated surgical skill assessment.

AI.tldr: PRA scores surgical skill videos by predicting a rater-weighted embedding of natural-language skill-level descriptions and projecting it onto a score path. It outperforms published baselines on AIxSuture and transfers zero-shot to JIGSAWS.
AI.motivation: Automated surgical skill assessment usually predicts fixed skill levels or scores tied to one rubric, and so does not transfer across equivalent criteria described in different language.
AI.method: Two variants: PRA-item uses learned queries for predefined items, and PRA-cond generates queries from textual item names. Adjacent description features define a score-parameterized path onto which the predicted embedding is projected.
AI.result: On AIxSuture, PRA outperforms published baselines in skill classification. Trained on two AIxSuture rubric items, PRA-cond gives positive score correlations on unseen JIGSAWS items without further training, with greater Grad-CAM overlap with instruments and suture than a description-matching baseline.
AI.conclusion: Predictive rubric alignment is a promising, flexible and explainable direction for automated surgical skill assessment.

title: Duo: A Reciprocal World Model for Full-Duplex Interaction
summary: In this report, we introduce the Reciprocal World Model (RWM) and present Duo v1, a full-duplex world model that continuously perceives audiovisual inputs while responding to users in real time. The RWM treats intelligence and physical reality as equally fundamental to what constitutes a world. Existing world models largely focus on simulating the latter, leaving reasoning and decision-making as external controls rather than intrinsic parts of the world itself. In RWM, we identify two equally fundamental capabilities: Intent, which provides the cognition underlying world interactions, and Realization, which generates coherent audio-visual behavior. To realize this formulation, Duo v1 introduces three key technical designs: (1) Leveraging autoregressive modeling for continuous interaction reasoning and participation decisions, rather than restricting it to instruction understanding for diffusion models. (2) Constructing chunk-specific conditions and synchronize tokens across Intent and Realization on a unified timeline. Module-specific attention masks enforce causal dependencies both within and across chunks, preventing access to future inputs. (3) Mitigating distribution shift in both modules through dual rollout distillation, training on autoregressively generated Intent tokens and synthesized audiovisual histories from Realization. Both modules continuously perceive real-time audio, video, and text, enabling full-duplex interaction with spontaneous conversations and interruptions. Beyond conversation, users can share real objects, reshape virtual scenes, guide assistants, or play audiovisual games without mouse or keyboard controls. The release of Duo v1 makes our first step, with the next version coming soon. We look forward to broader exploration of this emerging field.

AI.tldr: Duo v1 is a full-duplex audiovisual world model built on a Reciprocal World Model (RWM) that pairs Intent (cognition) with Realization (audio-visual generation). It continuously perceives input while responding in real time, including to interruptions.
AI.motivation: Existing world models simulate physical reality and leave reasoning and decision-making as external controls, rather than as intrinsic parts of the world.
AI.method: Autoregressive modeling handles continuous interaction reasoning and participation decisions. Chunk-specific conditions and synchronized tokens are placed on a unified timeline with module-specific attention masks enforcing causal dependencies. Dual rollout distillation mitigates distribution shift by training on autoregressive Intent tokens and synthesized audiovisual histories.
AI.result: The report gives no quantitative results in the abstract. It describes spontaneous conversation, interruptions, and users sharing real objects or reshaping virtual scenes without mouse or keyboard.
AI.conclusion: Duo v1 is a first step, and the authors expect broader exploration of this field and a next version.

title: Multi-View 3D Reconstruction Using V-JEPA Features
comment: 29 pages, 11 figures. Source code is available at this https URL
summary: Predictive video encoders provide dense visual representations, but adapting them to 3D reconstruction requires accurate depth, camera poses, and cross-view geometry. We study supervised RGB-only multi-view reconstruction using an architecture that combines video-pretrained features, camera estimation, scene aggregation, epipolar transport, and residual pointmaps. Experiments compare global and spatial camera regression with joint relative objectives on CO3D, alongside an independently trained TUM RGB-D model. On 168 CO3D five-view windows, the spatial-camera configuration achieves 29.3% lower absolute trajectory error than the global-camera configuration, but performs worse than identity poses in trajectory error and worse than the global configuration in depth error. The joint relative-objective configuration improves normalized intrinsics error and similarity-aligned Chamfer distance from 0.6447 to 0.5573, but increases raw Chamfer distance from 3.5535 to 4.4374. On 163 indoor windows, camera error is 0.3063 m versus 0.3694 m for identity poses, while depth error is 0.4279 versus 0.2516 for constant median depth. Refinement worsens indoor camera error, and additional experiments show competing depth and pose effects. Overall, the results distinguish representation adaptation, aligned shape, and raw reconstruction, highlighting the need for isolated component and encoder comparisons before attributing reconstruction gains to predictive video pretraining.

AI.tldr: The paper studies RGB-only supervised multi-view 3D reconstruction with V-JEPA features on CO3D and TUM RGB-D. Results show that representation adaptation, aligned shape and raw reconstruction must be separated, and that gains should not be credited to video pretraining without isolated comparisons.
AI.motivation: Predictive video encoders give dense features, but adapting them to 3D reconstruction needs accurate depth, camera poses and cross-view geometry.
AI.method: An architecture combines V-JEPA features, camera estimation, scene aggregation, epipolar transport and residual pointmaps. Global and spatial camera regression with joint relative objectives are compared on CO3D, along with an independently trained TUM RGB-D model.
AI.result: On 168 CO3D five-view windows, the spatial-camera configuration gives 29.3 percent lower absolute trajectory error than the global one but is worse than identity poses. The joint relative objective lowers similarity-aligned Chamfer distance from 0.6447 to 0.5573 but raises raw Chamfer distance from 3.5535 to 4.4374. On 163 indoor windows, camera error is 0.3063 m versus 0.3694 m for identity poses, while depth error is worse than constant median depth.
AI.conclusion: Reconstruction gains should not be attributed to predictive video pretraining until component and encoder comparisons are isolated.

title: Reframing Video Inverse Tone Mapping as Blind Posterior Inference via Latent Luminance Supervision
summary: High-dynamic-range (HDR) displays are now common, but most video content, such as archival footage, broadcast material, and the output of generative video models, exists only in standard dynamic range (SDR). The need is sharpest for generated video, which has no HDR master at all and is graded alongside live-action and visual-effects material finished in HDR. Converting SDR to HDR means undoing a tone-mapping operation that was never recorded, and clipping destroys the radiance wherever it acts, so HDR recovery is a blind inverse problem. Methods built on generative video priors fill clipped regions with plausible structure, but their reconstructions are systematically biased: in every public method we test, saturated content leans too bright or too dark, and the direction of the lean moves with the tone operator behind the input. We call this failure the luminance error, measure both its magnitude and its sign, and make it the focus of this work. Reframing ITM as posterior inference under an unknown operator locates the failure in two places and yields two corrections. A fixed affine functional of the video-diffusion latent reads log-luminance without decoding; on that coordinate an asymmetric loss selects an expectile of the posterior, applied only where clipping leaves luminance unconstrained. We also synthesize training SDR through an explicit family of tone operators, so the model marginalizes over what the observation cannot show. Trained this way, our luminance error stays flatter across operators and smaller on average than any public method, and the full system achieves the best perceptual quality on all three benchmarks.

AI.tldr: The paper reframes video inverse tone mapping as blind posterior inference, showing that generative video priors give biased luminance on clipped content. It proposes a latent-luminance coordinate with an asymmetric expectile loss, and trains on synthetic SDR from an explicit family of tone operators.
AI.motivation: Most video is SDR only, and generative video models produce no HDR master, but clipping makes HDR recovery a blind inverse problem. Existing generative methods show systematic luminance error whose sign shifts with the tone operator.
AI.method: A fixed affine functional of the video-diffusion latent reads log-luminance without decoding. An asymmetric loss selects an expectile of the posterior where clipping leaves luminance unconstrained. Training SDR is synthesized through an explicit family of tone operators.
AI.result: The luminance error is flatter across operators and smaller on average than any public method tested, and the full system gives the best perceptual quality on all three benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Posterior-aware correction of luminance bias improves SDR-to-HDR video conversion, and the model marginalizes over operators the observation cannot reveal.

title: From Concepts to Interactions: Dynamic Graph Semantic Recomposition for Safe Visual Generation
summary: Recent advances in flow-matching Transformers have greatly improved Text-to-Image (T2I) and Text-to-Video (T2V) generation, but unconstrained generation risks producing illegal or unethical content. Safety alignment must therefore suppress unsafe content while preserving legitimate generation. A concept's safety depends on context: a knife used for cooking is safe, whereas its use in violence is harmful. Yet most concept erasure methods indiscriminately suppress static, isolated representations, overlooking evolving semantic interactions. Consequently, safe scenes containing potentially sensitive terms may be unintentionally suppressed, compromising generation quality. To address this, we propose Dynamic Graph Semantic Recomposition (DGSR), which dynamically constructs and updates a semantic interaction graph from evolving text visual states during sampling. Context aware graph reasoning captures semantic dependencies, while paired safe/unsafe supervision distinguishes harmful from legitimate interactions, enabling precise identification of and selective intervention on high risk semantic relationships while preserving benign semantics. DGSR freezes the pretrained backbone and supports both image and video generation. Experiments show that DGSR achieves the lowest Attack Success Rate (ASR) in 10 of 12 T2I evaluations and reduces the average T2V unsafe frame rate by 41.2\% relative to the strongest baseline, while maintaining high generation fidelity and temporal consistency.

AI.tldr: DGSR is a concept-erasure method for T2I and T2V flow-matching models that builds a dynamic semantic interaction graph during sampling, so it intervenes only on harmful concept relations. It gives the lowest attack success rate in 10 of 12 T2I evaluations and cuts unsafe frame rate by 41.2 percent relative to the strongest baseline on T2V.
AI.motivation: Most concept erasure suppresses isolated concepts, which removes safe scenes that contain sensitive terms and degrades generation quality. Safety depends on context, such as a knife in cooking versus violence.
AI.method: The semantic interaction graph is updated from evolving text-visual states during sampling. Context-aware graph reasoning captures dependencies, and paired safe and unsafe supervision separates harmful from legitimate interactions. The pretrained backbone is frozen.
AI.result: DGSR achieves the lowest attack success rate in 10 of 12 T2I evaluations and reduces average T2V unsafe frame rate by 41.2 percent relative to the strongest baseline, with high fidelity and temporal consistency.
AI.conclusion: Context-dependent relation-level intervention can make safety alignment more selective while preserving benign generation quality.

title: MatrixSplat: Matrix-Parallel and Feature-Scalable 3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering on GPUs
summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) has emerged as a mainstream representation for real-time novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction. However, existing 3DGS rendering pipelines are poorly aligned with modern GPU architectures: depth-sorted alpha compositing introduces strong per-pixel sequential dependencies, limiting parallelism and resulting in scalar FMA-dominated execution that underutilizes high-throughput matrix units such as Tensor Cores. This mismatch becomes more severe for multimodal and semantically enriched 3DGS, where high-dimensional features must be accumulated from millions of Gaussians, leading to rapidly increasing computation and memory costs. We propose MatrixSplat, a matrix-parallel rendering framework for feature-scalable 3DGS on modern GPUs. We first identify the sequential dependency of alpha compositing as a key obstacle to efficient high-dimensional feature rendering, and adopt an order-independent weighted accumulation formulation that transforms feature rendering into matrix-oriented computation. Our framework features three key designs: (i) a tile-based splatting pipeline that maps feature accumulation to warp-level matrix-multiply-accumulate execution on Tensor Cores; (ii) a warp-granularity Gaussian packing strategy that mitigates visibility irregularity and improves feature reuse; and (iii) a lazy channel-batched feature-fetching pipeline that reduces shared-memory pressure, maintains high warp occupancy, and overlaps memory access with matrix execution for high-dimensional features. On Mip-NeRF 360, LERF, and 3D-OVS, MatrixSplat achieves up to 3.8$\times$ speedup over 3DGS and 2$\times$ over TC-GS while maintaining rendering quality and semantic accuracy, and further reduces render-kernel time by up to 36.7$\times$ for high-dimensional features. Integrated into existing fast renderers, it provides an additional 1.69-2.84$\times$ speedup.

AI.tldr: MatrixSplat is a 3D Gaussian Splatting renderer that reformulates feature accumulation as order-independent weighted sums executed on GPU Tensor Cores. It achieves up to 3.8 times speedup over 3DGS and 2 times over TC-GS, and up to 36.7 times lower render-kernel time for high-dimensional features.
AI.motivation: Depth-sorted alpha compositing creates per-pixel sequential dependencies that limit parallelism and underuse matrix units, and the cost worsens for high-dimensional semantic features.
AI.method: The sequential compositing is replaced by an order-independent weighted accumulation expressed as matrix operations. Three designs are used: a tile-based pipeline mapping to warp-level matrix-multiply-accumulate, warp-granularity Gaussian packing, and a lazy channel-batched feature fetch that reduces shared-memory pressure.
AI.result: On Mip-NeRF 360, LERF and 3D-OVS, MatrixSplat achieves up to 3.8 times speedup over 3DGS and 2 times over TC-GS while keeping rendering quality and semantic accuracy. Integrated into existing fast renderers, it gives an extra 1.69 to 2.84 times speedup.
AI.conclusion: Matrix-parallel, order-independent accumulation is an effective route to scalable feature rendering in 3DGS on modern GPUs.

title: CineMME: From Dialogue Grounding to Narrative Reasoning in Multimodal Video Understanding
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations & Datasets Track). Project page: this https URL
summary: Narrative video understanding requires more than recognizing visible events: models must extract evidence from dialogue, bind it to speakers, and use it to infer narrative meaning. Existing video benchmarks evaluate aspects of this problem, including video question answering, audio-visual reasoning, and temporal grounding, but rarely test whether these abilities form a coherent dialogue-to-plot evidence chain within the same clips. We introduce \textbf{CineMME}, a human-verified benchmark designed to diagnose dialogue-grounded plot understanding, supported by approximately $1,600$ expert person-hours of annotation. CineMME contains $975$ curated short narrative video clips and two linked tracks: \textit{CineMME-Grounding}, with $13,554$ timestamped speech segments and $33,083$ speaker face boxes for temporal dialogue localization, transcription, and active-speaker grounding; and \textit{CineMME-Reasoning}, with $1,600$ multiple-choice and $316$ open-ended questions spanning perception, audio, narrative, social, and scene-presentation understanding. Our main evaluation compares $20$ MLLMs on reasoning and $9$ omni-modal models on grounding. The results reveal a pronounced who-what-when decoupling: Gemini-3 Pro localizes dialogue in time ($68.34\%$ tIoU) and transcribes it with a WER of $28.99\%$, yet achieves only $7.74\%$ vIoU for active-speaker grounding while achieving $67.66\%$ MCQ accuracy on questions with extractable answers. Modality ablations further show that vision is not uniformly beneficial: it improves performance on perception-heavy questions but can hurt dialogue-centric reasoning. CineMME provides a compact diagnostic testbed for evaluating how multimodal video models connect dialogue, speakers, visual evidence, and narrative meaning.

AI.tldr: CineMME is a human-verified benchmark of 975 narrative video clips for testing whether models connect dialogue, speakers, visual evidence and plot, with two tracks: grounding and reasoning. Gemini-3 Pro localizes dialogue well but reaches only 7.74 percent vIoU for active-speaker grounding.
AI.motivation: Existing video benchmarks test visual QA, audio-visual reasoning and temporal grounding separately, but rarely test a coherent dialogue-to-plot evidence chain within the same clips.
AI.method: CineMME contains 975 clips with CineMME-Grounding (13,554 timestamped speech segments and 33,083 speaker face boxes) and CineMME-Reasoning (1,600 multiple-choice and 316 open-ended questions). About 20 MLLMs are evaluated on reasoning and 9 omni-modal models on grounding, with modality ablations.
AI.result: Gemini-3 Pro gives 68.34 percent tIoU for dialogue localization and a WER of 28.99 percent, yet 7.74 percent vIoU for active-speaker grounding, and 67.66 percent MCQ accuracy on questions with extractable answers. Vision improves perception-heavy questions but can hurt dialogue-centric reasoning.
AI.conclusion: The who-what-when decoupling shows that current multimodal video models do not integrate dialogue, speakers and visual evidence, and CineMME offers a compact diagnostic testbed.

title: Bridging Update Coordination and Flatness in Federated Learning
summary: Federated learning combines complementary knowledge across clients to alleviate local data limitations without sharing raw samples. However, data heterogeneity can cause conflicting updates and hinder generalization. Update coordination reduces interference among client updates, while flatness optimization reduces sensitivity to parameter perturbations to improve generalization. Existing joint designs largely target specific algorithms, limiting flexible combinations of these approaches. To address this problem, we propose a unified federated learning framework that bridges update coordination and flatness optimization. Clients separately accumulate descent signals and flatness corrections along the same local trajectory. The server coordinates both groups with independent states before fusing their outputs into a global update. Explicit conversion between trajectory signals and model updates enables different coordination strategies to work with compatible local or globally guided flatness mechanisms without changing the inference architecture. Experiments show that the evaluated combinations generally improve average and worst-client accuracy over update coordination alone, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed framework in combining these complementary optimization mechanisms.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a unified federated learning framework that combines update coordination with flatness optimization by accumulating descent signals and flatness corrections separately and fusing them at the server. It generally improves average and worst-client accuracy over update coordination alone.
AI.motivation: Data heterogeneity causes conflicting client updates, and existing joint designs are tied to specific algorithms, which limits flexible combinations.
AI.method: Clients accumulate descent signals and flatness corrections along the same local trajectory. The server coordinates both groups with independent states and fuses them into a global update, with explicit conversion between trajectory signals and model updates.
AI.result: The evaluated combinations generally improve average and worst-client accuracy over update coordination alone. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: The framework can flexibly combine update coordination and flatness mechanisms in federated learning without changing the inference architecture.

title: MAST: Medoid-Anchored Subspace Steering for Visual Grounding in Multimodal LLMs
summary: Existing activation steering methods for multimodal large language models (MLLMs) use the global activation mean as the steering vector, which tends to cause cross-task interference and unstable performance. We trace this failure to the multi-centered geometry of task activations. The global mean lands in the empty region between clusters and is faithful to no single task. Moreover, the steering signal in each task-pure local cluster is low-rank, and different query tasks benefit from emphasizing different families of local-basis directions under the shared routing protocol. To address this, we propose MAST (Medoid-Anchored Subspace Steering), a training-free, input-adaptive activation steering framework. MAST groups samples by task, performs multi-center clustering within each group, and selects one representative medoid per cluster. At inference time, each query is routed to multiple representative medoids. For each matched cluster, a low-rank local steering direction is extracted and aggregated across clusters to produce the final steering vector. Building on MAST, MAST-PR (Probe-Reweighted) uses a lightweight task-aware probe to reweight task-specialized local-direction families, yielding a further average improvement of +8.09 points over MAST.

AI.tldr: MAST is a training-free, input-adaptive activation steering method for MLLMs that uses medoid-anchored, multi-center subspaces instead of the global activation mean. MAST-PR adds a probe-based reweighting that gives a further average gain of +8.09 points over MAST.
AI.motivation: Global-mean steering vectors land between task clusters and cause cross-task interference and unstable performance, because task activations are multi-centered and the steering signal in each cluster is low-rank.
AI.method: Samples are grouped by task, clustered into multiple centers, and one medoid is chosen per cluster. Each query is routed to several medoids, a low-rank local direction is extracted per matched cluster, and these are aggregated into the final steering vector. MAST-PR reweights local-direction families with a lightweight task-aware probe.
AI.result: MAST-PR gives an average improvement of +8.09 points over MAST. The abstract gives no other numbers.
AI.conclusion: Input-adaptive, subspace-based steering with medoid anchors addresses cross-task interference in MLLM visual grounding without training.

title: GingivitisSeg: A Public Dataset and Comparative Benchmark for Gingivitis Segmentation in Intraoral Images
comment: Preprint. Under review at Journal of Imaging Informatics in Medicine. Dataset and code: this https URL. Dataset DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21098897
summary: Gingivitis segmentation from intraoral photographs can support computer-assisted periodontal assessment, but pixel-level delineation remains challenging due to severe foreground-background class imbalance, low-contrast boundaries, and variations in illumination and anatomy. We introduce GingivitisSeg, a public benchmark comprising 961 intraoral images with pixel-level annotations of gingival inflammation and predefined training (672), validation (144), and test (145) partitions. Seven semantic segmentation model-backbone configurations were compared using standardized partitions, input resolution, and evaluation metrics. Controlled ablation experiments examined class-weighted cross-entropy loss, Dice loss, and auxiliary supervision. UPerNet with ResNet50 achieved the highest mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) of 76.49% and gingivitis IoU of 54.91%. However, differences from DeepLabV3+ with ResNet50 and SegFormer with MiT-B2 were not statistically significant after Holm correction. The evaluated optimization components improved performance when combined in the UPerNet-ResNet50 configuration. Further analyses showed that performance was associated with gingivitis region size and decreased under stronger image blur. The dataset, benchmark splits, and source code are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: GingivitisSeg is a public benchmark of 961 intraoral images with pixel-level gingivitis annotations, comparing seven segmentation model-backbone configurations. UPerNet with ResNet50 achieves the highest mIoU at 76.49 percent and gingivitis IoU of 54.91 percent.
AI.motivation: Pixel-level gingivitis segmentation from intraoral photographs is hard because of class imbalance, low-contrast boundaries and variation in illumination and anatomy, and no public benchmark exists for it.
AI.method: Seven configurations are compared on standardized partitions (672 train, 144 validation, 145 test) with ablations on class-weighted cross-entropy, Dice loss and auxiliary supervision.
AI.result: UPerNet with ResNet50 gives the highest mIoU of 76.49 percent and gingivitis IoU of 54.91 percent. Differences from DeepLabV3+ with ResNet50 and SegFormer with MiT-B2 are not significant after Holm correction. The optimization components help when combined in UPerNet-ResNet50, and performance falls with smaller regions and stronger blur.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark gives a reference for gingivitis segmentation, and the top configurations are statistically indistinguishable.

title: OT-BLS: Optimal-Transport-based Backbone Layer Selection for Frozen DINOv3 in Cross-Domain Few-Shot Segmentation
comment: Accepted for publication at the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Visual Communications and Image Processing (VCIP 2026)
summary: Cross-domain few-shot segmentation (CD-FSS) aims to segment a target class in images from a previously unseen domain using only a few annotated support examples. Training-free CD-FSS methods, which typically leverage vision foundation models such as DINOv3, achieve competitive performance without parameter updates. However, the optimal DINOv3 layer for mask prediction varies across support--query episodes. Although several layer-selection criteria have been proposed, they do not explicitly evaluate whether the predicted query foreground and background labels agree with the corresponding support labels. To address this limitation, we propose a novel layer-selection criterion, Optimal-Transport-Based Backbone Layer Selection (OT-BLS). Our key insight is that an effective layer-selection criterion can be derived from the optimal-transport correspondence between query and support patch-token features. Based on this insight, we first estimate the transport plan using a well-established optimal transport algorithm and then compute a layer-selection score by aggregating the transported mass according to the foreground--background partition defined by each candidate query mask. The resulting score reflects how well the predicted foreground and background of the query correspond to those of the support. Experiments on eight benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of OT-BLS. It outperforms the conventional last-layer baseline in 12 of 16 dataset/shot settings. Furthermore, OT-BLS improves the average mIoU from 55.72 to 57.62 and achieves a 2.99-point improvement over the best-performing existing layer-selection criterion while running 3.7--14.6$\times$ faster.

AI.tldr: OT-BLS selects the DINOv3 backbone layer for each query by scoring optimal-transport agreement between query and support patch features, and improves on the last-layer baseline in 12 of 16 dataset-shot settings. It raises average mIoU from 55.72 to 57.62 and runs 3.7 to 14.6 times faster than existing criteria.
AI.motivation: The best DINOv3 layer for mask prediction varies across episodes, and existing layer-selection criteria do not check whether predicted query foreground and background agree with support labels.
AI.method: An optimal transport plan is estimated between query and support patch-token features, and a layer score aggregates transported mass according to each candidate query mask's foreground-background partition.
AI.result: Across eight benchmark datasets, OT-BLS beats the last-layer baseline in 12 of 16 dataset-shot settings, raises average mIoU from 55.72 to 57.62, and gains 2.99 points over the best existing layer-selection criterion while running 3.7 to 14.6 times faster.
AI.conclusion: Optimal-transport agreement is an effective, efficient criterion for training-free layer selection in cross-domain few-shot segmentation.

title: The Neighbour's Label: Opposite Subgroup Effects of Same-Dialogue Exposure in Next-Act Evaluation
summary: Window-based next-act evaluation often aims to measure generalisation across dialogues, yet overlapping windows and similarity retrieval can expose labelled examples from the test dialogue. The nearest such example is the target's labelled predecessor, whose act is correct when the target continues it and wrong when the target changes act; a model that copies it can gain and lose in two subgroups that one aggregate averages. We induce this exposure under controlled designs on SGD, STAR and AMI, whose official splits are clean. Randomly including the predecessor's row in training raises a lexical classifier's continuation scores and lowers its transition scores in all three corpora, and purging the adjacent rows removes most of the gain. With TF-IDF-retrieved demonstrations, two 7B instruction-tuned models show the same opposite pattern in all eight model-corpus-sample arms (some single-cell intervals include zero; one replication is partial), while natural-weight accuracy changes by only -0.05 to +0.04. Exposure frequency depends on the retrieval pipeline. We evaluate two diagnostic comparisons without model retraining and find that excluding the test dialogue does not detectably reduce accuracy on SGD. All exposure is induced; no published system was re-evaluated.

AI.tldr: Shows that same-dialogue exposure to a labelled predecessor example inflates next-act evaluation in opposite directions across subgroups (continuation gains, transition losses), so aggregate scores can hide it.
AI.motivation: Window-based next-act evaluation is meant to measure generalisation across dialogues, but overlapping windows and similarity retrieval can expose labelled examples from the test dialogue, which existing aggregate metrics average away.
AI.method: Induces this exposure under controlled designs on SGD, STAR and AMI by randomly including or purging the predecessor's row in training, and tests a lexical classifier and two 7B instruction-tuned models with TF-IDF-retrieved demonstrations.
AI.result: Including the predecessor raises continuation scores and lowers transition scores for the lexical classifier in all three corpora, and the 7B models show the same opposite pattern in all eight model-corpus-sample arms; natural-weight accuracy changes by only -0.05 to +0.04, and excluding the test dialogue does not detectably reduce accuracy on SGD.
AI.conclusion: Exposure to the test dialogue's labelled predecessor can distort subgroup-level next-act evaluation while leaving aggregate accuracy nearly unchanged, so evaluation protocols need to control for it; exposure frequency depends on the retrieval pipeline.

title: A General Concept-based Decomposition for Vision-Language Embeddings
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Project page at this https URL
summary: Vision-Language Models are designed to capture the compositional structure of the world through multi-modal alignment; however, it remains unclear whether their representations truly align with the way a human would naturally describe the same visual input. Prior works attempt to decompose visual embeddings into their concept-level contributions, but their instance-level optimization is inherently local and does not capture the model's global semantic structure, which is essential for compositional generalization across different inputs, tasks, and domains. We introduce GRACE, a method that learns this concept-based structure at the feature space level, producing semantic and general concept decompositions. To achieve this, we propose a novel training objective that preserves the geometric relations of different samples in the concept space, enabling a better understanding of how concepts compose and relate to each other. We validate GRACE on several image and video benchmarks, showing that its concept decomposition is aligned with human perception and achieves faithful decompositions across different tasks and domains. With minimal overhead, GRACE makes existing Vision-Language Models more interpretable, while preserving most of their original performance.

AI.tldr: Proposes GRACE, a method that learns concept-based decompositions of vision-language embeddings at the feature-space level, so that the decompositions are global and general rather than per-instance.
AI.motivation: Prior concept decomposition methods of visual embeddings optimise each instance locally and do not capture the model's global semantic structure, which compositional generalisation across inputs, tasks and domains requires.
AI.method: GRACE learns concept-based structure in feature space with a training objective that preserves the geometric relations between samples in the concept space.
AI.result: Validated on several image and video benchmarks, where the concept decompositions align with human perception and remain faithful across tasks and domains, with minimal overhead while preserving most of the original model performance.
AI.conclusion: GRACE makes existing vision-language models more interpretable at little cost in performance, offering a global alternative to instance-level concept decomposition.

title: Where is My Mug? Training-Free Framework for Personalized Image Segmentation
summary: \textbf{Personalized Image Segmentation (PIS)} aims to segment the specific object in a target image that matches a user-provided reference. Unlike category-based segmentation or few-shot segmentation, PIS must discriminate between multiple visually similar instances, a requirement central to deployed applications such as augmented reality, personalized content editing, robotics manipulation, inventory tracking, and fine-grained visual retrieval. We show that the strong numbers reported by existing PIS methods are largely an artifact of single-instance benchmarks: when evaluated on realistic scenes with several same-category look-alikes, prior point-prompt methods collapse, because the correct instance is frequently never surfaced as a prompt. We trace this to a recall bottleneck rather than a mask-quality one, and address it with a training-free, modular system. The pipeline first generates high-recall object proposals using an off-the-shelf class-agnostic detector, then matches each proposal to the reference using foundation-model features (e.g., BLIP-2), and finally refines the selected box with SAM. For robust matching we propose \textbf{top-$K$ Sinkhorn}, a patch-level distance that scores each candidate only on its most confidently matched patches; trimming the Sinkhorn dual potentials recovers the robustness of partial optimal transport at more than $100\times$ lower cost, keeping it inside the per-proposal candidate loop. To evaluate this regime, we introduce \textbf{\datasetname}, a realistic multi-instance benchmark. Across \datasetname, PerSeg, PerMIS, and DAVIS, our system surpasses PerSAM, $\mathrm{P}^2\mathrm{SAM}$, and PDM by up to $\sim\!48$ mIoU while matching their runtime and using fewer parameters, establishing a strong, deployable training-free baseline for real-world personalized segmentation.

AI.tldr: Presents a training-free system for personalized image segmentation that combines high-recall proposals, foundation-model matching and SAM refinement, and introduces a top-K Sinkhorn distance for robust matching among look-alike instances.
AI.motivation: Existing personalized segmentation methods report strong numbers on single-instance benchmarks, but they collapse in realistic scenes with several same-category look-alikes because the correct instance is often never surfaced as a prompt.
AI.method: The pipeline generates object proposals with an off-the-shelf class-agnostic detector, matches each proposal to the reference with BLIP-2 features using top-K Sinkhorn, a patch-level distance that scores only the most confidently matched patches, and refines the selected box with SAM; the authors also introduce a multi-instance benchmark.
AI.result: Across the new benchmark, PerSeg, PerMIS and DAVIS, the system surpasses PerSAM, P2SAM and PDM by up to about 48 mIoU while matching their runtime with fewer parameters; top-K Sinkhorn recovers partial optimal transport robustness at more than 100 times lower cost.
AI.conclusion: The failure is a recall bottleneck rather than a mask-quality one, and the modular training-free system is a strong, deployable baseline for real-world personalized segmentation.

title: Driving World Models Move the Camera, Not the Scene
comment: 23 pages. Project page: this https URL
summary: Plan-conditioned driving world models are used to compare candidate plans, so their forecast should change with the plan as the real scene would, yet widely used control metrics check only whether the camera follows the command. Recorded drives already contain real outcomes of plans that were never driven: retiming a log gives pose-matched images and LiDAR for other speeds, and a stereo rig records a laterally shifted view. Against these references, released world models move their camera but barely move the scene: their scene response, the share of the real change in distance that the forecast reproduces, reaches at most about a third of real video's, and the trajectory score cannot tell an executed speed command from an ignored one. Interventions inside the generator trace the failure to the plan's channel. The forecast geometry follows the context frames; once they carry the planned geometry, plan tokens add little. ReTime-Compose therefore delivers the plan as geometry, without training. It transports the frames of one logged-speed rollout to the planned cameras, and the frozen model completes only what no frame covers. Frozen generators then follow a 0.54 m lateral shift nearly as the real scene does on KITTI, nuScenes and Argoverse 2, and respond more than re-sampling to slow-down plans in three generators and to speed-up plans in two.

AI.tldr: Argues that released driving world models move the camera but barely move the scene in response to plans, and proposes ReTime-Compose, a training-free method that delivers the plan as geometry by transporting frames from a logged rollout.
AI.motivation: Widely used control metrics only check whether the camera follows the command, so they cannot reveal whether a plan-conditioned driving world model's forecast actually changes with the plan as the real scene would.
AI.method: Uses logged real drives as references for plans never driven (retimed logs and laterally shifted stereo views), measures scene response as the share of real change in distance that the forecast reproduces, and transports frames of one logged-speed rollout to the planned cameras so the frozen generator completes only uncovered content.
AI.result: Released world models reach at most about one third of real video's scene response; frozen generators with ReTime-Compose follow a 0.54 m lateral shift nearly as the real scene does on KITTI, nuScenes and Argoverse 2, and respond more than re-sampling to slow-down plans in three generators and speed-up plans in two.
AI.conclusion: Plan tokens add little once the context frames carry the planned geometry, so plan conditioning in driving world models should be delivered as geometry and evaluated against real outcome references rather than camera-following metrics.

title: PCLSegNet: Anatomy-Aware Deep Learning Framework for MRI-based Pancreatic Cyst Segmentation and Size Assessment
summary: Early detection and follow-up of pancreatic cystic lesions (PCLs) are crucial, as some of their subtypes, such as mucinous cystic neoplasms (MCNs) and intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasms, carry a significant risk of malignant transformation. Although most AI studies investigating PCLs rely on computed tomography (CT) scans, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offers superior soft tissue contrast, making it highly suitable for PCLs assessment. In this work, we propose an anatomy-aware two-stage deep learning framework for automated PCLs segmentation on abdominal MRI scans. First, a publicly available pancreas segmentation model is used to localize the pancreas. Then, we introduce the anatomyaware PCLSegNet, which incorporates anatomical priors as guidance for pancreas and PCLs segmentation. To address the class imbalance problem, we develop a Class-Specific ErrorWeighted (CSEW) loss function. Postprocessing is applied through anatomical this http URL proposed method outperforms multi-organ segmentation models such as TotalSegmentator, achieving substantially higher Dice scores for pancreas segmentation. Moreover, it also achieves a superior normalized surface Dice (NSD) and recall for PCLs segmentationcompared to other state-of-the-art models like nnU-Net, while also notably reducing the false negative rate, facilitating the automatic early detection and the noninvasive imaging-based assessment of PCLs.

AI.tldr: Proposes PCLSegNet, an anatomy-aware two-stage framework for segmenting pancreatic cystic lesions in abdominal MRI, guided by a pancreas localisation model and a class-specific error-weighted loss.
AI.motivation: Most AI studies on pancreatic cystic lesions use CT, whereas MRI gives better soft tissue contrast, and existing multi-organ and general segmentation models do not handle the lesion class imbalance and anatomical context well.
AI.method: A publicly available pancreas segmentation model localises the pancreas, then PCLSegNet uses anatomical priors to guide pancreas and lesion segmentation, trained with a Class-Specific Error-Weighted (CSEW) loss and followed by anatomy-based postprocessing.
AI.result: The method gives substantially higher Dice for pancreas segmentation than TotalSegmentator and higher normalised surface Dice and recall for lesion segmentation than nnU-Net and other state-of-the-art models, with a notably lower false negative rate.
AI.conclusion: The anatomy-aware design may support automatic early detection and noninvasive MRI-based follow-up of pancreatic cystic lesions.

title: Track4D: Representing Dense 3D Tracking for Video Diffusion Models
comment: NeurIPS 2026. Project page: this https URL
summary: We study how to repurpose video diffusion models (VDMs), pretrained on millions of videos, for dense 3D point tracking, where training data is scarce. Doing so is non-trivial, as it requires representing 3D tracks as video-like signals that may lie outside the natural-video distribution on which the VDM was trained. We thus systematically assess the effectiveness of two such video representations. The first, Residual 3D Tracking Video (RTV), encodes per-pixel 3D offsets relative to a query frame and allows recovery of 3D trajectories directly from the generated video. The second, Normalized Coordinate Map Video (NCMV), labels each pixel with a canonical coordinate invariant through time. This is closer to a natural video and easier for the VDM to learn, but requires additional post-processing with an off-the-shelf 2D tracker to recover 3D tracks. RTV tracks more accurately, while NCMV shows that a VDM can generate dense correspondence as a video. We instantiate both representations with LoRA adaptation of a frozen Wan backbone, conditioned on point maps from an off-the-shelf 3D reconstructor as a geometric scaffold. Trained with a single dynamic 3D tracking dataset, Track4D achieves competitive zero-shot tracking on four real and synthetic benchmarks. A regression readout that bypasses the video VAE and uses additional training data brings further improvement, demonstrating the potential of this direction for dense 3D tracking. We hope our analysis will inspire future work that leverages VDM priors for dense 3D tracking and 4D reconstruction. Project page: this https URL

AI.tldr: Repurposes pretrained video diffusion models for dense 3D point tracking by comparing two video-like track representations, and presents Track4D, which achieves competitive zero-shot tracking with LoRA-adapted Wan.
AI.motivation: Dense 3D tracking data is scarce, while video diffusion models are pretrained on millions of videos, but 3D tracks must be represented as video-like signals that may lie outside the natural-video distribution the model was trained on.
AI.method: Compares Residual 3D Tracking Video (RTV), which encodes per-pixel 3D offsets relative to a query frame, with Normalized Coordinate Map Video (NCMV), which labels each pixel with a time-invariant canonical coordinate; both are learned by LoRA adaptation of a frozen Wan backbone conditioned on point maps from an off-the-shelf 3D reconstructor.
AI.result: RTV tracks more accurately, while NCMV shows that a video model can generate dense correspondence as a video, and Track4D achieves competitive zero-shot tracking on four real and synthetic benchmarks; a regression readout that bypasses the video VAE and uses extra training data improves results further.
AI.conclusion: Video diffusion priors are a promising route to dense 3D tracking and 4D reconstruction, though the abstract reports the findings as analysis rather than a definitive best representation.

title: Beyond the Explicit: Benchmarking and Detecting Implicit Harm in Short Videos
summary: Short videos have become a dominant online medium, where harmful content is increasingly conveyed in implicit and fragmented forms. Prior work largely focuses on explicit categories, such as violence and hate speech, and often fails to detect videos that subtly promote misleading values through narrative context, emotional framing, or cross-modal cues, partly due to the lack of dedicated benchmarks for implicit harm. To bridge this gap, we construct DeepHarm-7K, a large-scale harmful short-video dataset comprising 7,110 samples annotated according to a fine-grained harmful-content taxonomy. The dataset systematically covers implicitly harmful videos across diverse real-world scenarios and is constructed through a rigorous multi-stage quality-control process. Building on this dataset, we propose DeepHarm-VL, a multimodal detection framework that integrates visual, audio, and cross-modal reasoning. The framework employs a two-round reasoning strategy to progressively identify surface-level evidence and infer latent harmful implications. Experimental results show consistent improvements over strong baselines and state-of-the-art methods across multiple open-source video-language models, demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting both explicit and implicit harmful short videos.

AI.tldr: Introduces DeepHarm-7K, a 7,110-video dataset of implicitly harmful short videos, and DeepHarm-VL, a multimodal two-round reasoning detector that outperforms baselines on explicit and implicit harm.
AI.motivation: Harm detection on short videos has focused on explicit categories such as violence and hate speech, and fails on videos that subtly promote misleading values through narrative, emotional framing or cross-modal cues, partly because no dedicated benchmark exists for implicit harm.
AI.method: Builds a dataset of 7,110 videos annotated with a fine-grained harmful-content taxonomy through a multi-stage quality-control process, and proposes DeepHarm-VL, which fuses visual, audio and cross-modal reasoning in two rounds: first surface-level evidence, then latent harmful implications.
AI.result: Consistent improvements over strong baselines and state-of-the-art methods across multiple open-source video-language models, for both explicit and implicit harmful short videos.
AI.conclusion: The dataset and two-round reasoning framework address a gap in harmful-content detection for implicit harm, which the abstract presents as an effective approach.

title: Arbor: When Labels Are Not Coarsened at Random
summary: Merging datasets labelled at different levels of a taxonomy leaves some images with only a coarse label, and some classes with no fine-grained label at all. Standard training scores a coarse label by the total probability of the classes under it. Coarse labels name superclasses, and the standard objective is exact only when every class within a superclass is equally likely to receive a coarse label. We call a class novel if it is never labelled finely, and known otherwise. A novel class violates the assumption, and the classifier assigns its images to a known sibling. We propose Arbor, which models how labels become coarse. In each superclass with a novel class, Arbor adds a virtual novel class, and a logistic gate divides the superclass's probability between it and the known classes. The gate is trained with the likelihood of the observed labels under this model, the coarsening likelihood. We prove that at its population optimum the gate equals the Elkan-Noto correction of positive-unlabelled learning, and show that training the correction into the classifier improves on applying it after training. Across Cars, CUB and Aircraft with 90% coarse labels, Arbor correctly assigns 76-85% of novel-class images to their superclass, more than hierarchical classifiers, hierarchical novelty detection and the Elkan-Noto correction. Its top-1 accuracy over the leaf classes on known-class images is within 1.6 points of the best baseline, although its final predictions return the superclass more often. On the more challenging iNaturalist-2019 benchmark, Arbor improves novel-class accuracy from 46% (uniform target, the strongest baseline) to 68%.

AI.tldr: Proposes Arbor, a method for training classifiers on datasets with taxonomy-mixed labels, which models coarse labelling with a logistic gate that corrects for classes never labelled finely (novel classes).
AI.motivation: When datasets labelled at different taxonomy levels are merged, standard training assumes every class in a superclass is equally likely to receive a coarse label, which fails for novel classes and causes known sibling misassignment.
AI.method: In each superclass with a novel class, Arbor adds a virtual novel class and a logistic gate that splits the superclass probability between it and the known classes, trained with the likelihood of observed labels under a coarsening model; the authors prove the optimum equals the Elkan-Noto correction from positive-unlabelled learning and train the correction into the classifier.
AI.result: With 90% coarse labels on Cars, CUB and Aircraft, Arbor assigns 76-85% of novel-class images to their superclass, outperforming hierarchical classifiers, hierarchical novelty detection and the Elkan-Noto correction, with leaf top-1 accuracy within 1.6 points of the best baseline; on iNaturalist-2019 it raises novel-class accuracy from 46% to 68%.
AI.conclusion: Modelling how labels become coarse, and training that correction jointly, handles novel classes better than post-hoc correction, at a small cost in fine-grained accuracy.

title: AcrossPlace: Do Vision--Language Models Recognize Places Beyond Their Source Views? A Comprehensive Benchmark
summary: Language-guided place recognition requires recovering geographic identity across visual observations beyond the image from which a description originates. However, aggregate retrieval scores often entangle observation transfer, gallery competition, and linguistic evidence, obscuring the underlying recognition capability. We introduce AcrossPlace, a provenance-aware benchmark establishing a systematic evaluation standard for bidirectional language--vision place recognition. Built upon GSV-Cities, AcrossPlace comprises 56,726 places across 23 cities, 156,800 automatically generated, rule-filtered descriptions, and 113,404 target images. Each description retains its source-image provenance, while retrieval operates on disjoint target observations. Text-to-image (T2I) and image-to-text (I2T) retrieval share a unified place-identity relevance criterion supporting multiple valid matches. Two geographic protocols evaluate unseen places within represented cities (P0) and generalization to held-out cities (P1). Paired observation comparisons, gallery-controlled evaluations, fixed-query scaling, and blinded annotation auditing systematically characterize retrieval performance. Across three training seeds, place-supervised SigLIP2 T2I Recall@1 decreases from 19.69% on source images to 12.31% on independent targets under P0. For fixed P1 queries, expanding the gallery from 500 to 8,425 places reduces Recall@1 from 14.67% to 2.87%. A 240-description audit further reveals discrepancies between automated acceptance and factual evidence. These findings establish AcrossPlace as a reproducible evaluation standard for assessing transferable place identity across visual observations and geographic environments.

AI.tldr: Introduces AcrossPlace, a provenance-aware benchmark of 56,726 places for bidirectional language-vision place recognition, showing that retrieval scores fall sharply when observations come from independent images and galleries grow.
AI.motivation: Aggregate retrieval scores for language-guided place recognition mix observation transfer, gallery competition and linguistic evidence, which obscures how well models recognise places beyond their source views.
AI.method: Builds on GSV-Cities with 156,800 generated and rule-filtered descriptions, each tied to its source image, and 113,404 target images with disjoint retrieval; it evaluates text-to-image and image-to-text retrieval under two geographic protocols (P0 for represented cities, P1 for held-out cities), with gallery-controlled comparisons and a 240-description audit.
AI.result: For place-supervised SigLIP2 text-to-image Recall@1 falls from 19.69% on source images to 12.31% on independent targets under P0 across three seeds, and for fixed P1 queries it falls from 14.67% to 2.87% when the gallery grows from 500 to 8,425 places; the audit shows discrepancies between automated acceptance and factual evidence.
AI.conclusion: AcrossPlace is presented as a reproducible standard for measuring transferable place identity across observations and geographic environments.

title: CaseScope: A Multi-Field Benchmark for Case-Level Pathology Diagnosis with Multimodal LLMs
summary: Pathologists rarely diagnose from a single image: they scan a section at low power for architecture, zoom into selected fields for cytology, and integrate the evidence across views and scales. Pathology benchmarks for multimodal large language models (MLLMs), however, mostly ask about one image or require whole-slide pipelines, and the few that show several fields draw nested regions from cancer slides of one public cohort. We introduce CaseScope, a benchmark of diagnosis from several curated fields of one lesion: CaseScope-Teaching, 436 cases from a residency-training image library, reconstructed, de-identified, harmonised against a WHO-based ontology and re-examined by a pathologist wherever an automated pre-review raised a doubt, and CaseScope-Atlas, 800 cases from 88 published atlases (387 of them figure series of one disease), labelled from the captions by two LLMs that must agree. They cover 843 entities across 18 organ systems and pose 4,679 items in six tasks, from open-ended and ten-way diagnosis with ontology-guided hard negatives under circular evaluation to the verification and location of morphological findings. Across twenty-eight open and four proprietary MLLMs, diagnoses are unstable -- the best open and proprietary models are correct under all ten option rotations on 17.9% and 61.7% of the teaching cases -- and wrong answers favour the classic look-alike; open models make little use of the additional fields on teaching cases, where the one-line specimen site matters more, although on atlas cases with three or more fields the fields count about as much as the site; and most open models verify findings barely above chance (median 62.0% vs. 50%, best 81.5%), gaining a median +3.4 points from images; proprietary models reach 83.2-93.2%. Rankings broadly replicate between the sources. The evaluation code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Introduces CaseScope, a benchmark of 4,679 items for case-level pathology diagnosis from several fields per lesion, and finds that 32 multimodal LLMs give unstable diagnoses and weak verification of morphological findings.
AI.motivation: Existing pathology benchmarks for multimodal LLMs mostly use one image or whole-slide pipelines, and the few multi-field benchmarks draw nested regions from a single public cancer cohort, which does not reflect how pathologists integrate views and scales.
AI.method: CaseScope-Teaching has 436 de-identified cases from a residency-training library, checked against a WHO-based ontology and re-examined by a pathologist where pre-review raised doubt; CaseScope-Atlas has 800 cases from 88 atlases labelled from captions by two LLMs that must agree; six tasks cover 843 entities across 18 organ systems, including ten-way diagnosis with ontology-guided hard negatives under circular evaluation.
AI.result: Across 28 open and four proprietary MLLMs, the best open and proprietary models are correct under all ten option rotations on 17.9% and 61.7% of teaching cases; median open-model verification is 62.0% against 50% chance (best 81.5%), versus 83.2-93.2% for proprietary models; open models make little use of extra fields on teaching cases, while on atlas cases with three or more fields the fields matter about as much as the site.
AI.conclusion: Current MLLMs give unstable case-level diagnoses and verify morphology poorly, especially open models, so multi-field pathology reasoning remains a weak point; rankings broadly replicate across the two sources.

title: Vision-Grounded Semantic Learning and Alignment for Scalable Multilingual Text-Based Person Retrieval
summary: Multilingual Text-Based Person Retrieval (TBPR) aims to retrieve individuals with texts in multiple languages. Despite its practical importance, it has been overlooked by existing research, which mainly focuses on English-only retrieval. The only prior attempt at multilingual TBPR suffers from (1) the absence of a large-scale, multilingual pretraining dataset and (2) a suboptimal model architecture for multilingual text encoding and cross-modal alignment, which employs a shared encoder that overlooks linguistic heterogeneity and relies on English as a pivot for cross-modal alignment, introducing English-centric bias. For this, we contribute MultiPedes, the first large-scale, pedestrian-centric multilingual pretraining dataset. It contains 10 million image-text pairs across four languages, constructed by a multilingual quality-aware data construction pipeline. We also propose ViSeLA (Vision-grounded Semantic Learning and Alignment), a novel framework featuring: (1) a semantic-aware multilingual learning module that extends the mixture-of-experts architecture by routing language-invariant semantics to specialized experts for improved multilingual feature learning; and (2) a vision-grounded cross-modal alignment module that employs a semantic probe to capture fine-grained semantics across modalities, enabling direct cross-modal alignment without relying on a pivot language. Extensive experiments on both multilingual and English-only TBPR datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of ViSeLA. The dataset and code are available at this https URL

AI.tldr: Presents MultiPedes, a 10-million-pair multilingual pedestrian image-text dataset, and ViSeLA, a framework that aligns multilingual text with images without English as a pivot language.
AI.motivation: Multilingual text-based person retrieval has been neglected, and the only prior attempt lacks a large multilingual pretraining dataset and uses a shared encoder with English as a pivot, which introduces English-centric bias.
AI.method: Constructs MultiPedes, with 10 million image-text pairs in four languages through a quality-aware pipeline, and proposes ViSeLA, which routes language-invariant semantics to specialised experts in a mixture-of-experts module and uses a semantic probe for vision-grounded cross-modal alignment without a pivot language.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multilingual and English-only text-based person retrieval datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of ViSeLA, according to the abstract, without specific numbers given.
AI.conclusion: Large-scale multilingual data and direct vision-grounded alignment are presented as a scalable route to multilingual person retrieval without English-centric bias.

title: CARE-Drive: Coupled Alternating Refinement for Ego-trajectories
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models bring multimodal understanding and world knowledge to end-to-end autonomous driving. To further improve the quality of predicted trajectories, existing studies introduce candidate refinement, residual denoising, and token correction. However, these methods typically focus on unified refinement of the entire trajectory, paying limited attention to the distinct physical quantities and their interactions. We further investigate physical specialization and coordination in trajectory refinement, centering on position and heading for simpler and more intuitive correction modeling. To this end, we propose CARE-Drive (Coupled Alternating Refinement for Ego-trajectories), which decomposes trajectory refinement into waypoint residual correction and position-conditioned heading generation. Through imitation learning and a future-token auxiliary task, the backbone provides predictive representations and a base trajectory. The position expert predicts bounded metric waypoint residuals, while the heading expert reconstructs vehicle orientation from adjacent angular increments conditioned on the corrected path. With the backbone frozen, the two experts are optimized alternately through supervised initialization and reinforcement fine-tuning. This design simplifies refinement through clear physical specialization while preserving conditional coupling during prediction and optimization. On NAVSIM v1, CARE-Drive achieves 88.8 PDMS, improving by 2.4 points over the unrefined base trajectories generated by the same backbone. Ablation studies further support the effectiveness of specialized experts and staged training.

AI.tldr: Proposes CARE-Drive, which decomposes trajectory refinement for vision-language-action driving models into separate position and heading experts, reaching 88.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1, 2.4 points above the unrefined base.
AI.motivation: Existing refinement methods for VLA driving models treat the whole trajectory as one unit and pay limited attention to the distinct physical quantities of position and heading and their interactions.
AI.method: With the backbone frozen, a position expert predicts bounded metric waypoint residuals and a heading expert reconstructs orientation from adjacent angular increments conditioned on the corrected path; the two are optimised alternately through supervised initialisation and reinforcement fine-tuning, on top of imitation learning and a future-token auxiliary task.
AI.result: On NAVSIM v1, CARE-Drive achieves 88.8 PDMS, improving by 2.4 points over the unrefined base trajectories from the same backbone, and ablations support the specialised experts and staged training.
AI.conclusion: Separating physical specialisation for position and heading while keeping them coupled yields better refined ego-trajectories for VLA driving.

title: ChartGalaxy++: A Richly Annotated Dataset for Chart Understanding and Generation
summary: Infographic charts communicate data through cohesive compositions of visual elements such as charts, text, and images. Existing infographic chart datasets primarily annotate individual elements with bounding boxes and category labels. Such element-level annotations do not capture hierarchical and spatial relationships, limiting their use for understanding how elements are organized and related within an infographic and for generating well-organized designs. To address this limitation, we introduce ChartGalaxy++, a richly annotated dataset of 217,195 infographic charts. At the core of this dataset is a scene graph representation, in which nodes represent visual elements and semantic groups, and edges encode their hierarchical and spatial relationships. For real infographics, we construct scene graphs by detecting and progressively grouping visual elements; for synthetic ones, we derive them directly from the generation process. We demonstrate the utility of ChartGalaxy++ through three applications: 1) image-to-scene-graph prediction, 2) scene-graph-augmented infographic question answering, and 3) evaluation of scene graph preservation in image generation. Together, these applications highlight the value of ChartGalaxy++ for advancing chart understanding and generation.

AI.tldr: Introduces ChartGalaxy++, a dataset of 217,195 infographic charts annotated with scene graphs that capture hierarchical and spatial relations among visual elements, and demonstrates three applications.
AI.motivation: Existing infographic chart datasets annotate individual elements with boxes and labels, which does not capture how elements are organised and related, limiting understanding and generation of well-structured designs.
AI.method: Scene graphs have nodes for visual elements and semantic groups and edges for hierarchical and spatial relations; real infographics are built by detecting and progressively grouping elements, while synthetic ones are derived from the generation process.
AI.result: The dataset is demonstrated on image-to-scene-graph prediction, scene-graph-augmented infographic question answering, and evaluation of scene graph preservation in image generation; the abstract reports no numbers.
AI.conclusion: Scene-graph annotation is presented as valuable for advancing chart understanding and generation.

title: Learning Motion-Appearance Coupling Priors for Solving Video Inverse Problems
summary: Reconstructing video from degraded measurements requires priors that capture both frame appearance and temporal dynamics. Many recent approaches combine pretrained image diffusion priors with motion guidance, sidestepping the costs of training large video models. Temporal consistency is often enforced via photometric losses or warping-based constraints, which implicitly assume that motion explains frame-to-frame or latent-to-latent changes up to small deviations, an assumption that fails under occlusions, lighting changes, and non-rigid deformation. In this paper, we propose to learn the coupling between motion and frame appearance as a generative prior. We learn the distribution of motion-induced appearance residuals with a conditional diffusion model and use it to regularize reconstruction in video inverse problems. Our motion-appearance prior acts as a plug-in regularizer for diffusion-based video reconstruction, preserving the benefits of image diffusion models while remaining compatible with existing appearance regularization techniques. Experiments on dynamic video inverse problems show that reconstruction with a learnt motion-appearance coupling prior outperforms photometric-consistency and noise-warping baselines, and that the approach also transfers to cardiac MRI reconstruction.

AI.tldr: Proposes learning a generative prior of motion-induced appearance residuals with a conditional diffusion model, used as a plug-in regulariser for diffusion-based video inverse problems.
AI.motivation: Photometric and warping-based temporal constraints assume motion explains frame changes up to small deviations, which fails under occlusion, lighting change and non-rigid deformation.
AI.method: A conditional diffusion model learns the distribution of motion-induced appearance residuals and regularises reconstruction within a pretrained image diffusion framework, remaining compatible with existing appearance regularisation.
AI.result: Outperforms photometric-consistency and noise-warping baselines on dynamic video inverse problems, and the learned coupling prior also transfers to cardiac MRI reconstruction.
AI.conclusion: Learning the coupling between motion and appearance is presented as a useful prior for video reconstruction, with transfer to a medical imaging task.

title: IncR-3DSGG: Incremental Posed RGB Image Based 3D Scene Graph Generation via Privileged Depth Supervision
summary: Scene graphs provide a compact, structured representation of environments by capturing objects and their spatial or semantic relationships in a form suitable for embodied agents.
