Existing 3D scene graph generation methods often rely on depth sensing at inference, either to associate object instances across views via point cloud overlap or to compute inter-object relations from geometric cues, limiting deployment to platforms with depth sensors. We propose IncR-3DSGG, which builds 3D scene graphs incrementally from posed\footnote{RGB images with camera extrinsics estimated by an off-the-shelf visual SLAM system.} RGB images, eliminating the use of depth sensors at inference. Our method leverages a Parametric Relation Predictor (PRP) that learns to estimate pairwise distances and relative angles between objects from 2D visual features and 2D geometric cues, using 3D geometric supervision available only during training. These learned pairwise measurements are fused across views through Pose Graph Optimization (PGO)~\cite{grisetti2010tutorial} to recover metrically grounded 3D object positions and build a globally consistent 3D scene graph incrementally. On the real-world 3RScan~\cite{wald2019rio} dataset, our method attains $52.2$ mean object recall and $30.8$ mean predicate recall under the 3DSSG~\cite{wald2020learning} evaluation protocol, against $27.0$ and $17.6$ for MonoSSG~\cite{wu2023incremental}, while using no depth or reconstructed geometry at inference. This shows that relations and metrically grounded 3D object representations can be predicted from posed RGB images alone.

AI.tldr: Presents IncR-3DSGG, which builds 3D scene graphs incrementally from posed RGB images without depth sensors at inference, using depth-based geometric supervision only during training.
AI.motivation: Existing 3D scene graph methods rely on depth at inference, either for instance association or relation geometry, which restricts deployment to platforms with depth sensors.
AI.method: A Parametric Relation Predictor estimates pairwise distances and relative angles between objects from 2D features and geometric cues, trained with 3D supervision, and these measurements are fused across views by pose graph optimisation over camera poses from an off-the-shelf visual SLAM system.
AI.result: On 3RScan under the 3DSSG protocol, it attains 52.2 mean object recall and 30.8 mean predicate recall, against 27.0 and 17.6 for MonoSSG, without depth or reconstructed geometry at inference.
AI.conclusion: Relations and metric 3D object positions can be predicted from posed RGB images alone, removing the need for depth sensing at inference.

title: Verifier Choice is a Benchmark Design Variable: Auditing Structural Counting Evaluation in Text-to-Image Models
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Evaluations and Datasets Track). 24 pages. Data: this https URL . Code: this https URL
summary: Automatic evaluation is now central to text-to-image benchmarking, but the verifier that converts generated images into scores is often treated as an implementation detail. We argue that this is unsafe: an automatic benchmark score is a property of the image generator, prompt distribution, verifier, verifier-use protocol, and scoring rule, not of the generator alone. We study this issue in structural counting, a controlled setting where human-visible counts can be audited. We construct a verifier-centric audit suite over seven counting objects: cell phones, chairs, and traffic lights for object counting, and clover leaflets, dresser drawer fronts, power-strip sockets, and turbine blades for substructure counting. Across 6,240 generated images from Qwen-Image-2512 and FLUX.2-dev, we compare open MLLM verifiers under count-only, reject-aware, zero-shot and few-shot protocols, plus TIFA-like target queries, a detector baseline, and frontier closed-model checks on two hard objects. On a balanced 2,280-image evaluation split, aggregate score matching can coexist with image-level disagreement, and verifier-use protocols and generator distributions change the measured reliability. Every verifier-protocol configuration also shrinks the human score difference between the two generators, by 7.5-25.0 pp, and with a third generator, Z-Image, all four tested protocols reverse the human ordering of Z-Image and FLUX.2-dev on our fixed prompt suite. GPT-5.5 and Claude Opus 4.7 checks do not remove the failure modes: GPT-5.5 still has only 59.92% clover valid-count fidelity, while Claude Opus 4.7 has lower same-slice agreement ($\kappa=0.432$). We propose reporting automatic benchmark scores with a factorized verifier reliability profile: aggregate score gap, image-level agreement, generator-comparison distortion, valid-image count fidelity, rejection behavior, output compliance, and directional bias.

AI.tldr: Audits automatic verifiers for text-to-image structural counting and shows that verifier choice, protocol and generator distribution can change benchmark scores and even reverse the human ordering of generators.
AI.motivation: Automatic text-to-image benchmark scores are treated as properties of the generator alone, although they also depend on the verifier and its protocol, which is rarely examined.
AI.method: Builds a verifier-centric audit suite over seven counting objects, with 6,240 images from Qwen-Image-2512 and FLUX.2-dev, and compares open MLLM verifiers under count-only, reject-aware, zero-shot and few-shot protocols, a TIFA-like baseline, a detector baseline and two frontier closed models on a balanced 2,280-image split.
AI.result: Every verifier-protocol configuration shrinks the human score gap between the two generators by 7.5-25.0 percentage points, and with a third generator, Z-Image, all four tested protocols reverse the human ordering of Z-Image and FLUX.2-dev; GPT-5.5 reaches only 59.92% clover valid-count fidelity, and Claude Opus 4.7 shows kappa 0.432 agreement.
AI.conclusion: Benchmark scores should be reported with a factorised verifier reliability profile covering score gap, image-level agreement, distortion, count fidelity, rejection, compliance and directional bias, since frontier verifiers do not remove these failures.

title: ThermalSplat: Generalizable Pose-Free Gaussian Splatting for Sparse-View Thermal 3D Reconstruction
summary: Thermal infrared imaging is vital for applications like search-and-rescue and autonomous navigation, yet trans- lating it into 3D scene representations remains a critical bottleneck. The low-texture nature and view-dependent emissivity of thermal images cause standard pose estima- tors to fail catastrophically, collapsing standard 3D Gaus- sian Splatting pipelines under sparse-view constraints. Fur- thermore, existing thermal reconstruction methods rely heavily on dense capture and computationally expensive per-scene optimization. Critically, many of these ap- proaches depend on aligned RGB-thermal datasets to ob- tain reliable camera poses and initial point clouds, ren- dering them unusable in purely thermal, unposed envi- ronments. To break this bottleneck, we present Thermal- Splat, the first generalizable, feed-forward Gaussian splat- ting framework that reconstructs 3D scenes directly from sparse thermal images without requiring known camera poses, RGB guidance, or per-scene training. We over- come thermal-specific challenges using a soft census loss for brightness-invariant structural matching and a bound- ary structure loss to explicitly supervise temperature discon- tinuities. Trained on an aggregated multi-source dataset, ThermalSplat synthesizes sharp reconstructions of unseen scenes in a single feed-forward pass. Extensive experi- ments demonstrate that ThermalSplat holds a strict advan- tage over scene-specific thermal splatting methods in the sparse regime. Furthermore, even compared against these baselines operating under their ideal dense capture set- tings, ThermalSplat achieves superior perceptual fidelity. By eliminating the need for computationally expensive per scene optimization, ThermalSplat offers an efficient and generalizable approach to thermal 3D reconstruction.

AI.tldr: Presents ThermalSplat, a feed-forward Gaussian splatting framework that reconstructs 3D scenes from sparse thermal images without known poses, RGB guidance or per-scene training.
AI.motivation: Standard pose estimators fail on low-texture, view-dependent thermal images, and existing thermal reconstruction needs dense capture, per-scene optimisation and aligned RGB-thermal data for poses.
AI.method: A generalisable feed-forward Gaussian splatting model trained on an aggregated multi-source dataset, using a soft census loss for brightness-invariant structural matching and a boundary structure loss that supervises temperature discontinuities.
AI.result: The abstract reports a strict advantage over scene-specific thermal splatting methods in the sparse regime, and superior perceptual fidelity even against those baselines under their dense capture settings; no numbers are given.
AI.conclusion: The approach offers an efficient, generalisable route to thermal 3D reconstruction without per-scene optimisation.

title: SteinPnP: Non-Parametric Uncertainty Quantification in the Perspective-N-Point Problem
summary: We propose SteinPnP, a probabilistic Perspective- N-Point (PnP) solver that models the full 6-DoF camera pose posterior using a non-parametric set of pose particles. By lever- aging Stein Variational Inference (SVI), SteinPnP combines the expressivity of particle-based representations with the efficiency of optimization-based solvers. However, a naive application of SVI struggles in the PnP problem, often missing alternative pose hypotheses or assigning incorrect probability weights to them. To address these limitations, we propose practical remedies that discover new potential poses, identify distinct hypothesis clusters, and balance their relative probability weights to capture the true underlying distribution. Our experiments across synthetic and real-world benchmarks demonstrate that SteinPnP accurately captures complex multimodal uncertainties while maintaining competitive accuracy.

AI.tldr: Proposes SteinPnP, a probabilistic perspective-n-point solver that models the full 6-DoF camera pose posterior with particles from Stein variational inference, with remedies for missed and misweighted hypotheses.
AI.motivation: Naive Stein variational inference in PnP often misses alternative pose hypotheses or assigns them incorrect weights, so it does not capture the true multimodal pose uncertainty.
AI.method: Uses a non-parametric set of pose particles and adds practical remedies that discover new candidate poses, identify distinct hypothesis clusters and balance their probability weights.
AI.result: Across synthetic and real-world benchmarks, SteinPnP is reported to capture complex multimodal uncertainty while keeping competitive accuracy; no numbers are given in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Particle-based pose posteriors can be made practical for PnP with these remedies, combining expressivity with optimisation-level efficiency.

title: Semantic Consistency of Vision Tokens: A Vision-Centric Perspective on Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: In computer vision, vision-language and self-supervised encoders are two unique paradigms characterized by global language alignment and high-quality vision-only patch representations, respectively. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often use the former because of language alignment, despite the recent rise in vision-centric tasks resembling traditional dense vision tasks that would likely benefit from the high-quality patch representations, raising the question whether self-supervised models could aid MLLMs in vision-centric tasks. To investigate this, we define semantic (in)consistency of patch tokens from language-aligned encoders and identify two sets of tokens, semantically consistent (SCTs) and semantically inconsistent (SITs). Through systematic probing via the removal of SCTs or SITs from the input of modern MLLMs, we show higher reliance on SCTs than SITs, as removal of the former induces larger performance drops. This demonstrates that MLLMs benefit from semantic consistency of vision tokens. With this in mind, we devise a simple yet effective extension of the MLLM training objective that combines traditional language modeling with semantic guidance via minimization of semantic inconsistency. This strategy, named Semantically-Guided Training (SGT), combines the signals of both loss terms to push the vision encoder towards providing semantically consistent tokens, while preserving language alignment. Extensive evaluation shows that SGT outperforms all baselines and MLLMs with specialized vision encoders on vision-centric benchmarks while keeping strong scores on text-centric benchmarks, thus setting state of the art on average across all tasks. Our results highlight the importance of combining language alignment and semantic consistency through the lens of MLLMs rather than independently from them and pave the way towards the design of better MLLM vision encoders.

AI.tldr: Shows that MLLMs rely more on semantically consistent vision tokens than inconsistent ones, and proposes Semantically-Guided Training (SGT), which adds a term that reduces semantic inconsistency to the language modelling objective.
AI.motivation: Language-aligned vision encoders are standard in MLLMs, but vision-centric tasks may benefit from the high-quality patch representations of self-supervised encoders, and it is unclear whether those could help MLLMs.
AI.method: Defines semantically consistent (SCT) and inconsistent (SIT) patch tokens from language-aligned encoders, probes models by removing either set, and trains with the language modelling loss plus a semantic inconsistency minimisation term that pushes the vision encoder towards consistent tokens.
AI.result: Removing SCTs causes larger performance drops than removing SITs, and SGT outperforms baselines and MLLMs with specialised vision encoders on vision-centric benchmarks while keeping strong text-centric scores, reaching state of the art on average across tasks.
AI.conclusion: Combining language alignment with semantic consistency is important for MLLM vision encoders, suggesting a route to better designs.

title: Reading the Unreadable: Text-Aware Image Super-Resolution Needs Reasoning
summary: Text-aware image super-resolution (TAISR) aims to recover high-resolution images from low-resolution inputs while preserving textual content. Existing methods treat this as a visual restoration problem, yet severely degraded text often cannot be read from local visual evidence alone. Humans instead read it by reasoning over image context, logical patterns, and prior knowledge. This raises a fundamental question: Does TAISR need reasoning? To answer this, we introduce two diagnostic tools. The first, ReasonText, is a human-curated benchmark that separates reasoning-required text from locally recoverable text. The second, Ground-Truth Text-Crop Accuracy (GTTCA), is a recognition-based metric that measures text restoration quality without text detection errors. Evaluating twelve recent super-resolution (SR) models, we find a consistent and substantial performance drop on reasoning-required text, revealing a systematic blind spot. Two observations point to a remedy. One is that text-conditioned SR models restore text substantially better when given ground-truth text. The other is that multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can read degraded text in low-resolution images through reasoning. We therefore propose Reasoning Transfer via Captioning (RTC), a training-free plug-in that uses an external MLLM to infer the degraded text and feeds the resulting caption to a text-conditioned SR model. RTC consistently improves all six text-conditioned SR models we evaluate, especially on reasoning-required text. Surprisingly, a real-world SR model with RTC can even outperform the TAISR model with RTC, suggesting that reasoning should be a core design axis for future TAISR.

AI.tldr: Introduces ReasonText and GTTCA to show that text-aware super-resolution fails on reasoning-required text, and proposes RTC, a training-free plug-in that adds an MLLM-inferred caption to text-conditioned SR models.
AI.motivation: Existing text-aware super-resolution treats text as a visual restoration problem, yet severely degraded text often cannot be read from local visual evidence alone, and this has not been measured.
AI.method: ReasonText is a human-curated benchmark separating reasoning-required from locally recoverable text, GTTCA is a recognition-based metric free of text detection errors, and Reasoning Transfer via Captioning (RTC) uses an external MLLM to infer degraded text and feeds the caption to a text-conditioned SR model.
AI.result: Twelve SR models show a consistent and substantial drop on reasoning-required text, and RTC consistently improves all six text-conditioned SR models evaluated, especially on reasoning-required text; a real-world SR model with RTC can outperform the TAISR model with RTC, according to the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Reasoning should be a core design axis for future text-aware super-resolution.

title: WaveFlow-UIE: A Single-Pipeline Wavelet-Domain Flow Model for Efficient Underwater Image Restoration
summary: Underwater image restoration remains challenging because color distortion, scattering, and detail loss affect low- and high-frequency image components differently. Recent diffusion-based methods have shown strong restoration quality, but often rely on multi-stage pipelines and costly iterative refinement. We present WaveFlow-UIE, a single-pipeline wavelet-domain flow model that directly learns to transform degraded underwater wavelet representations into clean ones. Our method applies a discrete wavelet transform, estimates lightweight physics-inspired degradation cues including transmission and ambient light, and conditions a velocity network trained with flow matching in wavelet space. The training objective combines flow-matching, frequency-weighted reconstruction, perceptual, color-consistency, and physics-consistency losses. Across UIEB, LSUI, UFO-120, and EUVP, WaveFlow-UIE achieves a strong quality-efficiency tradeoff, with especially competitive results on perceptual metrics. Relative to a strong wavelet-based diffusion baseline, the proposed model substantially reduces inference cost while maintaining or improving restoration quality on several paired benchmarks. We show that reducing the inference process from five flow steps to a single step preserves nearly all of the restoration quality while providing an additional speedup of about $4\times$ on UIEB at $256\times256$ resolution. This single-step result suggests that a single-pass wavelet-domain model is an effective alternative to heavier diffusion-style refinement.

AI.tldr: Presents WaveFlow-UIE, a single-pipeline wavelet-domain flow model for underwater image restoration that matches or improves on a wavelet diffusion baseline at lower inference cost.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-based underwater restoration gives strong quality but relies on multi-stage pipelines and costly iterative refinement.
AI.method: After a discrete wavelet transform and lightweight physics-inspired estimates of transmission and ambient light, a velocity network trained with flow matching in wavelet space maps degraded to clean wavelet representations, using flow-matching, frequency-weighted reconstruction, perceptual, colour-consistency and physics-consistency losses.
AI.result: Across UIEB, LSUI, UFO-120 and EUVP the model gives a strong quality-efficiency trade-off, with competitive perceptual metrics; a single flow step instead of five keeps nearly all restoration quality and gives about 4x extra speedup on UIEB at 256x256.
AI.conclusion: A single-pass wavelet-domain model is presented as an effective alternative to heavier diffusion-style refinement.

title: Fear of Memorizing Objects: End-to-End Zero-Shot Model-Based Object Detection
summary: This paper presents FOMO (Fear of Memorizing Objects), an end-to-end trainable transformer-based architecture for zero-shot model-based object detection. Existing approaches typically follow a proposal-and-match pipeline: target-agnostic mask proposals are generated and then matched to template features in a set of loosely coupled stages, making them susceptible to fragmented proposals in clutter and degraded matching under occlusions. FOMO elegantly replaces this paradigm by injecting object template information early in the detection pipeline: Bidirectional attention between learnable latent tokens, multi-view CAD templates, and query image features produces object-aware image features and conditioned queries which are subsequently decoded into bounding-box and confidence predictions. We train FOMO on Clutter6D, a novel large-scale synthetic dataset with over 500k images featuring more than 10k diverse object models rendered in highly cluttered scenes with multiple instances and varying occlusion levels, which addresses the limited object diversity and lack of realistic dense clutter in existing datasets for training zero-shot multi-instance algorithms. In true zero-shot fashion, FOMO achieves 54.2 mAP on BOP-Classic-Core at 0.23 s per image, ranking second overall with 3.8 pp difference to the top method while being more than 7x faster. Throughout comprehensive ablation studies we investigate and verify architectural design choices.

AI.tldr: Presents FOMO, an end-to-end transformer for zero-shot model-based object detection that injects CAD template information early, reaching 54.2 mAP on BOP-Classic-Core at 0.23 s per image.
AI.motivation: Proposal-and-match pipelines produce fragmented proposals in clutter and degrade matching under occlusion, because target-agnostic proposals are matched to templates in loosely coupled stages.
AI.method: Bidirectional attention between learnable latent tokens, multi-view CAD templates and query image features yields object-aware features and conditioned queries that are decoded into boxes and confidences; it is trained on Clutter6D, a synthetic dataset of over 500k images with more than 10k object models.
AI.result: In true zero-shot evaluation it reaches 54.2 mAP on BOP-Classic-Core at 0.23 s per image, ranking second overall with a 3.8 point gap to the top method while being more than 7 times faster.
AI.conclusion: Early template injection in an end-to-end model is a faster alternative to proposal-and-match detection, at a small accuracy cost relative to the best method.

title: Real Pairs Are Not Enough: Physically Anchored Supervision for Volumetric CT Super-Resolution
summary: Volumetric CT super-resolution (SR) models are commonly trained on synthetic or physically acquired pairs of low-resolution (LR) and high-resolution (HR) volumes. However, synthetic pairs miss real acquisition effects, whereas registered physical pairs retain inter-scan noise, artifact, and microstructure differences---causing direct voxelwise regression, and even naive synthetic-real mixing, to oversmooth fine porous structures. We introduce the Physically-anchored Implicit Network (PIN) with Real-Pair Dual-Anchor learning, which decouples physical-pair supervision into two complementary roles. The HR anchor teaches fine structure from registered HR through pair-conditioned spectral replay, while the LR anchor constrains the prediction from acquired LR via affine-calibrated low-pass projection. Together with exact synthetic supervision in one shared volumetric implicit model, PIN learns from both physical scans without forcing the acquired-LR reconstruction to match registered HR voxel by voxel. Inference requires only acquired LR. Across 30 external baseline configurations on real CT, PIN achieves the lowest full-volume LPIPS, reduces average symmetric surface distance by 42.3-49.5% and bone-volume-fraction error by 52.2-53.4% relative to the three strongest baselines for each metric, and lowers the erased reference-pore volume fraction from 37.3-72.9% to 10.4%. Code, pretrained models, and evaluation scripts will be publicly available.

AI.tldr: Proposes PIN with Real-Pair Dual-Anchor learning for volumetric CT super-resolution, using an HR anchor and an LR anchor so that registered physical pairs supervise without forcing voxel-level matching.
AI.motivation: Synthetic LR-HR pairs miss real acquisition effects, while registered physical pairs carry inter-scan noise, artefacts and microstructure differences, which cause direct voxelwise regression and naive mixing to oversmooth fine porous structures.
AI.method: A shared volumetric implicit network learns from exact synthetic supervision and two physical anchors: the HR anchor learns fine structure through pair-conditioned spectral replay, and the LR anchor constrains the prediction through an affine-calibrated low-pass projection of the acquired LR; inference needs only acquired LR.
AI.result: Across 30 external baseline configurations on real CT, PIN gives the lowest full-volume LPIPS, reduces average symmetric surface distance by 42.3-49.5% and bone-volume-fraction error by 52.2-53.4% relative to the three strongest baselines per metric, and lowers the erased reference-pore volume fraction from 37.3-72.9% to 10.4%.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling the two physical anchors preserves fine porous structure, and the authors state that code and pretrained models will be released.

title: SCR-Mamba: Skeleton-conditioned Mamba with cross-scale incremental refinement for efficient 3D human pose estimation
summary: Mamba-based methods for video-based 3D human pose estimation can model long sequences with linear complexity, but their selective state updates usually lack direct exploitation of skeletal relations. Meanwhile, stacking modeling blocks at the full temporal resolution leads to high computational overhead, while compressing the temporal sequence makes it difficult to retain per-frame details. To address these issues, we propose SCR-Mamba, whose core consists of Skeleton-Conditioned State Modeling (SCSM) and Cross-Scale Incremental Refinement (CSIR). SCSM generates a skeleton context from bone connections and left-right symmetry relations and generates the selective parameters of the spatial and temporal branches conditioned on it, so that structural relations are involved in the writing, propagation, and reading of state information. CSIR constructs multi-scale motion representations through content-adaptive aggregation and progressively refines the retained per-frame features with the increments produced by coarse-scale modeling, integrating long-range motion context while reducing full-resolution computation. On Human3.6M with Stacked Hourglass (SH) 2D detections and 243-frame inputs, SCR-Mamba-L achieves 36.8 mm MPJPE (P1) with 7.72 M parameters and 15.10 G MACs, less than 1/7 of the computational cost of StructMamPose-L with similar accuracy; SCR-Mamba-X further reaches 36.6 mm P1 and 30.9 mm P-MPJPE (P2), achieving state-of-the-art performance. On MPI-INF-3DHP, SCR-Mamba-X achieves a percentage of correct keypoints (PCK) of 99.3%, an area under the curve (AUC) of 88.1%, and an MPJPE of 14.2 mm.

AI.tldr: Proposes SCR-Mamba for efficient video-based 3D human pose estimation, conditioning Mamba state updates on skeleton relations and refining features across scales to cut full-resolution computation.
AI.motivation: Mamba models handle long sequences linearly but their selective state updates ignore skeletal relations, while full-resolution stacking is costly and temporal compression loses per-frame detail.
AI.method: Skeleton-Conditioned State Modeling (SCSM) builds skeleton context from bone connections and left-right symmetry to set selective parameters of spatial and temporal branches, and Cross-Scale Incremental Refinement (CSIR) builds multi-scale motion representations and refines per-frame features with coarse-scale increments.
AI.result: On Human3.6M with SH detections and 243-frame inputs, SCR-Mamba-L reaches 36.8 mm MPJPE with 7.72M parameters and 15.10G MACs, under 1/7 the cost of StructMamPose-L at similar accuracy; SCR-Mamba-X reaches 36.6 mm P1 and 30.9 mm P-MPJPE, and on MPI-INF-3DHP it gets 99.3% PCK, 88.1% AUC and 14.2 mm MPJPE.
AI.conclusion: The skeleton-conditioned, cross-scale design gives state-of-the-art accuracy at much lower computation, according to the authors.

title: MAGIC: Modality-Aware Gini Inspection for Clinical Hallucination Detection in LMMs
summary: Recent advances in medical large multimodal models (LMMs) have brought promising progress to clinical decision support, yet hallucination, the generation of confident but clinically unverifiable outputs, poses a critical threat to the reliability demanded in high-stakes medical settings. Existing hallucination detection methods, predominantly designed for unimodal settings, fail to capture the visual-linguistic dynamics inherent to medical imaging. We formulate the problem of hallucination detection in LMMs as disproportionate distribution of attention weights across the modalities during answer token generation. We quantify modality-specific attention concentration across layers and heads using the Gini coefficient and demonstrate statistically significant redistribution of attention mass between visual and textual tokens in hallucinated responses. We leverage these features to train a logistic regression-based classifier and evaluate it on two medical LMMs across three medical imaging modalities, demonstrating that our method achieves competitive or superior performance against contemporary hallucination detection baselines.

AI.tldr: Proposes MAGIC, a hallucination detector for medical large multimodal models that uses Gini coefficients of modality-specific attention and a logistic regression classifier.
AI.motivation: Hallucination detectors built for unimodal settings do not capture the visual-linguistic attention dynamics of medical imaging, where confident but clinically unverifiable answers are a serious risk.
AI.method: Measures the Gini coefficient of attention mass on visual versus textual tokens across layers and heads during answer generation, and trains a logistic regression classifier on these features.
AI.result: Hallucinated responses show statistically significant redistribution of attention between visual and textual tokens, and the method is competitive with or superior to contemporary baselines on two medical LMMs across three imaging modalities.
AI.conclusion: Modality-aware attention concentration is a useful signal for detecting clinical hallucinations in medical LMMs.

title: TraceKV: Policy-Preserving Low-Rank KV Cache Compression for Reasoning Vision-Language Models
summary: Reasoning vision-language models (VLMs) impose substantial KV cache demands from both large multimodal contexts and growing reasoning traces. Low-rank KV compression has emerged as a promising paradigm that stores low-dimensional latents of KV states and can be combined with quantization. However, existing low-rank methods often induce growing predictive policy drift from the dense model when compressing reasoning KV states, resulting in reasoning failures. We identify two key causes of this degradation: calibration-state mismatch between static contexts and on-policy reasoning states, and unequal error sensitivity across KV states. To address these challenges, we propose TraceKV, a training-free low-rank KV compression framework that unifies on-policy calibration, sensitivity-aware SVD, and global rank allocation under a single policy-preserving principle, substantially reducing policy-KL divergence during reasoning. Experiments across multiple VLMs and visual reasoning benchmarks demonstrate superior accuracy--memory trade-offs, achieving near-lossless reasoning accuracy with 5.64$\times$ KV cache compression when combined with quantization. Optimized low-rank attention kernels further deliver up to 1.83$\times$ end-to-end decoding speedup. Code will be available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Presents TraceKV, a training-free low-rank KV cache compression method for reasoning VLMs that reduces policy drift, reaching near-lossless accuracy at 5.64x compression when combined with quantisation.
AI.motivation: Low-rank KV compression causes growing policy drift from the dense model during long reasoning, due to calibration on static contexts that mismatches on-policy reasoning states and to unequal error sensitivity across KV states.
AI.method: TraceKV unifies on-policy calibration, sensitivity-aware SVD and global rank allocation under a policy-preserving principle that reduces policy-KL divergence, with optimised low-rank attention kernels.
AI.result: Across several VLMs and visual reasoning benchmarks it gives better accuracy-memory trade-offs, reaching near-lossless accuracy at 5.64x KV cache compression with quantisation and up to 1.83x end-to-end decoding speedup.
AI.conclusion: Policy-preserving calibration is presented as the key to low-rank KV compression for reasoning VLMs.

title: RipBench: A Unified Benchmark for Multi-Level Rip Current Detection, Classification and Segmentation
comment: Accepted to NeurIPS 2026, Evaluations & Datasets Track. 47 pages, 11 figures. See this https URL for dataset and project updates
summary: Rip currents are a serious and often under-addressed threat to beach safety and the leading cause of coastal drownings worldwide. They are difficult to detect due to their amorphous structure, similarity to the background, and large variability in viewpoints and environments. Despite their dangers and growing interest in automated detection, existing research remains fragmented across datasets, metrics, models, and approaches, leading to an incomplete understanding of model performance. We introduce RipBench, a unified benchmark that enables controlled evaluation of rip current detection spanning multiple tasks, including classification, axis-aligned and oriented object detection, and instance, semantic, and panoptic segmentation, on the same data with standardized splits. This allows direct comparison of model performance on all levels of visual abstraction. Across $304$ videos ($303{,}491$ frames, $51{,}011$ of them annotated for all six tasks) collected from diverse coastlines, our results expose a clear performance gap between coarse recognition and precise spatial understanding: frame-level classification reaches $F_2 = 0.93$, while the best detector and the best instance segmenter reach $0.72$ and $0.66$, with model rankings that change from task to task. Video-level confidence intervals, a blind inter-annotator study of the spatial labels, stratified analyses by viewpoint and visual signature, and video views with temporal baselines (single-seed, short-schedule reference runs) accompany the benchmark. All tasks are supported with carefully curated annotations and evaluated using standard metrics, with a focus on the $F_2$ score to emphasize recall in this safety-critical setting. RipBench, along with multiple baselines per task, is publicly available at this https URL to support progress in real-world, multi-task vision for beach safety.

AI.tldr: Introduces RipBench, a unified benchmark for rip current classification, detection and segmentation on 304 videos with standardised splits, showing a large gap between frame-level recognition and spatial localisation.
AI.motivation: Rip current research is fragmented across datasets, metrics and models, so model performance is not comparable across levels of visual abstraction.
AI.method: Evaluates classification, axis-aligned and oriented object detection, and instance, semantic and panoptic segmentation on the same data with standardised splits, using F2 to emphasise recall, with video-level confidence intervals, a blind inter-annotator study of spatial labels and stratified analyses.
AI.result: Across 304 videos (303,491 frames, 51,011 annotated for all six tasks), frame-level classification reaches F2 0.93 while the best detector and best instance segmenter reach 0.72 and 0.66, with model rankings that change between tasks.
AI.conclusion: Coarse recognition is far stronger than precise spatial understanding for rip currents, and the public benchmark with baselines is intended to support progress in beach safety vision.

title: FoveaDet: Software-Hardware Co-Design of Foveated CNN-Transformer for Object Detection
comment: 5 pages, 6 figures. Submitted to IEEE ISCAS 2027
summary: Deploying real-time object detection on power-constrained edge platforms is challenging as processing full-resolution frames is often computationally redundant. Inspired by biological foveation which assigns variable resolution based on visual saliency, we propose a novel software-hardware co-design framework called FoveaDet. On the software side, FoveaDet dynamically identifies salient regions to predict fixation points, followed by aggressive patch pruning in Vision Transformers (ViT) to discard irrelevant background data. To mitigate slowdowns from sequential patch generation, we implement optimized interpolation and patch selection algorithms. Evaluated on standard GPUs, this foveated approach reduces floating-point operations by 65.4% to 92.2% and accelerates inference by 4.76x, while suffering a negligible mAP drop compared to dense baselines. To eliminate hardware bottlenecks, we complement the algorithm with a custom RISC-V core featuring specialized instructions to accelerate the foveated processing pipeline. FoveaDet provides a scalable, efficient architecture capable of unlocking advanced vision processing on severely constrained mobile platforms.

AI.tldr: Presents FoveaDet, a software-hardware co-design that prunes ViT patches using predicted fixation points and adds a custom RISC-V core, reducing FLOPs by 65.4-92.2% and speeding inference 4.76x with negligible mAP loss.
AI.motivation: Real-time detection on power-constrained edge devices is wasteful when full-resolution frames are processed, since much of each frame is redundant.
AI.method: Predicts salient fixation points, prunes irrelevant patches in a Vision Transformer, and uses optimised interpolation and patch selection algorithms, with a custom RISC-V core that has specialised instructions for the foveated pipeline.
AI.result: On standard GPUs the foveated approach reduces floating-point operations by 65.4% to 92.2% and accelerates inference by 4.76x with a negligible mAP drop relative to dense baselines.
AI.conclusion: The co-designed architecture is presented as a scalable route to advanced vision on severely constrained mobile platforms.

title: Cat Royale Comprehensive Dataset: A Dataset for Pose Detection, Segmentation, Animal Action Recognition and Scene Understanding
comment: 26 pages, 4 figures, 6 tables. Submitted to the International Journal of Computer Vision. Dataset: this https URL
summary: Animal focused computer vision datasets are of a growing interest in the fields of both Computer Vision and Animal behaviour. The ability to make sense of complex scenes via a variety of Computer Vision tasks has substantial implications for behavioural understanding and welfare. The perfection of these tasks will help lead to better health and emotional outcomes for wild and domestic animals. In this work we present the Cat Royale Comprehensive Dataset (CRCD), a large, comprehensive, multi-modal dataset for feline understanding, based on a huge database of over 500 hours of video captured during the Cat Royale artwork and research project. Our dataset contains annotations for a range of computer vision problems including 20,000 images with instance segmentation masks, 5000 images with multi-subject pose coordinates, over 800 video clips with action classes, and over 800 clips with detailed text description. This is the first such dataset to link this wide range of annotation types together for multi-modal use. We release this entire dataset, and our custom annotation tools will also be made available, in order to allow for ongoing expansion. We also provide a series of benchmarks for the tasks of Instance Segmentation, Pose detection, Temporal Action Localisation, and finally video-text retrieval. The totality of this multi-modal dataset is the data needed to solve both these individual computer vision tasks as well as enabling more complex multi-modal tasks making use of a combination of annotations.

AI.tldr: Presents the Cat Royale Comprehensive Dataset, a multi-modal feline dataset from over 500 hours of video, with instance masks, poses, action clips and text descriptions, and benchmarks for four tasks.
AI.motivation: Animal-focused vision datasets are growing in importance for behavioural understanding and welfare, but few link several annotation types for the same data.
AI.method: Annotations include 20,000 images with instance masks, 5,000 images with multi-subject pose coordinates, over 800 action clips and over 800 clips with text descriptions, with benchmarks for instance segmentation, pose detection, temporal action localisation and video-text retrieval.
AI.result: The abstract reports the dataset and benchmarks but gives no benchmark numbers.
AI.conclusion: The dataset is presented as the first to link this range of annotation types for multi-modal use, with the release also including annotation tools for ongoing expansion.

title: CoCode-World: Shared 3D Proxy Representation for Multi-Player World Models
summary: Multiplayer generative world models must produce observations that agree on shared entities despite different camera motions and occlusions. Explicit world representations provide spatial control, but precise modeling of individual game maps limits scene diversity, while shared geometry alone cannot ensure consistent appearance across views. We present CoCode-World, a shared 3D proxy framework that separates structural control from visual synthesis for two-player video generation. Programmable proxies specify scene layout, motion, and occlusion, while RGB references guide character and scene appearance. To coordinate visual details across players, we concatenate paired proxy videos, appearance references, and target views in a consistent spatial layout and generate both views jointly with a pretrained video model. This formulation uses the model's native attention for cross-view communication within a single generation branch, with LoRA adaptation learning proxy adherence and appearance correspondence from paired observations. We construct a two-player GTA~V dataset that pairs synchronized RGB observations with proxy videos derived from shared map geometry and game-engine state. Experiments demonstrate appearance transfer to characters and scene styles unseen during training, with improvements in video quality and cross-view player identity over the evaluated baseline. Ablations further examine how proxy construction and cross-view communication affect generation. Project page: this https URL.

AI.tldr: Presents CoCode-World, a shared 3D proxy framework for two-player video world models that jointly generates both views with a pretrained video model to keep shared entities consistent.
AI.motivation: Multiplayer generative world models must agree on shared entities across camera motion and occlusion, but explicit representations limit scene diversity and shared geometry alone does not keep appearance consistent across views.
AI.method: Programmable proxy videos specify layout, motion and occlusion while RGB references guide appearance; paired proxy videos, appearance references and target views are concatenated in one spatial layout and generated jointly, with LoRA adaptation and the model's native attention for cross-view communication, trained on a two-player GTA V dataset.
AI.result: Appearance transfer to unseen characters and scene styles is shown, with improvements in video quality and cross-view player identity over the evaluated baseline; ablations examine proxy construction and cross-view communication.
AI.conclusion: Separating structural proxy control from visual synthesis helps keep multiplayer observations consistent across views.

title: Contrastive Bootstrap Representation Learning for Label-Efficient Agricultural Image Classification
summary: Expert annotation remains a major bottleneck in agricultural image classification, where collecting images is often easier than obtaining reliable labels from domain specialists. Self-supervised learning can reduce this dependence by pretraining transferable representations on unlabelled imagery. Contrastive and bootstrap methods provide two established but distinct training signals, motivating an empirical study of a formulation that applies both signals within one representation path under severe downstream label scarcity. We present Contrastive Bootstrap Representation Learning (CBRL), which jointly optimises SimCLR-style NT-Xent contrastive learning and bidirectional BYOL-style exponential-moving-average target prediction within a shared online projection space. Using a ViT-L/16 backbone and 10% of the downstream labels, we report single-seed point estimates on four primary agricultural test benchmarks plus an exploratory 33-image New Plant Diseases evaluation. CBRL records the highest macro-F1 point estimate on the four primary benchmarks. On DeepWeeds, its 79.77% test macro-F1 is 32.29 points above the random-initialisation, label-only baseline and 15.78 points above the next-highest comparison point estimate; on PlantVillage, its 98.14% macro-F1 is 10.43 and 0.43 points higher, respectively. On PlantDoc, however, all methods fail to reach practically useful performance. These results identify the evaluated joint formulation as a promising candidate for label-limited transfer, but they do not establish objective synergy, statistical superiority, or robustness across stochastic runs.

AI.tldr: Proposes CBRL, which jointly applies SimCLR-style contrastive and BYOL-style bootstrap objectives in one projection space, and reports the highest macro-F1 point estimates on four agricultural benchmarks with 10% labels.
AI.motivation: Expert annotation is a bottleneck in agricultural image classification, and it is unclear whether contrastive and bootstrap self-supervision work better together than separately under severe label scarcity.
AI.method: Uses a ViT-L/16 backbone with NT-Xent contrastive learning and bidirectional BYOL-style EMA target prediction in a shared online projection space, trained with 10% of downstream labels, with single-seed point estimates on four primary benchmarks and an exploratory 33-image evaluation.
AI.result: On DeepWeeds, CBRL reaches 79.77% test macro-F1, 32.29 points above the random-initialisation label-only baseline and 15.78 above the next-highest point estimate; on PlantVillage it reaches 98.14%, 10.43 and 0.43 points higher respectively; all methods fail on PlantDoc.
AI.conclusion: The joint formulation is a promising candidate for label-limited transfer, but the results do not establish objective synergy, statistical superiority or robustness across stochastic runs.

title: Learning-Based Interpolation of Detector Gaps in Photon-Counting X-ray Imaging
summary: Image detectors assembled from tiled modules have physical gaps in the field of view that must be filled before downstream processing such as phase retrieval or tomographic reconstruction. Unlike natural-image inpainting, detector-gap interpolation must leave all other pixels unmodified and preserve the intensity statistics of the filled region, since even a small shift in mean intensity can cause ring artifacts after reconstruction. We adapted two generative models, a Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty (WGAN-GP) and a conditional Pix2Pix model, to this task. We implemented a masking strategy that restricts all changes to the gap pixels and loss terms that constrain the mean intensity and the intensity distribution of the filled region. Both models were trained on nanoCT projections with simulated gaps and compared with linear interpolation, Navier--Stokes inpainting, and the deep image-inpainting network MADF, quantitatively on simulated gaps and visually on real detector gaps. WGAN-GP and Pix2Pix achieved the best perceptual similarity (LPIPS) and histogram distance and, apart from linear interpolation, the shortest inference time. Pix2Pix required about five times fewer training GPU-hours than WGAN-GP. Ablation studies showed that masking the network output contributes by far the most to plausible inpainting results. Applied to sinograms, Pix2Pix produced the most natural gap filling but improved the reconstruction only slightly compared with linear interpolation. The source code and the weights of the final Pix2Pix model are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Adapts a Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty and a conditional Pix2Pix model to fill detector gaps in photon-counting X-ray images, with masking that restricts changes to gap pixels and mean and distribution losses on the filled region.
AI.motivation: Detector gaps must be filled before phase retrieval or tomographic reconstruction, and natural-image inpainting does not preserve the intensity statistics needed, since small mean shifts cause ring artefacts.
AI.method: Trains WGAN-GP and Pix2Pix on nanoCT projections with simulated gaps, with an output mask restricting changes to gap pixels and losses constraining the mean and intensity distribution of the filled region, compared with linear interpolation, Navier-Stokes inpainting and MADF.
AI.result: WGAN-GP and Pix2Pix achieve the best LPIPS and histogram distance, and apart from linear interpolation the shortest inference time; Pix2Pix needs about five times fewer training GPU-hours than WGAN-GP; masking the output contributes most, and on sinograms Pix2Pix improves reconstruction only slightly over linear interpolation.
AI.conclusion: Pix2Pix gives the most natural gap filling at lower training cost, although its reconstruction gain over linear interpolation is small; the code and final weights are released.

title: WaveletLoRA: Frequency-Aware Content-Style Decomposition for Personalized Image Generation
summary: Content-style decomposition from a single image is a fundamental challenge in personalized image generation, aiming to separate subject identity from visual style for flexible recomposition. Existing approaches primarily operate in the spatial domain, without explicitly exploiting the distinct frequency characteristics naturally associated with content and style. In this paper, we propose WaveletLoRA, a novel frequency-aware framework for explicit content-style decomposition through wavelet-domain supervision. Specifically, we first apply a multi-level discrete wavelet transform (DWT) to decompose the reference image into low-frequency and high-frequency subbands. We then assign a dedicated LoRA branch to each subband, where the low-frequency branch models global appearance for style acquisition, while the high-frequency branches capture structural details for content preservation. To further improve disentanglement quality, we introduce a dense Mixture-of-Experts aggregation module together with a frequency-domain regularization objective, which reduces style leakage and enhance content fidelity. In addition, we establish WaveBench and develop a VLM-based evaluation protocol that explicitly measures both attribute similarity and attribute separation for disentanglement assessment. Extensive experiments demonstrate that WaveletLoRA consistently outperforms existing methods and produces results that better align with human preference.

AI.tldr: Proposes WaveletLoRA, which applies a multi-level wavelet transform and assigns a LoRA branch to each subband, separating style from content for personalised image generation, and introduces the WaveBench evaluation.
AI.motivation: Content-style decomposition from a single image is central to personalised generation, but existing methods work in the spatial domain and do not exploit the distinct frequency characteristics of content and style.
AI.method: A low-frequency branch models global appearance for style, high-frequency branches capture structure for content, and a dense mixture-of-experts aggregation and a frequency-domain regularisation reduce style leakage; a VLM-based protocol measures attribute similarity and separation on WaveBench.
AI.result: The abstract reports that WaveletLoRA consistently outperforms existing methods and better matches human preference, without specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Frequency-aware decomposition is presented as an effective way to disentangle content and style in personalised generation.

title: MemInStream: Memorizing or Merely Recognizing? Rethinking Streaming Video Memory Evaluation
summary: Streaming video understanding aims to continuously process incoming visual observations, making the retention and retrieval of relevant information increasingly important as the video history grows. Although existing benchmarks include memory-related questions, question-answering accuracy alone does not reliably measure memory capabilities. Incorrect predictions may arise from failures in visual understanding rather than forgetting, whereas correct predictions may rely on linguistic priors or recent observations without requiring historical memory. To address these ambiguities, we introduce MemInStream, a benchmark dedicated to evaluating memory capabilities in streaming video understanding. We develop an evidence-controlled validation protocol that associates each question with temporally localized evidence intervals. The protocol validates evidence solvability and memory necessity by retaining questions that models can answer from the annotated evidence but cannot resolve using recent observations, post-evidence observations, or textual input alone. This helps disentangle memory limitations from understanding failures while reducing memory-independent shortcuts. MemInStream provides a systematic evaluation of memory capabilities through four major categories, covering Episodic Retrieval, State Tracking \& Updating, Multi-Evidence Integration, and Contextual Memory across diverse video scenarios. Overall, \textsc{MemInStream} provides a comprehensive and reliable benchmark for systematically evaluating memory capabilities in streaming video understanding.

AI.tldr: Introduces MemInStream, a streaming video benchmark with an evidence-controlled protocol that keeps only questions requiring historical memory, to separate memory failures from understanding failures.
AI.motivation: Question-answering accuracy alone does not measure memory in streaming video, since errors may come from visual understanding and correct answers may come from linguistic priors or recent frames.
AI.method: Associates each question with temporally localised evidence intervals and retains only questions answerable from the evidence but not from recent observations, post-evidence observations or text alone; questions cover four categories: Episodic Retrieval, State Tracking and Updating, Multi-Evidence Integration and Contextual Memory.
AI.result: The abstract describes the protocol and categories but gives no model results or numbers.
AI.conclusion: MemInStream is presented as a comprehensive and reliable benchmark for memory capabilities in streaming video understanding.

title: Ultrasound Elastography: Excitation Methods and Low-Cost Alternative
summary: Ultrasound elastography (or elasticity imaging) is a method that characterizes the tissue mechanical properties with the purpose of aiding the diagnosis of certain pathologies. Many novel clinical applications use the assumption that these tissue properties are changed in the presence of pathological processes. Characterization of tissue mechanical properties is achieved by imaging the response of the tissue to an induced stress or excitation. A plethora of approaches have been used in the scientific community to induce excitation in tissue, which usually require additional tools or devices than are costly. Furthermore these are usually integrated in the imaging pipeline using additional software or hardware for control. An alternative that is simpler, faster to integrate (and low-cost) is proposed in this work, by using readily available smartphones as a source of mechanical excitation. The induced displacements are used to solve the elasticity inverse problem (IP) using a finite element method (FEM) approach. Preliminary elasticity reconstructions of a phantom that mimics tissue are similar to when using a dedicated actuator as means of inducing harmonic displacements, illustrating the feasibility of our low-cost ultrasound elasography approach.

AI.tldr: Proposes using smartphones as low-cost mechanical excitation sources for ultrasound elastography, with a finite element inverse solver, and reports reconstructions on a phantom similar to those from a dedicated actuator.
AI.motivation: Common excitation methods for ultrasound elastography need extra costly tools or hardware and software integration, which limits clinical adoption of tissue mechanical property imaging.
AI.method: Smartphones induce harmonic displacements in tissue, and the induced displacements are used to solve the elasticity inverse problem with a finite element method approach.
AI.result: Preliminary reconstructions of a tissue-mimicking phantom are similar to those obtained with a dedicated actuator for inducing harmonic displacements; the abstract reports no quantitative figures.
AI.conclusion: The low-cost smartphone approach is feasible for elastography, based on preliminary results.

title: Taming Neural Fields with a Frequency-Lipschitz Curriculum for Sparse-View CT Reconstruction
summary: Sparse-view computed tomography (SVCT) reduces radiation dose by acquiring fewer projection views, but the resulting under-determined inverse problem requires careful regularization to prevent reconstruction algorithms from fitting streak artifacts and hallucinated structures. Existing implicit neural representation (INR) methods rely on implicit spectral bias or iterative external denoising, yet they provide limited control over when high-frequency capacity is exposed during optimization. To address this limitation, we propose FLIC (Frequency-Lipschitz INR Curriculum), a capacity-controlled self-prior INR framework that makes the network's representational capacity explicit and schedulable. The core of our method is a joint frequency-Lipschitz curriculum that couples random Fourier feature encoding with spectrally normalized MLP decoding under non-uniform Lipschitz budgets, guiding reconstruction along a coarse-to-fine trajectory from stable global anatomy to fine details. The terminal capacity is automatically calibrated from FBP gradient statistics, enabling scan-adaptive regularization without per-scan manual tuning of the terminal Lipschitz budget. We further introduce a prior-guided adaptive ray sampling strategy that concentrates integration samples near high-gradient anatomical boundaries, improving forward-model fidelity. The entire framework operates in a single training stage without iterative denoising, enabling efficient per-image reconstruction. Extensive experiments on four public CT datasets under noise-free and low-dose settings show that our method achieves state-of-the-art unsupervised reconstruction quality with consistent performance across diverse anatomical structures.

AI.tldr: Proposes FLIC, a self-prior implicit neural representation for sparse-view CT that schedules network capacity through a joint frequency-Lipschitz curriculum, with the terminal capacity calibrated from FBP gradient statistics.
AI.motivation: Implicit neural representations for sparse-view CT either rely on spectral bias or on iterative external denoising, and give little control over when high-frequency capacity is exposed during optimisation.
AI.method: Couples random Fourier feature encoding with spectrally normalised MLP decoding under non-uniform Lipschitz budgets, a coarse-to-fine schedule, prior-guided adaptive ray sampling near high-gradient boundaries, and a single training stage without iterative denoising.
AI.result: The abstract reports state-of-the-art unsupervised reconstruction quality on four public CT datasets under noise-free and low-dose settings, with consistent performance across anatomical structures, without numbers.
AI.conclusion: Explicit, schedulable capacity control gives scan-adaptive regularisation for efficient per-image sparse-view CT reconstruction.

title: CGOcc: Learning Cross-Gaussian Dependencies for 3D Semantic Occupancy Prediction
summary: In Gaussian-based semantic occupancy prediction, overlapping primitives can provide ambiguous class predictions, making their joint interpretation important for voxel classification. However, current methods using spatially weighted mixtures neglect explicit modeling of cross-primitive dependencies, limiting the readout's ability to utilize category-specific relational evidence. Hence, we introduce CGOcc, a supervised multi-camera framework that explicitly models Cross-Gaussian dependencies for 3D semantic Occupancy prediction. CGOcc integrates appearance and geometric observations to refine Gaussian states and encodes cross-Gaussian dependencies in a diagonal-plus-low-rank representation. To incorporate these dependencies into voxel classification, CGOcc uses a class-conditional projection to extract diagonal and signed cross-Gaussian statistics without constructing a dense dependency matrix. The readout then refines occupied-class probabilities using these statistics while preserving a learned reference's occupied mass and free probability. Extensive experiments on nuScenes demonstrate CGOcc achieves state-of-the-art performance, with larger gains at high Gaussian overlap and improved predictions near boundaries. Ablation studies validate the effectiveness of covariance-aware prediction and support its synergy with geometric interaction.

AI.tldr: Proposes CGOcc, a multi-camera framework for 3D semantic occupancy prediction that models cross-Gaussian dependencies with a diagonal-plus-low-rank representation, reporting state-of-the-art results on nuScenes.
AI.motivation: Overlapping Gaussian primitives give ambiguous class predictions, and existing spatially weighted mixtures do not explicitly model dependencies between primitives.
AI.method: Refines Gaussian states from appearance and geometry, encodes cross-Gaussian dependencies as diagonal-plus-low-rank, and uses a class-conditional projection to extract diagonal and signed cross-Gaussian statistics, which refine occupied-class probabilities without building a dense matrix.
AI.result: On nuScenes, CGOcc achieves state-of-the-art performance, with larger gains at high Gaussian overlap and better predictions near boundaries; ablations support covariance-aware prediction.
AI.conclusion: Modelling cross-primitive dependencies helps occupancy readout, especially in regions of high Gaussian overlap.

title: How Far Can Frozen Vision-Language Models Go on Event Data? A Training-Free Study on EventBench
comment: "Technical report, EBMV @ ECCV 2026 Challenge. 13 pages, 9 figures
summary: We present a training-free system for the EBMV @ ECCV 2026 challenge "Event Stream Understanding with EventBench" (General Understanding track), which evaluates vision-language models on five event-camera understanding tasks. We use none of the challenge's training data: our goal is to measure how far off-the-shelf, RGB-pretrained models can go on event data through representation and prompting alone. For four of the five categories (gesture recognition, detailed understanding, causal reasoning, and event OCR) we render event bins as red/ON, blue/OFF frames, select a category-specific subset of bins, stitch them into a single grid image, and query the same frozen Qwen3.5 9B vision-language model with a category-specific prompt for all four tasks. The fifth category, action recognition, feeds every bin directly into the organizers' EventGPT-Plus-2B. The system reaches 62.28% overall accuracy across 2,084 test questions (rank 9/27), led by action recognition and causal reasoning (80.27%, 77.22%) and limited most by gesture recognition and event OCR (54.70%, 34.57%). We visualize test samples from every category together with the exact images the model receives, score six alternative representations against the evaluation server, and analyze the full test set post hoc. That analysis shows that our bounding-box crop almost never tightened around content, so event OCR text reached the model at roughly one fifth of its horizontal resolution, and that detailed-understanding predictions are skewed toward the first two answer options.

AI.tldr: Reports a training-free system for the EBMV @ ECCV 2026 EventBench challenge that renders event bins as RGB-style frames for a frozen Qwen3.5 9B model, reaching 62.28% overall accuracy and rank 9 of 27.
AI.motivation: The authors ask how far off-the-shelf RGB-pretrained vision-language models can go on event-camera data using representation and prompting alone, without the challenge's training data.
AI.method: For four of five categories, event bins are rendered as red/ON and blue/OFF frames, a subset is stitched into a grid, and the frozen Qwen3.5 9B answers with category-specific prompts; action recognition uses the organisers' EventGPT-Plus-2B on all bins.
AI.result: Overall accuracy is 62.28% across 2,084 test questions, led by action recognition and causal reasoning (80.27% and 77.22%) and limited by gesture recognition and event OCR (54.70% and 34.57%); post hoc analysis shows the bounding-box crop rarely tightened around content, so OCR text got about a fifth of its horizontal resolution.
AI.conclusion: Frozen RGB-pretrained models do reasonably on event data, but the crop and resolution choices limit event OCR, and detailed-understanding answers are skewed toward the first two options.

title: Image Deblending with Diffusion Models
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027. 22 pages, 10 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Image deblending is the task of decomposing a composite image back into its source images, which is an ill-posed problem, as a single blended image can be decomposed into multiple plausible source layers. While diffusion models are often used to solve inverse problems, they typically address single-output reconstruction problems. In this work, we formulate deblending as a joint inverse problem, employing diffusion posterior sampling to simultaneously reconstruct two source images, demonstrating that a single diffusion prior is expressive enough to disentangle two full images at once rather than just one. Drawing inspiration from human perception, where semantic understanding helps disentangle visual inconsistencies, we propose a training-free framework that leverages text prompts to constrain this solution space. We address the blind deblending task through a two-stage architecture: text-guided latent diffusion performs semantic separation using prompts as high-level cues, followed by a pixel-space refinement to recover fine details. Stochastic sampling produces multiple plausible decompositions that can be ranked without ground truth. Extensive experiments show that our training-free method achieves state-of-the-art results on unseen domains and extends to spatially-varying alpha maps, while remaining competitive with supervised baselines on standard scalar blending benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Proposes a training-free method that frames image deblending as a joint inverse problem, using diffusion posterior sampling to reconstruct two source images at once, guided by text prompts and followed by pixel-space refinement.
AI.motivation: Diffusion models usually solve single-output inverse problems, and deblending is ill-posed because one blended image can decompose into many plausible source pairs.
AI.method: Text-guided latent diffusion performs semantic separation with prompts as high-level cues, followed by pixel-space refinement; stochastic sampling yields multiple decompositions that can be ranked without ground truth.
AI.result: The training-free method achieves state-of-the-art results on unseen domains and extends to spatially varying alpha maps, while remaining competitive with supervised baselines on standard scalar blending benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: A single diffusion prior is expressive enough to disentangle two full images at once, offering a training-free route to blind deblending.

title: AIFR: Adaptive Identity Feature Recovery for Diffusion-Based Makeup and Anime Portraits
summary: Diffusion-based makeup and anime portraits are increasingly popular in online content creation (e.g., virtual makeup editing and anime avatar generation), but their altered appearances can hinder face recognition (FR) in identity-based content screening. Existing methods mainly adapt FR encoders or restore input images. The former require costly gallery re-encoding, while the latter may be incomplete or distort identity-related facial details. To address these limitations, we aim to correct identity features within a frozen FR model to recover its output embeddings in its original space. Appearance changes vary in strength and affect facial regions differently. To this end, we propose Adaptive Identity Feature Recovery (AIFR), a framework that inserts a lightweight recovery module at a single intermediate layer to predict sample-level correction strength and spatially adaptive residual updates. Module training uses fused identity targets to guide embedding recovery in the original FR space and an identity-shift score to regulate correction strength and limit unnecessary changes. At inference, AIFR processes a single portrait in one forward pass without reference images, producing recovered embeddings that can be directly matched with existing gallery templates without re-encoding. With only 1.22M trainable parameters, AIFR improves the average TAR at FAR=$10^{-4}$ from 66.1\% to 90.2\% over the original ArcFace, and further experiments show improvements across unseen makeup styles, stylization strengths, and generators. Beyond recognition, the recovered embeddings can directly condition a pretrained Arc2Face model to generate faces with improved identity preservation, showing compatibility with embedding-conditioned downstream generation.

AI.tldr: Proposes AIFR, a lightweight module inserted into a frozen face recognition model that corrects identity features for diffusion-made makeup and anime portraits, raising TAR at FAR=1e-4 from 66.1% to 90.2% over ArcFace.
AI.motivation: Diffusion-altered makeup and anime portraits hinder face recognition, and existing approaches either need costly gallery re-encoding by adapting the encoder or restore images in ways that may distort identity details.
AI.method: A lightweight recovery module at one intermediate layer predicts a sample-level correction strength and spatially adaptive residual updates, trained with fused identity targets and an identity-shift score; at inference it needs one forward pass and no reference image, with 1.22M trainable parameters.
AI.result: Average TAR at FAR=1e-4 rises from 66.1% to 90.2% over the original ArcFace, with improvements on unseen makeup styles, stylisation strengths and generators; recovered embeddings can also condition Arc2Face to improve identity preservation in generation.
AI.conclusion: Correcting embeddings in the original face recognition space avoids re-encoding galleries and supports both recognition and identity-preserving generation.

title: Prior-as-Skill: Remember Outside and Read Inside with On-Policy Self-Distillation for Self-Evolving VLM Agents
summary: Self-evolving visual agents keep what they learn as skills: key frames with step notes on a task's steps and their order. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is now a popular way to train such skills into a vision-language model that matches, on its own answers, a teacher that also reads the written order. At deployment, frames often go missing or show an unusual order, as when a person or a website reorders the steps. Existing internalization methods keep any order they store in the frame-reading weights: trained on full frames, the model guesses when they are missing, and trained with frames withheld, it stores the order, so memory can override what it sees. We propose PriorSplit, which fills in missing frames from an order kept outside the model, with no training beyond OPSD. It counts which of two neighboring steps comes first in training episodes, and the model checks if both asked steps are in view: if so, it answers from the frames, and otherwise the counts answer. Extensive experiments on synthetic skills with five models and on step-tagged order questions in new episodes of seen web, cooking and egocentric tasks demonstrate that, with frames missing, PriorSplit outperforms every compared method at OPSD's training cost. With Qwen3-VL-4B on synthetic skills, it also stays close to OPSD on unusual orders, where methods that gain most by storing the order fall behind.

AI.tldr: PriorSplit fills in frames missing at deployment from an order stored outside the model, so self-evolving VLM agents trained with on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) can use the step order without memorising it in the frame-reading weights. It adds no training beyond OPSD and outperforms the compared methods when frames are missing.
AI.motivation: OPSD internalises skills into a VLM, but existing methods store the step order in the frame-reading weights. When frames are missing the model guesses, and when trained with frames withheld it stores the order, so memory can override what the frames show, which fails for unusual step orders.
AI.method: PriorSplit keeps an order-count table outside the model, built from training episodes, that records which of two neighbouring steps comes first. At inference the model checks whether both asked steps are visible in the frames: if so it answers from the frames, otherwise the counts answer.
AI.result: On synthetic skills with five models and on step-tagged order questions in new episodes of seen web, cooking and egocentric tasks, PriorSplit outperforms every compared method with frames missing at OPSD's training cost. With Qwen3-VL-4B on synthetic skills it stays close to OPSD on unusual orders, where methods that store the order most fall behind.
AI.conclusion: Keeping the step order outside the model and using it only when frames are absent avoids memory overriding visual evidence, giving more robust self-evolving visual agents at no extra training cost.

title: VibePrevisBench: Evaluating Agentic Coding for 4D Scene Generation in Blender
summary: Controllable real-world video generation models can condition on a rendered graybox proxy video, which fixes layout, motion and camera. Coding agents can build such videos by reconstructing a 4D scene in Blender, yet no benchmark checks both these videos and the long, multi-shot scenes behind them. We introduce VibePrevisBench, a benchmark for 4D scene reconstruction: an agent turns a brief into an executable 4D scene and renders its proxy video. Its 242 tasks span four input kinds, including scripts, photos, continuations, and reference videos. Each delivery is scored along two evaluation dimensions. Rule-based Scene Check re-runs the code and compares the exported 4D scene with hidden ground truth facts in nine dimensions. VLM-based Screen Check asks a VLM judge whether the facts that pass can be recognized in the proxy video. We analyze the evaluation results and trajectories of 11 frontier coding agents and identify three key observations. First, multimodal understanding separates the agents, especially in understanding space and camera motion. Second, all agents seem to already master basic camera work and staging, and fail at challenging requests. Third, agents inspect their own renders but fail to correct their errors. Agents thus need better visual understanding of space and camera, explicit checks for challenging requests, and item-by-item verification of renders against the brief.

AI.tldr: VibePrevisBench is a benchmark for coding agents that reconstruct a 4D scene in Blender from a brief and render a proxy video, scored by a rule-based scene check and a VLM-based screen check over 242 tasks. Evaluation of 11 frontier coding agents finds that they handle basic camera work but fail on challenging requests and do not fix their own render errors.
AI.motivation: Controllable video generation can condition on rendered graybox proxy videos built by coding agents in Blender, but no benchmark checks both the resulting videos and the long, multi-shot scenes behind them.
AI.method: Each of the 242 tasks spans four input kinds: scripts, photos, continuations and reference videos. Rule-based Scene Check re-runs the code and compares the exported 4D scene with hidden ground-truth facts in nine dimensions. VLM-based Screen Check asks a VLM judge whether the facts that pass are recognisable in the proxy video.
AI.result: Across 11 frontier coding agents, multimodal understanding separates the agents, especially for space and camera motion. All agents handle basic camera work and staging but fail on challenging requests. Agents inspect their own renders but do not correct the errors they find.
AI.conclusion: Coding agents need better visual understanding of space and camera, explicit checks for challenging requests, and item-by-item verification of renders against the brief.

title: Fine-Grained Generative Hallucination Detection and Correction for Aerial Image Captioning
summary: Aerial imagery captured by unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) plays a vital role in applications such as surveillance, disaster response, and large-scale environmental monitoring. Automatic generation of textual descriptions for such imagery is essential for reducing manual inspection overhead and enabling better downstream decision-making. However, Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs), despite their impressive captioning capabilities, are prone to hallucination, producing descriptions that are inconsistent with the visual input. This problem is significantly amplified in aerial imagery due to its unique challenges such as extreme viewpoint variation, small objects, class imbalance, and ambiguous visual entities. Existing hallucination detection approaches either rely on computationally expensive large external models such as GPT-4, which perform poorly on aerial domains, or treat the problem as a rigid binary classification task, ignoring the inherent uncertainty in ambiguous cases. To address these limitations, we propose a lightweight, reference-free framework for hallucination detection and correction in free-form aerial image captioning. Our method leverages state-of-the-art MLLMs, specifically InternVL3 and Qwen2.5-VL, to detect hallucinated content in generated captions with minimal computational overhead. Detected hallucinations are corrected through a dedicated refinement module that improves the factual consistency of the original captions. Extensive experiments on the Labelled Illusion Dataset (LID) demonstrate that our framework significantly reduces hallucination rates while remaining practical for real-time deployment in resource-constrained environments. Code is available at: this https URL.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a lightweight, reference-free framework that uses MLLMs (InternVL3 and Qwen2.5-VL) to detect hallucinated content in free-form aerial image captions and corrects it with a refinement module. It reports significantly reduced hallucination rates on the Labelled Illusion Dataset (LID).
