AI.motivation: MLLMs produce hallucinated captions on aerial imagery because of extreme viewpoints, small objects, class imbalance and ambiguous entities. Existing detectors either depend on expensive large external models such as GPT-4, which perform poorly on aerial domains, or use rigid binary classification that ignores uncertainty.
AI.method: The framework uses state-of-the-art MLLMs, InternVL3 and Qwen2.5-VL, to detect hallucinated content in generated captions with minimal overhead. A dedicated refinement module then corrects the detected hallucinations to improve the factual consistency of the original captions.
AI.result: Experiments on the Labelled Illusion Dataset (LID) show that the framework significantly reduces hallucination rates. The abstract states that it remains practical for real-time use in resource-constrained settings.
AI.conclusion: A lightweight MLLM-based detect-and-correct pipeline offers a practical way to reduce hallucinations in aerial image captioning without relying on large external judges.

title: Where to Generate Touch: Do Image Latents Preserve Material Recognition?
summary: Generated touch could extend robot learning beyond recorded contacts. A tactile generator needs a latent space, and we choose one by testing whether a material classifier trained on real GelSight presses still works on encode-decode reconstructions from pretrained image models. On ObjectFolder Real, the classifier loses 6.5 to 9.7 points on reconstructions from three 16x discrete tokenizers and 0.3 points on those from the Stable Diffusion VAE (SD-VAE). The 16x tokenizers again lose far more on Touch and Go and on DIGIT object recognition (YCB-Slide). Retraining the classifier on reconstructions, with no new labels, narrows the discrete gap. SD-VAE reconstructions also keep object identity, with 76.7% object-matching accuracy against 78.9% for real touch and 67.0% for MAGVIT-v2. We therefore select SD-VAE latents and show a photo-to-touch generator trained in them. Code will be released upon acceptance.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether image latent spaces preserve material recognition for generating touch, and finds that the Stable Diffusion VAE keeps tactile material information far better than 16x discrete tokenizers. It selects SD-VAE latents and shows a photo-to-touch generator trained in them.
AI.motivation: Generated touch could extend robot learning beyond recorded contacts, but a tactile generator needs a latent space that keeps the information touch carries. The question is which pretrained image latent space preserves material recognition.
AI.method: A material classifier trained on real GelSight presses is applied to encode-decode reconstructions from pretrained image models. The paper compares three 16x discrete tokenizers with the Stable Diffusion VAE (SD-VAE) and also evaluates Touch and Go, DIGIT object recognition (YCB-Slide), and object-matching accuracy. Retraining the classifier on reconstructions, with no new labels, is also tested.
AI.result: On ObjectFolder Real the classifier loses 6.5 to 9.7 points on reconstructions from the 16x tokenizers but only 0.3 points on SD-VAE reconstructions. The 16x tokenizers also lose much more on Touch and Go and YCB-Slide. Retraining narrows the discrete gap. SD-VAE keeps object identity at 76.7% matching accuracy, against 78.9% for real touch and 67.0% for MAGVIT-v2.
AI.conclusion: SD-VAE latents preserve material and object information for touch, so they are a suitable latent space for photo-to-touch generation; code will be released upon acceptance.

title: Open Vision Banana: A Fully Open Recipe for Generative Visual Perception
summary: Recent work suggests that pretrained image generators encode real-world understanding beyond image synthesis. Vision Banana exploits this by framing vision tasks as conditional image editing. However, its data, weights, code, and implementation details are not public. We present Open Vision Banana (OVB), a fully open and reproducible recipe for converting pretrained generators into unified multi-task perception systems. Our analyses identify the design choices that matter most for generalization, including color encoding, prompt design, parameter adaptation, and task balancing. These choices interact, so individually helpful choices can hurt when combined with others. Starting from 4B and 9B parameter open-weight base models and using 2.1M-3.8M training pairs from public datasets, OVB surpasses Vision Banana's reported Cityscapes zero-shot performance (73.9 vs. 69.9 mIoU) and rivals state-of-the-art affine-invariant depth estimators. Its non-zero-shot variants come within five points of Vision Banana on referring and reasoning segmentation but remain further behind on instance segmentation. All models largely retain the base model's image-editing abilities. With legend ensembling, we introduce a test-time scaling method for generator-based perception. It segments an image under several class-color legends and fuses the results by majority vote, correcting unstable color-class bindings and improving mIoU by up to 8.7 points on Cityscapes and 15.0 points on COCO-Object without retraining. We release the dataset construction and processing pipeline, the training and evaluation code, as well as the final, intermediate, and ablation checkpoints. Project website: this https URL

AI.tldr: Open Vision Banana is a fully open and reproducible recipe for turning pretrained image generators into unified multi-task perception systems, with released data, code and checkpoints. It surpasses Vision Banana's reported Cityscapes zero-shot mIoU and adds a legend-ensembling test-time scaling method.
AI.motivation: Vision Banana shows that pretrained image generators can perform vision tasks as conditional image editing, but its data, weights, code and implementation details are not public.
AI.method: The authors analyse design choices, including colour encoding, prompt design, parameter adaptation and task balancing, which interact with each other. They start from 4B and 9B open-weight base models and train on 2.1M to 3.8M public image pairs. Legend ensembling segments an image under several class-colour legends and fuses the results by majority vote.
AI.result: On Cityscapes zero-shot, OVB reaches 73.9 mIoU against Vision Banana's reported 69.9 and rivals state-of-the-art affine-invariant depth estimators. Non-zero-shot variants are within five points of Vision Banana on referring and reasoning segmentation but trail on instance segmentation. Legend ensembling improves mIoU by up to 8.7 points on Cityscapes and 15.0 points on COCO-Object without retraining.
AI.conclusion: A fully open recipe can match or exceed a closed generator-based perception system, and test-time legend ensembling is a cheap way to improve generator-based perception, with the base models largely retaining their editing ability.

title: Lang-SVG: Hierarchical Image Vectorization with Language Priors
summary: Image vectorization reconstructs raster images as compact scalable vector graph- ics (SVG), providing a structured and editable code representation of images. However, most existing vectorization methods optimize for pixel-level render- ing fidelity, often producing SVGs that lack alignment with human-perceived object-part hierarchies, making them difficult to manipulate. To address this, we propose Lang-SVG, which introduces an explicit tree structure to organize SVG primitives with semantic labels and parent-child relationships. Lang-SVG incorporates granularity-controllable and open-vocabulary segmentation priors to initialize object-part hierarchies and leverages multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with SVG tree context to assign semantic labels to unlabeled nodes. To reduce redundancy, we introduce depth-adaptive simplification to reduce shape complexity and Tree-Guided Pruning and Merging to eliminate redundant SVG nodes. L1-SAM-Prompting further recovers missing regions to improve recon- struction fidelity and structural completeness. Beyond reconstruction fidelity, we introduce a new evaluation protocol that measures structural quality and semantic part alignment. Experiments demonstrate that Lang-SVG achieves state-of-the-art performance in both rendering fidelity and structural quality. Project website: this https URL.

AI.tldr: Lang-SVG is an image vectorisation method that organises SVG primitives into a semantically labelled tree of object parts, using segmentation priors and MLLMs, and reports state-of-the-art rendering fidelity and structural quality. It also introduces an evaluation protocol for structural quality and semantic part alignment.
AI.motivation: Most vectorisation methods optimise pixel-level rendering fidelity, so their SVGs lack alignment with human-perceived object-part hierarchies and are hard to edit.
AI.method: Lang-SVG adds an explicit tree with semantic labels and parent-child relations. It uses granularity-controllable, open-vocabulary segmentation priors to initialise object-part hierarchies, and MLLMs with SVG tree context to label unlabelled nodes. Depth-adaptive simplification, Tree-Guided Pruning and Merging, and L1-SAM-Prompting reduce redundancy and recover missing regions.
AI.result: Lang-SVG achieves state-of-the-art performance in both rendering fidelity and structural quality. The abstract reports no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Organising vectorisation around a semantic object-part tree yields editable SVGs that align with human perception without sacrificing reconstruction fidelity.

title: DuoJEPA: Cross-Modal Translation Between Unaligned Self-Supervised Embedding Spaces
summary: Learning from paired modalities is commonly equated with aligning them: two encoders are trained until the embeddings of a pair coincide in a shared space. We study whether cross-modal retrieval and classification can instead be obtained while the two encoders' own embedding spaces remain directly unaligned. DuoJEPA trains one encoder per modality with the self-supervised LeJEPA objective and appends to each encoder a single transformer layer that translates its embedding into the other encoder's space, supervised by a contrastive objective computed entirely within that target space. No loss term compares the two own spaces directly, although the encoders are optimised jointly through the translation objective. In our experiments, the translator's residual connections determine where the cross-modal pressure is absorbed: with a residual translator the two encoders become directly aligned, whereas with a skipless (residual-free) translator a paired-cosine test detects no alignment in the final models, and at most a weak one in the ablations, at comparable cross-modal performance. The learned class-token translation is well approximated by a single scaled rotation of the source space. We evaluate DuoJEPA on two modality pairs that differ in nearly every respect. On chest radiographs and reports from CheXpert Plus, it attains a zero-shot AUC of 86.6 and a cross-modal retrieval score of 78.5, compared with 60.0 and 64.2 for our reimplementation of LeVLJEPA with the same encoders and data. On Sentinel-2 optical and Sentinel-1 radar imagery, the frozen encoders fall within the range of published Sentinel foundation models under our reproduction of the Copernicus-Bench linear-probe protocol, the translator retrieves the paired image of the other sensor among 4,000 candidates in 77-79% of cases, and a patch-level extension transfers the within-image similarity structure of the scene.

AI.tldr: DuoJEPA trains one LeJEPA encoder per modality, adds a translator layer that maps each embedding into the other encoder's space, and shows that cross-modal retrieval and classification can work without aligning the two encoders' own spaces. The result depends on the translator's residual connections.
AI.motivation: Paired modalities are usually trained to align in a shared space. The question is whether cross-modal retrieval and classification can be achieved while the two encoders' own embedding spaces remain unaligned.
AI.method: Each encoder is trained with the self-supervised LeJEPA objective, and a single transformer layer appended to each encoder translates its embedding into the other encoder's space. The translator is supervised by a contrastive objective computed only within the target space, with no loss directly comparing the two own spaces. Residual and skipless translators are compared.
AI.result: On CheXpert Plus chest radiographs and reports, DuoJEPA reaches zero-shot AUC 86.6 and cross-modal retrieval score 78.5, against 60.0 and 64.2 for the authors' reimplementation of LeVLJEPA. With a residual translator the encoders become directly aligned, while a skipless translator yields no detectable alignment. On Sentinel-2 and Sentinel-1 imagery the translator retrieves the paired image from 4,000 candidates in 77 to 79% of cases.
AI.conclusion: Cross-modal pressure can be absorbed by the translator rather than by the encoders' own spaces, and the translator's residual connections determine whether alignment appears, a useful finding for designing multi-modal self-supervised models.

title: TRACE: Trajectory Synchronization for Training-Free Resolution Extension in Video Generation
summary: More text-to-video models are available, but many remain limited to low resolutions. Training them for higher resolutions is costly, while existing training-free methods still struggle with fine detail, scene structure, and efficiency. We propose TRACE, a training-free method that synchronizes low- and high-resolution generation trajectories. During early denoising, TRACE aligns predicted scene content at corresponding noise levels. It computes high-resolution updates from low-resolution predictions and the current high-resolution state, without high-resolution model inference. The high-resolution trajectory retains fine-grained variation for generating new details. Local window attention then refines fine details in a shared high-resolution latent state. TRACE checks suspected duplicate subjects against the corresponding low-resolution layout and corrects selected regions and their solver history while preserving detail elsewhere. Experiments across all kinds of video generation backbones and resolutions show improved perceptual quality and text-video alignment over FreeSwim, a state-of-the-art training-free method, with 2.0-2.9x end-to-end speedups. Our code and models will be released at this https URL.

AI.tldr: TRACE is a training-free method for extending text-to-video models to higher resolutions by synchronising low- and high-resolution generation trajectories and correcting duplicate subjects. It improves perceptual quality and text-video alignment over FreeSwim with 2.0 to 2.9x end-to-end speedups.
AI.motivation: Many text-to-video models are limited to low resolution. Training for higher resolution is costly, and existing training-free methods struggle with fine detail, scene structure and efficiency.
AI.method: During early denoising, TRACE aligns predicted scene content at corresponding noise levels and computes high-resolution updates from low-resolution predictions and the current high-resolution state, without high-resolution model inference. Local window attention refines details in a shared high-resolution latent. Suspected duplicate subjects are checked against the low-resolution layout and corrected, including their solver history.
AI.result: Across video generation backbones and resolutions, TRACE shows improved perceptual quality and text-video alignment over FreeSwim, a state-of-the-art training-free method, with 2.0 to 2.9x end-to-end speedups.
AI.conclusion: Synchronising low- and high-resolution trajectories gives a faster and better training-free route to high-resolution video generation.

title: Adaptive Distance Detection and Adaptive Instance Segmentation
comment: This is the paper from my Bachelor's degree in University of Birmingham
summary: This paper is about object detection model and semantic segmentation model in an FPS game Counter Strike: Condition Zero to detect enemies. Semantic segmentation is pixel-wise detection algorithm. We customized the architecture for semantic segmentation. We used YOLOv5s to train object detection model. After training, the inference time of semantic segmentation was compared to object detection. It was observed that object detection was slightly faster and semantic segmentation is slower but better at detecting the exact shape of the object. However, we found out that this slight difference of inference can grow exponentially if the both models get more complex. To solve this, we propose a novel approach called Adaptive distance detection which combines both algorithms. We will also introduce Adaptive instance segmentation to combine semantic segmentation and panoptic segmentation.

AI.tldr: The paper applies object detection (YOLOv5s) and semantic segmentation to enemy detection in the FPS game Counter-Strike: Condition Zero, and proposes Adaptive Distance Detection, which combines the two methods. It also introduces Adaptive Instance Segmentation, which combines semantic and panoptic segmentation.
AI.motivation: Semantic segmentation gives exact object shapes but is slower than object detection. The authors observe that this speed gap may grow with model complexity.
AI.method: The authors customise a semantic segmentation architecture and train a YOLOv5s detector, then compare their inference times. They propose Adaptive Distance Detection, which combines the two algorithms, and Adaptive Instance Segmentation, which combines semantic and panoptic segmentation.
AI.result: Object detection is slightly faster, while semantic segmentation is slower but better at detecting exact object shapes. The abstract gives no quantitative results for the proposed combinations.
AI.conclusion: The authors suggest that combining detection and segmentation can address the speed-versus-shape trade-off, but the abstract provides no evidence for this beyond the initial timing comparison.

title: Predicting the Needle in a Petabyte Scale Haystack: Open-Vocabulary Event Anticipation in Satellite Imagery
comment: 29 pages, 9 figures, to be published in NeurIPS 2026
summary: Satellite constellations now image the Earth daily, capturing the lifecycle of events from deforestation to urban construction. Anticipating these events before completion enables timely intervention, yet existing systems cannot jointly identify where a change occurs, what it will become, and when it will finish across an open vocabulary. Building such a model requires diverse event data, but events are like needles in a haystack, making manual annotation at global scale infeasible. We address this problem by representing change as the vector difference between vision-language model embeddings at distinct time points. This arithmetic approach allows us to search for semantic transformations directly in the latent space, enabling (1) an automated data engine for global event discovery without manual annotation and (2) the largest global satellite event dataset to our knowledge, comprising 21,000+ locations across 64+ event types with ~2M images from PlanetScope and Sentinel-2 spanning six continents, to train (3) a novel global-scale event anticipation model. Our model detects change with a 93.5% max F1 score, outperforms baselines 3.6x on predicted event retrieval, and forecasts completion dates with a 3-day median error, even nine months before completion. Code: this https URL

AI.tldr: This paper proposes open-vocabulary event anticipation in satellite imagery, using vision-language embedding differences to find change events automatically. It builds a dataset of 21,000+ locations and about 2M images across 64+ event types and trains a model that forecasts event completion dates.
AI.motivation: Anticipating events from satellite imagery enables timely intervention, but existing systems cannot jointly identify where a change occurs, what it will become and when it will finish across an open vocabulary. Manual annotation of rare events at global scale is infeasible.
AI.method: Change is represented as the vector difference between vision-language model embeddings at two time points, allowing semantic transformations to be searched directly in latent space. This drives an automated data engine for event discovery and builds a global dataset from PlanetScope and Sentinel-2 imagery. A global event anticipation model is trained on this data.
AI.result: The model detects change with a 93.5% max F1 score, outperforms baselines 3.6x on predicted event retrieval, and forecasts completion dates with a 3-day median error, even nine months before completion.
AI.conclusion: Embedding arithmetic offers an annotation-free route to a large, diverse satellite event dataset and a model that anticipates when events will finish.

title: Iris-Z: Scaling One Generative Model Past Specialist Geometry Models
comment: 14 pages, 9 figures, 6 tables. Code and models: this https URL
summary: Language moved from many task-specific models to one unified model: a single generative model with a single generative training task that handles all of them within the same backbone, and keeps improving with data, parameters and compute. We believe the bitter lesson applies just as much to computer vision, 3D and spatial understanding, in the end to visual intelligence: the effort should go into general architectures that solve all these tasks in a unified way, and into scaling them, rather than into task-specific designs. We test this on monocular geometry, a task that has belonged to specialised architectures for years. Iris-Z is a general image generator that produces appearance and geometry together. A single backbone denoises, reasons about and understands the image and its depth at the same time, and one set of weights generates images with their depth, estimates depth from photographs and paints images onto a given depth. At enough scale it surpasses state-of-the-art specialists on established depth benchmarks while keeping the generative abilities of the backbone it started from without specialized layers. We release two models for the community.

AI.tldr: Iris-Z is a single general image generator that produces appearance and geometry together, and at sufficient scale it surpasses specialist models on established monocular depth benchmarks while keeping its generative abilities. Two models are released to the community.
AI.motivation: Language moved from many task-specific models to one unified generative model that scales. The authors test whether monocular geometry, which has long relied on specialised architectures, can be handled the same way.
AI.method: A single backbone denoises, reasons about and understands an image and its depth together. One set of weights generates images with their depth, estimates depth from photographs and paints images onto a given depth. No specialised layers are added to the backbone the model starts from.
AI.result: At enough scale Iris-Z surpasses state-of-the-art specialist models on established depth benchmarks. The abstract does not give specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: A general generative architecture scaled up can replace task-specific geometry models while keeping its generative ability, supporting a bitter-lesson view of computer vision.

title: Topology-Aware 4D Gaussian Splatting for Egocentric Videos
summary: Reconstructing dynamic scenes and objects from monocular egocentric video is crucial for embodied AI, yet existing 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) approaches struggle with everyday interactions involving topological changes, such as cutting, assembly, opening, or closing. Since 4DGS methods rely on deforming a fixed representation, events that split, merge, or reveal surfaces cause severe visual artifacts. To address this challenge, we introduce TopoEgo, the first benchmark dedicated to topological changes in egocentric video (covering fission, fusion, open, and close), alongside Topo-4DGS, a topology-aware reconstruction method. Topo4DGS jointly models part-level motion and time-varying surface support by assigning independent rigid transformations to interacting parts and dynamically activating or deactivating Gaussians as surfaces appear, disappear, or separate. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Topo-4DGS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art 4DGS approaches across topological changes, especially on post-event frames. Code and data will be made publicly available.

AI.tldr: TopoEgo is a benchmark for topological changes in monocular egocentric video, such as fission, fusion, opening and closing, and Topo-4DGS is a topology-aware 4D Gaussian Splatting method that handles them. It significantly outperforms state-of-the-art 4DGS approaches, especially on post-event frames.
AI.motivation: Existing 4DGS methods deform a fixed representation, so everyday events that split, merge or reveal surfaces, such as cutting or opening, cause severe visual artefacts.
AI.method: Topo-4DGS jointly models part-level motion and time-varying surface support. It assigns independent rigid transformations to interacting parts and dynamically activates or deactivates Gaussians as surfaces appear, disappear or separate.
AI.result: Topo-4DGS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art 4DGS approaches across topological changes, with the largest gains on post-event frames. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Modelling topology changes explicitly is needed for faithful dynamic reconstruction of egocentric interactions, and code and data will be made public.

title: Sub-actions in Action: Text-Guided Hand-Role Alignment for Sub-Action Recognition
comment: Accepted at BMVC 2026, Supplementary material is available
summary: Our objective is to enhance VLMs ability to distinguish the roles of the left and right hands in egocentric actions. We introduce sub-action detection, a task that requires models to explicitly recognise the left- and right-hand roles and their manipulated objects within an ongoing high-level action. To address this challenge, we propose BiScopeNet, a framework that augments existing video-LLMs without modifying their vision encoders or language models. BiScopeNet incorporates two components: FocusAlign, a gated text-guided attention-based module that selectively aligns video features with textual context to emphasise action-relevant cues, and MetaLoss, a masked, object-weighted loss that prioritises visually grounded terms. To supervise sub-action detection, we introduce BiScopeCap-100K, a large-scale video-level dataset curated from existing egocentric datasets, providing dense captions that jointly describe high-level actions, left/right-hand roles, and manipulated objects, enriched with spatial metadata for grounding. Across the evaluated Video-LLM backbones, BiScopeNet improves action, hand-role, and object recognition over the corresponding supervised baselines, achieving the strongest aggregate performance among the evaluated configurations on BiScopeCap.

AI.tldr: BiScopeNet augments existing video-LLMs without changing their vision encoders or language models, to recognise the left and right hand roles and the manipulated objects in egocentric actions. It is trained on BiScopeCap-100K and achieves the strongest aggregate performance among the evaluated configurations on BiScopeCap.
AI.motivation: VLMs struggle to distinguish the roles of the left and right hands in egocentric actions, and existing benchmarks do not supervise sub-action detection at this level.
AI.method: BiScopeNet has two components: FocusAlign, a gated text-guided attention module that aligns video features with textual context, and MetaLoss, a masked, object-weighted loss that prioritises visually grounded terms. The supporting dataset, BiScopeCap-100K, is a video-level set curated from existing egocentric datasets, with dense captions and spatial metadata.
AI.result: Across the evaluated Video-LLM backbones, BiScopeNet improves action, hand-role and object recognition over the corresponding supervised baselines. It achieves the strongest aggregate performance among the evaluated configurations on BiScopeCap. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Text-guided alignment and object-weighted losses can add fine-grained hand-role understanding to existing video-LLMs without retraining their core components.

title: Pothole Risk Assessment with Geometrically Grounded Vision Language Models
comment: 22 pages, 8 figures, 17 tables. Submitted to IEEE Access. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Potholes impose billions of dollars in annual vehicle damage, yet detectors report only where potholes are, not how severe they are or what to do. Judging severity from a single RGB image is ill-posed, and ungrounded vision-language model (VLM) assessments tend to be over-conservative. We present a five-stage modular framework for the offline assessment of already-detected potholes that combines geometric measurements with VLM reasoning: perspective transformation, zero-shot SAM segmentation, geometric feature extraction, Gemini 2.5 Pro severity classification with composite risk scoring, and natural-language warning generation. We evaluate it on 3,092 potholes in 1,119 dashcam scenes against independent references. Severity agreement with a prediction-free three-annotator panel is weak (Cohen's $\kappa = 0.139$, 95% CI [0.00, 0.28]; $n = 101$) and far below the annotators' agreement with one another ($\kappa = 0.605$); against physically measured depth on an independent RGB-D dataset, it is also weak ($\kappa = 0.098$), although the predicted classes preserve the order of measured depths. The severity classes are therefore perceived visual categories, not depth measurements. Geometric grounding does change the warnings: relative to an image-only baseline, it moves 26.7% of scenes out of the high-urgency tier and raises critical-tier assignments by 109% (Stuart-Maxwell $p < 10^{-15}$), and in a blind study, three raters preferred the grounded warnings 3.5:1. A six-arm prompt ablation attributes the hybrid prompt's rule adherence to the per-pothole measurements rather than to the rubric or worked examples. At USD 0.105 per scene, it suits large-scale offline infrastructure assessment; its maneuver suggestions are advisory research outputs, not validated vehicle guidance.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a five-stage modular framework that combines geometric measurements with Gemini 2.5 Pro reasoning to assess the severity of already detected potholes and generate warnings. Severity agreement with human annotators is weak, but geometric grounding changes the warnings and is preferred in a blind study.
AI.motivation: Pothole detectors report where potholes are but not how severe they are or what to do. Judging severity from one RGB image is ill-posed, and ungrounded VLM assessments tend to be over-conservative.
AI.method: The pipeline applies perspective transformation, zero-shot SAM segmentation, geometric feature extraction, Gemini 2.5 Pro severity classification with composite risk scoring, and natural-language warning generation. A six-arm prompt ablation tests the hybrid prompt against rubric and worked-example variants.
AI.result: On 3,092 potholes in 1,119 dashcam scenes, agreement with a three-annotator panel is weak (Cohen's kappa 0.139) and far below inter-annotator agreement (0.605). Agreement with measured depth on an RGB-D dataset is also weak (kappa 0.098), though the classes preserve depth order. Relative to an image-only baseline, geometric grounding moves 26.7% of scenes out of the high-urgency tier and raises critical-tier assignments by 109%. Raters preferred the grounded warnings 3.5:1. The cost is USD 0.105 per scene.
AI.conclusion: Severity classes are perceived visual categories rather than depth measurements, but geometric grounding changes the warnings in a preferred way, making the framework suitable for offline assessment, with its manoeuvre suggestions remaining advisory research outputs.

title: Split-and-scale Latent 3D Representations
summary: Latent 3D representations have significantly expanded the capabilities of modern shape modeling, enabling compact encoding of 3D scenes and supporting powerful 3D generative models. Despite this progress, current representations struggle to capture the fine details of complex objects, fundamentally limited by the capacity of their latents. However, scaling latent capacity at training time is computationally expensive and often infeasible under memory limits, and naively increasing the number of latents at inference fails to make effective use of the added capacity. In this paper, we address both challenges with \textit{split-and-scale}, a method that effectively expands latent capacity at inference while keeping training cost tractable. Our key observation is that by representing 3D scenes as continuous functions of 3D coordinates, a single pretrained tokenizer can be applied at inference to arbitrarily small sub-regions of a scene, allocating the same latent capacity to a smaller spatial extent and thus capturing far higher detail. We validate this insight by conducting extensive ablations to study the trade-offs between compute, memory, latent capacity, and reconstruction quality, demonstrating our inference-time scaling method achieves quality competitive with much larger models that exceed single-GPU memory limits. We further demonstrate that split-and-scale supports high-quality generative modeling, training an autoregressive 3D generator that performs competitively with state-of-the-art baselines.

AI.tldr: Split-and-scale expands the latent capacity of a pretrained 3D tokenizer at inference by applying it to small sub-regions of a scene, while keeping training cost tractable. It reaches quality competitive with much larger models that exceed single-GPU memory and supports a competitive autoregressive 3D generator.
AI.motivation: Latent 3D representations struggle to capture the fine details of complex objects because their latent capacity is limited. Scaling latent capacity during training is expensive, and naively adding latents at inference does not use the added capacity effectively.
AI.method: Representing 3D scenes as continuous functions of 3D coordinates lets one pretrained tokenizer be applied to arbitrarily small sub-regions at inference. The same latent capacity then covers a smaller spatial extent, which captures higher detail. Ablations study the trade-offs between compute, memory, latent capacity and reconstruction quality.
AI.result: The inference-time scaling method achieves quality competitive with much larger models that exceed single-GPU memory limits. An autoregressive 3D generator trained with split-and-scale performs competitively with state-of-the-art baselines. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Spatial splitting at inference is an effective way to add detail to latent 3D representations without costly retraining, and it also supports high-quality generative modelling.

title: GOOSELoc: A Multimodal Benchmark for Ground-to-Aerial Localization in Unstructured Off-Road Terrain
summary: Cross-view pose estimation estimates a ground camera's geographic pose by matching onboard sensor data with geo-referenced overhead imagery. This is particularly relevant when GNSS is unreliable, for example under forest canopy or in urban canyons. Existing metric cross-view benchmarks, such as VIGOR and cross-view KITTI, are dominated by urban and road scenes with strong human-made structure without off-road terrain. We introduce GOOSELoc, a multimodal benchmark for ground-to-aerial localization in unstructured environments, including forests, fields, and rural tracks. GOOSELoc comprises 9,356 scenes recorded across all four seasons around Munich, Germany, pairing geo-referenced aerial orthophotos with surround-view RGB imagery and 3D LiDAR point clouds. Paved/unpaved labels enable analyzing the impact of terrain structure, while the seasonal recordings allow studying the appearance gap to mostly summer-captured orthophotos. To assess the transferability of existing methods, we adapt and fine-tune four state-of-the-art cross-view localization baselines on GOOSELoc. Despite task-specific fine-tuning, the performance degrades substantially in off-road environments. We therefore propose a multimodal baseline combining surround-view imagery and LiDAR geometry, improving localization performance and providing a stronger reference for future work. Data and baselines are released at this https URL.

AI.tldr: GOOSELoc is a multimodal benchmark for ground-to-aerial localisation in unstructured off-road terrain, with 9,356 scenes across four seasons pairing aerial orthophotos with surround-view RGB and LiDAR. Four existing cross-view baselines degrade substantially off-road, and a multimodal baseline combining imagery and LiDAR improves localisation.
AI.motivation: Existing cross-view benchmarks such as VIGOR and cross-view KITTI are dominated by urban and road scenes, which leaves off-road terrain unmeasured, although GNSS is unreliable under forest canopy or in urban canyons.
AI.method: The authors collect 9,356 scenes around Munich across all four seasons. Each scene pairs geo-referenced aerial orthophotos with surround-view RGB imagery and 3D LiDAR point clouds, with paved and unpaved labels. Four state-of-the-art cross-view localisation baselines are fine-tuned on GOOSELoc, and a multimodal baseline combines surround-view imagery with LiDAR geometry.
AI.result: Despite fine-tuning, the four baselines' performance degrades substantially in off-road environments. The proposed multimodal baseline improves localisation performance. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Off-road cross-view localisation is markedly harder than urban localisation, and the released data and multimodal baseline provide a stronger reference for future work.

title: SPEM: Scan-Prior Entropy Modeling for LiDAR Point Cloud Compression
summary: LiDAR point clouds exhibit scan-induced spatial regularities that are informative for geometry compression. Existing scan-aware approaches often exploit these regularities by transforming coded geometry into spherical or beam-aligned coordinate systems. However, this couples acquisition priors with geometry representation, altering spatial partitioning and quantization, and potentially preventing exact recovery of the original Cartesian geometry. We argue that acquisition priors should guide probability modeling rather than dictate the coding representation. We propose SPEM, a Scan-Prior Entropy Modeling framework that exploits LiDAR scanning regularities within the entropy model without requiring coordinate transformation. We introduce a multi-frequency spherical rotary positional encoding that captures scan-aligned spatial relationships in both backbone self-attention and decoded-context retrieval. Building upon this encoding, we develop a decoded-memory autoregressive predictor that efficiently exploits previously decoded occupancy information through reusable key/value caches. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in both lossy and lossless LiDAR geometry compression, highlighting the effectiveness of scan-prior modeling across different coordinate representations.

AI.tldr: SPEM is a scan-prior entropy modelling framework for LiDAR geometry compression that exploits scan regularities inside the entropy model without transforming coordinates. It reports state-of-the-art lossy and lossless compression across different coordinate representations.
AI.motivation: Existing scan-aware codecs convert geometry into spherical or beam-aligned coordinates, which changes spatial partitioning and quantisation and can prevent exact recovery of the original Cartesian geometry. The authors argue that acquisition priors should guide probability modelling rather than the coding representation.
AI.method: SPEM introduces multi-frequency spherical rotary positional encoding that captures scan-aligned relations in backbone self-attention and decoded-context retrieval. A decoded-memory autoregressive predictor reuses key and value caches to exploit previously decoded occupancy.
AI.result: The method achieves state-of-the-art performance in both lossy and lossless LiDAR geometry compression. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Scan priors are most useful when they guide the entropy model rather than the coordinate representation, which keeps exact Cartesian recovery possible.

title: WorldDraft: If Code Builds the World, Can Video Models Just Render It?
summary: Multimodal coding agents decouple 4D world construction from visual generation, repurposing video models from world generators toward generative renderers. This division of labor raises a fundamental question: if code builds the world, can video models just render it? A reliable generative renderer hinges on two complementary criteria: (i) world preservation, retaining prescribed 4D kinematics and camera paths; and (ii) visual realization, persistently binding text-specified target attributes over time. To evaluate this capability, we introduce WorldDraft, a benchmark of $432$ strictly paired test cases across $48$ executable 4D world families spanning six dynamic challenge categories. Under a $3 \times 3$ factorial design, WorldDraft orthogonally crosses draft granularity (abstract proxy to previs) and appearance alignment (neutral to conflicting) under identical dynamics. Extensive evaluations across $12$ representative models reveal that: (I) world preservation and visual realization remain in stark operational tension; (II) richer draft scaffolding anchors structure but paradoxically impairs appearance fidelity; and (III) conflicting source cues trigger severe source leakage (up to $64\%$), exposing fragile cross-modal disentanglement. To mitigate these bottlenecks, we propose WorldDraft-Primer, a plug-and-play visual prompting strategy that consistently improves both objectives across frozen video renderers. Together, WorldDraft and WorldDraft-Primer lay a foundation for bridging programmatic 4D simulation with video generation, advancing physically grounded generative rendering.

AI.tldr: WorldDraft is a benchmark of 432 paired test cases for testing whether video models can render 4D worlds built by code, and WorldDraft-Primer is a plug-and-play visual prompting strategy. It finds a tension between preserving world dynamics and realising target appearance, along with source leakage under conflicting cues.
AI.motivation: Multimodal coding agents build 4D worlds in code and video models are asked to render them. A reliable generative renderer needs both world preservation and visual realisation, and the question of whether video models can just render code-built worlds has not been measured.
AI.method: The benchmark has 432 strictly paired cases across 48 executable 4D world families in six dynamic challenge categories, in a 3 by 3 factorial design that crosses draft granularity (abstract proxy to previs) with appearance alignment (neutral to conflicting). Twelve representative models are evaluated. WorldDraft-Primer is a visual prompting strategy for frozen video renderers.
AI.result: World preservation and visual realisation remain in stark tension. Richer draft scaffolding anchors structure but impairs appearance fidelity. Conflicting source cues cause source leakage of up to 64%. WorldDraft-Primer consistently improves both objectives across frozen video renderers.
AI.conclusion: Bridging programmatic 4D simulation with video generation needs better cross-modal disentanglement, and the benchmark and primer lay a foundation for physically grounded generative rendering.

title: Disentangled Embedding Optimization for Diffusion-Based Dataset Distillation
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures. Accepted at the 34th ACM International Conference on Multimedia (ACM MM 2026)
summary: Dataset distillation aims to compress large-scale datasets into compact synthetic subsets that enable efficient model training with comparable performance to the original data. Recent advances show that diffusion models are highly effective for this task due to their strong generative capability. Existing diffusion-based approaches typically perform class-wise clustering and use the obtained cluster prototypes as diffusion inputs to generate distilled samples. However, the uniformly distributed original samples in a category inevitably lead to entanglement near cluster boundaries, pulling the cluster prototypes closer and reducing the inter-cluster separation. Consequently, the diffusion model receives overly similar latent inputs, resulting in synthetic data with limited diversity. To address this issue, we propose Disentangled Embedding Optimization (DEO), a simple yet effective framework that replaces static clustering with trainable embeddings. These embeddings are optimized to match the Gaussian statistics (i.e., mean and covariance) of the original data distribution, while a diversity regularizer is designed to encourage separation among these embeddings to improve the intra-class variability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our proposed DEO can generate more diversified and representative distilled data than existing cluster-based diffusion methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance and superior generalization across multiple datasets.

AI.tldr: DEO replaces static clustering in diffusion-based dataset distillation with trainable embeddings that match the Gaussian statistics of the original data, with a diversity regulariser that separates them. It reports more diverse distilled data and state-of-the-art performance over cluster-based diffusion methods.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion-based dataset distillation clusters each class and uses the prototypes as diffusion inputs. Samples near cluster boundaries entangle, pulling prototypes together, so the diffusion model receives overly similar latents and produces synthetic data with limited diversity.
AI.method: Disentangled Embedding Optimization (DEO) replaces static clustering with trainable embeddings. They are optimised to match the mean and covariance of the original data distribution, and a diversity regulariser encourages separation among them to improve intra-class variability.
AI.result: DEO generates more diversified and representative distilled data than existing cluster-based diffusion methods and achieves state-of-the-art performance and better generalisation across multiple datasets. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Trainable, separated embeddings fitted to the data's Gaussian statistics improve the diversity of diffusion-based distilled datasets.

title: ATune: Unsupervised Photo Retouching Through Image-Editor Controls
comment: 27 pages, 12 figures, 18 tables. Main paper 8 pages plus supplementary material
summary: Photo retouching models are trained on pairs of original and retouched photographs, usually edited by experts. Expert edits are costly, so the two main public sets, FiveK and PPR10K, hold only 16,161 originals. Good photographs on their own are far easier to find: commercial stock collections and free ones such as Pixabay and Unsplash hold millions. We learn retouching from them alone: we damage each photograph the way a camera or a careless edit would, which gives a worse and a better version of the same photograph. From these pairs, our model, ATune, learns how 13 measured attributes, such as brightness, contrast and sharpness, should change to raise a photograph's quality. The edit is declarative: ATune sets target values for the attributes, and a simple search adjusts the sliders of an out-of-the-box photo editor until the photograph reaches them. Every edit is a list of slider values a person can read and adjust. The same model can drive any editor that makes those changes; we test RawTherapee and darktable. We train on 10M photographs from a commercial stock collection and test on FiveK, PPR10K and SPAQ. Nine quality judges score every edit, and in a user study 157 human raters made 9,253 choices between our edit and another method's edit of the same photograph. When Claude Opus 5 and GPT-6 Astra edit the same photographs in the same editor, raters prefer our edits to GPT-6 Astra's (54.3%) and rate them even with Claude's (50.5%). We also compare with supervised retouchers on their home ground: NeurOP on FiveK and AdaInt on PPR10K, each trained on that set's own expert edits. Raters chose our edits in 46.3% of those comparisons. ATune, a 54M-parameter model trained without a single expert edit, now matches frontier models at setting an editor's sliders.

AI.tldr: ATune learns photo retouching without expert edits, from pairs of damaged and better versions of stock photos, and predicts target values for 13 attributes that a search maps to editor slider settings. It matches frontier models at setting an editor's sliders and is trained on 10M photographs.
AI.motivation: Retouching models need pairs of original and expert-retouched photos, but the main public sets hold only 16,161 originals. Millions of good photographs are available without expert edits.
AI.method: The authors damage each photograph in the way a camera or careless edit would, producing a worse and a better version. ATune learns how 13 measured attributes, such as brightness, contrast and sharpness, should change to raise quality. A simple search adjusts the sliders of an out-of-the-box editor, RawTherapee or darktable, until the targets are reached.
AI.result: Trained on 10M photographs and tested on FiveK, PPR10K and SPAQ, ATune is judged by nine quality judges and 157 raters who made 9,253 choices. Raters preferred its edits to GPT-6 Astra's (54.3%) and rated them even with Claude Opus 5's (50.5%). Against supervised retouchers NeurOP on FiveK and AdaInt on PPR10K, raters chose ATune in 46.3% of comparisons. The model has 54M parameters.
AI.conclusion: Declarative, readable slider edits learned without expert data can match frontier models at setting editor controls and come close to supervised retouchers on their own datasets.

title: Reconstruct What You Can: Distractor-free 4D Gaussian Splatting
summary: Dynamic reconstruction from casual video must preserve valid subject motion while suppressing transient occluders, shadows, and volumetric effects. Existing methods either suppress valid motion through static-scene assumptions or model all observations jointly, producing ghosting and unstable geometry. We introduce ReCan-GS, a 4D Gaussian Splatting framework that separates coherent scene content from inconsistent observations. It derives a Jacobian-based deformation-sensitivity score from the learned deformation field, using it as an empirical proxy for reconstruction ambiguity. The score guides separation into dynamic Core Gaussians and per-view Distractor Gaussians, or post-hoc pruning of sensitive Core Gaussians. The same criterion supports removal of spatial occluders, photometric artifacts, and evolving smoke or fog without masks, pretrained segmenters, or medium-specific supervision. Experiments on synthetic and real dynamic scenes and synthetic smoke/fog scenes demonstrate its usefulness across the evaluated distractor regimes.

AI.tldr: ReCan-GS is a 4D Gaussian Splatting framework that separates coherent scene content from transient distractors such as occluders, shadows, smoke and fog in casual video, without masks or segmenters. It uses a Jacobian-based deformation-sensitivity score to split Gaussians into dynamic Core and per-view Distractor sets.
AI.motivation: Dynamic reconstruction from casual video must keep valid subject motion while suppressing transient occluders, shadows and volumetric effects. Existing methods either suppress valid motion through static-scene assumptions or model all observations jointly, which causes ghosting and unstable geometry.
AI.method: A Jacobian-based deformation-sensitivity score computed from the learned deformation field serves as a proxy for reconstruction ambiguity. The score separates Gaussians into dynamic Core Gaussians and per-view Distractor Gaussians, or prunes sensitive Core Gaussians after the fact.
AI.result: The method is evaluated on synthetic and real dynamic scenes and on synthetic smoke and fog scenes, and the abstract reports its usefulness across the evaluated distractor regimes. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: A deformation-sensitivity criterion can remove spatial occluders, photometric artefacts and evolving smoke or fog without masks or medium-specific supervision.

title: FlowIR: Depth-driven Rectified Flow for Resolving Thermal Ambiguity in Infrared Super-Resolution
comment: Accepted to the 2026 IEEE International Conference on Multimedia & Expo (ICME 2026)
summary: Distinguishing different heat sources in low-resolution infrared (IR) images is inherently difficult, as multiple thermal emitters often collapse into ambiguous and overlapping responses. Existing super-resolution methods hallucinate structures from such ambiguous 2D evidence, leading to thermal drift, boundary merging, and unreliable restoration under infrared degradations. We propose FlowIR, a depth-driven rectified flow framework that resolves thermal ambiguity by injecting 3D geometric cues into the generation process. Pseudo-3D depth lifting and depth-guided 3D convolutions disentangle overlapping foreground objects, while cluster-wise inter-attention suppresses cross-source feature contamination. A Thermal-Geometry Consistency Loss further enforces geometric alignment during refinement. Built upon a lightweight rectified flow backbone, FlowIR restores IR images in only a few steps, producing sharply separated, degradation-robust, and geometrically faithful high-resolution results.

AI.tldr: FlowIR is a depth-driven rectified flow framework for infrared super-resolution that injects 3D geometric cues to separate overlapping heat sources. It restores images in a few steps and reports sharply separated, degradation-robust and geometrically faithful results.
AI.motivation: Multiple thermal emitters in low-resolution infrared images collapse into ambiguous, overlapping responses, and existing super-resolution methods hallucinate structure from this 2D evidence, causing thermal drift, boundary merging and unreliable restoration.
AI.method: Pseudo-3D depth lifting and depth-guided 3D convolutions disentangle overlapping foreground objects. Cluster-wise inter-attention suppresses cross-source feature contamination. A Thermal-Geometry Consistency Loss enforces geometric alignment during refinement. The model is built on a lightweight rectified flow backbone.
AI.result: FlowIR restores infrared images in only a few steps, producing sharply separated, degradation-robust and geometrically faithful high-resolution outputs. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Depth-driven geometric cues help resolve thermal ambiguity in infrared super-resolution while keeping inference efficient.

title: DEDCA: Test-Time Adaptation for Generalized AI-Generated Image Detection
summary: AI-generated image detectors face significant challenges when deployed in real-world environments, particularly when test samples are produced by unseen generators that deviate from the source training distribution. Existing detectors often rely on a single type of evidence, such as semantic representations or low-level generation traces, making them vulnerable when the corresponding cue becomes unreliable. Moreover, adapting detectors to newly emerging generators usually requires target labels or retraining, which is costly and impractical. To address these challenges, we propose Dual-Evidence Disagreement-Constrained Adaptation (DEDCA), a test-time adaptation framework for generalized AI-generated image detection. DEDCA constructs a dual-evidence detector by combining CLIP-based semantic evidence with trace evidence extracted from shuffled entropy and residual statistics, and introduces a reliability-aware gate to perform sample-specific adaptive fusion. Our key idea is to exploit the disagreement between the two evidence streams as an unlabeled adaptation signal, enabling the detector to adjust to target-domain shifts without relying on target labels or blindly trusting a single prediction stream. Experiments show that DEDCA achieves superior performance on the GenImage benchmark by outperforming state-of-the-art AI-generated image detectors and test-time adaptation methods with 92.0\% average accuracy.

AI.tldr: DEDCA is a test-time adaptation framework for AI-generated image detection that combines CLIP semantic evidence with trace evidence from shuffled entropy and residual statistics, and uses their disagreement as an unlabelled adaptation signal. It reports 92.0% average accuracy on GenImage.
AI.motivation: Detectors trained on one generator's distribution fail on unseen generators, and existing detectors rely on a single type of evidence. Adapting to new generators usually requires target labels or retraining.
AI.method: DEDCA builds a dual-evidence detector from CLIP-based semantic features and trace features from shuffled entropy and residual statistics. A reliability-aware gate performs sample-specific adaptive fusion. The disagreement between the two evidence streams is used as an unlabelled adaptation signal at test time.
AI.result: On the GenImage benchmark DEDCA achieves 92.0% average accuracy and outperforms state-of-the-art AI-generated image detectors and test-time adaptation methods.
AI.conclusion: Using disagreement between semantic and trace evidence as an unlabelled signal lets a detector adapt to new generators without target labels or blind trust in one stream.

title: Selective Generative Restoration for Video Deraining via Uncertainty-Aware Diffusion
summary: Video deraining is challenging due to rain streaks, occlusions, and atmospheric effects. Existing methods mainly follow a deterministic restoration paradigm, assuming that clean scenes can be uniquely recovered from rainy observations. However, rain degradation is spatially heterogeneous. Reliable regions require faithful reconstruction, whereas severely occluded regions contain ambiguous content that require stronger prior-driven inference. Therefore, conventional deterministic restoration often produces over-smoothed results, while global generative restoration may introduce unnecessary hallucinations. We introduce a Selective Generative Restoration paradigm for video deraining, where generative priors are adaptively activated according to restoration uncertainty. Based on this principle, we propose Selective Generative Video Deraining (SGVD), an uncertainty-aware diffusion framework that enables adaptive fidelity preservation and generative recovery. Specifically, SGVD exploits stochastic diversity between dual one-step diffusion predictions to estimate region-level restoration uncertainty, which determines where observation fidelity should be preserved and where generative inference should be activated. Furthermore, an anchor-guided trajectory consistency mechanism is proposed to regularize stochastic diffusion evolution across frames, reducing temporal generation drift and improving video coherence. To achieve practical efficiency, SGVD adopts one-step diffusion inference while maintaining uncertainty-aware generative capability. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SGVD achieves superior restoration performance, perceptual quality, and temporal consistency compared with state-of-the-art video deraining methods.

AI.tldr: SGVD is an uncertainty-aware diffusion framework for video deraining that activates generative priors only in regions where restoration is uncertain, and uses one-step diffusion inference with anchor-guided trajectory consistency. It reports superior restoration, perceptual quality and temporal consistency.
AI.motivation: Deterministic deraining over-smooths results, while global generative restoration introduces unnecessary hallucinations, because rain degradation is spatially heterogeneous.
AI.method: SGVD exploits stochastic diversity between two one-step diffusion predictions to estimate region-level restoration uncertainty. This decides where observation fidelity is kept and where generative inference is applied. An anchor-guided trajectory consistency mechanism regularises the diffusion evolution across frames to reduce temporal drift.
AI.result: Compared with state-of-the-art video deraining methods, SGVD achieves superior restoration performance, perceptual quality and temporal consistency. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Selectively activating generative restoration according to uncertainty balances fidelity and realism, and one-step inference keeps the approach efficient.

title: Hand in Silhouette: Synthetic-to-Real Multi-View Hand Reconstruction via Binary Masks
summary: Calibrated multi-view hand reconstruction has advanced rapidly, yet the effectiveness of existing methods depends strongly on real captured data, which is costly to acquire, limited in hand-geometry diversity, and often affected by imperfect annotations. Synthetic data offers a scalable alternative with accurate supervision, but a substantial synthetic-to-real appearance gap hinders its use. To address this, we introduce Hand in Silhouette (SilHand), a calibrated multi-view hand reconstruction framework that operates on binary hand masks, obtainable at low cost either automatically or manually, to reduce the synthetic-to-real observation gap. Rather than relying on RGB features for 3D lifting, SilHand projects metric 3D hypotheses into each view to query and fuse mask-ray evidence for hand reconstruction. This mask-centric formulation enables training on a large-scale synthetic dataset comprising 46.8k grasping poses and 60k free-hand samples, providing broad coverage of hand geometry while directly transferring to real captured hand geometry. Across five real-world benchmarks, SilHand improves relative reconstruction accuracy from 49.2% to 63.4% using masks rendered from reference hands. Moreover, reconstruction accuracy improves consistently as the synthetic training set grows, indicating that broader geometric coverage translates into better real-world performance. While achieving such diversity is difficult with real captured data, it becomes practical under our mask-centric formulation. Finally, SilHand remains robust under mask corruption, with reconstruction error increasing by at most 1.63 mm. Together, these results support binary masks as an effective interface for learning hand reconstruction from synthetic geometry.

AI.tldr: SilHand is a calibrated multi-view hand reconstruction framework that operates on binary hand masks instead of RGB, so it can train on a large synthetic dataset and transfer to real hands. It improves relative accuracy from 49.2% to 63.4% on five real benchmarks using masks rendered from reference hands.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-view hand reconstruction depends on costly real captured data, which is limited in hand-geometry diversity, and a synthetic-to-real appearance gap hinders the use of synthetic data.
AI.method: SilHand projects metric 3D hypotheses into each view to query and fuse mask-ray evidence, rather than lifting RGB features. Training uses a synthetic dataset of 46.8k grasping poses and 60k free-hand samples.
AI.result: Across five real-world benchmarks SilHand raises relative reconstruction accuracy from 49.2% to 63.4% using masks rendered from reference hands. Accuracy improves consistently as the synthetic training set grows. With mask corruption, reconstruction error rises by at most 1.63 mm.
AI.conclusion: Binary masks are an effective interface for learning hand reconstruction from synthetic geometry, and the mask-centric formulation makes broad geometric diversity practical.

title: ReliaGuard: Reconstruction-Aware Watermarking for Source Attribution and Blind Edit Localization
summary: Generative image editing facilitates content creation but complicates source attribution and edit verification. Existing watermarking methods combine copyright protection with tamper localization, yet background reconstruction can weaken spatial evidence even when source identifiers remain recoverable. We propose ReliaGuard, a reconstruction-aware watermarking framework for source attribution and blind edit localization. The writer optimizes keyed feature responses in both the protected image and its variational autoencoder reconstruction under image-distortion and source-preservation constraints. Using only the received image and a secret key, the reader combines watermark responses with local image context through residual evidence refinement and predicts an edit mask through native-resolution-guided multiscale reading. It is trained on complete editing outputs, locally spliced counterparts, and processed versions of both. On an independent test set of 300 source images and 900 editing cases from three image domains, our method achieves edit-region intersection-over-union scores of 85.61% for complete outputs and 94.90% for locally spliced outputs at a threshold calibrated to a nominal 1% background false-positive rate on complete outputs. The complete-output result exceeds the strongest baseline by 45.02 percentage points, while decoded identifier-bit accuracy reaches 100% in both conditions. Across seven families of image processing, the corresponding localization scores are 81.01% and 86.49%, with identifier-bit accuracies of 92.76% and 92.79%, respectively. These results support source recovery and blind edit localization under background reconstruction and subsequent image processing.

AI.tldr: ReliaGuard is a reconstruction-aware watermarking framework for generative image editing that embeds keyed watermarks in both the protected image and its VAE reconstruction. It recovers source identifiers and localises edits blindly, with an intersection-over-union of 85.61% on complete outputs.
AI.motivation: Existing watermarks combine copyright protection with tamper localisation, but background reconstruction by generative editors can weaken the spatial evidence even when source identifiers remain recoverable.
AI.method: The writer optimises keyed feature responses in the protected image and its variational autoencoder reconstruction under distortion and source-preservation constraints. The reader uses only the received image and the secret key, combines watermark responses with local context through residual evidence refinement, and predicts an edit mask through native-resolution-guided multiscale reading. Training uses complete edits, locally spliced edits and processed versions of both.
AI.result: On 300 source images and 900 editing cases from three domains, edit-region IoU is 85.61% for complete outputs and 94.90% for locally spliced outputs, at a threshold calibrated to a 1% background false-positive rate. The complete-output result exceeds the strongest baseline by 45.02 points, and identifier-bit accuracy reaches 100% in both conditions. Across seven processing families, localisation scores are 81.01% and 86.49%.
AI.conclusion: The framework supports source recovery and blind edit localisation under background reconstruction and subsequent image processing.

title: Description-Guided CLIP Adaptation with Local Evidence Calibration for Few-Shot Plant Disease Recognition
summary: Accurate plant disease recognition is essential for intelligent agriculture, but few-shot settings provide limited labeled samples that may not capture diagnostic symptoms and intra-class variations. Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs), such as CLIP, offer transferable visual-semantic knowledge. However, existing CLIP-based methods often rely on coarse class semantics and global visual representations, overlooking disease-specific diagnostic information and fine-grained local cues. Excessive few-shot adaptation may also cause over-specialization and weaken the generalization ability of large-scale pre-training. We propose a description-guided, two-stage CLIP adaptation method to address these issues. Symptom and comparative descriptions enrich class semantics with typical visual symptoms and discriminative cues between similar diseases. The enhanced semantics guide the aggregation of class-relevant patch evidence to calibrate global image-text matching with fine-grained cues. For adaptation, we first update the vision-language encoders with lightweight parameters, then freeze them and train a linear classifier. At inference, the classifier is used for in-domain prediction, while class prototypes from the adapted text encoder support cross-domain prediction and retain vision-language transferability. Experiments with two backbones show that our method achieves the highest mean accuracy in most few-shot settings on PlantVillage, Cassava, and Pear, reaching 93.16%, 79.30%, and 96.56%, respectively, with ViT-L/14 under 16-shot. On class-aligned cross-domain evaluation across 21 shared PlantDoc classes, it achieves 56.96% accuracy, outperforming all compared methods. These results demonstrate its effectiveness in fine-grained few-shot plant disease recognition and cross-domain generalization.

AI.tldr: A description-guided two-stage CLIP adaptation method for few-shot plant disease recognition, which enriches class semantics with symptom descriptions and calibrates image-text matching with class-relevant patch evidence. It reports the highest mean accuracy in most few-shot settings and 56.96% cross-domain accuracy on PlantDoc.
AI.motivation: Few-shot CLIP methods rely on coarse class semantics and global representations, so they overlook disease-specific symptoms and fine-grained local cues, and excessive adaptation weakens generalisation.
AI.method: Symptom and comparative descriptions enrich class semantics with typical symptoms and discriminative cues between similar diseases. These guide aggregation of class-relevant patch evidence to calibrate global image-text matching. The vision-language encoders are first updated with lightweight parameters, then frozen, and a linear classifier is trained. Class prototypes from the adapted text encoder support cross-domain prediction.
AI.result: With ViT-L/14 under 16-shot, accuracy reaches 93.16% on PlantVillage, 79.30% on Cassava and 96.56% on Pear. On cross-domain evaluation across 21 shared PlantDoc classes it reaches 56.96%, outperforming all compared methods.
AI.conclusion: Description-guided local evidence calibration improves fine-grained few-shot plant disease recognition and cross-domain generalisation while keeping the pretrained transferability.

title: RADIANT: Redundancy-Aware Information Allocation for Universal Multi-Modal Fusion
comment: 9 pages, 4 figures. Published in ACM Multimedia 2026 (MM '26). Code: this https URL
summary: Universal multi-modal fusion often fails not because modalities are insufficiently aligned, but because the fusion process allocates information poorly: redundant evidence is repeatedly amplified, modality-unique evidence is over-smoothed during alignment, and task-dependent synergistic evidence is insufficiently activated. We present RADIANT (Redundancy-Aware Dynamic Information Allocation Network), a task-general framework that organizes fusion around three complementary roles: suppressing redundant cross-modal overlap, preserving modality-unique evidence, and composing task-conditioned synergy through cross-modal interaction. Specifically, stable matrix-exponential projections are used to reduce interference among shared and modality-unique streams, while task memory with hard positive updates selects which synergistic interactions should be activated for the current fusion regime. Extensive experiments across six heterogeneous fusion tasks show consistent improvements over the compared methods. On FLIR, RADIANT improves downstream detection mAP@0.5 from 91.2% to 96.8%, a gain of 5.6 percentage points (6.1% relative) over GIF. RADIANT also exhibits strong direct cross-dataset transfer, with further gains from inference-time task-memory adaptation while keeping all network weights frozen. Additional ablations and sensitivity studies support the robustness of the allocation mechanism.

AI.tldr: RADIANT is a task-general multi-modal fusion framework that suppresses redundant cross-modal overlap, preserves modality-unique evidence and activates task-conditioned synergy. It improves FLIR detection mAP@0.5 from 91.2% to 96.8% over six heterogeneous fusion tasks.
AI.motivation: Fusion often fails because it allocates information poorly, not because modalities are misaligned: redundant evidence is amplified, unique evidence is over-smoothed during alignment, and synergistic evidence is under-activated.
AI.method: Matrix-exponential projections reduce interference between shared and modality-unique streams. A task memory with hard positive updates selects which synergistic interactions to activate for the current fusion regime.
AI.result: Across six heterogeneous fusion tasks RADIANT shows consistent improvements. On FLIR, downstream detection mAP@0.5 rises from 91.2% to 96.8%, a gain of 5.6 points (6.1% relative) over GIF. It transfers across datasets, with further gains from inference-time task-memory adaptation while network weights stay frozen.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly allocating information between redundant, unique and synergistic streams improves universal multi-modal fusion, with robustness supported by ablations and sensitivity studies.

title: TransXplainRRG: A Radiologist-Evaluated LVLM for Chest Radiograph Report Generation
summary: Recent advancements in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLM) enhance X-ray report generation, but often neglect clinical context, overlook workflow integration, and lack explainability, which hinders clinical adoption due to interpretability and reliability concerns. This paper addresses the dual challenges of performance and expert explainability in automated X-ray report generation for clinical AI applications. Our proposed approach, TransXplainRRG, utilises an off-the-shelf Swin Transformer model along with a transformer-based text encoder that incorporates patient medical history to generate a radiology report. Further, we explore an expert-guided `inside-out' approach and extract only abnormal findings for radiology report refinement. Thus, this study bridges the gap between high-performance automation and interpretability critical for clinical practice by combining state-of-the-art transformer-based vision encoders, text encoders, and LLMs. TransXplainRRG is trained and tested on the large-scale MIMIC-CXR dataset and further evaluated on the unseen IU X-Ray dataset to demonstrate its generalizability and robustness. We employed the GREEN metric as a complementary measure of clinical consistency, achieving scores of 0.327 on MIMIC-CXR and 0.605 on IU X-Ray, both higher than those achieved by MAIRA-2 under the same evaluation setting. It also performed competitively across standard evaluation metrics, frequently matching or surpassing state-of-the-art models. Additionally, we introduce qualitative evaluation metrics developed from radiologists' viewpoints and conduct a preliminary radiologist evaluation on 100 generated reports to assess their clinical relevance. Quantitative and qualitative analyses further demonstrate the potential of our TransXplainRRG framework for reliable and explainable radiology report generation.

AI.tldr: TransXplainRRG is a chest radiograph report generation model that uses a Swin Transformer, a text encoder over patient history, and expert-guided refinement of abnormal findings. It reports GREEN scores of 0.327 on MIMIC-CXR and 0.605 on IU X-Ray, both higher than MAIRA-2 under the same setting, and a preliminary radiologist evaluation of 100 reports.
AI.motivation: LVLM-based X-ray report generation often ignores clinical context and workflow, and lacks explainability, which hinders clinical adoption.
AI.method: The model uses an off-the-shelf Swin Transformer and a transformer-based text encoder that incorporates patient medical history. An expert-guided inside-out approach extracts only abnormal findings for report refinement. The approach combines vision encoders, text encoders and LLMs.
AI.result: Trained on MIMIC-CXR and tested on the unseen IU X-Ray dataset, the model scores 0.327 on MIMIC-CXR and 0.605 on IU X-Ray with GREEN, both higher than MAIRA-2 under the same evaluation. It performs competitively on standard metrics, frequently matching or surpassing state-of-the-art models. A radiologist evaluation covers 100 generated reports.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers a path to reliable and explainable report generation, although the radiologist evaluation is preliminary.

title: FuGIBench: Evaluating Reliable Preparation in Streaming Video
summary: An assistant watching a worker can prepare for an emerging need before the worker is ready to receive this http URL the need evolves, the assistant must maintain preparation until a response is due, or withdraw it if the need disappears. Video anticipation and interactive response benchmarks leave this interval between early evidence and response largely unmeasured. We introduce FuGIBench (Future-Grounded Interaction), a streaming-video benchmark in which a model chooses among waiting, reversible preparation, and response given a causal video prefix and a task contract. The benchmark contains 19,893 synthetic tool-assistance videos across ten tool tasks, in handover, ordinary-activity, and cancelled-need tracks. One primary score credits sustained preparation, incorporates response-interval alignment, and penalizes activity when the reference prescribes waiting. On a frozen set of 1,000 episodes, a reference system with a longer preparation lead has poorer response alignment, while similar handover leads accompany different levels of activity during ordinary work in matched scenarios. Together with cancellation analyses, these results show why evaluating preparation requires tracking decisions as needs develop, become actionable, or disappear.

AI.tldr: FuGIBench is a streaming-video benchmark in which a model chooses among waiting, reversible preparation and response, scored by one primary metric that credits sustained preparation and response-interval alignment. It shows that evaluating preparation requires tracking decisions as needs develop, become actionable or disappear.
AI.motivation: An assistant watching a worker should prepare before the worker needs help, maintain that preparation until a response is due, and withdraw it if the need disappears. Existing video anticipation and interactive response benchmarks do not measure this interval.
AI.method: The benchmark has 19,893 synthetic tool-assistance videos across ten tool tasks, in handover, ordinary-activity and cancelled-need tracks. Given a causal video prefix and a task contract, a model chooses among waiting, reversible preparation and response. The primary score penalises activity when the reference prescribes waiting. Analyses include cancellation.
AI.result: On a frozen set of 1,000 episodes, a reference system with a longer preparation lead has poorer response alignment. Similar handover leads accompany different levels of activity during ordinary work in matched scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Preparation should be evaluated over time, and tracking decisions across the need's lifecycle, including cancellation, reveals behaviour that single-point metrics miss.
