title: Teach with Blinks: Breaking Linguistic Momentum in On-Policy Distillation for Fine-Grained Multimodal Perception
summary: On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as an effective post-training approach to improving fine-grained perception in multimodal large language models by amortizing costly inference-time zooming operations into a single-pass recipe. However, vanilla OPD is inherently susceptible to linguistic momentum: the teacher can follow the student's erroneous prefixes, thus weakening corrective supervision. To address this, we propose Blink On-Policy Distillation (BlinkOPD), in which the teacher "blinks" at every token: it reads the same prefix once with its eyes open and once with its eyes closed. A first-glance gain further strengthens the correction on rollouts that conflict with the teacher. By extracting more effective supervision from each on-policy trajectory, BlinkOPD achieves state-of-the-art average performance across six fine-grained benchmarks using only 500 training images (12x less data) than existing OPD methods. Beyond fine-grained perception, BlinkOPD also demonstrates strong zero-shot improvements across ten held-out benchmarks spanning general visual perception, visual hallucination, and multimodal reasoning abilities. Code: this https URL

AI.tldr: BlinkOPD is an on-policy distillation method for fine-grained multimodal perception that counters linguistic momentum by having the teacher read each prefix both with eyes open and with eyes closed. It reaches state-of-the-art average performance on six fine-grained benchmarks with 12x less data (500 images).
AI.motivation: Vanilla on-policy distillation is susceptible to linguistic momentum: the teacher follows the student's erroneous prefixes, which weakens corrective supervision.
AI.method: At every token the teacher reads the same prefix once with its eyes open and once with its eyes closed. A first-glance gain strengthens the correction on rollouts that conflict with the teacher. This extracts more supervision from each on-policy trajectory.
AI.result: BlinkOPD achieves state-of-the-art average performance across six fine-grained benchmarks using only 500 training images, 12 times less data than existing OPD methods. It also shows zero-shot improvements on ten held-out benchmarks covering general perception, visual hallucination and multimodal reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Contrasting open-eye and closed-eye teacher readings yields stronger supervision per trajectory, improving fine-grained perception with far less data and transferring to other capabilities.

title: Gravity and Flight: Learning to Navigate Fine-Grained Remote Sensing Scenes
summary: Vision-language models are increasingly capable, yet their reasoning in complex remote sensing scenes can remain coarse-grained and insufficiently grounded in task-relevant visual evidence. We propose Gravity and Flight (G&F), a framework for scene specialization with limited supervision that separates visual and reasoning verification while coupling policy updates. It combines Evidence-of-Thought supervised fine-tuning (EoT-SFT) and Relational Transfer Policy Optimization (RTPO). EoT-SFT teaches fine-grained observation and faithful reasoning through description, analysis, and supported conclusions. RTPO independently samples responses to scene-matched image pairs with fine-grained visual differences under a shared task. Its rubric-based verification combines Gravity, which checks visual fidelity and description coverage, and Flight, which takes descriptions as premises to assess evidence use and relations between paired judgments. Their scores and task correctness yield a shared pair-level advantage that couples policy updates from both responses. Using 1,008 demonstrations and 500 training pairs for harbor specialization, G&F achieves a mean score of 69.12 across six evaluation sets, exceeding the backbone and supervised initialization by 9.76 and 4.56 points. Matched controls show gains over single-image and joint-input RL, and removing either verification view reduces performance. Applying G&F to urban specialization also improves on the base model and supervised initialization across three evaluation subsets. Project details and updates are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Gravity and Flight is a framework for specialising vision-language models to remote sensing scenes, combining EoT-SFT for evidence-based reasoning with RTPO, a pair-level policy optimisation that couples two verification views. It reaches a mean score of 69.12 across six evaluation sets, exceeding the backbone by 9.76 points.
AI.motivation: VLM reasoning in complex remote sensing scenes is coarse-grained and insufficiently grounded in task-relevant visual evidence, and scene specialisation must work with limited supervision.
AI.method: EoT-SFT teaches fine-grained observation and faithful reasoning through description, analysis and supported conclusions. RTPO samples responses to scene-matched image pairs with fine-grained differences. Gravity checks visual fidelity and description coverage, and Flight takes descriptions as premises to assess evidence use and relations between paired judgements. Their scores and task correctness give a shared pair-level advantage that couples the policy updates.
AI.result: Using 1,008 demonstrations and 500 training pairs for harbour specialisation, G&F reaches a mean score of 69.12 across six evaluation sets, exceeding the backbone and supervised initialisation by 9.76 and 4.56 points. Matched controls outperform single-image and joint-input RL, and removing either verification view reduces performance. Urban specialisation also improves on the base model.
AI.conclusion: Coupling two verification views in pair-level policy optimisation improves grounded reasoning for remote sensing specialisation with limited supervision.

title: RICapBench: A Fine-Grained Visual Understanding Benchmark Dataset for Vision-Language Models in Remote Sensing
summary: Advances in vision-language models (VLMs) have improved remote sensing image analysis and supported geospatial decision-making. However, fine-grained understanding of remote sensing imagery remains challenging for VLMs. Large variations in object scale, complex geospatial relations among instances, and limited visual detail hinder precise instance localization, visible attribute identification, and spatial relation understanding, potentially leading to descriptions that lack visual grounding. Existing datasets and benchmarks insufficiently assess end-to-end instance localization and captioning without target-specific textual cues. To support this evaluation, we introduce RICapBench, a dataset and benchmark that unifies instance localization and fine-grained captioning in remote sensing. RICapBench contains 245,466 instance-level annotations and 498,005 spatial relation tuples spanning general remote sensing, UAV remote sensing, and dense small-object scenarios. Each annotation pairs an object's oriented bounding box with a natural language description of its visible attributes and spatial relations to surrounding instances and environmental elements. To evaluate the accuracy and completeness of spatial relation captioning, we propose a remote sensing spatial relation parser and the RelCap-F1 metric. We combine RelCap-F1 with instance localization and attribute captioning metrics into a composite metric, RICScore. Our evaluation of 15 advanced open-source and closed-source VLMs identifies instance localization as a major bottleneck for these models. LocateAnything achieves the highest RICScore of 31.68, but scores lower on spatial relation captioning than other task-fine-tuned open-source VLMs. Code and dataset are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: RICapBench is a dataset and benchmark that unifies instance localisation and fine-grained captioning for remote sensing VLMs, with 245,466 instance annotations and 498,005 spatial relation tuples. It finds instance localisation to be the main bottleneck, with LocateAnything achieving the highest RICScore of 31.68.
AI.motivation: VLMs struggle with object scale, geospatial relations and limited detail in remote sensing imagery, and existing benchmarks do not assess end-to-end localisation and captioning without target-specific textual cues.
AI.method: Each annotation pairs an oriented bounding box with a natural-language description of the object's visible attributes and spatial relations. The benchmark spans general, UAV and dense small-object scenes. The authors propose a remote sensing spatial relation parser and the RelCap-F1 metric, combined with localisation and attribute metrics into the composite RICScore.
AI.result: Of 15 open-source and closed-source VLMs evaluated, LocateAnything achieves the highest RICScore of 31.68 but scores lower on spatial relation captioning than some task-fine-tuned open-source VLMs. Instance localisation is identified as a major bottleneck.
AI.conclusion: Localisation is the main limitation for current VLMs on fine-grained remote sensing captioning, and the benchmark makes this measurable.

title: VBot Exo2Ego Policy: Lightweight Data Collection and Exocentric-to-Egocentric Video Generation
summary: We present VBot Exo2Ego Policy, a video generation model that turns third-person videos into first-person observations of a selected actor, offering a practical way to expand first-person operation data from abundant real-world footage. To support this goal, we introduce a lightweight data collection pipeline and mobile app that support first-person recording, third-person recording, and synchronized capture of both views. This setup combines accessible single-view collection with paired RGB and camera geometry for learning cross-view correspondence. Building on a pretrained video diffusion transformer, our model incorporates geometric guidance and auxiliary supervision from semantic masks and hand keypoints to facilitate optimization and improve the fidelity of hand-object interactions. Camera geometry is injected stochastically during training and gradually removed, allowing inference without target-camera calibration. To accommodate the diversity of Internet videos, we combine source-video perception and reasoning, optional actor references, and multi-shot adaptation to identify the intended actor and follow an operation across camera cuts. The collection system and generation model provide a foundation for expanding first-person operation data across tasks, scenes, and participants.

AI.tldr: VBot Exo2Ego Policy is a video diffusion model that turns third-person videos into first-person views of a chosen actor, supported by a lightweight mobile data-collection app that records paired first- and third-person views. It injects camera geometry during training, removes it gradually, and does not need target-camera calibration at inference.
AI.motivation: First-person operation data is scarce, while third-person footage is abundant. The aim is to expand first-person data from real-world footage with accessible collection.
AI.method: The model builds on a pretrained video diffusion transformer and adds geometric guidance and auxiliary supervision from semantic masks and hand keypoints to improve hand-object interactions. Camera geometry is injected stochastically during training and gradually removed. Source-video perception and reasoning, optional actor references and multi-shot adaptation identify the intended actor across camera cuts.
AI.result: The abstract describes the model and data pipeline but gives no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: The collection system and generation model provide a foundation for expanding first-person operation data across tasks, scenes and participants.

title: Model Distribution-Aware Multimodal Dataset Distillation
summary: Multimodal dataset distillation (MDD) aims to reduce the cost of vision-language pre-training by synthesizing compact image-text datasets. Although recent feature-matching methods have improved distillation efficiency, synthetic data may become specialized to the model representations encountered during optimization, limiting generalization to unseen model states. We propose Model Distribution-Aware Multimodal Dataset Distillation (MDA-DD), which leverages supervision from a dynamic staggered queue of models at different training stages. We further introduce asymmetric dual projection for complementary alignment in visual and linguistic spaces and an uncentered second-order moment objective that retains mean-related cross-modal information. Experiments on Flickr30K and MS-COCO demonstrate consistent retrieval improvements over existing methods across synthetic-data budgets. With only 100 synthetic pairs, MDA-DD improves IR@1 and TR@1 on Flickr30K by 12.9 and 18.2 percentage points, respectively, over the strongest baseline at the same budget, outperforming all compared methods using 500 pairs on both datasets across all six retrieval metrics.

AI.tldr: MDA-DD is a multimodal dataset distillation method that supervises synthetic image-text pairs with a dynamic staggered queue of models at different training stages, improving retrieval. With 100 synthetic pairs it improves Flickr30K IR@1 and TR@1 by 12.9 and 18.2 points over the strongest baseline at the same budget.
AI.motivation: Feature-matching distillation can specialise synthetic data to the model states seen during optimisation, which limits generalisation to unseen model states.
AI.method: MDA-DD uses supervision from a dynamic staggered queue of models at different training stages. It adds asymmetric dual projection for complementary alignment in visual and linguistic spaces, and an uncentred second-order moment objective that keeps mean-related cross-modal information.
AI.result: On Flickr30K and MS-COCO, retrieval improves consistently over existing methods across synthetic-data budgets. With 100 synthetic pairs, IR@1 and TR@1 on Flickr30K rise by 12.9 and 18.2 points over the strongest baseline at the same budget, outperforming all compared methods using 500 pairs on all six retrieval metrics.
AI.conclusion: Distilling against a distribution of training states rather than a single trajectory yields more general synthetic multimodal datasets, which is most valuable at very small budgets.

title: PhysCapBench: A Cross-Domain Benchmark for Physically Grounded Video Captioning
summary: Physical AI aims to learn transferable physical knowledge from real-world experience to understand, predict, and act in the physical world. Internet videos and embodied demonstrations provide complementary observations of motion, interaction, and state evolution. A foundational data challenge is to measure and preserve this physical information as training supervision. In video-language pretraining, captions express observed processes in language, yet a semantically correct description can omit the interactions and transitions that define those processes. Rich physical experience in video does not automatically translate into sufficient language supervision. This gap calls for a yardstick to assess annotation quality, compare captioning strategies, and guide training-data refinement. Motivated by our data construction for world-model pretraining, we introduce PhysCapBench, to our knowledge the first unified physical-caption benchmark spanning all three domains: third-person scenes, egocentric manipulation, and handheld-gripper demonstrations. It provides human-verified annotations for 1,500 video sequences and evaluates accuracy and coverage through seven physical dimensions. We examine downstream utility through video reconstruction and manipulation-policy fine-tuning. Physical captions reduce reconstruction LPIPS by 8.6-9.5% on third-person videos and 26.9-30.9% on egocentric videos relative to metadata captions. Training-instruction enrichment improves both PhysCapBench scores and policy success, including a 7.5-percentage-point gain for pi0.5 on a RoboTwin 2.0 subtask. PhysCapBench makes the physical content of language supervision inspectable and comparable, providing a cross-domain basis for its evaluation and improvement.

AI.tldr: PhysCapBench is a cross-domain benchmark of human-verified physical captions for 1,500 videos spanning third-person scenes, egocentric manipulation and handheld-gripper demonstrations, scored on seven physical dimensions. Physical captions reduce reconstruction LPIPS relative to metadata captions, and enrichment improves policy success.
AI.motivation: Captions can be semantically correct yet omit the interactions and transitions that define physical processes, so rich physical experience in video does not automatically become language supervision. A yardstick is needed to assess annotation quality.
AI.method: The benchmark provides human-verified annotations for 1,500 video sequences across three domains and evaluates accuracy and coverage through seven physical dimensions. Downstream utility is tested through video reconstruction and manipulation-policy fine-tuning.
AI.result: Physical captions reduce reconstruction LPIPS by 8.6 to 9.5% on third-person videos and 26.9 to 30.9% on egocentric videos relative to metadata captions. Training-instruction enrichment improves PhysCapBench scores and policy success, including a 7.5-point gain for pi0.5 on a RoboTwin 2.0 subtask.
AI.conclusion: PhysCapBench makes the physical content of language supervision inspectable and comparable across domains, supporting better captioning and training-data refinement.

title: DesignTaste: Benchmarking AI-Generator Visual Design Against Award-Wining Works
comment: 31 pages, 12 figures, including appendices. Code and data: this https URL
summary: Text-to-image benchmarks commonly assess text-image alignment or overall preference. Whether models can produce good designs when a brief leaves the appearance open remains less well understood. We introduce DesignTaste, a visual design benchmark that compares generated images with award-winning works. From these works and their publicly available context, we derive 403 design briefs: 100 poster tasks from 100 Beste Plakate 2025 and 303 tasks spanning 20 categories from ADC 2026. Six leading commercial text-to-image models each generate an image from the same brief. A single model judge scores each output and the corresponding award-winning work independently on five evaluation dimensions. On each dataset, only ArtArk achieves a higher mean overall score than the award-winning works. All six models score lower in Creative Originality on both datasets. These results show that producing finished, visually appealing images does not imply that a model can develop good design solutions.

AI.tldr: DesignTaste benchmarks text-to-image models against award-winning designs, using 403 briefs derived from Beste Plakate 2025 and ADC 2026. Only one of six commercial models, ArtArk, beats the award-winning works on mean overall score, and all six score lower on Creative Originality.
AI.motivation: Text-to-image benchmarks assess alignment or overall preference, but not whether models produce good designs when a brief leaves the appearance open.
AI.method: The authors derive 403 design briefs from award-winning works and their public context: 100 poster tasks from Beste Plakate 2025 and 303 tasks across 20 categories from ADC 2026. Six commercial text-to-image models generate an image per brief. A single model judge scores each output and the award-winning work independently on five dimensions.
AI.result: On each dataset, only ArtArk achieves a higher mean overall score than the award-winning works. All six models score lower in Creative Originality on both datasets.
AI.conclusion: Producing finished, visually appealing images does not mean a model can develop good design solutions, and creative originality remains a clear gap.

title: HIFC-IQA: Train-Free Cross-Domain Image Quality Assessment via Dual-Process Cognition
summary: The gap between controlled synthetic distortions and complex real-world degradations introduces a critical domain shift challenge for No-Reference Image Quality Assessment. Although Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) approaches attempt to address this issue, they remain constrained by substantial retraining overhead and cumulative error propagation inherent in iterative pseudo-labeling. Inspired by the dual-process theory of human cognition for remarkable generalization ability, we propose Hierarchical Intuitive and Fuzzy Consensus (HIFC), a completely train-free Cross-Domain IQA framework. HIFC employs asymmetric perceptual decomposition to disentangle semantic content from distortion-sensitive representations. The final quality score is fused through the synergy of two complementary branches: a memory consensus branch that retrieves a stable Fuzzy Quality Centroid from a synthetic reference gallery, and an intuitive branch that captures aesthetic polarization via zero-shot vision-language alignment. Extensive experiments show that HIFC achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks, attaining the highest average SRCC and PLCC among competing UDA methods. Most notably, in the challenging synthetic-to-authentic cross-domain setting, HIFC achieves a substantial performance margin over competing methods, demonstrating remarkable robustness and generalization.

AI.tldr: HIFC-IQA is a train-free cross-domain image quality assessment framework that combines a memory consensus branch, which retrieves a fuzzy quality centroid from a synthetic reference gallery, with a zero-shot vision-language intuitive branch. It reports the highest average SRCC and PLCC among UDA methods, with the largest margin in synthetic-to-authentic transfer.
AI.motivation: No-reference IQA suffers a domain shift between controlled synthetic distortions and real-world degradations. UDA methods need costly retraining and suffer error accumulation from iterative pseudo-labelling.
AI.method: Inspired by dual-process cognition, HIFC uses asymmetric perceptual decomposition to separate semantic content from distortion-sensitive representations. The final score fuses a memory consensus branch, which retrieves a Fuzzy Quality Centroid from a synthetic reference gallery, with an intuitive branch that captures aesthetic polarisation through zero-shot vision-language alignment.
AI.result: HIFC achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmarks, with the highest average SRCC and PLCC among competing UDA methods. In the synthetic-to-authentic setting it shows a substantial margin over competing methods. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: A train-free, dual-branch design can generalise across domains without retraining or pseudo-label drift.

title: Can an LVLM Perceive Event Boundaries Like a Human?
summary: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) reason effectively about video content, but whether they perceive its event boundaries in a manner consistent with humans remains unclear. We first investigate this through Generic Event Boundary Detection (GEBD), which identifies event boundaries naturally perceived by humans in continuous video, without relying on predefined event categories. On Kinetics-GEBD dataset, LVLMs miss many boundaries when predicting directly from frames, but effectively refine candidates proposed by an unsupervised discovery method, achieving state-of-the-art unsupervised GEBD performance. We extend this discovery-refinement approach to hour-long egocentric video, where boundary discovery requires a broader semantic scale and whole-video LVLM refinement becomes impractical. We address these challenges through coarse-to-fine temporal discovery and localized LVLM accept/reject judgments. Human evaluation shows that the LVLM's agreement with group consensus falls within the range observed among human annotators, with disagreements concentrated on low-consensus cases. Using this pipeline, we construct EgoBoundary, a benchmark for event boundary detection in hour-scale egocentric video. Representative supervised and unsupervised methods degrade substantially on EgoBoundary, highlighting the challenge of long-horizon event boundary detection.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that LVLMs miss many event boundaries when predicting from frames directly, but refine candidates from an unsupervised discovery method to reach state-of-the-art unsupervised GEBD performance. It extends this to hour-long egocentric video and introduces the EgoBoundary benchmark.
AI.motivation: LVLMs reason well about video content, but it is unclear whether they perceive event boundaries as humans do. Whole-video LVLM refinement becomes impractical for hour-long egocentric video.
AI.method: On Kinetics-GEBD the authors use LVLMs to accept or reject candidate boundaries proposed by an unsupervised discovery method. For hour-long egocentric video they use coarse-to-fine temporal discovery and localised LVLM accept or reject judgements. EgoBoundary is constructed with this pipeline.
AI.result: On Kinetics-GEBD the pipeline achieves state-of-the-art unsupervised GEBD performance. Human evaluation shows the LVLM's agreement with group consensus falls within the range observed among human annotators, with disagreements concentrated on low-consensus cases. Representative supervised and unsupervised methods degrade substantially on EgoBoundary.
AI.conclusion: LVLMs can serve as reliable refiners of event boundary candidates, and long-horizon egocentric boundary detection remains a substantial challenge.

title: PiLLVD: A Real-World Low-Light Video Dataset for Dynamic Scenes Captured with Off-the-Shelf Cameras
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures, 5 tables. Dataset available on Zenodo: this https URL
summary: Low-light image and video enhancement has received increasing attention in recent years. However, most existing enhancement methods are developed and evaluated on still images, while progress in low-light video enhancement remains limited by the lack of real-world paired video datasets. Acquiring paired low-light and normal-light video sequences is challenging because it requires spatially and temporally aligned captures while avoiding motion blur, exposure mismatch, and correspondence errors in dynamic scenes. To address this gap, we introduce PiLLVD, the Pi-based Low-Light Video Dataset, a paired low-light video dataset captured using an accessible Raspberry Pi-based multi-camera system with off-the-shelf cameras. PiLLVD provides paired low-light and aligned normal-light reference sequences for dynamic indoor and outdoor scenes, including diverse human and object motion under varying illumination conditions. Unlike existing datasets that are often image-based, static, synthetic, or limited to simple motion patterns, PiLLVD focuses on motion-rich scenes where frame-to-frame stability and motion-related artefacts are important for evaluation. In addition to presenting the dataset and acquisition pipeline, we benchmark representative pre-trained low-light video enhancement methods on PiLLVD under a zero-shot setting. The results show that existing methods do not generalise uniformly across the proposed sequences, highlighting the challenges posed by the proposed dataset and its value for both benchmarking existing methods and supporting the development of future low-light video enhancement algorithms.

AI.tldr: PiLLVD is a paired low-light video dataset for dynamic indoor and outdoor scenes, captured with a Raspberry Pi multi-camera system and off-the-shelf cameras. Benchmarking pretrained low-light video enhancement methods zero-shot shows that they do not generalise uniformly across its sequences.
AI.motivation: Low-light video enhancement lacks real-world paired video data, since paired captures of dynamic scenes are hard to align and avoid motion blur and exposure mismatch. Existing datasets are image-based, static, synthetic or limited to simple motion.
AI.method: The authors build an accessible Raspberry Pi-based multi-camera system with off-the-shelf cameras. It captures paired low-light sequences and aligned normal-light references of motion-rich indoor and outdoor scenes with diverse human and object motion under varying illumination.
AI.result: Representative pretrained low-light video enhancement methods are benchmarked zero-shot on PiLLVD, and their performance does not generalise uniformly across the proposed sequences. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: PiLLVD offers a valuable benchmark for evaluating existing methods and for developing future low-light video enhancement algorithms, with frame-to-frame stability important for evaluation.

title: UniSpark: Exploring Hybrid Attention for Multimodal Understanding and Generation
summary: We present UniSpark-9B, a unified multimodal model that investigates hybrid attention for visual understanding and generation. Built on a Mixture-of-Transformer-Experts backbone with approximately 9B parameters in each branch, UniSpark combines full attention for explicit token interactions with GatedDeltaNet linear attention for compact context propagation. Autoregressive text prediction and visual flow matching jointly support visual question answering, text-to-image generation, instruction-guided editing, and interleaved text-image prediction. In interleaved generation, noisy visual targets are isolated from subsequent predictions, while clean visual representations provide context for later outputs. A blockwise protocol enforces this distinction through attention masks in full-attention layers and recurrent-state retention rules in linear-attention layers. The selected training sources contain 159.7M generation samples, 213.4M understanding samples, and 624.8K interleaved sequences. A four-stage curriculum jointly trains multimodal understanding and visual generation, refining answer accuracy and instruction following while extending image synthesis to 2K. UniSpark scores 2470.3 on MME-S and 0.83 on GenEval. Qualitative examples further illustrate its capabilities in interleaved image generation, video synthesis, and video editing. Together, these results demonstrate that hybrid attention provides an effective backbone for unified multimodal understanding and generation.

AI.tldr: UniSpark-9B is a unified multimodal model that uses hybrid attention, combining full attention with GatedDeltaNet linear attention, for both visual understanding and visual generation.
AI.motivation: Unified multimodal models need one backbone that supports understanding, generation and interleaved text-image prediction; the abstract does not detail the shortcomings of prior models.
AI.method: A Mixture-of-Transformer-Experts backbone with about 9B parameters per branch combines full attention for explicit token interactions with GatedDeltaNet linear attention for compact context propagation. Autoregressive text prediction and visual flow matching are trained jointly, and a blockwise protocol uses attention masks in full-attention layers and recurrent-state retention rules in linear-attention layers so that noisy visual targets are isolated from later predictions. A four-stage curriculum is used.
AI.result: Training sources contain 159.7M generation samples, 213.4M understanding samples and 624.8K interleaved sequences. UniSpark scores 2470.3 on MME-S and 0.83 on GenEval, extends image synthesis to 2K, and gives qualitative examples of interleaved image generation, video synthesis and video editing.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid attention provides an effective backbone for unified multimodal understanding and generation.

title: Context-Predictive Low-Rank Adaptation for Face Presentation Attack Detection
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE for possible publication. Copyright may be transferred without notice, after which this version may no longer be accessible
summary: Face presentation attack detection requires representations that distinguish physical spoofing cues across changes in acquisition devices, subjects, and attack media. Large visual encoders offer transferable representations, but conventional binary fine-tuning supervises their final decisions without explicitly constraining how local facial evidence is represented under partial observation. We present CP-JEPA, a context-predictive adaptation framework that combines low-rank tuning of a pretrained CLIP image encoder with a joint-embedding predictive objective. A student predicts complete-image teacher features at masked spatial locations, while unmasked classification, masked classification, and prediction consistency retain the connection to the live/spoof task. An exponential-moving-average teacher supplies evolving latent targets. The auxiliary components are used only during training; inference requires only the LoRA-adapted CLIP visual encoder and binary classifier. {We evaluate CP-JEPA under single-source and multi-source OCIM transfer, additional CelebA-Spoof training, transfer to CelebA-Spoof, two-source training, and unseen-attack evaluation on SiW-Mv2.} On the standard OCIM benchmark, CP-JEPA achieves 3.74\% mean HTER and 98.73\% mean AUC. {Single-source evaluation achieves 11.36\% mean HTER across twelve source--target combinations.} With CelebA-Spoof added to the three OCIM training sources, CP-JEPA reduces mean HTER from 3.45\% to 2.35\% and increases mean AUC from 98.68\% to 99.32\%. On SiW-Mv2, it achieves 3.36\% mean HTER across the held-out attack categories. Controlled loss ablations examine the contributions of latent prediction, masked classification, and prediction consistency. The results show that context-predictive adaptation can improve cross-dataset PAD performance, although the gains vary with the training sources and evaluation setting.

AI.tldr: CP-JEPA adapts a pretrained CLIP image encoder with LoRA and a joint-embedding predictive objective for face presentation attack detection, improving cross-dataset performance, though gains vary with training sources and evaluation setting.
AI.motivation: Conventional binary fine-tuning supervises only the final live/spoof decision and does not explicitly constrain how local facial evidence is represented under partial observation.
AI.method: Low-rank tuning of a pretrained CLIP image encoder combined with a joint-embedding predictive objective: a student predicts complete-image teacher features at masked spatial locations, with an exponential-moving-average teacher supplying latent targets. Unmasked classification, masked classification and prediction consistency keep the link to the live/spoof task. Auxiliary components are used only in training; inference needs only the LoRA-adapted encoder and binary classifier.
AI.result: On the standard OCIM benchmark, 3.74% mean HTER and 98.73% mean AUC; 11.36% mean HTER across twelve single-source combinations; with CelebA-Spoof added to the three OCIM sources, mean HTER falls from 3.45% to 2.35% and mean AUC rises from 98.68% to 99.32%; 3.36% mean HTER across held-out attack categories on SiW-Mv2.
AI.conclusion: Context-predictive adaptation can improve cross-dataset PAD performance, although the gains depend on the training sources and evaluation setting.

title: Pl@ntNet machine-to-machine identification service with Pl@ntNet API: enabling automated biodiversity monitoring through large-scale plant identification
summary: 1. Monitoring plant biodiversity requires identifying large numbers of plants across space and time. Although artificial intelligence (AI) can now identify plant species from images with high accuracy, most existing systems rely on users manually submitting images. As ecological monitoring increasingly generates large image collections from cameras, drones, robots and online platforms, there is a growing need for plant identification services that can be directly integrated into automated data-processing workflows. 2. Here, we present Pl@ntNet's machine-to-machine AI plant identification service. This service uses an application programming interface (API) to provide programmatic access to Pl@ntNet's plant recognition models and the associated taxonomic processing. This service enables the implementation of automated identification workflows without human intervention and can thus directly link large image collections and automated observation systems to an AI-based plant identification system. 3. We establish that this service, which covers 85,000 species from around the world, (1) has a species prediction accuracy of 0.89, (2) process images up to 666 times faster than workflows requiring human intervention, (3) and has processed over 84 million identification requests since its launch, including more than 40 million in 2025 alone. We demonstrate how it has already enabled the implementation of a new generation of ecological workflows: identifying plants from images of insects to reconstruct the plant-pollinator interactions, analysing geolocated images from social media to study plant distribution, detecting invasive plants using images taken at the roadside, and identifying weeds using agricultural robots. Finally, we illustrate its application using a reproducible example: identifying plants from insect photos on iNaturalist. In approximately 30 min on a standard laptop, 2,424 images were processed to generate a dataset of 708 plant-pollinator interactions, with a weighted precision of 0.98 for flower detection and an accuracy of 0.88 for genus plant identification. 4. In conclusion, this machine-to-machine species identification is already operating on a considerable scale and meets a genuine need. All of this paves the way for a new paradigm in biodiversity monitoring, in which automated sensors and image collections can be directly connected to AI-based identification services.

AI.tldr: Pl@ntNet presents a machine-to-machine plant identification API for automated biodiversity monitoring, reporting a species prediction accuracy of 0.89 and over 84 million identification requests processed since launch.
AI.motivation: Most existing AI plant identification systems rely on users submitting images manually, whereas large image collections from cameras, drones, robots and online platforms need identification services that integrate directly into automated workflows.
AI.method: An application programming interface gives programmatic access to Pl@ntNet's plant recognition models and associated taxonomic processing, covering 85,000 species, so identification can run without human intervention.
AI.result: Species prediction accuracy of 0.89; images processed up to 666 times faster than workflows requiring human intervention; over 84 million requests since launch, including more than 40 million in 2025. In a reproducible iNaturalist example, 2,424 images processed in about 30 min on a standard laptop yielded 708 plant-pollinator interactions, with weighted precision 0.98 for flower detection and accuracy 0.88 for genus-level plant identification.
AI.conclusion: The service already operates at considerable scale and points toward a paradigm in which automated sensors and image collections connect directly to AI-based identification.

title: ActWorld-JEPA: Action-Conditioned JEPA World Models Meet Latent Planning for End-to-End Autonomous Driving
comment: 19 pages, including appendix. Code: this https URL. Project: this https URL
summary: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) enable future prediction in latent space without pixel reconstruction. However, latent predictive consistency alone does not establish the relative driving quality of candidate plans. We present ActWorld-JEPA, a joint-embedding formulation for candidate-based driving. Where Plan-Conditioned JEPA (PC-JEPA) uses global and step-wise trajectory intentions to guide recurrent latent prediction, then combines the predicted future with the current scene through gated cross-attention; Relational Residual Reranking ($R^3$) models agreement and discrepancy between plan and future representations under planning supervision, yielding bounded, gated residual corrections to the base planning scores. This formulation connects latent prediction to candidate selection using only observed context and proposed trajectories at inference. Benchmark-specific implementations report 94.1 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, with the final selector calibrated using aggregate NAVTEST feedback, and 91.6 and 42.7 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navtest and navhard, respectively. The nuScenes evaluation reports a mean $L_2$ error of 1.20 m and a predicted collision rate of 0.76% over 1--6 s. This work provides an effective path from JEPA's predictive representations to driving decisions informed by anticipated consequences.

AI.tldr: ActWorld-JEPA links JEPA latent prediction to candidate trajectory selection for end-to-end autonomous driving, using a relational residual reranking module on top of plan-conditioned latent prediction.
AI.motivation: Latent predictive consistency alone does not establish the relative driving quality of candidate plans.
AI.method: Plan-Conditioned JEPA (PC-JEPA) uses global and step-wise trajectory intentions to guide recurrent latent prediction and fuses the predicted future with the current scene through gated cross-attention. Relational Residual Reranking (R3) models agreement and discrepancy between plan and future representations under planning supervision, producing bounded, gated residual corrections to the base planning scores. Inference uses only observed context and proposed trajectories.
AI.result: 94.1 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, with the final selector calibrated using aggregate NAVTEST feedback; 91.6 and 42.7 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navtest and navhard; on nuScenes, mean L2 error of 1.20 m and predicted collision rate of 0.76% over 1 to 6 s.
AI.conclusion: The work offers an effective path from JEPA predictive representations to driving decisions informed by anticipated consequences.

title: Do the Details Help the Whole? One-Way Transfer from Person Actions to Group Intent in VLMs on JRDB-Social
summary: Social scene datasets label people at two levels: what each person is doing and what the group is there for. Training on both levels at once is often assumed to help each of them. We test this assumption for vision-language models (VLMs) on JRDB-Social, treating person actions as the details and group intent as the whole. We fine-tune Qwen3.5 4B under eight training arms with three seeds, repeat the core arms on Qwen3.5 9B and Qwen3-VL 4B, and judge every arm with a verdict rule fixed before testing. Writing each member's actions before the intent raises intent macro-F1 from 30.1 to 31.0, and writing the intent first reaches 31.2, while action F1 stays within 0.2 points of an action-only model. Under the selected recipe, no arm trained with intent improves actions. The gain requires correct, image-grounded actions: empty action lists or actions borrowed from another group with the same intent lower intent F1. Forced-prefix tests, occlusion, member masking, linear probes and component grafting show that the intent follows the written actions, relies more on people and partly resides in the vision tower. Supplying actions as input instead of as targets hurts both levels.

AI.tldr: On JRDB-Social, fine-tuning vision-language models on person actions improves group intent recognition, but training with intent does not improve action recognition, so the transfer runs one way.
AI.motivation: Social scene datasets label people at two levels, individual actions and group intent, and training on both is often assumed to help each; this assumption is tested for VLMs.
AI.method: Qwen3.5 4B is fine-tuned under eight training arms with three seeds, with core arms repeated on Qwen3.5 9B and Qwen3-VL 4B; every arm is judged by a verdict rule fixed before testing. Analyses include forced-prefix tests, occlusion, member masking, linear probes and component grafting.
AI.result: Writing each member's actions before the intent raises intent macro-F1 from 30.1 to 31.0, and writing the intent first reaches 31.2, while action F1 stays within 0.2 points of an action-only model. No arm trained with intent improves actions. The gain needs correct, image-grounded actions, since empty or borrowed action lists lower intent F1. Intent follows the written actions, relies more on people, and partly resides in the vision tower. Supplying actions as input rather than as targets hurts both levels.
AI.conclusion: Person-level details help group-level intent, but intent training does not help person-level actions, so the transfer is one-way.

title: ReFineR: Single image to dense point cloud registration at pixel level with point splatting
summary: Cameras and LiDARs (Light Detection and Ranging) provide complementary observations of the same scene: cameras capture rich appearance cues while LiDAR sensors provide accurate geometric measurements. In this work, we address the problem of fine image-to-point cloud registration from a single image and a roughly estimated camera pose. On robotic platforms, residual reprojection errors of several pixels are commonly observed even after calibration due to temporal desynchronization, mechanical vibrations, or inaccuracies in point cloud reconstruction. Such errors can lead to decimeter-level geometric discrepancies at moderate distances and significantly affect multiple downstream tasks, such as dense cross-modal supervision, texture mapping, and semantic label transfer. To address this challenge, we introduce ReFineR: an offline framework to finely register individual images to pre-reconstructed point clouds. ReFineR builds upon differentiable point splatting rasterization and a smooth Gradient Orientation Measure (GOM) to iteratively refine the camera pose through analysis-by-synthesis optimization. We evaluated the method on a curated dataset of manually calibrated images collected from heterogeneous data sources. Furthermore, we show that an automatic point cloud rescale factor can be estimated prior to optimization, enabling robust refinement across a wide range of scenarios using a single scale-invariant formulation. The project page can be found at this https URL

AI.tldr: ReFineR is an offline framework that refines a camera pose from a single image against a pre-reconstructed point cloud by analysis-by-synthesis, using differentiable point splatting and a smooth Gradient Orientation Measure.
AI.motivation: On robotic platforms, residual reprojection errors of several pixels remain after calibration because of temporal desynchronization, vibration and point cloud inaccuracies, causing decimeter-level discrepancies that hurt dense cross-modal supervision, texture mapping and semantic label transfer.
AI.method: Starting from a roughly estimated camera pose, the camera pose is refined iteratively by analysis-by-synthesis optimization built on differentiable point splatting rasterization and a smooth Gradient Orientation Measure (GOM). An automatic point cloud rescale factor is estimated before optimization, and a single scale-invariant formulation handles a wide range of scenarios.
AI.result: Evaluated on a curated dataset of manually calibrated images collected from heterogeneous data sources; the abstract reports no numerical results.
AI.conclusion: The framework is presented as enabling robust pixel-level registration of individual images to point clouds across a wide range of scenarios.

title: Towards Democratising Low-Data Medical Image Classification: CPU-Trainable ZACH-ViT and Its Geometric Variants
summary: Medical image classification in resource-constrained settings must contend with limited annotations and computational capacity. We evaluate four ZACH-ViT variants with linear, Euclidean prototype, Poincare and spherical heads alongside two compact multiple-instance-learning baselines. All models are trained from scratch with fewer than 260,000 parameters across seven MedMNIST+ datasets and three external benchmarks (PCam, ISIC2017 and Shenzhen tuberculosis radiographs). The low-data protocol uses 50 training images per class and five seeds, with validation-selected checkpoints at 23 and 47 epochs; a full-data reference uses one seed. Compact-TransMIL achieves the highest ten-dataset mean test Macro-F1 at 23 epochs (53.34%) and with full data (73.93%). At 47 epochs, ZACH-Linear narrowly leads (57.76% versus 57.54% for Compact-TransMIL). Extending training improves Macro-F1 in 239 of 300 paired comparisons. On ISIC2017, hZACH-Spherical has the highest 47-epoch low-data Macro-F1 (44.09% with SD 4.09%), whereas ZACH-EuclideanProto leads with full data (51.27%). We additionally conduct 40 CPU-only training runs on ISIC2017 and Shenzhen using four CPU threads; model-only single-image inference requires approximately 4-9 ms, while image decoding and preprocessing substantially increase end-to-end latency. The results demonstrate the feasibility of CPU-only training on the tested platform and the task- and regime-dependence of compact medical imaging under strict resource constraints.

AI.tldr: On medical image classification with fewer than 260,000 parameters trained from scratch, Compact-TransMIL leads the ten-dataset mean Macro-F1 at 23 epochs and with full data, while ZACH-Linear narrowly leads at 47 epochs; CPU-only training is shown to be feasible.
AI.motivation: Medical image classification in resource-constrained settings must contend with limited annotations and limited computational capacity.
AI.method: Four ZACH-ViT variants with linear, Euclidean prototype, Poincare and spherical heads are compared with two compact multiple-instance-learning baselines, all trained from scratch on seven MedMNIST+ datasets and three external benchmarks (PCam, ISIC2017, Shenzhen tuberculosis radiographs). The low-data protocol uses 50 training images per class and five seeds with validation-selected checkpoints at 23 and 47 epochs; a full-data reference uses one seed.
AI.result: Compact-TransMIL has the highest ten-dataset mean test Macro-F1 at 23 epochs (53.34%) and with full data (73.93%); at 47 epochs ZACH-Linear narrowly leads (57.76% versus 57.54% for Compact-TransMIL); extended training improves Macro-F1 in 239 of 300 paired comparisons; on ISIC2017, hZACH-Spherical has the highest 47-epoch low-data Macro-F1 (44.09% with SD 4.09%), while ZACH-EuclideanProto leads with full data (51.27%). Model-only single-image inference takes about 4 to 9 ms, and image decoding and preprocessing substantially increase end-to-end latency; 40 CPU-only training runs on ISIC2017 and Shenzhen used four CPU threads.
AI.conclusion: CPU-only training is feasible on the tested platform, and the best compact model depends on the task and training regime.

title: Improved CNN-Transformer Network for Neutron Image Super-Resolution
summary: The spatial resolution of neutron images is of great importance for material defect diagnosis, structural characterization, and nondestructive testing. However, owing to limitations in neutron beam quality, scintillator conversion efficiency and light scattering, detector pixel size, and noise levels, conventional neutron images often suffer from speckle noise, blurred edges, and missing details, making them inadequate for high-precision analysis. To address these issues, an improved super-resolution model combining convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and Transformers is proposed. First, to overcome the difficulty of obtaining high-quality and clear training images for neutron imaging, a pretrained image restoration model is fine-tuned using real neutron images and then employed to enhance existing neutron images, thereby providing high-quality reference images for subsequent super-resolution model training. Second, an improved CRAFT-based super-resolution network is developed by incorporating a hybrid prior-guided channel fusion module (HPCF), a mean-standard deviation dual-statistics squeeze-and-excitation block (MS-SEBlock), and a partial convolution feed-forward network (PCFN), with the aim of improving the reconstruction of important information, such as textures and fine details, in neutron images. Simulation results demonstrate that, compared with bicubic interpolation, SRCNN, SRGAN-VGG, and other methods, the proposed network achieves superior performance in both full-reference metrics, including PSNR and SSIM, and no-reference metrics, including AGM and SMD. The visual quality and structural fidelity of the reconstructed images are also significantly improved. This study provides a new approach to improving neutron image quality.

AI.tldr: An improved CRAFT-based CNN-Transformer super-resolution network for neutron images, with reference images from a fine-tuned restoration model, outperforms bicubic interpolation, SRCNN and SRGAN-VGG in simulation.
AI.motivation: Neutron images often suffer from speckle noise, blurred edges and missing details because of beam quality, scintillator conversion efficiency, light scattering, detector pixel size and noise, and high-quality clear training images are hard to obtain.
AI.method: A pretrained image restoration model is fine-tuned on real neutron images and used to enhance existing neutron images, providing high-quality references for training. The super-resolution network is an improved CRAFT with a hybrid prior-guided channel fusion module (HPCF), a mean-standard deviation dual-statistics squeeze-and-excitation block (MS-SEBlock) and a partial convolution feed-forward network (PCFN).
AI.result: In simulation, the network outperforms bicubic interpolation, SRCNN, SRGAN-VGG and other methods on full-reference metrics (PSNR and SSIM) and no-reference metrics (AGM and SMD), with visual quality and structural fidelity also improved.
AI.conclusion: The study provides a new approach to improving neutron image quality.

title: When Chekhov's Gun Fires Anyway: Over-Realization in Text-to-Image Models
summary: In text-to-image generation, a target that the prompt mentions often appears in the generated image in a way the prompt does not call for. We call this failure over-realization. Mental-spaces theory points to the situations where it can happen: under a negation, inside what a character believes or imagines, as the vehicle of a figurative comparison, or behind a viewpoint that hides the target. Prior work has studied only negation in depth, and the conventional alignment and preference metrics do not penalize the failure. We build OverReal to measure it: OverReal-Gen, 698 prompts covering the four situations, on which we measure each generator's over-realization rate; and OverReal-Det, 2,841 generated images human-labeled for whether and how the target is over-realized, on which we verify the automatic judge that produces this rate. Our evaluation of eight text-to-image systems reveals that all of them over-realize, and that conventional metrics such as CLIPScore reward the failure rather than penalize it. Prompt expansion only partly mitigates the failure. Inside the generator, the diffusion backbone attends to a mentioned target almost as much as to a requested one. The cue words that should hold the target back receive less attention than ordinary words.

AI.tldr: OverReal measures over-realization, where a target mentioned in a text-to-image prompt appears in the image when the prompt does not call for it; all eight evaluated systems over-realize, and CLIPScore rewards the failure rather than penalizing it.
AI.motivation: Prior work has studied only negation in depth, and conventional alignment and preference metrics do not penalize over-realization.
AI.method: Guided by mental-spaces theory, the authors cover four situations (negation, what a character believes or imagines, figurative comparison, and a viewpoint that hides the target). OverReal-Gen has 698 prompts for measuring each generator's over-realization rate; OverReal-Det has 2,841 generated images, human-labeled, for verifying the automatic judge that produces the rate.
AI.result: All eight evaluated text-to-image systems over-realize, and conventional metrics such as CLIPScore reward the failure. Prompt expansion only partly mitigates it. Inside the generator, the diffusion backbone attends to a mentioned target almost as much as to a requested one, and cue words that should hold the target back receive less attention than ordinary words.
AI.conclusion: Over-realization is a systematic failure that conventional metrics miss, and current mitigation is only partial.

title: Learning the Missing Derivative: Neural Multiple-Scattering Operators for Inverse Volume Rendering
summary: Reconstructing optically thick media from photographs requires modeling multiple scattering and its response to changes in extinction. Frozen-source tomography discards this derivative; differentiable path tracing estimates it through expensive, noisy sampling. We instead predict the multiple-scattering field with a neural operator and differentiate through it during inverse rendering, while computing transmittance and single scattering directly. A further challenge arises during optimization: an operator that predicts the field accurately on held-out media can still produce poor derivatives at the density states visited by the optimizer. We address this by fine-tuning on states generated during inversions driven by the operator, using Monte Carlo scattering-field supervision. On held-out optically thick clouds, our method improves relighting over frozen-source tomography at equal time and outperforms differentiable path tracing given substantially more time. Training on inversion trajectories also improves derivative alignment at visited states and reduces optimization drift.

AI.tldr: A neural operator predicts the multiple-scattering field for inverse volume rendering and is differentiated through during inversion; fine-tuning on operator-driven inversion states improves relighting of optically thick media.
AI.motivation: Frozen-source tomography discards the derivative of the multiple-scattering response to changes in extinction, while differentiable path tracing estimates it through expensive, noisy sampling.
AI.method: A neural operator predicts the multiple-scattering field and is differentiated through during inverse rendering, while transmittance and single scattering are computed directly. The operator is fine-tuned on states generated during inversions it drives, using Monte Carlo scattering-field supervision.
AI.result: On held-out optically thick clouds, relighting improves over frozen-source tomography at equal time and outperforms differentiable path tracing given substantially more time. Training on inversion trajectories improves derivative alignment at visited states and reduces optimization drift.
AI.conclusion: Accurate field prediction on held-out media is not enough for good derivatives at the states an optimizer visits; training on inversion trajectories addresses this.

title: MuViRL: Multimodal View-Invariant Visual Speech Representation Learning via Calibrated View Aggregation
summary: Multimodal representation learning combines complementary signals to capture shared semantic information. For dynamic scenes, these representations need to remain consistent across views while preserving distinctions between temporal states. In visual speech representation learning, view variation changes the visibility and reliability of articulation cues, making it difficult to learn such representations from synchronized audio and video. To address this challenge, we propose MuViRL, a self-supervised framework for multimodal view-invariant visual speech representation learning via calibrated view aggregation. The framework combines synchronized 3D Gaussian view synthesis with multimodal self-supervision to learn consistent representations from real and synthesized data. A multimodal decision model learns relative view utility from teacher prediction losses, and its calibrated scores guide the aggregation of complementary information. Aggregation-to-Single Distillation transfers the aggregated predictions to a single branch. Real-synthetic alignment matches synchronized windows across views while preserving their temporal relations. Experiments on real and synthesized multiview data demonstrate that MuViRL improves multimodal representation consistency and visual speech recognition performance across views.

AI.tldr: MuViRL is a self-supervised framework for view-invariant visual speech representation learning that combines 3D Gaussian view synthesis with calibrated view aggregation and distillation.
AI.motivation: View variation changes the visibility and reliability of articulation cues, which makes consistent visual speech representations hard to learn from synchronized audio and video.
AI.method: Synchronized 3D Gaussian view synthesis is combined with multimodal self-supervision. A multimodal decision model learns relative view utility from teacher prediction losses, and its calibrated scores guide aggregation of complementary information across views. Aggregation-to-Single Distillation transfers aggregated predictions to a single branch, and real-synthetic alignment matches synchronized windows across views while preserving temporal relations.
AI.result: Experiments on real and synthesized multiview data show improved multimodal representation consistency and visual speech recognition performance across views; the abstract gives no numbers.
AI.conclusion: Calibrated view aggregation helps learn view-consistent visual speech representations.

title: Sprint3D: Accelerating End-to-End 3D Asset Generation through Pipeline Optimization

summary: Image-to-3D generative models now produce asset-quality textured meshes, but at minutes per asset they remain slow to iterate with and costly to deploy. Prior work has mostly accelerated the sampling of the networks, and where it also optimizes the mesh processing, it trains its own generators. We instead start from a publicly released pipeline and ask how much of its end-to-end time can be saved. Profiling the public Pixal3D pipeline shows that its latency is dominated by what happens after the networks: the four rectified flows take 14% of the wall-clock time and mesh post-processing takes 85%, most of it in CPU-based UV unwrapping. We therefore first rebuild the mesh post-processing on the GPU and take it off the critical path, then cut the per-evaluation overhead of the flows and distill them from 76 to 8 network evaluations. The resulting pipeline, Sprint3D, reduces the median time per asset from 133 s to 4.05 s on one H200 GPU at the same export settings (33$\times$). At the same time, on 2,653 held-out Toys4K objects it improves every input-view normal metric of the Pixal3D protocol, with a slightly lower mean silhouette IoU, lower point-cloud alignment scores and less fine texture detail. The rebuilt post-processing alone also speeds up TRELLIS.2, which uses the same export code, by 6.7$\times$ without a detectable change in the evaluated metrics.

AI.tldr: Sprint3D speeds up an existing image-to-3D asset pipeline about 33 times, mainly by moving mesh post-processing to the GPU and distilling the rectified flows from 76 to 8 network evaluations, at a slight cost in silhouette IoU.
AI.motivation: Image-to-3D models take minutes per asset, and prior acceleration work has focused on sampling the networks; profiling the public Pixal3D pipeline shows that most time is spent after the networks, mostly in CPU-based UV unwrapping.
AI.method: Mesh post-processing is rebuilt on the GPU and taken off the critical path. The per-evaluation overhead of the four rectified flows is cut, and the flows are distilled from 76 to 8 network evaluations.
AI.result: Median time per asset falls from 133 s to 4.05 s on one H200 GPU at the same export settings (33x). On 2,653 held-out Toys4K objects, every input-view normal metric of the Pixal3D protocol improves, with a slightly lower mean silhouette IoU, lower point-cloud alignment scores and less fine texture detail. The rebuilt post-processing alone speeds up TRELLIS.2 by 6.7x without a detectable change in the evaluated metrics.
AI.conclusion: Most end-to-end latency lies outside the networks, so optimizing post-processing gives large speedups at a modest quality trade-off.

title: What Limits Thermal Infrared Drone Detection? A Cross-Dataset Benchmark Analysis
comment: Accepted at 2027 IEEE/CVF Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision Workshops (WACVW), Workshop "Real World Surveillance: Applications and Challenges, 7th"
summary: Thermal infrared (IR) imaging enables drone detection with reduced dependence on ambient illumination, supporting continuous surveillance beyond the limitations of visible-spectrum sensing. However, substantial and often undocumented variability in camera systems, processing pipelines, and annotation practices across public IR drone datasets complicates the assessment of detector performance and cross-domain generalization. To examine these sources of variability and their implications for drone detection, we systematically characterize existing IR datasets and establish an artifact taxonomy reflecting their origins across the acquisition and processing pipeline, encompassing optical and sensor effects, tone mapping and image enhancement, and recording-related artifacts. Focusing on long-wave IR data, we investigate the impact of training data composition and model characteristics on YOLO-based detection performance, generalization, and condition-dependent failure modes. Our results demonstrate that detection performance is governed more strongly by training data composition than by YOLO generation or model capacity, while cross-dataset generalization exhibits pronounced asymmetries. Even the best-performing configuration fails to detect over 40\% of drones, with elevated miss rates for very small targets, cluttered urban backgrounds, and thermal crossover, highlighting the shortcomings of existing datasets.

AI.tldr: A cross-dataset analysis of long-wave infrared drone detection finds that training data composition matters more than YOLO generation or model capacity, and even the best configuration fails to detect over 40% of drones.
AI.motivation: Public IR drone datasets vary in camera systems, processing pipelines and annotation practices in undocumented ways, which complicates assessing detector performance and cross-domain generalization.
AI.method: An artifact taxonomy covers optical and sensor effects, tone mapping and image enhancement, and recording-related artifacts across the acquisition and processing pipeline of existing IR datasets. Focusing on long-wave IR data, the authors study how training data composition and model characteristics affect YOLO-based detection, generalization and condition-dependent failure modes.
AI.result: Detection performance is governed more strongly by training data composition than by YOLO generation or model capacity, and cross-dataset generalization shows pronounced asymmetries. Even the best configuration fails to detect over 40% of drones, with higher miss rates for very small targets, cluttered urban backgrounds and thermal crossover.
AI.conclusion: The shortcomings of existing datasets limit thermal drone detection, so training data composition is the key lever.

title: From Foundation VLM to Versatile Driving VLM: A Triplet Incremental Training Approach
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. Accepted at the 10th Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL 2026)
summary: Adapting general Vision-Language Models (VLMs) to Autonomous Driving (AD) is thought to require heavy 3D spatial priors or intrusive architectural overhauls to compensate for a lack of spatial grounding. In this work, we present a counterintuitive pilot study: off-the-shelf general VLMs already exhibit remarkable adaptability across diverse driving tasks, while precise metric depth remains the primary missing link, a bottleneck readily addressable via onboard sensors and depth foundation models. To this end, we introduce the Triplet Incremental Training Framework, a non-intrusive paradigm that seamlessly instills 3D geometric awareness into a general VLM backbone while fully preserving its open-world capabilities. Driven by automatically constructed (image, depth, QA pair) triplets, our framework operates via a unified tri-stream training pipeline: an unfrozen primary VLM stream to adapt to driving tasks, an auxiliary depth stream that guides the visual backbone to implicitly imagine 3D scene geometry via explicit geometric constraints, and a frozen twin VLM stream employing logit-level KL distillation to prevent semantic drift. Crucially, the auxiliary depth branch is discarded during deployment, ensuring the enhanced geometric awareness comes with zero inference overhead. We evaluate our framework across four major benchmarks targeting four diverse capabilities spanning 3D spatial perception, driving-oriented language reasoning, end-to-end planning, and general multimodal understanding. Our approach outperforms state-of-the-art driving VLMs, rivals domain-specific expert models in 3D perception, and successfully retains its original general reasoning capabilities. This demonstrates that Triplet Incremental Training offers a unified, deployment-ready paradigm for transforming general foundation models into robust driving intelligences.

AI.tldr: The Triplet Incremental Training Framework adds 3D geometric awareness to a general VLM for driving through depth-supervised training, discards the depth branch at deployment, and reports outperforming driving VLMs while retaining general reasoning.
AI.motivation: Adapting general VLMs to autonomous driving is thought to require heavy 3D priors or intrusive architectural changes, but a pilot study suggests general VLMs already adapt well, with metric depth as the main missing link.
AI.method: Automatically constructed (image, depth, QA pair) triplets train a tri-stream pipeline: an unfrozen primary VLM stream adapts to driving tasks; an auxiliary depth stream guides the visual backbone to implicitly model 3D geometry through explicit geometric constraints; and a frozen twin VLM stream uses logit-level KL distillation to prevent semantic drift. The depth branch is discarded at deployment.
AI.result: Evaluated on four major benchmarks covering 3D spatial perception, driving-oriented language reasoning, end-to-end planning and general multimodal understanding. The approach outperforms state-of-the-art driving VLMs, rivals domain-specific expert models in 3D perception and retains general reasoning; the abstract gives no numbers.
AI.conclusion: The framework is presented as a unified, deployment-ready route to turning general foundation models into driving systems with zero inference overhead.

title: Fog-FWL: A Large-Scale Full-Waveform LiDAR Dataset for Recovering Fog-Hidden Objects
summary: LiDAR is a core sensor for autonomous driving, yet it is highly vulnerable to fog. Fog scattering produces strong backscatter near the sensor and attenuates reflections from objects behind it, so weak object returns are often discarded by the peak detection that converts received signals into point clouds. Full-waveform LiDAR (FWL), which records the received optical signal before peak detection, retains these weak returns, but the lack of suitable data has prevented research on recovering fog-hidden objects from FWL. We present Fog-FWL, a dataset foundation for this task that consists of a real-world benchmark, Fog-FWL-Real, and a large-scale synthetic training set, Fog-FWL-Sim. Fog-FWL-Real contains 7,527 real foggy FWL frames from 8 scenes and 58 sequences, which is 579x larger than the only existing real foggy FWL data, together with histogram-level Object/Fog/Noise labels, 10,719 3D bounding boxes, and three difficulty levels defined by the attenuation of object reflections. Fog-FWL-Sim contains 12,000 frames generated by our physics-based simulator, Fog-FWL-Simulator, which integrates spatially heterogeneous fog density fields, time-resolved light transport including multiple scattering, and a photon-counting SPAD receiver model. The two subsets share the same sensor format and annotation protocol, enabling a strict sim-to-real evaluation in which no real waveforms are used for training. Our analysis shows that, under the hardest condition, object returns are included in the three strongest peaks for only 34.9% of object rays, underscoring the need for waveform-level recovery. Fog-FWL-Real, Fog-FWL-Sim, and the Fog-FWL-Simulator will be publicly released to facilitate research on fog-robust LiDAR perception.

AI.tldr: Fog-FWL is a dataset foundation for recovering fog-hidden objects from full-waveform LiDAR, pairing a real foggy benchmark with a large physics-based synthetic training set for strict sim-to-real evaluation.
AI.motivation: Fog backscatter and attenuation cause weak object returns to be discarded by peak detection, and although full-waveform LiDAR retains them, suitable data for research has been lacking.
AI.method: Fog-FWL-Real has 7,527 real foggy FWL frames from 8 scenes and 58 sequences, with histogram-level Object/Fog/Noise labels, 10,719 3D bounding boxes and three difficulty levels. Fog-FWL-Sim has 12,000 frames from a physics-based simulator with spatially heterogeneous fog density fields, time-resolved light transport including multiple scattering, and a photon-counting SPAD receiver model. Both subsets share the same sensor format and annotation protocol.
AI.result: Fog-FWL-Real is 579 times larger than the only existing real foggy FWL data. Under the hardest condition, object returns are among the three strongest peaks for only 34.9% of object rays. No real waveforms are used for training in the sim-to-real evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The results underscore the need for waveform-level recovery, and the datasets and simulator will be released to support fog-robust LiDAR perception.

title: PhysLoop: Harnessing LLMs' Physics Awareness for Self-Improving Video Generation Models
summary: Video generation models produce visually realistic videos but still struggle with physical dynamics and causal consistency. Learning from generated videos requires fine-grained physical supervision, yet reliable quality judgments, correction pairs, and controlled variations are difficult to obtain. Large language models (LLMs) possess physical knowledge, but struggle to reliably guide video generation models in producing their training videos. We present PhysLoop, a unified harness designed to support physically grounded self-improvement in video generation models. The harness guides and constrains LLMs throughout video generation, selection, and correction, distilling their physical knowledge into physically consistent videos. The framework supports controllable training-data construction and inference-time video repair. By identifying and correcting failures, PhysLoop marks a key milestone toward recursive self-improvement (RSI) in video generation models with limited human intervention. We release 100K videos spanning diverse, realistic indoor and outdoor scenes, along with generation tools and two evaluation datasets: PhysLoop-Gen and PhysLoop-Repair. We evaluate controllable generation and localized repair on these datasets, respectively, and assess physical behavior on the external Physics-IQ Verified benchmark.

AI.tldr: PhysLoop is a harness that constrains LLMs to guide video generation, selection and correction, enabling physically grounded self-improvement of video generation models, with 100K videos released.
AI.motivation: Generated videos still struggle with physical dynamics and causal consistency, and fine-grained physical supervision such as quality judgments, correction pairs and controlled variations is hard to obtain, while LLMs' physical knowledge does not reliably guide video generation.
AI.method: A unified harness guides and constrains LLMs throughout video generation, selection and correction, distilling their physical knowledge into physically consistent videos. It supports controllable training-data construction and inference-time video repair.
AI.result: 100K videos across diverse indoor and outdoor scenes are released, with generation tools and two evaluation datasets (PhysLoop-Gen and PhysLoop-Repair). Controllable generation and localized repair are evaluated on these datasets, and physical behavior is assessed on the external Physics-IQ Verified benchmark; the abstract gives no numbers.
AI.conclusion: Identifying and correcting failures is presented as a milestone toward recursive self-improvement of video generation models with limited human intervention.

title: ORCA:Orthogonal Residual Consensus Alignment for Multi-View Clustering
summary: Deep multi-view clustering often suffers from redundant information accumulation during fusion and indiscriminate alignment across representation levels. We propose Orthogonal Residual Consensus Alignment (ORCA) to address these challenges. Its semantic incremental recurrent fusion module extracts cross-view orthogonal residuals as non-redundant increments and adaptively weights recurrent states through divergence-guided gating. Its consensus-calibrated hierarchical contrastive alignment module uses the global consensus to weight contrastive alignment of view-level, pairwise, and recurrent representations. Together, these modules balance view-specific structure with cross-view consistency. Experiments on five benchmarks against fifteen competing methods demonstrate ORCA's effectiveness, including a 5.25 percent accuracy improvement over the strongest baseline on 100leaves. Ablation studies validate both modules. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: ORCA is a deep multi-view clustering method that reduces redundant fusion through orthogonal residual increments and aligns views using global consensus, reporting a 5.25 percent accuracy gain over the strongest baseline on 100leaves.
AI.motivation: Deep multi-view clustering accumulates redundant information during fusion and aligns representations indiscriminately across representation levels.
AI.method: A semantic incremental recurrent fusion module extracts cross-view orthogonal residuals as non-redundant increments and adaptively weights recurrent states through divergence-guided gating. A consensus-calibrated hierarchical contrastive alignment module uses the global consensus to weight contrastive alignment of view-level, pairwise and recurrent representations.
AI.result: Across five benchmarks against fifteen competing methods, including a 5.25 percent accuracy improvement over the strongest baseline on 100leaves; ablations validate both modules.
AI.conclusion: The two modules together balance view-specific structure with cross-view consistency; the abstract states that code is available.

title: Efficient Periocular Recognition through Model Scaling and Cross Spectral VIS NIR Verification
comment: Munuscript In revision Process, abstract limited to 1920 ch
summary: Periocular recognition offers an efficient alternative to full-face verification when facial regions are occluded or image resolution is limited. We present AdaEye, a systematic study of input and backbone scaling for periocular verification in visible-spectrum (VIS) and cross-spectral (VIS/NIR) settings. Using an AdaFace-style framework, we compare full-face, masked-face, and dedicated 80x40 periocular inputs while varying backbone width and embedding dimensionality. Across four VIS/VIS and VIS/NIR protocols, we assess verification accuracy, computational cost, inference throughput, training memory, template size, and training stability.
