Direct periocular processing reduces recognition cost from 6.30 to 1.64 GMACs per image and increases measured throughput by approximately threefold. Its effectiveness depends on the evaluation protocol: periocular models perform better on native UFPR periocular images, whereas face-based protocols favor retaining more input information. Moderate backbone width reductions maintain comparable mean verification performance on CASIA and ND-NIVL while reducing computation. Embedding compression decreases template-storage requirements, primarily benefiting deployment. Multi-seed experiments reveal that some configurations require numerical stabilization, particularly when embedding and backbone reductions are combined. These findings support selecting compact periocular architectures according to the target protocol and deployment constraints, balancing accuracy, efficiency, storage, and robustness.

AI.tldr: AdaEye is a systematic study of input and backbone scaling for periocular verification, showing that periocular inputs cut recognition cost from 6.30 to 1.64 GMACs per image, with effectiveness depending on the evaluation protocol.
AI.motivation: Periocular recognition offers an efficient alternative to full-face verification when facial regions are occluded or image resolution is limited, and its trade-offs in visible and cross-spectral settings need to be understood.
AI.method: Using an AdaFace-style framework, the authors compare full-face, masked-face and dedicated 80x40 periocular inputs while varying backbone width and embedding dimensionality. Four VIS/VIS and VIS/NIR protocols are used to assess verification accuracy, computational cost, inference throughput, training memory, template size and training stability.
AI.result: Direct periocular processing reduces cost from 6.30 to 1.64 GMACs per image and raises measured throughput about threefold. Periocular models perform better on native UFPR periocular images, while face-based protocols favor retaining more input information. Moderate backbone width reductions keep mean verification comparable on CASIA and ND-NIVL. Embedding compression reduces template storage, and some configurations need numerical stabilization when embedding and backbone reductions are combined.
AI.conclusion: Compact periocular architectures should be selected according to the target protocol and deployment constraints, balancing accuracy, efficiency, storage and robustness.

title: Evaluating Video LLMs' Understanding of Corner Cases in Autonomous Driving
summary: Natural language explanations promised by modern Video Large Language Models (Video LLMs) offer autonomous driving systems a path toward detailed scene description and interpretable decision making on the road. While recent benchmarks have begun assessing these models on driving scenes, they mainly target routine traffic conditions and general comprehension tasks based on existing driving datasets and therefore fail to evaluate model performance on the rarest and most safety-critical driving events, also known as "corner cases". To provide a comprehensive evaluation of Video LLMs on precisely these scenarios, we introduce DashBench, a benchmark testing 25 Video LLMs on 1,709 carefully curated driving videos spanning not only collision-related corner cases but also rare non-collision ones. Through extensive prompts and open-ended question answering, we expose a critical capability gap: all evaluated models perform substantially below the threshold required for safety-critical driving applications, frequently misjudging or missing dangerous events on the road ahead and hallucinating non-existent agents or actions in their explanations. We believe DashBench, combining an extensive dataset with a rigorous evaluation toolkit and a detailed diagnosis of current model limitations, drives progress toward safer, more explainable autonomous driving systems. The code and data will be shared at: this http URL

AI.tldr: DashBench is a benchmark of 1,709 driving videos for testing 25 Video LLMs on collision and rare non-collision corner cases; all evaluated models fall well below the level required for safety-critical driving.
AI.motivation: Existing driving benchmarks mainly target routine traffic and general comprehension, so they fail to evaluate model performance on rare, safety-critical corner cases.
AI.method: DashBench tests 25 Video LLMs on 1,709 curated driving videos spanning collision-related and rare non-collision corner cases, using extensive prompts and open-ended question answering, with a rigorous evaluation toolkit.
AI.result: All evaluated models perform substantially below the threshold required for safety-critical applications, often misjudging or missing dangerous events and hallucinating non-existent agents or actions in their explanations.
AI.conclusion: Combining the dataset, the evaluation toolkit and the diagnosis of model limitations is intended to drive progress toward safer, more explainable driving systems.

title: EG360: Efficient and Generalizable $360^\circ$ Depth Estimation via Adaptive Panorama-Perspective Distillation and Spherical Cross-Level Feature Fusion
summary: Generalized panorama depth estimation has witnessed great advances in recent years. These methods typically achieve robust zero-shot generalization performance using large pretrained models, but their high computational cost makes real-time inference on embedded platforms challenging. In contrast, previous lightweight panorama models have mostly been developed for single-domain evaluations and cannot generalize well due to domain shifts. To reduce the gap between these two types of models, we introduce EG360, an efficient and generalizable panorama depth estimation model. Specifically, building on a lightweight depth model, we design an Adaptive Panorama-Perspective Distillation (APPD) strategy guided by scene geometry, along with a Spherical Cross-Level Feature Fusion (SCFF) module for global semantic perception. As a result, with only 6.593M parameters after reparameterization, EG360 achieves strong zero-shot performance on real-world benchmarks and runs at 35 FPS on a Jetson Orin NX 16GB in MAXN mode, whereas a previous ViT-small model runs at less than 2 FPS. Our code will also be made public for future research.

AI.tldr: EG360 is an efficient, generalizable 360-degree depth estimation model with 6.593M parameters after reparameterization, running at 35 FPS on a Jetson Orin NX 16GB while achieving strong zero-shot performance on real-world benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Large pretrained panorama depth models generalize well but are too computationally costly for real-time embedded inference, while previous lightweight panorama models were developed for single domains and generalize poorly under domain shift.
AI.method: Built on a lightweight depth model, EG360 uses an Adaptive Panorama-Perspective Distillation (APPD) strategy guided by scene geometry and a Spherical Cross-Level Feature Fusion (SCFF) module for global semantic perception.
AI.result: 6.593M parameters after reparameterization; strong zero-shot performance on real-world benchmarks; 35 FPS on a Jetson Orin NX 16GB in MAXN mode, whereas a previous ViT-small model runs at less than 2 FPS.
AI.conclusion: The model narrows the gap between generalizable large panorama models and lightweight ones suited to embedded platforms; code will be made public.

title: Kosmo-GFM: A Production-Ready Geometry Foundation Model
summary: We present Kosmo-GFM, a scene reconstruction system that integrates a geometry foundation model (GFM), a pose optimization engine (PoseEngine), and reconstruction-derived supervision from KosmoWorld. GFM predicts camera parameters, depth, cross-view correspondences, and dynamic 3D points from images and videos. PoseEngine combines these predictions with geometric optimization to recover scene-level camera poses and geometry for downstream 3D and 4D Gaussian Splatting. KosmoWorld generates images and geometric supervision from reconstructed real-world scenes to improve GFM's geometric predictions. On the Sparse and Medium subsets of SpatialBench, GFM achieves the lowest absolute relative depth error and the highest relative-pose AUC at 5 degrees among the compared methods. It also achieves the lowest mean endpoint errors for dynamic points and scene flow across the five evaluated datasets. Across 34 scenes completed by all compared reconstruction systems, PoseEngine achieves the highest scene-averaged pose AUC at thresholds of 1, 3, and 5 degrees, with a cumulative runtime of 14.07 hours, approximately 20% of GLUEMAP's 69.67 hours. PoseEngine Flash provides a further accuracy-efficiency trade-off, with a measured mixed-precision runtime of 2.62 hours, approximately 4% of GLUEMAP's runtime. Separate scaling experiments show generally favorable trends with increased data, model computation, and training budgets. These results support the use of learned geometric priors within a scene-level reconstruction pipeline.

AI.tldr: Kosmo-GFM is a scene reconstruction system combining a geometry foundation model, a pose optimization engine and reconstruction-derived supervision, reporting the best depth error and pose AUC on SpatialBench subsets at about 20% of GLUEMAP's runtime.
AI.motivation: Scene-level reconstruction for downstream 3D and 4D Gaussian Splatting needs accurate camera poses and geometry recovered from images and videos.
AI.method: The geometry foundation model (GFM) predicts camera parameters, depth, cross-view correspondences and dynamic 3D points. PoseEngine combines these predictions with geometric optimization to recover scene-level camera poses and geometry. KosmoWorld generates images and geometric supervision from reconstructed real-world scenes to improve GFM's predictions.
AI.result: On the Sparse and Medium subsets of SpatialBench, GFM achieves the lowest absolute relative depth error and the highest relative-pose AUC at 5 degrees. It also achieves the lowest mean endpoint errors for dynamic points and scene flow across five datasets. Across 34 scenes, PoseEngine achieves the highest scene-averaged pose AUC at 1, 3 and 5 degrees, with a cumulative runtime of 14.07 hours against 69.67 hours for GLUEMAP; PoseEngine Flash runs in 2.62 hours at mixed precision.
AI.conclusion: The results support using learned geometric priors within a scene-level reconstruction pipeline, and separate scaling experiments show generally favorable trends.

title: Visual Cipher Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Visual Reasoning
summary: While language-model agents excel at long-horizon coding and terminal tasks, this success relies on two conditions: explicit text specifications and immediate execution feedback. However, neither condition holds in real-world problems where critical information exists only in images, leaving it unclear whether long-horizon capability transfers from text to visual reasoning. In such visual settings, because rules and clues resist text transcription and lack test-case feedback, agents must repeatedly inspect images, simulate spatial transformations, and autonomously cross-check clues. Despite this challenge, existing evaluations fail to capture such capability: visual reasoning benchmarks largely reduce tasks to single-turn, short-chain question answering, whereas agent benchmarks focus on text-based environments or interactive states that permit trial-and-error. To bridge this gap, we introduce Visual Cipher Bench, a collection of 40 original visual puzzles across four categories: spatial manipulation and simulation, logical constraints and planning, rule induction, and knowledge-based decoding. Each puzzle provides only one to three black-and-white line drawings and a minimal submission instruction, requiring agents to discover the underlying solving mechanism entirely from the images. Across 29 reasoning-effort configurations of eight frontier models, even the strongest model, GPT-6 Astra (max), achieves only 26.7% accuracy, while five of the eight models score below 1%. Yet on a ten-task subset, providing a single non-spoiler mechanism hint boosts accuracy from 7.8% to 55.6%. This sharp contrast shows that the primary bottleneck of current agents lies not in executing multi-step plans, but in autonomously discovering rules from visual evidence. Visual Cipher Bench thus provides a rigorous benchmark for measuring long-horizon visual reasoning in agents.

AI.tldr: Visual Cipher Bench tests LLM agents on 40 visual puzzles that require discovering rules from black-and-white line drawings; the strongest model reaches 26.7% accuracy, and a single mechanism hint raises accuracy on a ten-task subset from 7.8% to 55.6%.
AI.motivation: Agent benchmarks rely on explicit text specifications and immediate execution feedback, while real problems often place critical information only in images, and visual reasoning benchmarks reduce tasks to single-turn, short-chain question answering.
AI.method: 40 original visual puzzles in four categories (spatial manipulation and simulation, logical constraints and planning, rule induction, knowledge-based decoding), each giving one to three black-and-white line drawings and a minimal submission instruction. Evaluation covers 29 reasoning-effort configurations of eight frontier models.
AI.result: The strongest model, GPT-6 Astra (max), achieves 26.7% accuracy, and five of the eight models score below 1%. On a ten-task subset, a single non-spoiler mechanism hint boosts accuracy from 7.8% to 55.6%.
AI.conclusion: The primary bottleneck for current agents is autonomously discovering rules from visual evidence rather than executing multi-step plans.

title: Raysemble: Metric 3D Bone Reconstruction from a Single X-ray
summary: Raysemble reconstructs eight lumbar and pelvic bones from a single X-ray by separating shape and placement. Each 3D query samples regional and global features at its image projection. A shared decoder predicts normalized bone shapes. Predicted depth and camera geometry determine 3D centers and scales for resampling these shapes onto a common grid in millimeters. Evaluation uses 23 held-out patients with 43 CT scans, each generating one simulated anteroposterior radiograph. Without rigid alignment to CT,Raysemble leads 15 evaluated methods, averaging 65.24% Dice, 9.09 mm HD95, and 3.32 mm ASSD over three random seeds. With identical inputs, it improves Dice over VolumeNeRF by 5.86 percentage points.

AI.tldr: Raysemble reconstructs eight lumbar and pelvic bones in metric 3D from a single X-ray by separating shape from placement, and leads 15 evaluated methods, averaging 65.24% Dice and 9.09 mm HD95 without rigid alignment to CT.
AI.motivation: Reconstructing metric 3D bone geometry from one X-ray requires both the shape of each bone and where it sits in space; the abstract does not describe the limitations of prior methods.
AI.method: Each 3D query samples regional and global features at its image projection. A shared decoder predicts normalized bone shapes. Predicted depth and camera geometry determine 3D centers and scales, which are used to resample the shapes onto a common grid in millimeters.
AI.result: Evaluated on 23 held-out patients with 43 CT scans, each generating one simulated anteroposterior radiograph. Without rigid alignment to CT, Raysemble leads 15 evaluated methods, averaging 65.24% Dice, 9.09 mm HD95 and 3.32 mm ASSD over three random seeds. With identical inputs, it improves Dice over VolumeNeRF by 5.86 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Separating shape from placement enables metric 3D bone reconstruction from a single X-ray; the abstract does not discuss clinical utility.

title: TokenStream: Multi-Subject Personalized Video Generation with Token-wise LoRA and Guided Attention
summary: We introduce TokenStream, an optimization-based framework that composes independently learned subject identities in text-to-video generation without a reference-video training dataset or joint optimization of each new subject combination. Learning from a single reference image makes subject appearance difficult to separate from static-image bias, while merging independently trained adapters can mix identities. Token-wise LoRA (ToRA) restricts low-rank updates to the cross-attention value projections of subject-associated text tokens, providing a separate adaptation path for each subject. A T2V-guided stream copies queries and keys from the frozen base model during early denoising to reuse its layout and motion priors while retaining personalized values. We also introduce Multi-DB, a 30-subject, 122-prompt benchmark with appearance-free prompts and varied interactions. On Multi-DB at 1.3B, TokenStream improves identity preservation from 0.422 for DreamBooth to 0.467 and textual alignment from 0.652 to 0.688.

AI.tldr: TokenStream composes independently learned subject identities in text-to-video generation without a reference-video dataset or joint optimization, improving identity preservation over DreamBooth on the Multi-DB benchmark.
AI.motivation: Learning from a single reference image makes subject appearance hard to separate from static-image bias, and merging independently trained adapters can mix identities.
AI.method: Token-wise LoRA (ToRA) restricts low-rank updates to the cross-attention value projections of subject-associated text tokens, giving each subject a separate adaptation path. A T2V-guided stream copies queries and keys from the frozen base model during early denoising to reuse its layout and motion priors while keeping personalized values.
AI.result: On Multi-DB at 1.3B (30 subjects, 122 prompts), identity preservation improves from 0.422 for DreamBooth to 0.467, and textual alignment from 0.652 to 0.688.
AI.conclusion: Token-wise adaptation combined with guided attention allows personalized subjects to be composed in video generation without joint optimization.

title: Automated PD-L1 Tumor Proportion Scoring with Uncertainty-Guided Triage in Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer
comment: 55 pages (29-page main text with 5 figures and 3 tables, followed by 26 pages of supplementary material)
summary: Programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) tumor proportion score (TPS) informs immunotherapy selection in non-small cell lung cancer. Near the 1% and 50% cutoffs, the score should also indicate when closer review is warranted. We designed a three-stage framework to follow the sequence of TPS assessment. Stage 1 identifies tumor regions and excludes macrophage-rich patches. Stage 2, a dual-branch cell counting network (D2Count-Net), counts PD-L1-positive and PD-L1-negative tumor cells in these regions to calculate TPS. Stage 3, TPS-Guard, an uncertainty-guided triage mechanism, reports model uncertainty as the disagreement among independently trained models, refers the most uncertain slides, and flags scores near the 1% or 50% cutoff when model estimates disagree across that cutoff. Flags state the reason for referral or alert the pathologist to possible scoring errors on auto-reported slides. In a retrospective, single-center study, 154 whole-slide images were scored by three pathologists, and the model and each pathologist were compared in turn with the mean of the other two. On the 114 slides unseen in training, model mean absolute error (MAE) was 6.96 percentage points, within the range of the three pathologists (4.24 to 8.29), and model uncertainty correlated with absolute TPS error (Spearman rho = 0.77) and inter-pathologist disagreement (rho = 0.71). After referral of the 15% most uncertain slides, model and pathologist MAE both decreased. Applied without retraining to an external, publicly available dataset, TPS-Guard still directed review to higher-error cases, and referring more uncertain cases raised sensitivity at the 50% cutoff. TPS-Guard provides reasons for reviewing individual automated scores and identifies slides that also produce greater disagreement among pathologists. Prospective reader studies should assess TPS-Guard's effect on TPS reporting.

AI.tldr: A three-stage framework automates PD-L1 tumor proportion scoring in non-small cell lung cancer with uncertainty-guided triage; the model's mean absolute error on 114 unseen slides is 6.96 percentage points, within the pathologists' range of 4.24 to 8.29.
AI.motivation: The PD-L1 tumor proportion score informs immunotherapy selection, and scores near the 1% and 50% cutoffs should also indicate when closer review is warranted.
AI.method: Stage 1 identifies tumor regions and excludes macrophage-rich patches. Stage 2, a dual-branch cell counting network (D2Count-Net), counts PD-L1-positive and PD-L1-negative tumor cells to calculate the score. Stage 3, TPS-Guard, reports uncertainty as disagreement among independently trained models, refers the most uncertain slides, and flags scores near the 1% or 50% cutoff when model estimates disagree across that cutoff.
AI.result: In a retrospective single-center study of 154 whole-slide images scored by three pathologists, model MAE on the 114 unseen slides is 6.96 points. Uncertainty correlates with absolute score error (Spearman rho 0.77) and inter-pathologist disagreement (rho 0.71). After referral of the 15% most uncertain slides, model and pathologist MAE both decrease. On an external public dataset without retraining, TPS-Guard still directs review to higher-error cases and referring more uncertain cases raises sensitivity at the 50% cutoff.
AI.conclusion: TPS-Guard gives reasons for reviewing individual automated scores and identifies slides that also produce greater pathologist disagreement; prospective reader studies should assess its effect on reporting.

title: Report of the 8th LSVOS Challenge: Mobile Unified Multimodal Understanding
comment: 13 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Report of the MUMU track of the 8th LSVOS Challenge, held in conjunction with ECCV 2026. Project page: this https URL
summary: This report summarizes the Mobile Unified Multimodal Understanding (MUMU) track of the 8th Large-scale Video Object Segmentation (LSVOS) Challenge, held in conjunction with ECCV 2026. MUMU asks for a single unified model that jointly performs multi-concept image tagging over quality, scene, and event vocabularies, open-vocabulary object detection, and concise image captioning, within a budget of 0.5B parameters and 8 GB of peak inference memory. Submissions are ranked by a weighted task score scaled by an efficiency factor. We describe the tasks, rules, and evaluation protocol, report the final results, and review the methods of the top three teams. All three leading solutions build on the compact Florence-2-base model, but extend it in different ways: lightweight tagging heads with cross-task inference refinement, a shared low-rank adapter trained on coverage-aware multi-source data with task-dependent decoding, and a training-free pipeline that maps captions to tags and applies detection test-time augmentation. The results show that a compact prompt-based vision-language model can serve all three outputs when supervision, decoding, and cross-task cues are designed for each task, while open-vocabulary detection on novel categories remains the main bottleneck.

AI.tldr: This report summarizes the Mobile Unified Multimodal Understanding track of the 8th LSVOS Challenge, where the top three teams all build on Florence-2-base and open-vocabulary detection of novel categories remains the main bottleneck.
AI.motivation: The report describes the track's tasks, rules and evaluation protocol under a budget of 0.5B parameters and 8 GB peak inference memory, and reports the final results.
AI.method: A single unified model must perform multi-concept image tagging over quality, scene and event vocabularies, open-vocabulary object detection and concise captioning; submissions are ranked by a weighted task score scaled by an efficiency factor. The top three teams used lightweight tagging heads with cross-task inference refinement, a shared low-rank adapter trained on coverage-aware multi-source data with task-dependent decoding, and a training-free pipeline mapping captions to tags with detection test-time augmentation.
AI.result: All three leading solutions build on the compact Florence-2-base model; the abstract gives no numeric scores.
AI.conclusion: A compact prompt-based vision-language model can serve all three outputs when supervision, decoding and cross-task cues are designed for each task, while open-vocabulary detection on novel categories remains the main bottleneck.

title: A Disease-specific Retinal Aging Biomarker for Predicting Progression to Late Age-related Macular Degeneration
summary: Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is a leading cause of irreversible vision loss in older adults. While chronological age is a primary risk factor, it inadequately reflects individual variations in retinal aging, limiting effective AMD risk stratification and timely intervention. Here, we propose and validate fundus-based AMD age (FAA), which quantifies disease-specific retinal aging in AMD and captures accelerated AMD-related retinal aging, thereby improving prognostic precision over chronological age. Trained on 36,782 images from 2,192 participants in the Age-Related Eye Disease Study (AREDS) dataset and validated across AREDS and AREDS2 cohorts, our model demonstrates significant improvements over traditional chronological age-based approaches. Specifically, integrating the proposed FAA into Cox proportional-hazards models significantly enhances prediction performance. FAA improved the C-index from 0.836 to 0.888 and reduced the 5-year Brier score from 0.050 to 0.046 in AREDS, with consistent gains observed in AREDS2 (C-index 0.715 to 0.756; 2-year Brier 0.078 to 0.076). FAA showed improved prognostic performance across the two datasets and under different phenotype definitions (reading center-defined vs. specialist-defined grading), supporting its potential utility for AMD risk stratification. These findings highlight the advantage of incorporating FAA into AMD risk prediction frameworks, supporting further evaluation of FAA for AMD risk stratification.

AI.tldr: Fundus-based AMD age (FAA), a disease-specific retinal aging biomarker, improves prediction of progression to late AMD over chronological age, raising the AREDS C-index from 0.836 to 0.888.
AI.motivation: Chronological age is a primary risk factor for age-related macular degeneration but inadequately reflects individual variation in retinal aging, which limits risk stratification and timely intervention.
AI.method: A model trained on 36,782 images from 2,192 AREDS participants quantifies disease-specific retinal aging. FAA is integrated into Cox proportional-hazards models and validated across the AREDS and AREDS2 cohorts.
AI.result: In AREDS, the C-index improves from 0.836 to 0.888 and the 5-year Brier score falls from 0.050 to 0.046. In AREDS2, the C-index rises from 0.715 to 0.756 and the 2-year Brier score changes from 0.078 to 0.076. Gains hold under reading-center-defined and specialist-defined phenotype definitions.
AI.conclusion: FAA may be useful for AMD risk stratification and merits further evaluation.

title: ElasticDino: Dense Semantic Features Using Elastic Deformations
summary: Vision transformers (ViTs) serve as the backbone for countless vision tasks, including dense prediction tasks, such as segmentation and depth estimation, even though the quadratic complexity of self-attention severely limits feature resolution and induces spatial artifacts. In this work, we introduce ElasticDino, a lightweight adapter which produces high-resolution feature maps, adhering to the fine details of the input image. As a key insight, we observe the consistency of artifacts across channels, and simultaneously resolve them to match the input image structure. Using a slim architecture based on spatial deformations, ElasticDino produces pixel-aligned, high-resolution feature maps efficiently. Leveraging deformations allows strictly preserving sharp semantics, and thereby avoiding the smoothness biases inherent to alternative approaches. Due to the absence of ground truth, we employ pixel-level semantic segmentation and depth estimation with linear heads to predict a set of downstream dense tasks, guiding the deformation process without leaking task-specific semantics into the model. We demonstrate superior accuracy over current methods on a range of popular dense task benchmarks, with better computational performance.

AI.tldr: ElasticDino is a lightweight adapter that uses elastic spatial deformations to produce high-resolution, pixel-aligned dense feature maps from vision transformers, reporting superior accuracy over current methods on popular dense benchmarks.
AI.motivation: The quadratic complexity of self-attention limits ViT feature resolution and induces spatial artifacts that hurt dense prediction tasks such as segmentation and depth estimation.
AI.method: A slim architecture based on spatial deformations resolves artifacts, which are consistent across channels, so that the feature maps match the input image structure. With no ground truth available, pixel-level semantic segmentation and depth estimation with linear heads guide the deformation without leaking task-specific semantics into the model.
AI.result: Superior accuracy over current methods on a range of popular dense task benchmarks, with better computational performance; the abstract gives no numbers.
AI.conclusion: Deformation-based features preserve sharp semantics without the smoothness biases of alternative approaches, providing efficient high-resolution dense features.

title: AURA 2.0: From User-Driven Responses to Model-Initiated Conversations in Streaming Video
summary: Most AI assistants respond only when prompted, remaining silent even when events in the video stream offer meaningful opportunities for conversation. To move beyond purely user-driven interaction, we present AURA 2.0, a streaming video large language model that introduces three core upgrades to AURA. The key advance is Model-Initiated Conversation (MIC), which enables the model to identify topics worth discussing in the evolving visual stream and initiate conversations at appropriate moments without a user query. Stream-Aware Tool Calling (SATC) enables the model to invoke external tools using the current visual and conversational context and incorporate returned information into the ongoing interaction. Interactive Visual Grounding (IVG) supports visual grounding in both user inputs and model outputs. The model can identify objects marked by users on video frames and produce frame-aligned bounding boxes to link its responses to specific objects and regions. To develop these capabilities, we construct a dedicated streaming interaction dataset and adopt a three-stage training scheme to integrate the new behaviors with AURA's existing streaming interaction abilities. We further incorporate Long-Horizon Interaction Memory (LHIM) to maintain contextual continuity over extended video streams. Evaluations on public streaming benchmarks show that AURA 2.0 achieves leading performance among open-source streaming models, while targeted evaluations further validate its new interaction capabilities. We open-source the model weights and inference code.

AI.tldr: AURA 2.0 is a streaming video LLM that initiates conversations without a user query, calls tools using the current stream context, and grounds objects in video frames, with model weights and inference code open-sourced.
AI.motivation: Most AI assistants respond only when prompted, remaining silent even when events in a video stream offer meaningful opportunities for conversation.
AI.method: Three upgrades to AURA: Model-Initiated Conversation (MIC), Stream-Aware Tool Calling (SATC) and Interactive Visual Grounding (IVG). A dedicated streaming interaction dataset is built, a three-stage training scheme integrates the new behaviors, and Long-Horizon Interaction Memory (LHIM) maintains contextual continuity over extended streams.
AI.result: AURA 2.0 achieves leading performance among open-source streaming models on public streaming benchmarks, and targeted evaluations validate its new interaction capabilities; the abstract gives no numbers.
AI.conclusion: The model weights and inference code are open-sourced.

title: Ropedia Xperience 2: A Gold Standard for Scaling Physical AI Environments and Behaviors
summary: Large foundation models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 have recently been shown to control robots directly from visual observations. They nevertheless remain brittle on long-horizon, contact-rich tasks in real-world environments. Further progress depends on two complementary resources: demonstrations of human behavior that supervise how tasks are performed, and interactive environments in which policies can be rolled out, evaluated, and improved in closed loop. Language models have advanced along well-characterized scaling laws; the corresponding question for physical AI is how capability scales with environments and behaviors, which first requires identifying which data to scale and how to produce and reuse such data continuously. To address this question, we introduce Ropedia Xperience 2, comprising 1,589 released metric-scale 3D scans and a collection of 4,230 egocentric recordings of 74 tasks (131 hours). We further show that each capture can be repurposed for robot learning: scenes are converted into physically interactive simulation environments, human motion is retargeted to whole-body robot trajectories, and additional robot behaviors are obtained through virtual teleoperation and automated long-horizon trajectory generation. We propose this joint capture of environments and behaviors as a gold standard for physical AI data collection, laying a data foundation for establishing scaling laws over environments and behaviors.

AI.tldr: Ropedia Xperience 2 is a dataset of 1,589 released metric-scale 3D scans and 4,230 egocentric recordings of 74 tasks (131 hours), proposed as a gold standard for jointly capturing environments and behaviors for physical AI.
AI.motivation: Foundation models remain brittle on long-horizon, contact-rich tasks in real-world environments, and progress depends on human demonstrations and interactive environments, but how capability scales with them is not yet characterized.
AI.method: Each capture is repurposed for robot learning: scenes are converted into physically interactive simulation environments, human motion is retargeted to whole-body robot trajectories, and additional robot behaviors come from virtual teleoperation and automated long-horizon trajectory generation.
AI.result: The release comprises 1,589 metric-scale 3D scans and 4,230 egocentric recordings of 74 tasks (131 hours); the abstract reports no policy performance numbers.
AI.conclusion: Joint capture of environments and behaviors is proposed as a gold standard for physical AI data collection, laying a data foundation for establishing scaling laws over environments and behaviors.

title: SALT: State-Aligned Low-Rank Transfer for Single-Temporal Cross-Dataset Structural Localization in Remote Sensing
comment: Accepted at the Third Workshop on Computer Vision for Geospatial Image Analysis (GeoCV), IEEE/CVF WACV 2027
summary: Change detection in remote sensing conventionally relies on spatially aligned bi-temporal imagery, which may be unavailable or unreliable in practical scenarios. Recent single-temporal approaches address this limitation by learning structural evidence, such as building regions, from a labeled source dataset and transferring it to unseen target imagery using only the current image. However, adaptation to the source dataset can over-specialize pretrained features and reduce their cross-dataset generalization, a risk that this paper argues is higher when the feature adaptation is parameterized independently of the states used for prediction. To address this issue, the current study introduces SALT, a State-Aligned Low-Rank Transfer framework. SALT keeps a DINOv3 backbone frozen and learns negative and positive structural states that both score each patch and, through State-Aligned Low-Rank Adaptation (SALA), span the rank-2 subspace in which patch features are corrected. Directional State Alignment supervises these corrections to raise the evidence of positive patches and lower that of negative ones, while Geometry Preservation limits changes to the pairwise relations among pretrained patch features. Experiments on LEVIR-CD and the WHU aerial building dataset show that, at the pixel level and in both transfer directions, SALT outperforms four baselines reproduced under a common source-only protocol, improving over the strongest reproduced baselines by 9.45 and 5.79 points in pixel-level AP and by 27.69 and 14.25 points in IoU (LEVIR-CD to WHU and WHU to LEVIR-CD, respectively), with only 0.068M trainable parameters and 40.2 ms per image. In order to facilitate reproducibility and further research, the source code of SALT is available at this https URL

AI.tldr: SALT is a single-temporal change detection framework that learns negative and positive structural states over a frozen DINOv3 backbone, outperforming four reproduced baselines in both LEVIR-CD and WHU transfer directions with 0.068M trainable parameters.
AI.motivation: Adapting to the source dataset can over-specialize pretrained features and reduce cross-dataset generalization, a risk the paper argues is higher when feature adaptation is parameterized independently of the states used for prediction.
AI.method: A DINOv3 backbone is kept frozen. Learned negative and positive structural states score each patch and, through State-Aligned Low-Rank Adaptation (SALA), span a rank-2 subspace in which patch features are corrected. Directional State Alignment supervises the corrections to raise the evidence of positive patches and lower that of negative ones, and Geometry Preservation limits changes to pairwise relations among pretrained patch features.
AI.result: At the pixel level and in both transfer directions, SALT improves over the strongest reproduced baselines by 9.45 and 5.79 points in pixel-level AP and by 27.69 and 14.25 points in IoU (LEVIR-CD to WHU and WHU to LEVIR-CD, respectively), with 0.068M trainable parameters and 40.2 ms per image.
AI.conclusion: State-aligned low-rank transfer can improve single-temporal cross-dataset structural localization with few trainable parameters; the source code is released.

title: Joint Null-Space Projection for Data-Free Model Merging
summary: Merging independently fine-tuned checkpoints into a single multi-task model requires no data, no labels, and no gradient steps. In practice the task vectors of different tasks interfere, and the standard remedies--averaging, magnitude pruning, sign election--operate entry by entry, ignoring that each delta induces a low-dimensional update on the hidden features it acts upon. We recast merging as a subspace interference problem. For every two-dimensional weight tensor we take the top-r right-singular subspace of each task's delta--the input directions along which that task moves the representation most--and remove from each task vector the component lying in the union of the other tasks' subspaces. The resulting Joint Null-Space Projection (JNSP) is closed-form and order-independent, needs no forward pass, and is defined entirely by the checkpoint set. On eight CLIP image-classification tasks JNSP merges ViT-B/16 experts to 89.45% average accuracy without using a single image, 11.88 points above the strongest parameter-wise training-free baseline (TIES-Merging, 77.57%), 14.22 above Task Arithmetic, and 0.98 above WUDI's data-free consensus merge (88.47%). The gain holds across three backbones on the independently trained TALL release (+10.8, +12.6, +9.1 over TIES for ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32, ViT-L/14) and replicates there at 89.20%; controls confirm the source--a single shared subspace instead of per-task ones loses 2.9 points, and a sequential variant collapses to 69.6%. On RoBERTa-large the same projection underperforms plain task arithmetic, which we report rather than hide. Code is available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Joint Null-Space Projection merges fine-tuned checkpoints without data by removing from each task vector the components lying in other tasks' top right-singular subspaces, reaching 89.45% average accuracy on eight CLIP image classification tasks.
AI.motivation: Task vectors interfere when merged, and standard entry-wise remedies (averaging, magnitude pruning, sign election) ignore that each task delta induces a low-dimensional update on the hidden features it acts upon.
AI.method: For every two-dimensional weight tensor, the top-r right-singular subspace of each task's delta is computed, and each task vector has the component lying in the union of the other tasks' subspaces removed. The projection is closed-form and order-independent, needs no forward pass, and is defined entirely by the checkpoint set.
AI.result: On eight CLIP image classification tasks, merging ViT-B/16 experts gives 89.45% average accuracy without any image, 11.88 points above TIES-Merging (77.57%), 14.22 above Task Arithmetic and 0.98 above WUDI's data-free consensus merge (88.47%). On the independently trained TALL release across three backbones, gains over TIES are +10.8, +12.6 and +9.1 for ViT-B/16, ViT-B/32 and ViT-L/14. A single shared subspace loses 2.9 points, and a sequential variant collapses to 69.6%. On RoBERTa-large the projection underperforms plain task arithmetic.
AI.conclusion: Subspace-aware merging is effective for CLIP vision models, though not uniformly, as the RoBERTa-large result shows; code is available.

title: TuMAP: A Dual-View, Morphotype-Aware Pathomics Pipeline for Quantifying Renal Tubular Remodeling
comment: 5 pages, 3 figures, 1 table. Submitted to IEEE ISBI 2027
summary: Quantifying disease-associated renal tubular remodeling is challenging because tubular appearances are heterogeneous. We introduce TuMAP (Tubular Morphotype-Aware Pathomics), a pipeline combining (1) dual-view foundation-model representations and provisional morphotype annotation, (2) compositional and within-morphotype pathomics, and (3) patient-level statistical inference. From 456,158 tubules in 358 PAS-stained kidney biopsy slides, TuMAP identified eight image-based morphotypes, seven of which showed stable subsampling assignments. Across 219 patients in six diagnostic groups, diabetic nephropathy (DN) and tubulointerstitial nephritis/acute tubular injury (TIN/ATI) each differed from minimal change disease in seven morphotype proportions, while IgA nephropathy differed in six. DN showed reduced nuclear solidity and increased eccentricity across all eight morphotypes. Area-normalized nuclear density exposed additional within-morphotype differences. TuMAP provides a framework for separating changes in tubular morphotype composition from phenotypic differences within morphotypes.

AI.tldr: TuMAP is a dual-view, morphotype-aware pathomics pipeline that identifies eight tubular morphotypes in PAS-stained kidney biopsies and tests patient-level differences in morphotype composition and within-morphotype nuclear features.
AI.motivation: Quantifying disease-associated renal tubular remodeling is challenging because tubular appearances are heterogeneous.
AI.method: The pipeline combines dual-view foundation-model representations with provisional morphotype annotation, compositional and within-morphotype pathomics, and patient-level statistical inference, applied to 456,158 tubules from 358 PAS-stained kidney biopsy slides.
AI.result: Eight image-based morphotypes were identified, seven of which showed stable subsampling assignments. Across 219 patients in six diagnostic groups, diabetic nephropathy (DN) and tubulointerstitial nephritis/acute tubular injury (TIN/ATI) each differed from minimal change disease in seven morphotype proportions, and IgA nephropathy in six. DN showed reduced nuclear solidity and increased eccentricity across all eight morphotypes.
AI.conclusion: The framework separates changes in tubular morphotype composition from phenotypic differences within morphotypes.

title: Predicting Ethanol Drinking Status from Nonhuman Primate Liver Histology: A Proof of Concept for Parameter-efficient Fine-tuning in Few-Shot Vision-Language Modeling
comment: 3 pages, 2 figures. Accepted for publication in the proceedings of IEEE BIBM 2026. The code is publicly available: this https URL
summary: Combining vision-language models (VLMs) with parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) offers a promising approach to few-shot whole-slide image (WSI) classification in computational pathology. This study evaluates this approach for predicting ethanol drinking status from nonhuman primate liver histology. Adapters are evaluated against non-PEFT configurations on a subset of the Monkey Alcohol Tissue Research Resource (MATRR). All evaluated PEFT configurations achieve higher mean balanced accuracy than the non-PEFT baselines. For example, in the four-shot setting, attention-based multiple instance learning (ABMIL) alone achieves 43.5% mean balanced accuracy, compared with 78.1% after adding an adapter. Qualitative attention analysis shows that textual pathway adaptations produce localized attention heatmaps, while visual pathway adaptations produce more diffuse ones. A pathologist's review identified similar histological features across adaptations.

AI.tldr: Adding parameter-efficient adapters to a vision-language model improves few-shot whole-slide image classification of ethanol drinking status from nonhuman primate liver histology; four-shot ABMIL rises from 43.5% to 78.1% mean balanced accuracy with an adapter.
AI.motivation: Combining VLMs with parameter-efficient fine-tuning is a promising approach to few-shot WSI classification in computational pathology, and this study tests it on nonhuman primate liver histology.
AI.method: Adapters are evaluated against non-PEFT configurations on a subset of the Monkey Alcohol Tissue Research Resource (MATRR), with attention-based multiple instance learning (ABMIL) as the classifier; textual and visual pathway adaptations are compared using attention heatmaps and pathologist review.
AI.result: All PEFT configurations achieve higher mean balanced accuracy than the non-PEFT baselines. In the four-shot setting, ABMIL alone achieves 43.5% mean balanced accuracy, compared with 78.1% after adding an adapter. Textual pathway adaptations produce localized attention heatmaps and visual pathway adaptations produce more diffuse ones, and a pathologist found similar histological features across adaptations.
AI.conclusion: The study is a proof of concept that PEFT of VLMs can support few-shot WSI classification in this setting.

title: STeP-C: Real-Time Neural Compression for Distributed Fiber-Optic Sensing at Scale
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027 (Applications Track). 10 pages, 9 figures, 3 tables
summary: Distributed fiber-optic sensing (DFOS) technologies such as Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) generate continuous, high-resolution spatio-temporal data at rates exceeding hundreds of megabytes per second, creating severe challenges for real-time storage and transmission. While neural compression methods can achieve strong rate-distortion performance on sensing data, prior approaches either require per-segment retraining incompatible with streaming, or have only been validated offline. None have been demonstrated end-to-end on a continuously streaming DAS acquisition system at scale. We present STeP-C (Spatio-Temporal Predictive Compression), a neural compression framework that decouples spatial encoding, temporal prediction, and entropy-optimized residual coding, trained end-to-end with a rate-distortion objective motivated by conditional entropy reduction. Critically, we identify entropy coding as the dominant bottleneck for streaming deployment. We address it through GPU-side symbol computation, cached probability tables, and parallel GIL-free arithmetic coding, together with FP16 inference and batched entropy coding, enabling a full real-time pipeline built around a GPU ring buffer. We validate this pipeline on a live DAS testbed, achieving a 98.85% file size reduction at 31.04 dB full-band PSNR and an average throughput of 535 MB/s, exceeding the 324 MB/s requirement for 1 kHz, 81 km DAS streams. We further show that STeP-C substantially outperforms conventional codecs at practical streaming bitrates, can be applied to unseen channel ranges within the same acquisition system without retraining, and largely maintains downstream detector consistency, with 96.62% high-confidence class agreement and 100% Jaccard similarity on detected event types.

AI.tldr: STeP-C is a neural compression framework for distributed acoustic sensing that runs in real time on a live testbed at 535 MB/s, exceeding the 324 MB/s needed for 1 kHz, 81 km streams, with a 98.85% file size reduction at 31.04 dB full-band PSNR.
AI.motivation: DAS generates continuous data at hundreds of megabytes per second, and prior neural compression methods either need per-segment retraining incompatible with streaming or have only been validated offline.
AI.method: STeP-C decouples spatial encoding, temporal prediction and entropy-optimized residual coding, trained end-to-end with a rate-distortion objective. Entropy coding is identified as the dominant bottleneck and addressed with GPU-side symbol computation, cached probability tables, parallel GIL-free arithmetic coding, FP16 inference and batched entropy coding, within a GPU ring buffer pipeline.
AI.result: 98.85% file size reduction at 31.04 dB full-band PSNR and average throughput of 535 MB/s, against a 324 MB/s requirement. STeP-C outperforms conventional codecs at practical streaming bitrates and can be applied to unseen channel ranges without retraining. Downstream detector consistency holds, with 96.62% high-confidence class agreement and 100% Jaccard similarity on detected event types.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline achieves real-time neural compression on a continuously streaming DAS system at scale while largely maintaining downstream detection consistency.

title: HiVE-VQA: Hierarchical Interaction via Volumetric Embedding for Video Quality Assessment
comment: Accepted to WACV 2027, 11 pages, 3 figures, 6 tables
summary: The proliferation of user-generated video content has made accurate and robust no-reference video quality assessment (NR-VQA) a highly important challenge. Existing research increasingly relies on architecturally complex multi-branch pipelines or computationally intensive fine-tuning of single-branch backbones. In this paper, we investigate whether a single frozen video foundation model can serve as an effective NR-VQA backbone, and propose HiVE-VQA, the first framework (to our knowledge) to apply a JEPA-based video encoder to this task. HiVE-VQA extracts token grids from multiple depths of a pre-trained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder and stacks them into a hierarchical spatio-temporal volume, which a compact 3D convolutional head fuses across its layer, spatial, and temporal axes, combining low-level distortion cues from shallow layers with the semantic and temporal context captured at greater depths. The encoder remains frozen throughout, so only the head is trained: 5.2M parameters (5.7\% of the total), with no auxiliary multi-modal models and an inference cost that is invariant to video resolution. Trained solely on LSVQ and evaluated without any fine-tuning, HiVE-VQA outperforms 17 state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in SROCC and PLCC on both intra-dataset (LSVQ-test, LSVQ-1080p) and cross-dataset (KoNViD-1k, LIVE-VQC) benchmarks. These results indicate that hierarchical, depth-wise fusion of features from a single frozen video foundation model provides a more effective and efficient basis for NR-VQA than task-specific multi-network fusion. Code and model checkpoints are available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: HiVE-VQA applies a frozen V-JEPA 2.1 encoder to no-reference video quality assessment, fusing hierarchical multi-depth token grids with a compact 3D convolutional head, and outperforms 17 state-of-the-art methods while trained only on LSVQ.
AI.motivation: No-reference VQA has relied on architecturally complex multi-branch pipelines or costly fine-tuning of single-branch backbones; the paper asks whether one frozen video foundation model can serve as an effective backbone.
AI.method: Token grids are extracted from multiple depths of a pretrained V-JEPA 2.1 encoder and stacked into a hierarchical spatio-temporal volume, which a compact 3D convolutional head fuses across its layer, spatial and temporal axes. Only the head is trained, with 5.2M parameters (5.7% of the total), and inference cost is invariant to video resolution.
AI.result: Trained solely on LSVQ without fine-tuning, HiVE-VQA outperforms 17 state-of-the-art methods in SROCC and PLCC on intra-dataset (LSVQ-test, LSVQ-1080p) and cross-dataset (KoNViD-1k, LIVE-VQC) benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical depth-wise fusion of a single frozen video foundation model is more effective and efficient than task-specific multi-network fusion for no-reference VQA.

title: SpotDiff: A Plug-and-Play Framework for Zero-Shot Change Detection in Remote Sensing Imagery
summary: Remote sensing change detection usually relies on large collections of temporally aligned, pixel-level annotations, which limits its scalability across regions, imaging platforms and application domains. Recent zero-shot approaches reduce the need for supervision, but they often localize fine-grained changes poorly because their features are coarse or inconsistent across time. We present SpotDiff, a training-free, plug-and-play framework for zero-shot change detection built by composing complementary vision foundation models. SpotDiff uses DINOv3 for semantically robust features, AnyUp to reconstruct them at pixel resolution, and SAM 3 for text-guided region-of-interest proposals, which an inference-time multi-scale strategy (SWIMS) makes reliable on small objects. Change is then measured by comparing the reconstructed features of the two dates inside the proposed regions, with no learnable components, fine-tuning or change labels. To our knowledge, SpotDiff is the first change detection method to use a universal feature upsampler, which alone adds 13.8 F1 over bilinear upsampling of the same features. On LEVIR-CD, SpotDiff reaches 82.46 F1, 2.06 points above the strongest prior training-free method, and on the multi-class SECOND benchmark it improves building change detection by 10.3 IoU and the six-class average by 2.2 IoU. Qualitative results on PlanetScope (3 m) and Sentinel-2 (10 m) imagery show that the same pipeline transfers across resolutions without modification. Our results indicate that composing modern foundation models is an effective route to scalable, label-free change detection.

AI.tldr: SpotDiff is a training-free framework for zero-shot change detection that composes DINOv3, AnyUp feature upsampling and SAM 3 region proposals, reaching 82.46 F1 on LEVIR-CD, 2.06 points above the strongest prior training-free method.
AI.motivation: Zero-shot change detection localizes fine-grained changes poorly because its features are coarse or inconsistent across time.
AI.method: DINOv3 provides semantically robust features, AnyUp reconstructs them at pixel resolution, and SAM 3 produces text-guided region-of-interest proposals, made reliable on small objects by an inference-time multi-scale strategy (SWIMS). Change is measured by comparing the reconstructed features of the two dates inside the proposed regions, with no learnable components, fine-tuning or change labels.
AI.result: 82.46 F1 on LEVIR-CD, 2.06 points above the strongest prior training-free method. On the multi-class SECOND benchmark, building change detection improves by 10.3 IoU and the six-class average by 2.2 IoU. The feature upsampler alone adds 13.8 F1 over bilinear upsampling. The pipeline transfers without modification to PlanetScope (3 m) and Sentinel-2 (10 m) imagery.
AI.conclusion: Composing modern foundation models is an effective route to scalable, label-free change detection.

title: Validation-Guided Prompt Selection for Differential Morphing Attack Detection
summary: Differential morphing attack detection (D-MAD) compares a trusted live capture with a document image that may contain a facial morph. We investigate whether labelled validation data can improve a frozen-parameter vision-language evaluator through prompt selection rather than model fine-tuning. Version~1 generates 50 candidate prompts and selects the top-ranked instruction using a security-oriented loss that prioritises missed morph attacks (MACER) while accounting for bona fide classification errors (BSCER), response failures, parse failures, and decision inconsistency. Version~2 recursively revises prompts using aggregate validation feedback. On a subject-disjoint test set of 160 pairs spanning LMA, MIPGAN-2, and PIPE, the selected Version~1 prompt achieves a (19.17\%) morph attack classification error rate (MACER), with (0.00\%) observed bona fide sample classification error rate (BSCER), compared with (70.00\%) MACER for a controlled manual prompt. The paired (50.83) percentage-point difference has a (95\%) subject-bootstrap interval of ([43.33,58.33]). Recursive revision does not surpass the best Generation~0 validation loss; the reported revised descendant obtains (31.67\%) test MACER. All 23 attacks missed by Version~1 are landmark-based (LMA) morphs. Overall, the results show that prompt formulation can substantially influence frozen-parameter VLM-based D-MAD performance, while also highlighting the challenge of recursive prompt refinement under a compact 10-subject validation setting.

AI.tldr: Selecting prompts with labelled validation data improves a frozen-parameter vision-language evaluator for differential morphing attack detection, cutting morph attack classification error from 70.00% for a manual prompt to 19.17% on a 160-pair test set.
AI.motivation: Differential morphing attack detection compares a trusted live capture with a document image that may contain a morph; the question is whether validation data can improve a frozen VLM through prompt selection rather than fine-tuning.
AI.method: Version 1 generates 50 candidate prompts and selects the top-ranked one using a security-oriented loss that prioritises missed morph attacks (MACER) while accounting for bona fide errors (BSCER), response failures, parse failures and decision inconsistency. Version 2 recursively revises prompts using aggregate validation feedback.
AI.result: On a subject-disjoint test set of 160 pairs spanning LMA, MIPGAN-2 and PIPE, the selected Version 1 prompt achieves 19.17% MACER and 0.00% observed BSCER, versus 70.00% MACER for a controlled manual prompt; the paired difference is 50.83 points with a 95% subject-bootstrap interval of [43.33, 58.33]. Recursive revision does not surpass the best Generation 0 validation loss; the reported revised descendant obtains 31.67% test MACER. All 23 attacks missed by Version 1 are LMA morphs.
AI.conclusion: Prompt formulation can substantially influence frozen-parameter VLM D-MAD performance, while recursive prompt refinement is challenging under a compact 10-subject validation setting.

title: Consensus Capture in Reference-Based UAV Video Stabilization: A Benchmark on Dynamic Urban Scenes
comment: 50 pages, 17 figures, 24 tables. Code at this https URL and data at this https URL and this https URL
summary: Reference-frame stabilization registers every frame of a hovering-drone video onto one reference frame, keeping object positions comparable. The registration pipelines it relies on are selected on feature-matching benchmarks in which only the camera moves. Over a busy intersection, vehicles moving together supply mutually consistent correspondences that can draw the robust homography estimate toward their motion: consensus capture, which inlier statistics cannot flag. A two-part benchmark measures it and the object masking meant to prevent it. A static protocol scores ten pipelines under exactly known homographies on 4K aerial frames, tuned on a site-disjoint split at a matched resolution and feature budget. A dynamic protocol scores them at an offline and a real-time budget on hovers selected from the video alone to span the amount and coherence of moving foreground, plus a stationary control. It measures background alignment, object position error and the share of a moving group's displacement an estimate follows, against a pseudo-ground-truth reference audited with manually annotated ground control points, which also score every candidate. On static scenes, tuned AKAZE, RootSIFT, SIFT and BRISK lead, retuning the matcher thresholds raises the mean average accuracy (mAA) by at most 0.0062, and masking costs less than 0.005. Unmasked ORB is captured on 28 of 304 real-time dynamic pairs and on 6 offline; its real-time captured estimates have a median corner error of 18.8 px yet typical inlier counts and ratios. Masking removes capture for every pipeline and leaves the leading pipelines unchanged. Code, data and results are released.

AI.tldr: A two-part benchmark shows that moving vehicles can pull robust homography estimates in reference-based UAV video stabilization ("consensus capture"), that unmasked ORB is captured on 28 of 304 real-time dynamic pairs, and that object masking removes this for every pipeline.
AI.motivation: Reference-frame stabilization of hovering-drone video relies on pipelines selected on feature-matching benchmarks where only the camera moves, so vehicles moving together can supply consistent correspondences that bias the homography, and inlier statistics cannot flag this.
AI.method: A static protocol scores ten pipelines under exactly known homographies on 4K aerial frames. A dynamic protocol scores them at offline and real-time budgets on hovers selected to span the amount and coherence of moving foreground, plus a stationary control, measuring background alignment, object position error and the share of a moving group's displacement that an estimate follows, against a pseudo-ground-truth audited with manually annotated ground control points.
AI.result: On static scenes, tuned AKAZE, RootSIFT, SIFT and BRISK lead; retuning matcher thresholds raises mAA by at most 0.0062, and masking costs less than 0.005. Unmasked ORB is captured on 28 of 304 real-time dynamic pairs and on 6 offline pairs, with a median corner error of 18.8 px despite typical inlier counts and ratios. Masking removes capture for every pipeline and leaves the leading pipelines unchanged.
AI.conclusion: Consensus capture is a real failure mode on dynamic urban scenes, and masking mitigates it without changing the leading pipelines; code, data and results are released.

title: eDMD: Endpoint Distribution Matching for Few-Step Diffusion Distillation
comment: Code Link: see this https URL
summary: Distribution matching distillation (DMD) has emerged as a leading paradigm for distilling diffusion models into few-step students, where an auxiliary fake score model tracks the student's distribution and the discrepancy between the teacher and fake predictions drives the student toward the teacher. In multi-step distillation, although only the student's final output is delivered, existing methods train the fake model on intermediate states or across all denoising steps. Consequently, the student's update signal becomes entangled with intermediate distributions, which can distort the matching direction and remain nonzero even after the student's final outputs already match the teacher distribution. To resolve this mismatch, we propose Endpoint Distribution Matching Distillation (eDMD), which trains a single shared fake model exclusively on the student's final outputs and uses it to correct every denoising step. Our theoretical analysis proves that this endpoint reference guarantees that the distribution matching term vanishes if and only if the student's final output distribution matches the teacher's, regardless of intermediate distributions. Beyond the fake reference, we further strengthen teacher supervision through a precise teacher (PT) that replaces single-step guided predictions with short multi-step trajectories on the final noise interval, paired with a calibrated query density for intermediate steps. Experiments on SD3-Medium, FLUX.2-klein (4B and 9B), and Qwen-Image-2.1 demonstrate that eDMD consistently outperforms existing distribution matching methods for 4-step generation.

AI.tldr: eDMD trains a single shared fake model only on the student's final outputs for distribution matching distillation, proves the matching term vanishes exactly when final output distributions match, and reports consistent gains for 4-step generation.
AI.motivation: In multi-step distribution matching distillation, existing methods train the fake model on intermediate states or across all denoising steps, so the student's update is entangled with intermediate distributions that can distort the matching direction and remain nonzero after final outputs already match.
AI.method: A single shared fake model is trained exclusively on the student's final outputs and used to correct every denoising step. A precise teacher (PT) replaces single-step guided predictions with short multi-step trajectories on the final noise interval, paired with a calibrated query density for intermediate steps.
AI.result: The theoretical analysis shows the distribution matching term vanishes if and only if the student's final output distribution matches the teacher's, regardless of intermediate distributions. Experiments on SD3-Medium, FLUX.2-klein (4B and 9B) and Qwen-Image-2.1 show that eDMD consistently outperforms existing distribution matching methods for 4-step generation.
AI.conclusion: The endpoint reference resolves the intermediate-distribution mismatch in multi-step distillation, improving few-step generation.

title: MALNISI-Infused Graph Construction and Weighted Contrastive Loss based GAT for Unsupervised Representation Learning in HSI
summary: Hyperspectral images (HSI) possess discriminating spectral characteristics with respect to land utilization due to high-dimensional information. Recently, unsupervised representation learning using graph neural networks has unveiled these utilization-specific complex spectral relations. This article has three main contributions. First, it proposes an index, the Mean Absolute Local Neighborhood Inverse Spectral Index (MALNISI), which measures the similarity between two pixels based on their neighborhood information. The index is used to construct a weighted adjacency matrix, giving the HSI a graph structure. Second, it proposes an upgraded Graph Attention Network that learns compact latent representations of hyperspectral data from the constructed graph. In this network, an enhanced multi-head attention mechanism incorporates the MALNISI weights as an auxiliary feature to emphasize learned attention between neighboring pixels. To alleviate over-smoothing and preserve fine-grained spectral details, the architecture integrates residual connections, skip projections, and feature normalization, which together enhance representation capability, stabilize learning, and accelerate convergence. Third, it proposes a weighted contrastive loss function that incorporates neighborhood-aware MALNISI between connected pixels, encouraging strongly connected pixels in the high-dimensional space to remain close in the latent space, and weakly connected pixels to stay apart. The resulting discriminative low-dimensional embeddings are then clustered using spectral clustering. Experimental analysis on six benchmark HSI datasets demonstrates the efficiency and necessity of the three aforementioned contributions, and the comparative study highlights superior performance over fourteen state-of-the-art approaches.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a pixel-similarity index (MALNISI) to turn a hyperspectral image into a weighted graph, then learns unsupervised pixel embeddings with an upgraded Graph Attention Network and a MALNISI-weighted contrastive loss, followed by spectral clustering. It reports superior results over fourteen state-of-the-art approaches on six benchmark HSI datasets.
AI.motivation: Hyperspectral images carry land-use-specific spectral relations, but unsupervised graph neural network methods have not exploited local neighborhood similarity in a way that captures them well, and deep graph models suffer from over-smoothing and loss of fine spectral detail.
AI.method: MALNISI, a neighborhood-based similarity index, defines a weighted adjacency matrix for the image graph. An enhanced multi-head GAT uses MALNISI weights as auxiliary attention features and adds residual connections, skip projections and feature normalization. A weighted contrastive loss pulls strongly connected pixels together and pushes weakly connected ones apart, and the embeddings are clustered with spectral clustering.
AI.result: Ablations on six benchmark HSI datasets show each of the three contributions is needed, and the method outperforms fourteen state-of-the-art approaches in the comparative study.
AI.conclusion: Neighborhood-aware graph construction combined with a weighted contrastive objective yields compact, discriminative unsupervised embeddings for hyperspectral clustering.

title: Objects as Addresses: Instance Binding in Vision Transformer Attention
summary: Humans naturally parse visual scenes into coherent individual objects rather than scattered features, a capability cognitive science calls object binding. While recent work shows that pretrained Vision Transformers (ViTs) intrinsically acquire this ability, how native self-attention computations mechanistically keep object instances separate remains unresolved. By studying this across eight pretrained ViTs, we found that instance separation is expressed more strongly in attention routing than in token content: selected query-key relations distinguish individual objects more reliably than value similarity or residual representations. Inside heads, patches belonging to one individual tend to read from a common image region, which we term their attention address. Visually distinct parts of one person share an address, whereas identical duplicated instances receive separate, movable addresses. These shared destinations arise in part because query interactions with the spatial structure of keys direct attention toward consistent regions for one object and elsewhere for another. In DINOv2 and most other backbones we tested, editing this query component at the selected head redirects its attention address toward another individual. Grouping patches by this query component separates same-category instances, reaching .615 FG-ARI versus .289 for the same clustering of final-layer features, which tend to merge them.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how pretrained Vision Transformers keep object instances separate inside self-attention, and finds that instance separation is carried more strongly by attention routing (query-key relations) than by token content. Editing the query component at a selected head redirects attention to a different individual in DINOv2 and most other tested backbones.
AI.motivation: Pretrained ViTs are known to acquire object binding, but the mechanism by which native self-attention keeps object instances separate has not been explained.
AI.method: Across eight pretrained ViTs, the authors compare instance separation in query-key attention routing, value similarity and residual token representations, identify per-head attention addresses shared by patches of one object, and intervene by editing the query component of a selected head.
AI.result: Query-key relations distinguish individual objects more reliably than value similarity or residual representations. Grouping patches by the query component reaches 0.615 FG-ARI for same-category instances, versus 0.289 for clustering final-layer features.
AI.conclusion: Instance binding in ViTs is implemented largely through attention routing, which gives a mechanistic handle to read and steer object-level grouping.

title: Consistent Video-to-Video Translation via Explicit Correspondences
comment: ECCV 2026. Project Website: this https URL
summary: Interactive video-to-video applications require real-time generation while maintaining long-range temporal consistency. However, recent methods achieve speed by restricting attention to a fixed-length causal window. This limits long-range consistency whenever relevant history falls outside the context window. To address this limitation, we introduce vid2vid-long, a correspondence-based approach grounded in a simple observation. Video-to-video translation provides an explicit cross-frame reference: the regions that match in the input video should match in the output video too. Concretely, we compute patch-level correspondences in the input, guiding retrieval of previously generated outputs in the corresponding regions, and condition the model on these patches through correspondence cross-attention. Our experiments demonstrate that vid2vid-long consistently improves long-range temporal consistency across recent video models while preserving generation quality and real-time performance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes vid2vid-long, a correspondence-based method for real-time video-to-video translation that keeps long-range temporal consistency beyond a fixed causal attention window. It matches patches between input frames and retrieves corresponding previously generated outputs as conditioning.
AI.motivation: Fast interactive video translation restricts attention to a fixed-length causal window, so consistency breaks when relevant history lies outside that window.
AI.method: Patch-level correspondences are computed in the input video. These guide retrieval of earlier generated outputs at matching regions, and the model is conditioned on those patches through correspondence cross-attention.
AI.result: The approach consistently improves long-range temporal consistency across several recent video models while preserving generation quality and real-time performance, according to the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Explicit cross-frame correspondences from the input provide an effective reference for long-range consistency in real-time video-to-video generation.

title: FLEX-LBP: Learning Local Binary Patterns with Exact Binary Inference for Texture Classification
comment: 21 pages, 5 figures, 8 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Local Binary Patterns (LBP) remain among the most widely used texture descriptors, from industrial inspection to medical imaging. Yet their radius, sampling angles, color transform and thresholds are fixed by hand for each dataset. We present FLEX-LBP, which learns these parameters by backpropagation while every forward pass computes exact binary codes and hard histogram counts. A straight-through estimator acts only in the backward pass, so the deployed descriptor is an interpretable hard-binary LBP with 90 learnable parameters and unchanged inference cost. In a controlled ablation on six color texture benchmarks, the component worth learning is dataset-dependent. One configuration, applied unchanged everywhere, learns the geometry and thresholds with the color transform frozen. It improves the nearest-neighbor accuracy of the identical fixed descriptor by 3.55 points on average over five seeds, significantly on five of six benchmarks and never significantly worse. With a linear discriminant readout, it gains 0.9 points; the fully learned descriptor gains 2.7 and has the highest mean. FLEX-LBP is more accurate than five classical LBP-family descriptors, PCANet and a neural LBP on five of six benchmarks. Its mean nearest-neighbor accuracy exceeds that of frozen ImageNet ResNet-50 features (23.5 million parameters). On the Kather colorectal cancer histology benchmark, the fully learned descriptor reaches 93.8%, significantly above the best classical descriptor (Completed LBP, 92.8%). The learned radii adapt in directions that recur across seeds. Noise drowns single-pixel comparisons and illuminant change flips inter-channel ones; median sampling or gray-world normalization restores 96-97%. The code is available as a drop-in PyTorch layer at this https URL.

AI.tldr: FLEX-LBP learns the parameters of Local Binary Patterns (radius, sampling angles, color transform, thresholds) by backpropagation while keeping exact binary codes and hard histograms in the forward pass, so the deployed descriptor remains an interpretable LBP with 90 learnable parameters. It improves over fixed LBP and several baselines on color texture benchmarks.
AI.motivation: LBP texture descriptors are widely used, but their parameters are hand-tuned for each dataset, and differentiable relaxations usually change the descriptor that is deployed.
AI.method: A straight-through estimator is used only in the backward pass, so forward computation stays exact binary LBP with hard histogram counts. Four variants are compared in a controlled ablation, in which the learned parts differ by dataset, and one configuration learns geometry and thresholds with the color transform frozen.
AI.result: The frozen-color configuration raises nearest-neighbor accuracy of the identical fixed descriptor by 3.55 points on average over five seeds, significant on five of six benchmarks. The fully learned descriptor reaches 93.8% on Kather colorectal histology versus 92.8% for Completed LBP, and its mean nearest-neighbor accuracy exceeds frozen ResNet-50 features.
AI.conclusion: Learning the LBP parameters yields gains without changing inference cost or interpretability, although the useful components depend on the dataset, and median sampling or gray-world normalization restores accuracy under noise or illuminant change.

title: Spatial Foundry: A Multimodal Dataset for Spatial Intelligence
summary: Spatial intelligence requires connecting visual observations to the geometry, objects, and persistent state of an environment. Images alone leave these relationships implicit, while disconnected annotations make it difficult to study appearance, camera motion, and scene changes under a common reference. We introduce Spatial Foundry, a collection of 5,280 furnished residential 3D scene configurations with editable assets and aligned visual, geometric, and temporal data. Its modalities include floor plans, perspective and panoramic RGB, metric depth, point clouds, meshes, instance-level 3D bounding boxes, and camera trajectories paired with video. Shared scene coordinates link observations across views and time; editable source scenes enable additional camera paths and controlled object changes. We describe the data representation and construction workflow, and discuss applications in floor-plan-conditioned 3D generation, geometric reconstruction, instance-level perception, camera-conditioned video generation, shared world modeling, and scene editing. Controlled camera and scene variations support spatial perception and world-model research. The public project page provides videos and an interactive colored point-cloud preview.

AI.tldr: Spatial Foundry is a multimodal dataset of 5,280 furnished residential 3D scene configurations with editable assets and aligned visual, geometric and temporal data. It is intended for spatial intelligence research such as 3D generation, reconstruction, perception, camera-conditioned video generation and world modeling.
