AI.motivation: Images alone leave spatial relations implicit, and existing annotations are disconnected, which makes it hard to study appearance, camera motion and scene change under a shared reference.
AI.method: The dataset provides floor plans, perspective and panoramic RGB, metric depth, point clouds, meshes, instance-level 3D bounding boxes and camera trajectories paired with video, all in shared scene coordinates. Editable source scenes allow extra camera paths and controlled object changes.
AI.result: The abstract reports no quantitative benchmark results; it describes the data representation, construction workflow and a set of application directions, with a public project page offering videos and an interactive point-cloud preview.
AI.conclusion: The dataset offers a controllable, aligned multimodal resource for studying spatial perception and world models.

title: BrickFlow: Connectivity-Guided Brick Reconstruction
summary: Given a set of LEGO parts and an image of an assembled object, our task is to infer the pose of each part to assemble the object. In contrast with traditional 3D reconstruction, doing so requires satisfying discrete physical constraints, which provide structure but render the problem combinatorial and highly sensitive to small pose errors. To learn a prior over how parts fit together, we train a set-conditioned SE(3) flow model on procedurally generated assemblies. We then finetune this model to inject image conditioning, using 1% as much data. However, while the learned flow captures global structure, it does not enforce connectivity. To address this, we introduce an analytic connectivity-field guidance to pull predictions toward connected assemblies at test time. Through this, we demonstrate improved build quality with model size, pretraining, and guidance. We make our models and data available for research purposes at this https URL

AI.tldr: BrickFlow infers the pose of each LEGO part from an image of the assembled object by training a set-conditioned SE(3) flow model on procedurally generated assemblies, then adding image conditioning and an analytic connectivity-field guidance at test time. It reports improved build quality with model size, pretraining and guidance.
AI.motivation: Recovering LEGO assemblies requires satisfying discrete physical connectivity constraints, which makes the problem combinatorial and sensitive to small pose errors, and learned flow models capture global structure but do not enforce connectivity.
AI.method: A set-conditioned SE(3) flow model is pretrained on procedurally generated assemblies, then finetuned with image conditioning using 1% as much data. An analytic connectivity field guides predictions toward connected assemblies at test time.
AI.result: The abstract reports improved build quality as model size, pretraining and guidance increase. It gives no numerical values.
AI.conclusion: Combining a learned pose prior with explicit connectivity guidance is a practical route to image-conditioned discrete assembly reconstruction; models and data are released for research.

title: K2V: Generative Keyframing For Physically Plausible Video Generation
summary: Video diffusion models are able to generate samples with high-quality appearance and textural qualities. However, content produced by these methods is known to exhibit significant physical errors. This is because, in a classical video generation setting, all physical reasoning must take place simultaneously and exclusively within the diffusion this http URL propose to resolve these issues by redistributing the task of physical reasoning onto a language model-backed keyframe generation module, which allows for explicit reasoning in language, and fine-grained control over the appearance of the video at important moments in the video. We then condition a video generation model with these keyframes, reducing the role of the diffusion model to the simpler task of interpolating between physically-correct intermediate states, rather than inferring an entire sequence with diffusion. Results demonstrate that our approach significantly outperforms existing approaches, achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Physics-IQ Verified benchmark and PhyGenBench.

AI.tldr: K2V separates physical reasoning from appearance synthesis in video generation: a language-model-backed module generates physically meaningful keyframes, and a video diffusion model only interpolates between them. It reports state-of-the-art results on the Physics-IQ Verified benchmark and PhyGenBench.
AI.motivation: Diffusion video generators produce high-quality appearance but often contain physical errors, because all physical reasoning must happen implicitly inside the diffusion process.
AI.method: A language-model-backed keyframe generation module reasons explicitly in language about physical states and sets fine-grained appearance at key moments. A video generation model is conditioned on these keyframes and interpolates between them.
AI.result: The approach significantly outperforms existing methods and reaches state-of-the-art performance on Physics-IQ Verified and PhyGenBench. The abstract gives no specific numbers.
AI.conclusion: Explicit language-based keyframe planning is an effective way to improve physical plausibility in generated video.

title: TTB: Test-time Baking for Efficient Rendering of Decoder-only View Synthesis Models
comment: NeurIPS 2026 (Spotlight). Project page: this https URL
summary: Decoder-only Large View Synthesis Models (LVSMs) with KV-cache have recently achieved state-of-the-art quality by regressing novel views from neural networks without reconstructing 3D geometry, while Test-Time Training (TTT) layers save computation but sacrifice quality. We propose Test-Time Baking (TTB), a strategy that learns to bake global scene information from cross-view attention into a lightweight MLP, enabling fast and high-fidelity novel-view decoding. The first key is to repurpose the fast-weight MLP of TTT to learn the cross-view attention mapping explicitly from its input-output pairs, rather than replacing attention entirely, achieving the same rendering efficiency as TTT while delivering substantially higher quality. The second key addresses a modality misalignment between context prefilling and novel-view rendering: we disentangle context tokens into camera-only context rendering tokens to serve as TTB input, and context ground-truth tokens with image content to serve as the TTB mapping target, ensuring the baked MLPs are relieved of the modality generalization challenge between context and novel-view processing. Our method achieves up to **23x** rendering speedup with quality on par with the state-of-the-art across several benchmarks. Project page: this https URL

AI.tldr: TTB (Test-Time Baking) speeds up decoder-only Large View Synthesis Models by baking cross-view attention into a lightweight MLP, reusing the fast-weight MLP of Test-Time Training layers. It reports up to 23x rendering speedup at quality comparable to the state of the art.
AI.motivation: Decoder-only LVSMs with KV-cache give state-of-the-art view synthesis quality but are slow, while TTT layers are fast but lose quality.
AI.method: The fast-weight MLP of TTT is trained to learn the cross-view attention mapping from its input-output pairs rather than replacing attention. Context tokens are split into camera-only rendering tokens used as input and context ground-truth tokens used as the mapping target, which removes the modality mismatch between context prefilling and novel-view rendering.
AI.result: The method achieves up to 23x rendering speedup, with quality on par with the state of the art across several benchmarks, according to the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Baking global scene information from attention into a small MLP gives TTT-level efficiency with near-attention quality for novel-view decoding.

title: Unbundling Multimodal Vision Encoding
summary: How multimodal language models should encode visual input remains up for debate. Most models use a pretrained vision encoder, while some recent recipes train the encoder from scratch with the language model or remove it entirely. Vision encoders bundle together three design choices: a visual prior from upstream pretraining, dedicated vision capacity, and pre-fusion placement of that capacity (i.e., before the multimodal backbone). Because published models also differ in data, architecture, and compute, comparing them cannot isolate the effect of each choice. We disentangle these choices via a controlled framework where we pretrain all models from scratch on common data and compare them on visual question answering and language benchmarks at matched lifetime compute. We find that the visual prior is not necessary; an encoder trained jointly from scratch is on par with a pretrained one, without a separate training stage. What matters instead is dedicated vision capacity: an encoder-free model trails on visual understanding even when its backbone is enlarged by the encoder's parameter count. Yet that capacity need not precede multimodal fusion, as vision-only modules added in-fusion to early backbone layers perform comparably to a pre-fusion encoder and can lower time to first token. These results also hold across backbone sizes, when encoder pretraining is treated as free, and when starting from a pretrained language model. Overall, our findings favor dedicated vision capacity trained jointly with the backbone and placed early within it.

AI.tldr: This controlled study pretrains multimodal models from scratch on common data and finds that a pretrained visual prior is not necessary, while dedicated vision capacity placed early in the backbone matters. Vision-only modules inserted early in the language backbone perform comparably to a pre-fusion encoder and can reduce time to first token.
AI.motivation: Published multimodal models differ in data, architecture and compute, so existing comparisons cannot isolate the effect of the vision encoder, which bundles a visual prior, dedicated capacity and pre-fusion placement.
AI.method: The three design choices are disentangled in a framework where all models are pretrained from scratch on common data and compared on visual question answering and language benchmarks at matched lifetime compute, with extra controls for backbone size, free encoder pretraining and starting from a pretrained language model.
AI.result: An encoder trained jointly from scratch matches a pretrained one. An encoder-free model trails on visual understanding even when its backbone is enlarged by the encoder's parameter count. In-fusion vision-only modules in early layers perform comparably to a pre-fusion encoder.
AI.conclusion: Dedicated vision capacity trained jointly with the backbone and placed early within it is the key design factor, rather than a pretrained visual prior.

title: Back to Pixels: Lifting Latent Video Diffusion into Pixel Space
summary: Frontier video generation models work in a VAE latent space that compresses video in both space and time. This compression made training tractable, but now limits high-resolution, controllable, and interactive generation -- doubling resolution quadruples token count, conditions apply to groups of frames rather than individual ones, and each response must wait for the rest of its multi-frame block. We present PixVid, a simple yet effective method that lifts a pretrained latent video model to directly generate every frame in pixel space. PixVid keeps the diffusion transformer and replaces the VAE decoder with a convolutional head that renders its outputs into pixels. We find that predicting clean video rather than velocity, together with a larger noise shift, is key to quality. Finetuned from Wan2.1-14B, PixVid is competitive with the latent baseline within $\sim 1.3$M training clips. Working framewise in pixels, it generates at $2\times$ higher resolution with the same per-frame token count, keeps depth-conditioned video editing aligned under fast motion, and responds to each action at the next frame. Project page: this https URL

AI.tldr: PixVid adapts a pretrained latent video diffusion transformer to generate every frame directly in pixel space by replacing the VAE decoder with a convolutional head. Finetuned from Wan2.1-14B, it matches the latent baseline within about 1.3M training clips and generates at 2x higher resolution with the same per-frame token count.
AI.motivation: Latent VAE video models compress space and time, which makes high resolution, per-frame control and interactive response costly, since doubling resolution quadruples the token count and conditions apply to groups of frames.
AI.method: The diffusion transformer is kept and a convolutional head renders its outputs into pixels. Predicting clean video rather than velocity, together with a larger noise shift, is identified as key to quality.
AI.result: PixVid is competitive with the latent baseline within about 1.3M clips, generates at 2x higher resolution at the same per-frame token count, keeps depth-conditioned editing aligned under fast motion, and responds to each action at the next frame.
AI.conclusion: Framewise pixel-space generation with a lifted latent model is a practical route to higher resolution, finer control and lower response latency in video generation.

title: Learning Low-Latency Action Verification for Frozen Vision-Language-Action Models
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have made significant progress in general-purpose robotic manipulation. However, sampled action sequences can be ineffective, while evaluating alternatives with computationally expensive verifiers adds latency at each policy query. In this work, we propose HDH, a lightweight framework that uses hindsight from a frozen VLA's own deployments to improve action verification. The framework has three stages. First, we deploy the policy and collect its autonomous rollouts. We then train a compact action verifier to assign each action chunk a predicted task-success score. Finally, the frozen VLA generates action candidates, and the verifier selects the candidate with the highest score for execution. Across four LIBERO-10 tasks, HDH achieves an average success rate of 82.3\% and on three real-world manipulation tasks, HDH improves average success over the baseline policy by 22.6\%.

AI.tldr: HDH is a lightweight framework that trains a compact action verifier on the rollouts of a frozen vision-language-action policy, then uses it to select the best of several sampled action chunks at inference. It reports 82.3% average success on four LIBERO-10 tasks and a 22.6% relative improvement on three real-world tasks.
AI.motivation: Sampled action sequences from VLA policies can be ineffective, and verifying them with expensive verifiers adds latency at every policy query.
AI.method: The policy is deployed to collect autonomous rollouts, a compact verifier is trained to assign each action chunk a predicted task-success score, and the frozen VLA generates candidates, from which the verifier selects the highest-scoring one for execution.
AI.result: Average success is 82.3% across four LIBERO-10 tasks. On three real-world manipulation tasks, average success improves over the baseline policy by 22.6%.
AI.conclusion: Hindsight from a frozen policy's own deployments can train a cheap verifier that improves action selection without modifying the VLA.

title: Emergent Vision-Shaped Thinking in Text-Only Reasoning through Multimodal Training
summary: Does multimodal training shape how a language model thinks, even when the input is text only? We test this with targeted causal ablations across 10 multimodal configurations from 6 model families, with matched text-only backbones and cross-family transfer controls. We contrast spatial-imagery tasks that invite mental scene construction with symbol-manipulation tasks solvable by symbolic rules alone. We identify a vision-language axis in hidden-state space and ablate its projection at inference. In Chameleon-7B, this ablation drops accuracy on BIG-Bench Hard (BBH) navigate by 27.6 pp while leaving boolean expressions intact (+5.6 pp), a 33.2 pp double dissociation. The effect is direction-specific and layer-localized, extends to mental-simulation tasks such as mental rotation, paper folding, and perspective taking, and is not explained by task difficulty, reasoning depth, or sequential update load. Together, these results reveal emergent vision-shaped thinking (EVT): text-only reasoning that causally recruits representations introduced or strengthened by vision-language training, without assuming an image-like internal format. The measured effect is spatially concentrated at 7-8B and broadens to non-spatial visual attribute binding in the tested 32B configuration. In dual-path unified models (BAGEL, Janus-Pro), the causal handle localizes to the generation pathway as a compact one-dimensional carrier. The understanding pathway also encodes spatial information in a higher-rank, probe-decodable form, but is not the causal handle. To separate decodability from causal use, we analyze concentration, alignment, and semantic location. These diagnostics explain why behavior, probing, and intervention can diverge. Multimodal training thus reshapes the geometry of text-only reasoning, not just how visual input is processed.

AI.tldr: The paper reports that multimodal training changes how a text-only reasoning model thinks: a vision-language direction in hidden-state space is causally used for text-only spatial reasoning. Ablating it drops BBH navigate accuracy by 27.6 points in Chameleon-7B while leaving boolean expressions intact, which the authors call emergent vision-shaped thinking.
AI.motivation: It is unclear whether multimodal training affects reasoning on text-only inputs, and whether any effect reflects causal use or just decodable information.
AI.method: Targeted causal ablations are run across 10 multimodal configurations from six model families, with matched text-only backbones and cross-family transfer controls. A vision-language axis in hidden-state space is identified and its projection ablated at inference, with separate analyses of concentration, alignment and semantic location.
AI.result: In Chameleon-7B, ablation reduces BBH navigate accuracy by 27.6 points and increases boolean expression accuracy by 5.6 points, a 33.2-point double dissociation. The effect extends to mental rotation, paper folding and perspective taking, and is not explained by difficulty, reasoning depth or update load. In BAGEL and Janus-Pro the causal handle lies in the generation pathway.
AI.conclusion: Vision-language training reshapes the geometry of text-only reasoning, and decodability of visual information should not be taken as evidence of causal use.

title: One Block Is Enough: LoopMR for Accelerated MRI Reconstruction
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, 6 tables. Code: this https URL
summary: Deep-learning unrolled networks are the leading approach to accelerated MRI reconstruction. State-of-the-art models such as PromptMR+ learn a distinct block for every cascade, so their size grows with the number of cascades. Sharing one block across iterations avoids adding parameters, but earlier shared-weight models typically used a tiny block and produced worse images than models with distinct weights. Therefore, it remained unclear whether weight sharing itself or the choice of block was the problem. Recent advances in looped transformers, which reuse the same block across layers, show that they can match or outperform their distinct-weight counterparts on several tasks. Motivated by this, we propose LoopMR, which reuses a single Restormer block at every iteration as its core. Besides the current image estimate, the block receives data-consistency inputs and latent images. On four datasets covering the brain (CC359), knee (fastMRI), heart (CMRxRecon2023) and carotid (in-house), LoopMR significantly outperforms E2E-VarNet, PromptMR and PromptMR+ in PSNR and SSIM at every acceleration factor (p < 0.01), with about 1/9 of PromptMR+'s parameters (10.3M versus 92.9M). It also keeps its lead at unseen acceleration factors and on an unseen dataset. With our transformer block, the shared model matches or outperforms its distinct-weight counterpart at 6, 12 and 24 iterations. At a fixed number of iterations, shared transformer blocks match or outperform their distinct-weight versions, while shared CNN blocks perform worse. These results suggest that looping one well-chosen block can outperform stacking distinct cascades in MRI reconstruction, with a fraction of the parameters.

AI.tldr: LoopMR reuses one Restormer block across all iterations of an unrolled MRI reconstruction network. With about 10.3M parameters versus 92.9M for PromptMR+, it significantly outperforms E2E-VarNet, PromptMR and PromptMR+ in PSNR and SSIM across four datasets and acceleration factors.
AI.motivation: State-of-the-art unrolled MRI networks use a distinct block per cascade, so their size grows with cascades, and earlier weight-shared models used tiny blocks that underperformed, leaving unclear whether weight sharing or block choice was the cause.
AI.method: A single Restormer block is looped at every iteration as the core, and it receives the current image estimate, data-consistency inputs and latent images. Shared transformer and shared CNN blocks are compared against distinct-weight versions at fixed iteration counts.
AI.result: LoopMR significantly outperforms E2E-VarNet, PromptMR and PromptMR+ in PSNR and SSIM at every acceleration factor (p < 0.01) on CC359, fastMRI, CMRxRecon2023 and an in-house carotid dataset, and keeps its lead at unseen acceleration factors and on an unseen dataset. Shared transformer blocks match or outperform distinct-weight versions at 6, 12 and 24 iterations, while shared CNN blocks perform worse.
AI.conclusion: Looping one well-chosen transformer block can match or beat stacking distinct cascades in MRI reconstruction with a fraction of the parameters.

title: Adapting Monocular Depth Estimation in Novel Scenes through Disparity Refinement and Robot Ego-Motion
summary: The geometric understanding of a scene is a crucial component for safe and efficient robotic operations in novel and unstructured environments. The recent emergence of foundation models for Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) has provided an opportunity to enrich robotic perception capabilities with dense long-range depth predictions, replacing expensive onboard hardware (e.g., LiDARs and stereo cameras). However, these offline models are primarily trained on affine-invariant depth representations, and their generalization to novel scenes remains unclear. In this work we present EM-ViT, a monocular depth estimation model that learns to adapt online relative depth inputs from a foundation model prior to the metric scale with observations collected during robotic operations. Motivated by the stereo camera parameterization, our method decomposes depth prediction via dense disparity refinement to recover the scene's relative structure and an effective baseline scalar prediction to determine the missing metric scale. The learning process leverages sparse LiDAR points and, optionally, the robot's Ego-Motion (EM) to rapidly train a lightweight Vision Transformer (ViT), while an internal gradient matching loss preserves the fine-grained semantic structure of the input disparity in real-time. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on publicly available sequences, such as KITTI, and show that our online learning pipeline can adapt to novel scenes faster and with higher accuracy than existing MDE foundation models. The code and supplementary materials will be publicly available at this https URL.

AI.tldr: EM-ViT adapts relative depth from a monocular depth foundation model to metric scale online, using sparse LiDAR points and optionally the robot's ego-motion. It decomposes depth into dense disparity refinement and a predicted baseline scalar, and reports faster and more accurate adaptation to novel scenes than existing MDE foundation models on KITTI and related sequences.
AI.motivation: Foundation models for monocular depth are trained for affine-invariant depth, and their generalization to novel robotic scenes is unclear, while replacing LiDAR or stereo needs metric scale.
AI.method: Motivated by stereo parameterization, depth prediction is split into dense disparity refinement, which recovers relative structure, and an effective baseline scalar, which fixes metric scale. A lightweight Vision Transformer is trained online with sparse LiDAR supervision, optionally ego-motion, and a gradient matching loss that preserves the input disparity's fine structure.
AI.result: The abstract reports that the online pipeline adapts to novel scenes faster and with higher accuracy than existing MDE foundation models on publicly available sequences such as KITTI, without giving numerical values.
AI.conclusion: Online adaptation with sparse LiDAR and ego-motion can turn a relative depth prior into metric depth for robotic perception in novel scenes.

title: Poison-then-Hide: Finetuning-Activated Backdoor Attack on Pretrained Vision Encoders
summary: Backdoor attacks threaten the integrity of machine learning models by allowing attackers to control model behavior through triggers. Models can be compromised during finetuning by backdoor attacks through either poisoned data or adversarial training objectives. Because existing finetuning-activated attacks assume limited domain shift or frozen encoder layers, they often fail under full-model finetuning. We target a stealthy finetuning-activated attack where a dormant backdoor is implanted in a pretrained encoder, and later activated by finetuning on clean downstream data. We propose Poison-then-Hide, a novel attack that remains effective when the entire model is finetuned in a domain transfer. Our approach consists of three components: trigger optimization, base encoder poisoning, and targeted unlearning to conceal the backdoor. We evaluate our method on six datasets and three model architectures, and achieve state-of-the-art (up to 97%) attack success rates. We find that jointly learning the benign target task alongside the poisoning is critical to the attack's success. We demonstrate standard detection and mitigation defenses cannot fully remove the backdoor, which can reappear after benign finetuning.

AI.tldr: Poison-then-Hide implants a dormant backdoor in a pretrained vision encoder that is activated when the whole model is finetuned on clean downstream data. It combines trigger optimization, base encoder poisoning and targeted unlearning, and reports up to 97% attack success rate across six datasets and three architectures.
AI.motivation: Existing finetuning-activated backdoors assume limited domain shift or frozen encoder layers and often fail under full-model finetuning across domain transfer.
AI.method: Three components: trigger optimization, poisoning of the base encoder, and targeted unlearning that conceals the backdoor. Joint learning of the benign target task alongside the poisoning is identified as critical.
AI.result: The attack reaches state-of-the-art attack success rates of up to 97% on six datasets and three model architectures. Standard detection and mitigation defenses do not fully remove the backdoor, which can reappear after benign finetuning.
AI.conclusion: Pretrained vision encoders are vulnerable to stealthy, finetuning-activated backdoors that survive common defenses, which calls for more robust defenses in the pretrain-finetune pipeline.

title: Aggregate Accuracy Hides Diagnosis-Specific Failure in Medical Vision-Language Models
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Medical Reasoning with Vision Language Foundation Models (Med-Reasoner). 16 pages including NeurIPS checklist, 1 figure, 5 tables
summary: Medical vision-language models (VLMs) are compared mainly by accuracy averaged across findings, a summary that can hide complete failure on a single diagnosis. We audit five open medical VLMs (MedGemma-4B, Lingshu-7B, HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B, and MedVLM-R1) on 6,048 ChestX-ray14 questions balanced by sex, age, finding, and label. On the 432 pneumothorax-positive X-rays, HuatuoGPT-Vision and Qwen2.5-VL detect zero cases while MedGemma and Lingshu detect 38% and 67% of the same images. The two failing models answer "no" to all 864 pneumothorax cases (balanced accuracy 0.500, chance), yet produce fluent, anatomically specific explanations that name the signs of a collapsed lung and then deny them, with no hedge or abstention. This failure is not an artifact of prompting, image resolution, label ambiguity, or model scale. It persists across four prompt formats, at native resolution, and on single-label cases. A within-model control shows the same forced prompt gives HuatuoGPT 79% recall on nodule but only 6% on pneumothorax. It survives a tenfold scale increase (Qwen2.5-VL-72B detects 4%) and replicates on SIIM-ACR, an independent dataset with radiologist-drawn masks, where the failing models detect 0 of 432 confirmed pneumothoraces, including 0 of the 144 largest lesions. Reading the models' logits and internal states shows this is not blindness. The two failing models are highly confident yet no better than chance and a linear probe recovers pneumothorax from their hidden representations even where recall is zero, so the finding is represented internally but suppressed at the output. Aggregate accuracy therefore cannot establish that a medical VLM can see a given finding, because a model that misses one can still describe it convincingly. Reporting per-finding recall and specificity on balanced cases is needed to tell the difference.

AI.tldr: An audit of five open medical vision-language models on ChestX-ray14 finds that two models detect zero of 864 pneumothorax cases while answering "no" with fluent explanations, so aggregate accuracy hides diagnosis-specific failure. The authors recommend per-finding recall and specificity on balanced cases.
AI.motivation: Medical VLMs are compared mainly by accuracy averaged over findings, which can conceal complete failure on a single diagnosis.
AI.method: Five models (MedGemma-4B, Lingshu-7B, HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B and MedVLM-R1) are evaluated on 6,048 ChestX-ray14 questions balanced by sex, age, finding and label. Controls cover prompt formats, resolution, label ambiguity, scale (Qwen2.5-VL-72B), logits, hidden states with a linear probe, and replication on SIIM-ACR.
AI.result: HuatuoGPT-Vision and Qwen2.5-VL detect zero of 432 pneumothorax-positive X-rays, while MedGemma and Lingshu detect 38% and 67%. The failing models have balanced accuracy of 0.500, and a linear probe recovers pneumothorax from their hidden states even where recall is zero. On SIIM-ACR, the failing models detect 0 of 432 confirmed pneumothoraces.
AI.conclusion: Aggregate accuracy cannot show that a medical VLM can see a given finding, since the finding can be represented internally yet suppressed at the output, so per-finding recall and specificity are needed.

title: Coarse-to-Fine 3D MRI Reconstruction via Resolution-Agnostic Neural Operators
summary: Deep-learning-based 3D MRI reconstruction is limited in practice by the GPU memory and compute cost of full-volume training; 3D acquisitions are thus most often reconstructed by 2D models applied slice-by-slice and then stacked, which ignores through-plane (stacking-axis) structure. We reconstruct in full 3D and ask whether a model can be trained at low resolution (fast and memory-feasible) yet deployed at higher resolution. This coarse-to-fine strategy needs reliable cross-resolution performance, but standard networks are resolution-specific and degrade substantially when evaluated outside the training setting. We therefore use resolution-agnostic neural operators (NOs) and propose KIR-NO (k-space-to-Image Reconstruction Neural Operator), a discretization-agnostic framework for accelerated 3D MRI reconstruction. KIR-NO is trained with full backpropagation on low-resolution volumes and applied zero-shot to higher-resolution volumes at inference. Its core building block is a 3D neural operator based on discrete-continuous convolutions: convolutional filters are parameterized in a continuous basis and sampled at arbitrary voxel resolutions while preserving the local inductive bias of convolution. KIR-NO integrates these learned operators with physics-based consistency: a k-space neural-operator head first refines the undersampled Fourier measurements, and image-space neural-operator cascades then refine the reconstruction through interleaved data-consistency updates. Across 3D knee and brain MRI benchmarks, KIR-NO improves over classical and CNN baselines: it improves over a state-of-the-art 3D CNN by 2.2 dB PSNR at half resolution under 4x acceleration on SKM-TEA, with gains persisting at 8x and 16x. These results show that resolution-agnostic operators make coarse-to-fine 3D MRI reconstruction - cheap low-resolution training with high-resolution deployment - practical across anatomies.

AI.tldr: KIR-NO is a resolution-agnostic neural operator for 3D MRI reconstruction, trained on low-resolution volumes and applied zero-shot at higher resolution. It improves over a state-of-the-art 3D CNN by 2.2 dB PSNR at half resolution under 4x acceleration on SKM-TEA, with gains persisting at 8x and 16x.
AI.motivation: Full-volume 3D MRI training is limited by GPU memory and compute, so 2D slice-wise models are common and ignore through-plane structure, while standard networks degrade when evaluated at other resolutions.
AI.method: Convolutional filters are parameterized in a continuous basis and sampled at arbitrary voxel resolutions, forming discrete-continuous 3D neural operators. A k-space neural-operator head refines undersampled Fourier measurements, and image-space neural-operator cascades refine the reconstruction with interleaved data-consistency updates.
AI.result: On 3D knee and brain benchmarks, KIR-NO improves over classical and CNN baselines, including a 2.2 dB PSNR gain over a state-of-the-art 3D CNN at half resolution under 4x acceleration on SKM-TEA, with gains at 8x and 16x.
AI.conclusion: Resolution-agnostic operators make cheap low-resolution training with high-resolution deployment practical for 3D MRI reconstruction across anatomies.

title: AROMA: Adaptive Representation-Oriented Multimodal Actuation for Vision-Language Model Control
summary: Mechanistic localization does not by itself yield usable control: causal sensitivity may occupy little activation energy, an accurate local direction may fail at finite scale, and a reachable numeral target may be wrong. We introduce AROMA (Adaptive Representation-Oriented Multimodal Actuation), a frozen-VLM control framework separating where to intervene, which geometry and gain to use, how to reach a target, which target to pursue, and when to act. In Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct, four dimensions of a causally validated cross-attention head explain 89.82% of cardinality sensitivity but only 9.52% of median activation energy; magnitude-normalized causal subspace actuation converts this mismatch into finite control, improving exact-count accuracy on untouched procedural data by +8.00 pp. Iterative Minimal-Effort Actuation (MEA) reaches 81.25% of oracle targets versus 15.18% for a frozen direction under matched step budgets. With target and gate frozen before evaluation, targeted MEA improves the previous frozen policy from 34.444% to 38.730% on a new natural Stage-2 cohort (N=630; paired p=4.63e-7) and yields 65.741% versus 65.153% over all 7,992 examples while editing only 63 inputs. Prospective routing, replication across heads and models, and comparisons with attribution-steering baselines further characterize each stage, separating localization, actuation, reachability, target quality, and selective deployment as distinct control problems.

AI.tldr: AROMA is a control framework for a frozen vision-language model that separates localization, actuation, reachability, target choice and gating. In Llama-3.2-11B-Vision-Instruct it turns a causally validated cross-attention head into finite control, with iterative minimal-effort actuation reaching 81.25% of oracle targets versus 15.18% for a frozen direction.
AI.motivation: Locating a causally sensitive mechanism does not by itself give usable control, because the sensitivity may carry little activation energy, a local direction may fail at finite scale, and a reachable target may be wrong.
AI.method: Magnitude-normalized causal subspace actuation edits four dimensions of a validated head, and Iterative Minimal-Effort Actuation (MEA) moves toward a target within a step budget. Target and gate are frozen before evaluation, and the policy is tested on a new natural Stage-2 cohort.
AI.result: The four dimensions explain 89.82% of cardinality sensitivity but only 9.52% of median activation energy. Targeted MEA raises a previous frozen policy from 34.444% to 38.730% on N=630 (paired p=4.63e-7), and reaches 65.741% versus 65.153% over all 7,992 examples while editing 63 inputs.
AI.conclusion: Localization, actuation, reachability, target quality and selective deployment are separate control problems, and each has to be solved for finite control of a frozen VLM.

title: Are We Ready for Snow-tonomous Driving? Challenges Toward Robust Automated Driving in Extreme Weather
summary: Automated driving has gained remarkable momentum over the past decade, with both industry and academia investing substantial resources in developing perception and control solutions to advance vehicle autonomy. However, these efforts have largely focused on clear-weather scenarios, leaving harsh conditions, such as snow, rain, and fog, comparatively understudied. As a result, inclement weather remains one of the most significant hurdles for autonomous vehicles, often leading to substantial performance degradation in downstream perception and control tasks. In this paper, we present insights from the EU-funded Horizon Europe project ROADVIEW, which aims to develop robust, weather-aware perception and control modules for connected and automated vehicles operating under severe conditions, including snow, rain, and fog. Drawing on four years of large-scale development and real-world demonstrations across multiple vehicle platforms in different locations, we identify ten key challenges that hinder the development of weather-resilient autonomy, including data scarcity, domain shifts, limitations in multimodal perception, control robustness, and validation gaps, among others. We summarize these challenges and lessons learned toward enabling reliable snow-autonomous driving, highlighting critical directions for future research and standardization.

AI.tldr: This paper reports lessons from the EU Horizon Europe project ROADVIEW on automated driving in snow, rain and fog. It identifies ten key challenges for weather-resilient autonomy, including data scarcity, domain shift, multimodal perception limits, control robustness and validation gaps.
AI.motivation: Automated driving research has concentrated on clear weather, leaving severe conditions such as snow, rain and fog understudied, although weather is a major obstacle for autonomous vehicles.
AI.method: Four years of large-scale development and real-world demonstrations on several vehicle platforms at different locations are summarized, and the authors distill ten challenges and lessons learned.
AI.result: The paper names ten challenges, including data scarcity, domain shifts, limits of multimodal perception, control robustness and validation gaps. The abstract gives no quantitative results.
AI.conclusion: Reliable snow-capable autonomous driving needs research and standardization on the listed challenges, and the authors highlight directions for future work.

title: Supervision-Aware Evaluation of MedGemma for Reference-Assisted Radiotherapy Contour Ranking
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, 3 tables. Submitted to IEEE ISBI 2027
summary: Radiotherapy contour ranking can support quality assurance, but vision-language model (VLM) gains may reflect supervision, score construction, available inputs, or representation access. We evaluated frozen MedGemma 1.5 in a single-institution study, a 12-patient held-out HaN-Seg test, five-fold cross-fitting on 30 non-test HaN-Seg patients, and transfer without refitting to 120 SegRap2023 patients. On held-out HaN-Seg, a supervised readout of the final prompt state exceeded a supervised readout of the model's yes/no output probabilities by +0.3047 pooled average precision (AP; 95% patient-bootstrap interval [+0.2822, +0.3269]); the advantage persisted against a parameter-count-matched nonlinear control. A readout of projected visual tokens exceeded the final-state readout in cross-fitting and transfer (+0.0706 AP averaged equally across patients on SegRap; 95% interval [+0.0607, +0.0804]), while a structured panel-feature readout remained competitive with visual tokens. The anatomy-conditioned readout did not demonstrate an advantage over the native-feature comparator. These results motivate visual-token and structured-feature controls in medical-imaging VLM evaluations; outcomes were computational or synthetic, not clinical acceptability.

AI.tldr: A supervision-aware evaluation of frozen MedGemma 1.5 for ranking radiotherapy contours on head and neck data finds that a readout of projected visual tokens beats a readout of yes/no output probabilities. The paper also reports that the anatomy-conditioned readout shows no advantage over the native-feature comparator.
AI.motivation: VLM gains in radiotherapy contour ranking may come from supervision, score construction, available inputs or representation access, rather than from the model's understanding, so these factors must be separated.
AI.method: Frozen MedGemma 1.5 is evaluated in a single-institution study with a 12-patient held-out HaN-Seg test, five-fold cross-fitting on 30 non-test HaN-Seg patients, and transfer without refitting to 120 SegRap2023 patients. Supervised readouts are compared, including final prompt state, yes/no output probabilities, projected visual tokens and structured panel features.
AI.result: On held-out HaN-Seg, a supervised readout of the final prompt state beats the yes/no probability readout by +0.3047 pooled average precision (95% interval [+0.2822, +0.3269]). A visual-token readout beats the final-state readout by +0.0706 AP in cross-fitting and transfer (95% interval [+0.0607, +0.0804]).
AI.conclusion: Medical VLM evaluations need visual-token and structured-feature controls, since the reported gains depend on the readout, and the results are computational or synthetic rather than evidence of clinical acceptability.

title: SkillEarth: Teaching General-Purpose Agents to Act on Earth via Skill Evolution
summary: Recently developed remote sensing (RS) agents execute real-world tasks with complex workflows through multi-step tool invocation. These agents, however, typically rely on predefined expertise or parameter updates. They thus require updating expert knowledge or retraining models whenever new tools, tasks, or execution patterns emerge, limiting their continual adaptability in dynamic Earth environments. In this work, we seek to equip general-purpose agents with RS tool-call knowledge that can be automatically extracted from demonstrated trajectories without expert intervention or parameter updates. Specifically, we propose SkillEarth, a self-evolving skill extraction method that externalizes RS tool-call knowledge as reusable, retrievable, and evolvable skill files and refines them through observation-grounded evolution. Unlike existing automatic skill extraction methods that rely on outcome-based reflection to refine skills holistically, SkillEarth grounds skill evolution in real tool-chain execution and combines dual-judge feedback with a grounded observation routing graph for precise component-level refinement. The resulting skills are generalizable, reliable, and transferable: they improve overall RS tool-call performance across three frontier LLMs and four open-source LLMs, are refined through real tool execution feedback, and support cross-model reuse without retraining. Experiments on OpenEarth-Bench and Earth-Bench demonstrate that SkillEarth achieves better tool selection, argument correctness, execution-order consistency, and task completion than existing RS agents and skill extraction methods.

AI.tldr: SkillEarth automatically extracts remote sensing tool-call knowledge from demonstrated trajectories as reusable, retrievable and evolvable skill files, without parameter updates. Skills are refined using real tool-chain execution with dual-judge feedback and a grounded observation routing graph, and they improve tool use across seven LLMs.
AI.motivation: Remote sensing agents rely on predefined expertise or retraining, which limits adaptation to new tools, tasks and execution patterns, and existing skill extraction refines skills holistically from outcome-based reflection.
AI.method: Skills are extracted from demonstrated trajectories and evolved using observation-grounded routing of tool-chain execution feedback, with dual-judge feedback for component-level refinement.
AI.result: The skills improve overall tool-call performance across three frontier LLMs and four open-source LLMs and transfer across models without retraining. On OpenEarth-Bench and Earth-Bench, SkillEarth improves tool selection, argument correctness, execution-order consistency and task completion over existing remote sensing agents and skill extraction methods.
AI.conclusion: Externalized, execution-grounded skill files give general-purpose agents continual remote sensing tool-use ability without retraining.

title: What Makes a VLA Reactive? A Study of Execution Strategies for Dynamic Manipulation
comment: 13 pages, 7 figures, Efficient Foundation Models for Real-Time Embodied AI, CoRL 2026 Workshop
summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models predict chunks of future actions, and when objects move, those chunks go stale before they are executed. We study what makes a pretrained VLA reactive, using \pihalf{} on two dynamic simulation benchmarks and three real-robot tasks. We vary the prediction and execution horizons, compare synchronous and asynchronous inference, test methods that deliver actions sooner or keep successive chunks continuous, and adapt the policy with motion cues and latent-space reinforcement learning. The best prediction horizon is about one second, and the best execution horizon depends on the checkpoint. Short horizons help more with asynchronous execution, and methods that keep the trajectory continuous outperform those that only reduce latency. Adapting the policy repairs targeted failures, but on the conveyor task changing the execution horizon gained as much. Reactivity depends on the execution pipeline as much as on the policy, so both should be evaluated together.

AI.tldr: This study of pretrained VLA policies on dynamic manipulation finds that reactivity depends on the execution pipeline as much as on the policy. A prediction horizon of about one second works best, and methods that keep trajectories continuous outperform those that only reduce latency.
AI.motivation: VLA models predict action chunks that go stale when objects move, so their reactivity to dynamic scenes is poorly understood.
AI.method: The pi-0.5 policy is evaluated on two dynamic simulation benchmarks and three real-robot tasks. Prediction and execution horizons are varied, synchronous and asynchronous inference are compared, methods that deliver actions sooner or keep chunks continuous are tested, and the policy is adapted with motion cues and latent-space reinforcement learning.
AI.result: The best prediction horizon is about one second and the best execution horizon depends on the checkpoint. Short horizons help more with asynchronous execution. On the conveyor task, changing the execution horizon gains as much as policy adaptation.
AI.conclusion: Reactivity must be evaluated jointly for the policy and the execution pipeline, since either can dominate the outcome.

title: Reading the Table: Sim-to-Real Game State Detection for the Chef's Hat Card Game
comment: Presented at the Dungeons, Neurons, and Dialogues workshop (DnD-SIDC 2026) at ICANN 2026, this https URL
summary: Tabletop games offer a compelling scenario to study the interaction between artificial and human agents, combining social interaction with game state tracking and physical manipulation. To assess the game state, a robot needs to precisely detect closely related game objects, such as different card designs, requiring dedicated training data that is costly to annotate in the real world. Instead, we develop a fully automated synthetic data collection pipeline, using re-projection of known 3D coordinates to generate labels automatically and domain randomization to bridge the reality gap. This approach is used to collect a dataset of 25413 samples to finetune an object detection and a segmentation model, which are combined to assign detected cards to game-relevant zones and infer the game state. When evaluated on a real NICO humanoid robot, our pipeline achieves an F1-score of 0.906 for card-to-zone assignment, thus providing the perceptual foundation for a robot that can autonomously play Chef's Hat against human players.

AI.tldr: The paper builds a fully automated synthetic data pipeline for detecting Chef's Hat cards on a table, using re-projection of known 3D coordinates for automatic labels and domain randomization. A detector and a segmenter trained on 25,413 synthetic samples assign cards to game zones and reach an F1-score of 0.906 on a real NICO humanoid robot.
AI.motivation: Game state tracking requires distinguishing closely related card designs, and labeling such data in the real world is costly.
AI.method: Labels are generated automatically by re-projecting known 3D coordinates, and domain randomization bridges the sim-to-real gap. An object detector and a segmentation model are finetuned on the synthetic data and combined to assign detected cards to game-relevant zones and infer the game state.
AI.result: On a real NICO humanoid robot, the pipeline achieves an F1-score of 0.906 for card-to-zone assignment.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic data with automatic labels can provide the perception base for a robot that tracks the state of a tabletop game against human players.

title: EMS-Nav: Embodied Multi-Scale Navigation
summary: Industrial inspection robots must reach work areas and specific equipment. These destinations span spatial scales from regions to objects, so robots must relate each target to its surroundings to interpret the task and determine where to go. Existing methods support multi-scale navigation through rich environment representations, but at substantial computational and storage cost. These costs limit deployment where wireless coverage is incomplete and robots must rely on onboard computation to keep navigating. We introduce EMS-Nav, a biologically inspired multi-scale navigation framework for online, on-device operation. Its core innovation is to organize perception, spatial understanding, and navigation around regions, making local spaces the basic units of both environmental understanding and computation. EMS-Nav groups objects and their relationships into functionally meaningful spaces and builds a hierarchy from local areas to the broader environment. This organization supports efficient map construction alongside the interpretation and execution of language goals at different scales. In multi-scale navigation experiments, EMS-Nav achieves the highest success rates across all four target categories: objects, rooms, regions, and specific instances. It outperforms state-of-the-art open-vocabulary mapping and navigation methods, improving overall first-attempt success by 9.39 percentage points over the strongest baseline while reducing mapping overhead and language-model input size. Local deployment in real indoor environments further demonstrates its applicability to on-device embodied navigation. By establishing regions as the organizing basis for perception, spatial understanding, and language-guided action, EMS-Nav provides a system that combines multi-scale understanding with computational efficiency to support diverse language goals on resource-constrained robots.

AI.tldr: EMS-Nav is a multi-scale navigation framework for on-device robot operation that organizes perception, spatial understanding and navigation around regions and builds a hierarchy from local areas to the wider environment. It improves overall first-attempt success by 9.39 percentage points over the strongest baseline across objects, rooms, regions and specific instances.
AI.motivation: Industrial inspection robots must reach targets at several spatial scales, but existing multi-scale navigation needs rich environment representations that are costly in computation and storage, which is a problem where wireless coverage is incomplete.
AI.method: Objects and their relations are grouped into functionally meaningful spaces, and a hierarchy is built from local regions to the broader environment. This supports efficient map construction and the interpretation of language goals at different scales, with reduced language-model input size.
AI.result: EMS-Nav achieves the highest success rate in all four target categories (objects, rooms, regions and specific instances), improves overall first-attempt success by 9.39 points over the strongest open-vocabulary baseline, reduces mapping overhead, and runs locally in real indoor environments.
AI.conclusion: Regions as the organizing basis for perception and language-guided action combine multi-scale understanding with the efficiency needed on resource-constrained robots.

title: Physics-based simulation unlocks scaling laws for generalizable MRI reconstruction
summary: Deep-learning-based magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reconstruction holds great promise for accelerating acquisitions, yet its clinical translation remains bottlenecked by poor generalizability across unseen scanners, populations, anatomies, and protocols. Gathering sufficiently diverse clinical datasets to overcome this bottleneck is hindered by high acquisition costs, privacy restrictions, and institutional biases. Here, we introduce Scalable Inverse Model (SIM), a framework that systematically co-designs physics-simulated training data, model architecture, and learning paradigms around scalability--leveraging compute scaling to overcome historical data bottlenecks and achieve robust zero-shot MRI reconstruction. Across 14 public and in-house datasets--spanning seven international centers, five vendors, field strengths of 0.3-7 T, over ten anatomical regions, more than ten acquisition protocols, downstream quantitative and molecular tasks, and a 150-scan blinded radiologist study--SIM demonstrates robust zero-shot generalizability, recovering fine anatomical details while suppressing aliasing artifacts where conventional deep-learning methods fail. Attention-map analyses confirm that SIM learns physically explainable, dynamically adaptive reconstruction primitives rather than anatomy-specific priors. SIM establishes a scalable, privacy-preserving, and democratized infrastructure for universal MRI reconstruction, providing a blueprint for generalizable AI across inverse problems in medical imaging.

AI.tldr: SIM is a scalable inverse model for MRI reconstruction, trained on physics-simulated data, that achieves robust zero-shot reconstruction across 14 public and in-house datasets, seven centers and five vendors. Attention analyses suggest it learns physically explainable reconstruction primitives rather than anatomy-specific priors.
AI.motivation: Deep MRI reconstruction generalizes poorly to unseen scanners, populations, anatomies and protocols, and collecting diverse clinical data is expensive, restricted by privacy, and subject to institutional bias.
AI.method: Physics-simulated training data, model architecture and learning paradigm are co-designed around scalability, using compute scaling in place of large clinical datasets.
AI.result: Across 14 datasets spanning field strengths of 0.3-7 T, more than ten anatomical regions and more than ten protocols, SIM recovers fine anatomical detail and suppresses aliasing where conventional deep-learning methods fail, including in a 150-scan blinded radiologist study.
AI.conclusion: Physics-based simulation with scaling provides a privacy-preserving infrastructure for universal MRI reconstruction, and a blueprint for generalizable AI in medical inverse problems.

title: MOSAIC: Modular Obstacle and Spatial-Aware Framework for Manipulation In Cluttered Scenes
summary: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong performance in robotic manipulation, yet most rely primarily on 2D visual observations and language instructions, leaving scene geometry and obstacle relationships to be inferred implicitly. This limitation is particularly problematic in cluttered environments, where small spatial errors can lead to unintended contacts or collisions. We propose MOSAIC, a modular spatial- and obstacle-aware framework that can be integrated with pretrained VLA policies to improve object-level scene understanding and action generation. Our method augments the VLA backbone with an auxiliary semantic grounding task that predicts role-specific masks for the target object, destination region, and surrounding obstacles. We further combine the target and destination masks with depth estimated from 3D scene reconstruction to construct role-specific geometric tokens that are injected directly into the action expert. In addition, we propose obstacle-aware attention supervision that emphasizes obstacles near the robot body during task execution. The resulting attention features are subsequently injected into later action-expert layers to further guide action generation. Together, these components provide explicit semantic, geometric, and obstacle-aware cues while preserving the underlying pretrained VLA architecture. We evaluate our framework on pretrained VLA model using the RoboPRO benchmark, including visual perturbation tests, and further validate it on real-world manipulation tasks. MOSAIC improves the success rate by 5.1% in cluttered scenes, and by 9.7% under visual perturbations, with gains of up to 25.0% in the most challenging environment. We will release our code and dataset upon acceptance at the following Github page: this https URL

AI.tldr: MOSAIC augments a pretrained VLA policy with role-specific masks for the target, destination and obstacles, geometric tokens from depth, and obstacle-aware attention supervision, while keeping the base architecture. It improves success by 5.1% in cluttered scenes and by 9.7% under visual perturbations on the RoboPRO benchmark, with gains up to 25.0% in the hardest setting.
AI.motivation: VLA models rely mainly on 2D observations and language, so scene geometry and obstacle relations are implicit, which causes contacts and collisions in cluttered scenes.
AI.method: An auxiliary semantic grounding task predicts role-specific masks for the target object, destination region and surrounding obstacles. Target and destination masks combined with depth from 3D reconstruction form geometric tokens injected into the action expert, and obstacle-aware attention supervision emphasizes obstacles near the robot body.
AI.result: On RoboPRO, success improves by 5.1% in cluttered scenes and by 9.7% under visual perturbations, with gains up to 25.0% in the most challenging environment. Real-world manipulation tasks are also reported.
AI.conclusion: Explicit semantic, geometric and obstacle-aware cues can be added to a pretrained VLA without changing its architecture, which improves performance in clutter.

title: I See What You Want: Decoding Hierarchical Operator Intent from Visual Teleoperation History
comment: 8 pages, 6 figures. Project page: this https URL
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) have become a powerful foundation for robotic scene understanding, task planning, and language-conditioned control. A natural question follows: can these models also decode what a human operator intends while teleoperating a robot, without any explicit instruction? We formulate this as hierarchical intent prediction, jointly inferring the ongoing atomic action and the broader mission it serves from a short visual teleoperation history. To study this, we introduce VI AMO (Vision Intention Action and Mission Ongoing), a dataset of 6,600 episodes from eleven robot sources with 13,653 temporally aligned action annotations and 9,702 mission annotations. Large proprietary models struggle with this problem: on held-out episodes, GPT-4o reaches Sentence-BERT similarities of only 0.563 and 0.470 for action and mission, and GPT-5.6 Luna achieves only 0.581 and 0.554. Fine-tuning a VLM on VI AMO yields our Vision-Intention Model (VIM), which raises these scores to 0.825 and 0.821 and still reaches 0.726 and 0.717 on the 35.4% of test actions with both labels absent from training. Finally, as a downstream application, VIM's predicted mission enables a vision-language-action (VLA) policy to take over from the operator mid-task in a real-world environment unseen during VIM fine-tuning, reducing human teleoperation time by 34.6% relative to GPT-4o and 39.8% relative to GPT-5.6 Luna, while cutting intent-prediction latency by roughly 70% on average.

AI.tldr: VI AMO is a dataset of 6,600 teleoperation episodes for hierarchical intent prediction, and VIM, a VLM finetuned on it, infers the current atomic action and the mission from a short visual teleoperation history. VIM substantially outperforms GPT-4o and GPT-5.6 Luna, and its predicted mission lets a VLA policy take over mid-task, reducing teleoperation time by 34.6% versus GPT-4o.
AI.motivation: Large proprietary VLMs struggle to decode what a human operator intends from visual teleoperation history, so intent prediction is an open problem.
AI.method: The VI AMO dataset provides 6,600 episodes from eleven robot sources with 13,653 action annotations and 9,702 mission annotations. A VLM is finetuned on it to form the Vision-Intention Model (VIM), and its predicted mission is used to hand control to a VLA policy in a real-world environment.
AI.result: On held-out episodes, GPT-4o reaches Sentence-BERT similarities of 0.563 for action and 0.470 for mission, and GPT-5.6 Luna 0.581 and 0.554. VIM reaches 0.825 and 0.821, and 0.726 and 0.717 on the 35.4% of test actions with both labels unseen in training. Teleoperation time falls by 34.6% relative to GPT-4o and 39.8% relative to GPT-5.6 Luna, and intent-prediction latency drops by about 70%.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuned VLMs can decode hierarchical operator intent from visual history, and the predicted mission enables useful handover from teleoperation to autonomous control.

title: From State of THE ART to Human Prediction Algorithms
summary: Human curiosity and longing for the future have driven human progress from ancient times to the present. With the advancement of AI technology, human prediction algorithms have also drawn increasing attention from researchers. However, as AI technology continues to advance, we observe a counterintuitive phenomenon. Take human trajectory prediction algorithms as an example. Although models' quantitative prediction performance has improved, yielding one state-of-the-art model after another, the consideration of human behaviors, future thoughts, and social interactions themselves presents a gradually diminishing trend in the construction of these prediction algorithms, buried beneath numbers and metrics. In this manuscript, taking interactive art and human trajectory prediction algorithms as examples, we attempt to adopt a different analytical perspective to analyze the structural and developmental commonalities between these two fields. By examining specific interactive artworks and prediction algorithms, we aim to explore how human intuitions and art are associated with AI algorithms through three aspects, including perception, interaction, and timing, thereby providing new insights for the understanding and further research in this domain. We also observe an interesting phenomenon that certain art-inspired prediction algorithms can actually deduce intriguing patterns of human behaviors from the data, offering new potential avenues for understanding the relationship between human activities, state of The Art, and AI algorithms.

AI.tldr: This perspective paper compares interactive art and human trajectory prediction algorithms, arguing that prediction research increasingly optimizes metrics while neglecting human behavior, future thinking and social interaction. It analyzes the two fields through perception, interaction and timing, and notes that some art-inspired prediction methods recover interpretable patterns of human behavior from data.
AI.motivation: Trajectory prediction models keep improving on benchmark numbers, but the human and social aspects of prediction are receding in their design.
AI.method: The authors take interactive artworks and trajectory prediction algorithms as examples and analyze their structural and developmental commonalities through three aspects: perception, interaction and timing.
AI.result: The paper reports no experiments; it describes an observation that some art-inspired prediction algorithms can deduce intriguing patterns of human behavior from data.
AI.conclusion: Cross-reading art and prediction research offers new insights and possible directions for understanding human activity and designing AI prediction algorithms.

title: Safety as a Budget: Calibrating the Control Channel of Constrained GRPO for Vision-Language Models
summary: Reinforcement learning can teach vision-language models (VLMs) to decline harmful image-text requests, but how safe the result becomes is set indirectly, through reward weights found by trial runs. Stating safety as budgets on the rate of harmful assistance and the rate of over-refusal, enforced by Lagrange multipliers inside GRPO with an off-the-shelf scorer as the cost, is the natural fix, and it fails twice. The multiplier compares the scorer's mean with the budget, and scorers built for ranking get the mean wrong: a fixed-point analysis shows that the mean bias, not the budget, then decides whether the multiplier settles, saturates or switches off. And standard GRPO standardizes the penalized reward within each group, which cancels the multiplier before it reaches the gradient. Two-channel constrained GRPO repairs both: the base reward keeps the raw score for the within-group comparison, the penalty and the constraint estimate pass through a monotone map fitted on judge-labeled training responses, and the advantage keeps the multiplier. On a Qwen3-VL-2B policy with a training-free readout of an open 4B model as the scorer, held-out harm on 1,037 adversarial prompts falls from 8.9% under standard GRPO to 4.8%, lower in every seed, where the uncalibrated budget gives 7.6%; over-refusal stays at most 2% on 400 benign queries and MMBench is unchanged. The gain is largest where the intent sits in the image (10.1% -> 5.1%) and grows on the unseen HADES benchmark (28.9% -> 12.8%). Order-preserving distortions of the scores reproduce each predicted controller state in every seed, and the results hold under a map fitted on another judge's labels, an image-reading judge and a human audit.

AI.tldr: Two-channel constrained GRPO calibrates safety budgets for VLMs by separating the base reward, which keeps the raw scorer output, from the penalty and constraint estimate, which pass through a monotone map fitted on judge labels. On Qwen3-VL-2B, held-out harm falls from 8.9% under standard GRPO to 4.8% on 1,037 adversarial prompts, with over-refusal at most 2% on 400 benign queries.
AI.motivation: Reward weights set safety only indirectly. Stating safety as harm and over-refusal budgets with Lagrange multipliers in GRPO fails, because scorers built for ranking have a biased mean, and standard GRPO standardizes penalized rewards within groups, which cancels the multiplier.
AI.method: Two channels are used. The base reward keeps the raw score for within-group comparison, while the penalty and constraint estimate pass through a monotone map fitted on judge-labeled training responses, and the advantage keeps the multiplier. A fixed-point analysis explains the controller states.
AI.result: Held-out harm falls from 8.9% under standard GRPO to 4.8%, lower in every seed, versus 7.6% for an uncalibrated budget. Over-refusal stays at most 2% on 400 benign queries, MMBench is unchanged, and harm on the HADES benchmark falls from 28.9% to 12.8%.
AI.conclusion: Calibrating the scorer's mean and keeping the multiplier in the advantage makes a stated safety budget effective in constrained GRPO, and the gains hold across other judges and human audit.

title: Asymmetric Multimodal Learning with Decomposed JEPAs
summary: Cross-modal alignment is the standard objective for building multimodal representations. We show that alignment as a \emph{sole} objective is lossy wherever modalities are informationally asymmetric---where neither can express what the other carries. Visual question answering is an obvious case: a question is a selective relational operator probing a dense visual field whose fine-grained features no query recovers, so what alignment preserves is not what the task requires. We prove an \textbf{Alignment Redundancy Bound}: alignment-only Dirichlet energy minimization retains at most the redundant information atom $\Red(Z; X_1, X_2)$, annihilating private modality-specific structure $\Unq(Z; X_m)$ and cross-modal synergy $\Syn(Z; X_1, X_2)$. We introduce \textbf{Decomposed JEPA (D-JEPA)}, which factorizes latents into an aligned shared core and private modality-specific fibers. The shared core retains most of the structure alignment targets; the private fibers recover what alignment discards, via contextual masked prediction and asymmetric cross-subspace independence. Under information asymmetry, alignment-only training undergoes catastrophic semantic collapse on compositional reasoning benchmarks, surviving only on binary queries. D-JEPA averts this collapse, substantially improving downstream accuracy over both alignment-only and alignment-with-reconstruction baselines, and restoring a positive multimodal synergy gap in place of the baseline's inverted gap. Information-theoretic audits confirm that D-JEPA recovers most of the mutual information available from a frozen backbone, and causal fiber-swap interventions demonstrate that the recovered information is causally localized in the private fibers.

AI.tldr: D-JEPA factorizes multimodal latents into an aligned shared core and private modality-specific fibers, which prevents the information loss of alignment-only objectives under informational asymmetry. It substantially improves downstream accuracy over alignment-only and alignment-with-reconstruction baselines, and avoids catastrophic semantic collapse on compositional reasoning benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Cross-modal alignment is the standard objective, but it is lossy when neither modality can express what the other carries, as in visual question answering, because alignment keeps only redundant information and discards private and synergistic structure.
AI.method: The paper proves an Alignment Redundancy Bound, which says alignment-only Dirichlet energy minimization retains at most the redundant atom and annihilates private and synergy atoms. D-JEPA learns a shared core and private fibers through contextual masked prediction and asymmetric cross-subspace independence.
AI.result: Alignment-only training collapses on compositional reasoning benchmarks and survives only on binary queries. D-JEPA avoids this collapse, improves accuracy over both baselines, and restores a positive multimodal synergy gap. Information-theoretic audits show it recovers most of the mutual information available from a frozen backbone, and fiber-swap interventions show the recovered information lies in the private fibers.
AI.conclusion: Private modality-specific structure must be modeled alongside alignment when modalities are informationally asymmetric.

title: Dataset Distillation via Drifting
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. Project Page: this https URL
summary: The task of dataset distillation concerns the learning of a small set of synthetic samples that can serve as an effective replacement for a large real dataset when used for downstream tasks. While many solutions have been proposed since the problem's inception, most of them primarily seek to optimize the distilled data with respect to a classifier. In this work, we propose a new distillation method that learns a set of samples such that they directly approximate the per-class data distribution. Specifically, we "drift" our distilled data in the latent space of a feature extractor such that they move both toward the real data and away from each other without using a classification objective. We find that our drifted data cover the real distribution significantly better than existing methods while still serving as powerful training samples for classification. Furthermore, we showcase our method's use as a visualization tool for better interpreting models and extend it beyond images to other modalities. Our work advances the frontier of dataset distillation, offering a novel synthesis method and proposing distribution-based metrics as a complementary evaluation. More broadly, our findings help address the growing need to understand both data and models by uncovering more about how they interact.

AI.tldr: Dataset distillation via drifting learns a small synthetic set whose samples are moved in a feature extractor's latent space toward the real data and away from each other, approximating the per-class distribution without a classification objective. The drifted samples cover the real distribution better than existing methods while still training classifiers well.
AI.motivation: Most dataset distillation methods optimize synthetic data for a classifier, so they do not directly approximate the per-class data distribution.
AI.method: Synthetic samples are drifted in the latent space of a feature extractor, attracted to real data and repelled from one another, with no classification loss. The approach is also applied to visualization and beyond images.
AI.result: The drifted data cover the real distribution significantly better than existing methods, and remain effective training samples for classification. The abstract proposes distribution-based metrics as a complementary evaluation.
AI.conclusion: Distribution-based distillation offers a new synthesis method and a tool for interpreting data and models.

title: AgriSense: Vision-Language Decision Support and Robotic Intervention in a Virtual Greenhouse Copy title
summary: Autonomous greenhouse management increasingly requires robotic systems that integrate perception, navigation, environmental regulation, and plant-level intervention. This paper presents AgriSense, a framework combining an Isaac Sim virtual greenhouse, a quadruped mobile manipulator, RGB and LiDAR-inertial sensing, environmental control, and supervised vision-language decision support. Frozen DINOv2 and BERT encoders, together with structured environmental inputs, support joint prediction of twelve environmental references, a target zone, and an intervention flag. Checkpoint replay reproduces 41/43 zone decisions. Across five seeds on a source-grouped test set, the full, image-removed, and language-removed configurations each achieve 43/44 correct zone decisions, providing no evidence of incremental multimodal zone-accuracy improvement. The full model achieves mean absolute errors of 0.249 degrees C for temperature, 2.030 percentage points for humidity, and 0.997 percentage points for soil moisture. Sensor-only inputs match full-model zone accuracy, while language-only inputs achieve 68.64%. External real-image benchmarks reveal distribution-shift limitations. Five offline Point-LIO routes yield rigidly aligned trajectory errors of 5.22-17.32 mm. Of 40 virtual-arm targets, 32 satisfy geometric acceptance criteria and eight are rejected at boundaries. Six long-horizon climate cases and fault protocols characterize integration limits. Navigation and integrated treatment rely on simulator-state inputs; physical greenhouse performance and agronomic treatment efficacy remain unvalidated. The contribution is an evaluated decision-support and robotic-intervention framework for a virtual greenhouse.

AI.tldr: AgriSense is a framework for a virtual greenhouse in Isaac Sim, combining a quadruped mobile manipulator with vision-language decision support that predicts environmental references, a target zone and an intervention flag. Sensor-only inputs match full-model zone accuracy, and the abstract states that physical greenhouse performance is not validated.
AI.motivation: Autonomous greenhouse management needs robots that combine perception, navigation, climate control and plant-level intervention, and the paper evaluates such a decision-support and robotic intervention framework in simulation.
AI.method: Frozen DINOv2 and BERT encoders, with structured environmental inputs, support joint prediction of twelve environmental references, a target zone and an intervention flag. The system uses RGB and LiDAR-inertial sensing and offline Point-LIO trajectories.
AI.result: Checkpoint replay reproduces 41/43 zone decisions. Across five seeds, the full, image-removed and language-removed configurations each get 43/44 correct zone decisions, and language-only inputs reach 68.64%. Temperature MAE is 0.249 degrees C and humidity MAE 2.030 percentage points, and 32 of 40 virtual-arm targets pass geometric acceptance.
AI.conclusion: The results give no evidence that multimodal inputs improve zone accuracy, and the framework is a virtual-greenhouse decision-support system whose physical efficacy remains unvalidated.

title: Spatiotemporal learning improves quantification of pore-space evolution and fluid displacement
comment: 48 pages, 9 figures, 18 tables, including Supplementary Information
summary: Pore-space evolution and fluid displacement influence how rocks transmit and store fluids, affecting geological carbon storage, underground hydrogen storage and groundwater contaminant transport. A single time-resolved micro-CT experiment may produce tens to hundreds of three-dimensional images, and segmentation is required to quantify physical properties and run image-based simulations. Traditional methods such as thresholding perform poorly on noisy, low-contrast images and need manual adjustment per image; 3D deep learning networks segment each image without temporal information, so their errors vary between images and could be mistaken for physical change. Here we introduce a transformer-based 4D segmentation framework combining spatial and temporal information. It uses sequential images to resolve ambiguous phase assignments and separate physical change from segmentation error. The method is tested on images of mineral dissolution: it measures pore-volume growth and rock boundaries more accurately than an equivalent 3D model that ignores temporal information.
