It also captures the increase in permeability verified against reference segmentations and flow simulations. The advantage transfers to another dissolution sample without retraining. On two other datasets of fluid displacement, it reduces spurious changes in predicted rock and porosity fluctuations and accurately identifies filling events. Spatiotemporal segmentation turns sequences of hundreds of three-dimensional images into more reliable quantitative measurements of pore-space evolution and fluid displacement without per-image parameter adjustment to support the analysis of time-resolved CT imaging.

AI.tldr: A transformer-based 4D segmentation framework uses sequences of micro-CT images to separate physical pore-space change from segmentation error. It measures pore-volume growth and rock boundaries more accurately than an equivalent 3D model without temporal information, and captures the rise in permeability in mineral dissolution.
AI.motivation: Per-image 3D segmentation of time-resolved micro-CT varies from image to image, so these errors can be mistaken for physical change, while thresholding performs poorly on noisy, low-contrast images.
AI.method: A transformer-based 4D framework combines spatial and temporal information from sequential images to resolve ambiguous phase assignments.
AI.result: The method outperforms an equivalent 3D model on mineral dissolution images, captures the permeability increase verified against reference segmentations and flow simulations, transfers to another dissolution sample without retraining, and reduces spurious changes on two fluid displacement datasets while identifying filling events.
AI.conclusion: Spatiotemporal segmentation yields more reliable measurements of pore-space evolution and fluid displacement without per-image parameter tuning.

title: UAV-Flow++: A Unified Suite for Benchmarking and Learning Language-Guided UAV Flight
summary: Language-guided UAV navigation has largely focused on long-horizon route planning, leaving short-range, object-relative flight maneuvers underexplored. To address this gap, we formulate Flying-on-a-Word (Flow), a task requiring a UAV to convert concise natural-language instruction, egocentric visual observation, and current state dynamics into continuous flight actions. Flow encompasses both primitive motion commands and complex object-interactive behaviors, assessing motion intent comprehension and spatial context grounding. To enable policy learning and closed-loop evaluation, we introduce UAV-Flow, a comprehensive dataset comprising 30,692 expert-piloted real-world trajectories across eight distinct motion categories, alongside 10,109 simulation trajectories in the UAV-Flow-Sim environment equipped with task-specific completion criteria. Furthermore, we develop FlowVLA, which undergoes imitation pretraining on mixed real-sim demonstrations and online post-training via Tail-Aware GRPO (TGRPO). By leveraging group reward distributions, TGRPO effectively reinforces high-reward action sequences. Evaluated on 273 held-out UAV-Flow-Sim episodes, pretrained FlowVLA achieves a mean success rate of 75.58%, outperforming the strongest baseline by 6.72 percentage points, which TGRPO post-training further elevates to 93.16% with superior sample efficiency. Physical UAV experiments demonstrate robust execution of object-relative commands in both indoor and outdoor real-world scenes. Together, Flow establishes a novel benchmark and learning framework for language-conditioned flight maneuvers.

AI.tldr: UAV-Flow++ introduces the Flying-on-a-Word task and a dataset of 30,692 real and 10,109 simulated expert-piloted UAV trajectories for language-guided short-range flight, along with FlowVLA trained with Tail-Aware GRPO. FlowVLA reaches 75.58% success on 273 held-out simulated episodes, rising to 93.16% after TGRPO.
AI.motivation: Language-guided UAV navigation has focused on long-horizon route planning, leaving short-range object-relative maneuvers underexplored.
AI.method: Imitation pretraining on mixed real and simulated demonstrations, followed by online post-training with Tail-Aware GRPO (TGRPO), which reinforces high-reward action sequences using group reward distributions. The dataset spans eight motion categories and includes primitive and object-interactive behaviors.
AI.result: Pretrained FlowVLA achieves a mean success rate of 75.58% on 273 held-out UAV-Flow-Sim episodes, 6.72 points above the strongest baseline, and TGRPO raises it to 93.16% with better sample efficiency. Physical UAV experiments show robust execution of object-relative commands indoors and outdoors.
AI.conclusion: Flow provides a benchmark and learning framework for language-conditioned flight maneuvers, with real-world feasibility shown in preliminary physical tests.

title: Neural Render Proxies for Interactive and Differentiable Lighting
comment: Accepted at Computer Graphics Forum (Proc. EGSR 2026)
summary: Within the CG animation production pipeline, the challenges artists tackle in Lighting can be immense. Even minor adjustments require re-rendering massive scenes with slow offline renderers; global illumination has to be sampled and complex shaders have to be evaluated, leading to iteration times of minutes to hours per frame. To accelerate this process, we introduce a novel neural render proxy (NRP) that enables differentiable relighting of static scenes with fixed camera and materials at interactive rates. Our main insight is the decoupling of traditional rendering into path sampling and emission computation. From a single, light-agnostic render pass, we collect light transport data in the form of path samples. This enables rapidly sampling lighting conditions on the fly, and training a scene-specific lightweight neural network that learns how light is transported from any scene location to any image pixel. This approach is compatible with non-differentiable production renderers, induces minimal memory requirements during inference, and scales only with resolution and the number of light sources and parameters, but independently of scene and appearance complexity. Our evaluation demonstrates interactive frame rates for relighting (~30-60 Hz) while closely approximating the visual fidelity of ground-truth path tracing. In addition, the differentiable NRP enables fast, gradient-based inverse workflows, allowing artists to efficiently solve for lighting parameters from intuitive image-space edits or generative targets.

AI.tldr: Neural Render Proxies (NRP) enable differentiable, interactive relighting of static scenes with fixed camera and materials, by learning a scene-specific network from light transport path samples collected in one light-agnostic render pass. It reports about 30-60 Hz relighting while closely approximating ground-truth path tracing.
AI.motivation: Lighting iteration in CG production takes minutes to hours per frame with offline renderers, because global illumination and complex shaders must be re-evaluated for each change.
AI.method: Path sampling is decoupled from emission computation. From one light-agnostic render pass, path samples are collected and used to train a lightweight network that maps scene locations to image pixels, which can be sampled under new lighting on the fly and works with non-differentiable renderers.
AI.result: The method reaches interactive relighting rates of roughly 30-60 Hz while closely approximating ground-truth path tracing, and the differentiable proxy supports gradient-based inverse lighting from image-space edits or generative targets.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling path sampling from emission gives artists fast relighting and gradient-based inverse lighting, with cost that scales with resolution and light count rather than scene complexity.

title: ProtoVis-Nav: Prototypical Visual Imagination for Visual-Spatial Aligned UAV Navigation
summary: Vision language navigation (VLN) is very challenging for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) since small errors in 3D motion prediction can lead to navigation errors and collisions. Unable to fathom execution outcomes in 3D environments, existing methods often struggle to predict accurate navigation waypoints from language instructions. To solve this, we introduce the Prototypical Visual Imagination framework, shortened as ProtoVis-Nav, which forces the model to imagine an outcome-associated local visual representation for the intended next UAV movement. Specifically, we predict feature prototypes and use their linear combination to estimate the visual feature of the target region. In this manner, the VLN model first imagines the local visual representation of the next intended location, and then uses predicted prototypes as context for generating the final action, promoting alignment between visual context and waypoint outputs. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the ProtoVis-Nav framework and show substantial improvements over existing baselines.

AI.tldr: ProtoVis-Nav improves vision-language navigation for UAVs by having the model imagine the visual feature of the intended next location, estimated as a linear combination of predicted feature prototypes, before generating the action. The abstract reports substantial improvements over existing baselines.
AI.motivation: Small errors in 3D motion prediction cause navigation errors and collisions for UAVs, and existing methods struggle to predict accurate waypoints because they cannot anticipate the outcome of an action.
AI.method: The model predicts feature prototypes and combines them linearly to estimate the visual feature of the target region. These predicted prototypes then serve as context for generating the final action, aligning visual context with waypoint outputs.
AI.result: The abstract reports extensive experiments showing the effectiveness of the framework and substantial improvements over existing baselines, without giving numerical values.
AI.conclusion: Imagining the outcome-associated local visual representation before acting improves the alignment between visual context and waypoint prediction for UAV navigation.

title: Delaunay-Based Nearest Neighbor Search with Grid-Accelerated Queries and Parallel Construction
summary: Nearest-neighbor search is a fundamental primitive in computer graphics, with applications in distance field computation, surface reconstruction, and point cloud registration. In many graphics applications, data points lie on a surface manifold embedded in 3D space, whereas queries are distributed throughout the surrounding volume, a setting in which spatial partitioning structures such as k-d trees and grids can become inefficient. Dynamic-programming-based nearest-neighbor search (DP-NNS) offers an alternative: it traverses a successor DAG that records the history of incremental Delaunay construction and often outperforms spatial partitioning structures. However, its sequential construction is slow, and naive parallelization degrades query performance, limiting its practical adoption. We accelerate both queries and construction in DP-NNS. For queries, we introduce a grid-based initialization strategy that precomputes valid starting points on the successor DAG, shortening search paths while preserving exactness and enabling a twofold speedup. For construction, we analyze how parallel insertion affects query cost and develop a parallel algorithm that preserves logarithmic expected query cost under stated geometric assumptions. Our parallel construction algorithm achieves a 10x speedup over the sequential baseline while maintaining nearly the same query cost. We further reorder query points to improve cache locality. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms widely used libraries in nearest-neighbor query performance.

AI.tldr: The paper accelerates dynamic-programming nearest-neighbor search (DP-NNS) on Delaunay successor DAGs, with a grid-based initialization that gives a twofold query speedup and a parallel construction that gives a 10x construction speedup. Query cost stays nearly the same and remains logarithmic in expectation under stated assumptions.
AI.motivation: DP-NNS on surfaces embedded in 3D is fast for queries, but its sequential construction is slow and naive parallelization degrades query performance, while k-d trees and grids are inefficient for queries spread through the volume.
AI.method: A grid-based strategy precomputes valid starting points on the successor DAG to shorten search paths while keeping exactness. A parallel insertion algorithm for construction is analyzed for its effect on query cost, and query points are reordered for cache locality.
AI.result: Queries get a twofold speedup, and parallel construction reaches a 10x speedup over the sequential baseline with nearly the same query cost. The method outperforms widely used libraries in query performance.
AI.conclusion: Parallel Delaunay-based construction and grid-accelerated queries make DP-NNS practical for graphics applications such as distance fields and point cloud registration.

title: PIM: A Physical Intuition Model for Low-Latency Prediction of Object Interaction Outcomes
summary: Predicting object interaction outcomes from initial conditions is a central problem in data-driven physical reasoning. Existing methods often use rigid-body-level states or predict the evolution through autoregressive rollouts. Coarse representations cannot represent local deformation, while rollout errors may compound over long prediction horizons. Instead, we introduce PIM, a Physical Intuition Model that directly predicts a physical system's equilibrium state from its initial mesh geometry, kinematics, and physical attributes. PIM combines local k-nearest-neighbor (KNN) attention to encode intra-object geometry, anchor-based cross-object attention to model interactions, and a dual-branch decoder that predicts object-level translations and per-vertex residual displacements. Across MuJoCo scenarios involving both rigid and deformable interactions, PIM achieves lower vertex and centroid errors than the evaluated baselines. By predicting complete equilibrium states in a single forward pass, PIM substantially reduces latency relative to autoregressive learned models and MuJoCo rollouts under the evaluated protocols, enabling low-latency inference when only the final outcome is required.

AI.tldr: PIM predicts the equilibrium state of an object interaction in a single forward pass from initial mesh geometry, kinematics and physical attributes, combining KNN attention with anchor-based cross-object attention and a dual-branch decoder. It achieves lower vertex and centroid errors than the evaluated baselines on MuJoCo rigid and deformable scenarios, with substantially lower latency.
AI.motivation: Coarse rigid-body states cannot represent local deformation, and autoregressive rollouts accumulate errors over long horizons, while MuJoCo rollouts are slow.
AI.method: Local k-nearest-neighbor attention encodes intra-object geometry, anchor-based cross-object attention models interactions, and a dual-branch decoder predicts object-level translations and per-vertex residual displacements.
AI.result: Across MuJoCo scenarios with rigid and deformable interactions, PIM achieves lower vertex and centroid errors than the evaluated baselines, and it substantially reduces latency relative to autoregressive learned models and MuJoCo rollouts under the evaluated protocols.
AI.conclusion: Direct prediction of equilibrium states is a low-latency alternative when only the final outcome is needed.

title: Finite-Cadence Refresh Equilibria for Streaming Prior-Anchored Ridge: A Closed-Form Forgetting Window and Spectral Correction
comment: 67 pages, 7 figures. Lean 4 formalization and code: [this https URL](this https URL)
summary: Recursive estimators on drifting streams must forget stale data fast enough to track the target, yet slowly enough to average out noise. In prior-anchored ridge regression, this trade-off admits a closed-form spectral decomposition in which each eigen-direction interpolates between the data solution and the prior with pull weight $s_i = \rho / (\mu_i + \rho)$. When the anchor is refreshed every $k$ steps, we show that the moving-frame offset converges to a finite-cadence equilibrium that lags the pure-leaky path by an explicit $\Delta_k(s)$ while reducing estimation variance by a factor $\Psi(s, r_k)$. Minimizing the cycle-averaged risk gives $\omega^* = (4\nu^2 \Sigma / c')^{1/3}$, $c' = \sigma^2 d_{\mathrm{eff}}(\rho)$, and the plug-in strength $\rho^* = \sigma^2 / (n\delta^2)$. A random-matrix deterministic equivalent extends both laws to finite dimension, renormalizing the anchor to $\rho_{\mathrm{eff}} = \rho (e^{\zeta q} - 1) / (\zeta q)$; it matches simulation within 5% at fixed operating points and within 13% at the method's own, and rank-deficient populations reduce exactly to their active subspace. The resulting method, SPAR, calibrates window and strength online from residuals. On a 27-configuration grid the calibrated window opens on drift without divergence, and the grid defaults transfer to an hourly electricity stream and to BCI IV 2b. The core algebra, refresh chain, and regret bounds are formalized in Lean 4.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes prior-anchored ridge regression on drifting streams with periodic anchor refresh, giving a finite-cadence equilibrium, a closed-form forgetting window and a calibrated method, SPAR, that tunes window and strength online. A random-matrix deterministic equivalent matches simulation within 5% at fixed operating points, and the core algebra is formalized in Lean 4.
AI.motivation: Recursive estimators on drifting streams must forget stale data quickly enough to track the target and slowly enough to average out noise, and the trade-off has not been characterized when the prior anchor is refreshed every k steps.
AI.method: Each eigen-direction interpolates between data and prior with pull weight s_i = rho/(mu_i + rho). The authors derive the moving-frame equilibrium, an optimal window omega* and strength rho*, extend the laws by a random-matrix deterministic equivalent with renormalized anchor strength, and build SPAR, which calibrates from residuals.
AI.result: The analysis matches simulation within 5% at fixed operating points and within 13% at the method's own operating points. On a 27-configuration grid the calibrated window reacts to drift without divergence, and the defaults transfer to an hourly electricity stream and BCI IV 2b.
AI.conclusion: Closed-form forgetting windows with online calibration give stable tracking on drifting streams, with the core algebra and regret bounds formally verified in Lean 4.

title: An Eyring-Kramers Formula for Singular Wells
summary: Understanding the persistence of learned behaviors in AI safety motivates an investigation of the dynamical counterpart to the equilibrium geometry studied in singular learning theory. We analyze this persistence through transitions between singular wells. We establish an Eyring-Kramers formula for a low temperature Langevin diffusion between two compact connected zero components of a real-analytic potential. The wells may be singular and nonisolated, and the unique minimizing gate is a nondegenerate index-one saddle, with gates understood as inclusion-minimal sets meeting every minimizing path. A boundary-gate construction shows that uniqueness of this inclusion-minimal gate is equivalent to every minimizing path passing through the saddle and one such path meeting the communication level only there. Compact semianalytic topology provides a separating function away from a fixed saddle neighborhood; analytic Morse coordinates give matching capacity bounds by first sending the temperature to zero and then shrinking that neighborhood. An anchored energy estimate and a small-ball potential-theoretic identity give uniformity for deterministic starting points. The leading constant is expressed in terms of the sublevel-volume coefficient, a Gamma factor, and the saddle Hessian.

AI.tldr: The paper proves an Eyring-Kramers formula for the transition rate of a low-temperature Langevin diffusion between two singular wells of a real-analytic potential, where the unique minimizing gate is a nondegenerate index-one saddle. It gives the leading constant in terms of a sublevel-volume coefficient, a Gamma factor and the saddle Hessian.
AI.motivation: The persistence of learned behaviors in AI safety calls for a dynamical counterpart to the equilibrium geometry of singular learning theory, which requires transitions between singular, possibly non-isolated wells.
AI.method: The authors establish the formula for wells that are compact connected zero components of a real-analytic potential. A boundary-gate construction shows uniqueness of the inclusion-minimal gate is equivalent to all minimizing paths passing through the saddle, and separating functions, analytic Morse coordinates, capacity bounds and an anchored energy estimate are used.
AI.result: The leading constant is expressed through the sublevel-volume coefficient, a Gamma factor and the saddle Hessian, and the estimate holds uniformly for deterministic starting points.
AI.conclusion: Under the uniqueness of the minimizing gate, transition rates between singular wells follow an Eyring-Kramers law with an explicit constant.

title: Robbing Peter to Pay Paul: Cross-Attribute Externalities of Fairness Interventions
summary: Fairness interventions often targets disparities associated with a single sensitive attribute in binary classification tasks. However, when multiple sensitive attributes are associated with a data subject, improving fairness with respect to one attribute does not necessarily improve it across all attributes: it may exacerbate disparities associated with other sensitive attributes, including those that are unavailable to the practitioner. We refer to these unintended effects as cross-attribute externalities of fairness. We study how fairness with respect to one sensitive attribute varies when an initially unfair classification or regression model is corrected with respect to another attribute. We characterize these externalities using Wasserstein barycentric disparities and develop a distributional framework that captures changes in both marginal and joint fairness measures. This highlights a limitation of conventional fairness evaluation, in which the success of an intervention is assessed mainly for the attribute it targets. In a jointly Gaussian model, we derive explicit trajectories for marginal and joint disparities and identify conditions under which an intervention eliminates disparities with respect to its target attribute while increasing disparities associated with another attribute. We also derive sharp partial-identification bounds on the resulting externalities when a sensitive attribute is unavailable and extend our results to categorical sensitive attributes. We illustrate these externalities using classification and regression real-data: in the classification experiments, interventions increase unfairness with respect to the hidden attribute in the majority of scenarios across more than half of the datasets considered; in the regression experiments on the ACSIncome dataset, correcting for race reduces sex disparities, whereas subsequently correcting for age increases them.

AI.tldr: Shows that correcting a classifier or regressor for one sensitive attribute can increase unfairness with respect to other attributes, including hidden ones, and gives a distributional framework based on Wasserstein barycentric disparities to characterize these cross-attribute externalities.
AI.motivation: Fairness interventions are usually evaluated only for the single attribute they target, although a model may be unfair along several sensitive attributes at once and the effects on the others are not tracked.
AI.method: The authors model fairness correction as moving toward Wasserstein barycenters, derive explicit disparity trajectories for marginal and joint fairness in a jointly Gaussian model, give conditions under which an intervention removes disparity for its target while increasing it for another attribute, and derive sharp partial-identification bounds when an attribute is unavailable; results extend to categorical attributes.
AI.result: In classification experiments on real datasets, interventions increased unfairness with respect to the hidden attribute in most scenarios across more than half of the datasets; in regression on ACSIncome, correcting for race reduced sex disparities while subsequently correcting for age increased them.
AI.conclusion: Conventional fairness evaluation, which judges an intervention only on its target attribute, is limited, and fairness audits should consider effects on other attributes, including those the practitioner cannot observe.

title: Don't Match the Noise: Distribution Matching under Unknown Measurement Error with an Audit Sample
summary: Real-world machine learning systems often operate on imperfect measurements: sensors are noisy, annotations are produced by non-experts, and scientific observations are often indirect. In these settings, classic distribution comparison tools such as maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) can be systematically biased, matching artifacts of the measurement process rather than the underlying mechanisms of interest. We study a practical regime in which noisy observations are abundant, but only a small audited subset contains ground-truth measurements. We propose measurement-error-corrected MMD (MEC-MMD), an audit-based estimator that debiases kernel evaluations without requiring a noise model. MEC-MMD is exactly unbiased for the oracle MMD under simple random auditing, admits an explicit variance decomposition, and is consistent for the population MMD, achieving the standard $O_p(N^{-1/2})$ rate when the audit size scales with the dataset. We demonstrate the utility of distributional matching with MEC-MMD loss for both parameter estimation and unsupervised applications, showing that MEC-MMD consistently outperforms MMD and alternative methods. These results provide a principled foundation for robust distribution comparison, simulation-based inference, and learning in noisy real-world machine learning pipelines.

AI.tldr: Proposes MEC-MMD, an audit-based, noise-model-free version of maximum mean discrepancy that debiases kernel evaluations using a small audited subset with ground-truth measurements.
AI.motivation: Standard MMD can be biased when observations are noisy measurements, so distribution matching may fit measurement artifacts rather than the true underlying distribution, and the noise model is often unknown.
AI.method: Given abundant noisy observations and a small audit sample with ground truth, MEC-MMD corrects kernel evaluations by audit-based debiasing under simple random auditing; the estimator has an explicit variance decomposition and is used as a loss for parameter estimation and unsupervised learning.
AI.result: MEC-MMD is exactly unbiased for the oracle MMD under simple random auditing and consistent for the population MMD at the standard O_p(N^-1/2) rate when the audit size scales with the dataset; it consistently outperformed MMD and alternative methods in the reported experiments.
AI.conclusion: Provides a principled basis for robust distribution comparison, simulation-based inference and learning from noisy data without specifying the noise.

title: Improved last-iterate bounds for SGD with and without replacement
summary: In this work, we study last-iterate convergence bounds for stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on convex and $\beta$-smooth loss functions and improve the bound from $\cO((\log T)^3/T)$ to $\cO((\log T)^3/(T\log\log T))$ in the interpolation regime. The improvement comes from applying a horizon-dependent multiscale estimate of gradients to the comparison of trajectories. The bound applies to both sampling with replacement and sampling without replacement within one pass.

AI.tldr: Improves last-iterate convergence bounds for SGD on convex, beta-smooth losses in the interpolation regime, from O((log T)^3/T) to O((log T)^3/(T log log T)), for both sampling with and without replacement within one pass.
AI.motivation: Prior last-iterate bounds for SGD on smooth convex losses in the interpolation regime left room for improvement in the dependence on T, and the analysis needed to cover both sampling schemes.
AI.method: The improvement uses a horizon-dependent multiscale estimate of gradients, applied in the comparison of SGD trajectories.
AI.result: The bound improves the rate from O((log T)^3/T) to O((log T)^3/(T log log T)) and holds for both sampling with replacement and sampling without replacement within one pass.
AI.conclusion: A sharper last-iterate guarantee for SGD in the interpolation regime, applicable to both common sampling schemes.

title: Synthetic Data Augmentation for Fairness under Data Imbalance: Theory and Adaptive Allocation
summary: Data imbalance across sensitive groups and class labels is common in classification problems and can contribute to substantial fairness disparities. We study how such imbalance affects Equal Opportunity and how synthetic data augmentation can mitigate the resulting unfairness. We first identify two mechanisms, prevalence imbalance and group-size imbalance, through which changes in the training distribution shift the learned decision boundary and induce disparities in group true positive rates. Motivated by this analysis, we study exact full-balance augmentation, which equalizes all group-label cells. We establish conditions under which full balancing strictly improves Equal Opportunity together with a prediction-error comparison under the oracle balanced distribution, and show that the Equal Opportunity gap of the synthetic-data classifier converges to that of the oracle balanced classifier as the sample size grows and the generator error vanishes. The finite-sample convergence rate agrees, up to logarithmic factors and generator-approximation error, with the information-theoretic lower-bound rate under the corresponding regularity regimes. Since exact balancing need not provide the best fairness-accuracy trade-off in practice, we further propose Accuracy-Constrained Adaptive Synthetic Augmentation (ACASA), which learns both where and how much to augment by minimizing estimated fairness disparity subject to a constraint on predictive accuracy. We provide a finite-sample guarantee comparing the selected augmentation allocation with the population-optimal accuracy-feasible allocation. Simulation studies and real data application support the theoretical findings and demonstrate that synthetic augmentation can substantially reduce fairness disparities while achieving favorable empirical fairness-accuracy trade-offs.

AI.tldr: Analyses how group and label imbalance affects Equal Opportunity, shows that full-balance synthetic augmentation can improve it, and proposes ACASA, an adaptive allocation of synthetic data that minimizes estimated fairness disparity under an accuracy constraint.
AI.motivation: Imbalance across sensitive groups and labels causes fairness disparities, and exact balancing of the training data may not give the best fairness-accuracy trade-off in practice.
AI.method: The authors identify prevalence imbalance and group-size imbalance as two mechanisms that shift the decision boundary and cause group true positive rate gaps; they study full-balance augmentation that equalizes all group-label cells and propose ACASA, which learns where and how much to augment by minimizing estimated disparity subject to an accuracy constraint.
AI.result: Theory gives conditions under which full balancing strictly improves Equal Opportunity, and the Equal Opportunity gap of the synthetic-data classifier converges to that of the oracle balanced classifier as sample size grows and generator error vanishes, with a finite-sample rate matching the information-theoretic lower bound up to logarithmic and generator-approximation factors; ACASA has a finite-sample guarantee against the population-optimal accuracy-feasible allocation. Simulations and a real data application show substantial disparity reduction with favorable fairness-accuracy trade-offs.
AI.conclusion: Synthetic augmentation can reduce fairness disparities, and an adaptive, accuracy-constrained allocation can be preferable to exact balancing.

title: Nested Ensemble Learning with Topological Data Analysis for Graph Classification and Regression
comment: This is the published version of the article. Published in International Journal of Topology, MDPI, DOI: https://doi.org/10.3390/ijt2040017. Link to the official version: this https URL
summary: We propose a nested ensemble learning framework that utilizes Topological Data Analysis (TDA) to extract and integrate topological features from graph data, with the goal of improving performance on classification and regression tasks. Our approach computes persistence diagrams (PDs) using lower-star filtrations induced by three filter functions: closeness, betweenness, and degree2 centrality. To overcome the limitation of relying on a single filter, these PDs are integrated through a data-driven, three-level architecture. At Level-0, diverse base models are independently trained on the topological features extracted for each filter function. At Level-1, a meta-learner combines the predictions of these base models for each filter to form filter-specific ensembles. Finally, at Level-2, a meta-learner integrates the outputs of these filter-specific ensembles to produce the final prediction. We evaluate our method on both simulated and real-world graph datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that our framework consistently outperforms base models and standard stacking methods, achieving higher classification accuracy and lower regression error. It also surpasses existing state-of-the-art approaches, ranking among the top three models across all benchmarks.

AI.tldr: Proposes a three-level nested ensemble that builds persistence diagrams from three centrality-based lower-star filtrations and combines the resulting topological features for graph classification and regression.
AI.motivation: Relying on a single filter function limits the topological information extracted from graphs, and standard stacking does not exploit the structure of multiple filters.
AI.method: Persistence diagrams are computed with lower-star filtrations induced by closeness, betweenness and degree2 centrality; at Level-0 base models are trained on each filter's features, at Level-1 a meta-learner forms a filter-specific ensemble, and at Level-2 a meta-learner integrates these ensembles into the final prediction.
AI.result: The framework consistently outperforms base models and standard stacking, achieving higher classification accuracy and lower regression error on simulated and real graph datasets, and ranks among the top three models across all benchmarks compared with existing state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: Combining topological features from several filter functions in a nested ensemble improves graph learning over single-filter and standard stacking approaches.

title: Communication-Efficient Federated Multi-View Clustering via View-Aware Quantization
summary: Federated multi-view clustering (FedMVC) has recently attracted increasing attention for its ability to exploit complementary clustering structures across multiple clients while preserving data privacy. However, existing FedMVC methods often suffer from high communication overhead due to the repeated transmission of high-dimensional representations, which limits their scalability in practical federated systems. Moreover, different views may contribute unequally to the clustering performance, calling for adaptive communication strategies. In this paper, we propose a view-aware quantization algorithm for communication-efficient FedMVC. By dynamically assigning quantization bits based on iteratively updated view importance scores, the proposed algorithm effectively balances clustering performance and communication efficiency under a global bit budget constraint. To validate its generality, we integrate our approach into four state-of-the-art FedMVC methods. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that view-aware quantization achieves up to 6.59x communication reduction while maintaining and in some cases surpassing baseline clustering performance, confirming the effectiveness and scalability of the proposed approach.

AI.tldr: Proposes a view-aware quantization algorithm that allocates bits across views by their importance for communication-efficient federated multi-view clustering, reporting up to 6.59x communication reduction.
AI.motivation: Federated multi-view clustering repeatedly transmits high-dimensional representations, causing high communication overhead, and views contribute unequally to clustering, so uniform communication is inefficient.
AI.method: Quantization bits are assigned dynamically from iteratively updated view importance scores under a global bit budget; the approach is integrated into four state-of-the-art FedMVC methods.
AI.result: On multiple benchmark datasets, view-aware quantization achieves up to 6.59x communication reduction while maintaining or in some cases surpassing baseline clustering performance.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, view-aware bit allocation is an effective and scalable way to reduce communication in federated multi-view clustering.

title: Bet Imaginatively, not Historically in Independent-Data Sequential Testing
summary: Sequential testing avoids some of the many controversies and drawbacks related to traditional batch testing with p-values. In particular, the testing by betting paradigm has developed rapidly in recent years; it frames the level of evidence against the null as the wealth of a player in a betting game. Naturally, how much a player should bet is a key consideration, and should reflect their confidence in what they know about the next observed data point. Much current work uses standard betting strategies developed for adversarial problems. In the stochastic setting, where the observed data is independent and stationary, these approaches may be suboptimal. We propose a simple betting strategy, follow the leave-one-out e-power (FLOE), that exploits the i.i.d. nature of a data stream to estimate the e-power of our current test on the underlying distribution. We average not over the historical evidence collected so far, as generic online learning-based methods do, but instead over the equally-likely possible data sequences we might have seen based on shuffling the data. With an additional principled regularization technique, this simple drop-in method yields substantial improvements in testing performance on a variety of kernel two-sample and independence testing problems.

AI.tldr: Proposes FLOE, a betting strategy for sequential testing with i.i.d. data that averages over shuffled data sequences to estimate the e-power of the current test, yielding substantial gains on kernel two-sample and independence tests.
AI.motivation: Standard betting strategies come from adversarial settings and may be suboptimal when data are independent and stationary, while generic online-learning methods average over the historical evidence rather than exploiting the i.i.d. structure.
AI.method: Follow the leave-one-out e-power (FLOE) exploits the i.i.d. nature of the stream: it estimates the e-power of the current test on the underlying distribution by averaging over the equally likely data sequences obtained by shuffling the data, together with an additional regularization technique.
AI.result: The simple drop-in method yields substantial improvements in testing performance on a variety of kernel two-sample and independence testing problems.
AI.conclusion: Betting strategies tailored to the stochastic setting can improve sequential testing, and a shuffling-based estimate of bet size is a practical drop-in replacement.

title: Learning Mixtures of Exponential Family
summary: Motivated by causal inference and physical computing systems, we consider the problem of learning mixture of two bounded-support exponential-family distributions with a shared interaction parameter matrix and mixture component-specific linear parameter vectors. The unknown sequence of component labels belongs to a known structured class. We propose an estimator based on a convex loss that avoids the log-partition function; for each fixed label assignment, estimation is a convex optimization problem. We show that the conditional population loss uniquely identifies the interaction matrix and the linear parameter attached to each sample. For a global empirical minimizer, we establish finite-sample bounds on the interaction error in Frobenius norm and the average squared linear-parameter error. The bounds depend on the logarithm of the number of admissible label assignments, and, for fixed dimension and model bounds, imply consistency when this complexity grows sublinearly with sample size. Additional occupancy and separation conditions yield component and label recovery.

AI.tldr: Gives an estimator for mixtures of two bounded-support exponential-family distributions with a shared interaction matrix, based on a convex loss that avoids the log-partition function, with finite-sample error bounds.
AI.motivation: Motivated by causal inference and physical computing systems, the problem requires learning mixtures with shared interaction parameters and unknown structured label assignments, where the log-partition function complicates estimation.
AI.method: The estimator minimizes a convex loss that avoids the log-partition function; for each fixed label assignment estimation is a convex optimization problem, and a global empirical minimizer is taken over admissible label assignments.
AI.result: The conditional population loss uniquely identifies the interaction matrix and the linear parameter of each sample; finite-sample bounds are given on the Frobenius-norm interaction error and the average squared linear-parameter error, depending on the log of the number of admissible label assignments; occupancy and separation conditions yield component and label recovery.
AI.conclusion: The error bounds imply consistency when the complexity of the label-assignment class grows sublinearly with sample size, and the additional conditions allow recovery of components and labels.

title: Global-Local and Window-Concatenated Functional Random Forests: Early and Late Fusion of Window-Specific Functional Principal Components
summary: Functional random forests built on a single functional principal component decomposition of the whole domain may dilute features confined to short intervals, whose location is rarely known in advance. We propose two random forests based on window-specific functional principal components. The global-local functional random forest (GL-FRF) is a late-fusion method that stacks a tuned full-curve forest and one forest per window with penalised convex weights; it contains the full-curve forest as a feasible solution, and its weights indicate which parts of the domain drive the prediction. The window-concatenated functional random forest (WC-FRF) is an early-fusion method that trains a single tuned forest on the concatenated window-specific scores. On twenty UCR datasets, GL-FRF improved on a tuned full-curve forest with the same number of trees on 16, with Brier score reductions of up to 0.21, significantly after Holm adjustment. No method was best on more than six datasets. WC-FRF was more accurate than GL-FRF on 13 datasets but failed when the signal required the full curve, whereas GL-FRF had the smallest mean and maximum excess over the best method across all 32 simulated and real settings, which makes it the safer choice when the location of the signal is unknown.

AI.tldr: Proposes two functional random forests built on window-specific functional principal components: GL-FRF, a late-fusion stacking method, and WC-FRF, an early-fusion method, for functional data whose informative interval is unknown.
AI.motivation: A single functional PCA over the whole domain can dilute features confined to short intervals whose location is rarely known in advance.
AI.method: GL-FRF stacks a tuned full-curve forest and one forest per window with penalised convex weights, which include the full-curve forest as a feasible solution; WC-FRF trains one tuned forest on concatenated window-specific scores.
AI.result: On twenty UCR datasets, GL-FRF improved on a tuned full-curve forest on 16 with Brier score reductions up to 0.21, significantly after Holm adjustment; no method was best on more than six datasets. WC-FRF was more accurate than GL-FRF on 13 datasets but failed when the signal required the full curve; GL-FRF had the smallest mean and maximum excess over the best method across 32 settings.
AI.conclusion: GL-FRF is the safer choice when the location of the signal is unknown, while WC-FRF is more accurate on some datasets but fails when the full curve is needed.

title: Distribution-First Framework for Learning Risk-Sensitive Individualized Treatment Rules
summary: Learning a risk-sensitive individualized treatment rule (ITR) with patient covariates is challenging when the treatment criterion depends on the full conditional outcome distribution rather than only its conditional mean. Existing methods are largely criterion-specific, making it difficult to compare multiple treatment criteria within a common pipeline, such as quantiles, conditional value-at-risk (CVaR), and complex preference-based objectives such as cumulative prospect theory. We propose a distribution-first framework for risk-sensitive ITR learning that first estimates treatment-specific conditional outcome distributions and then constructs the target ITR by plug-in criterion evaluation. The proposed framework unifies treatment rule learning across multiple criteria and accommodates hard-to-optimize objectives within the same estimation pipeline. On the theoretical side, it yields a general error propagation result for locally Hölder-stable criteria, linking first-stage distribution estimation error to downstream criterion estimation and treatment regret, together with sharper regret bounds under standard margin conditions. Empirically, we show that the proposed framework outperforms direct criterion-specific methods in multiple settings and further evaluate it on the ACTG175 HIV clinical trial, a randomized study comparing several antiretroviral regimens in HIV-infected adults.

AI.tldr: Proposes a distribution-first framework for risk-sensitive individualized treatment rules: estimate treatment-specific outcome distributions, then plug them into any criterion such as quantiles, CVaR or cumulative prospect theory.
AI.motivation: Existing risk-sensitive ITR methods are criterion-specific, making it hard to compare several treatment criteria within one pipeline, and some objectives are hard to optimize directly.
AI.method: The framework estimates treatment-specific conditional outcome distributions and constructs the target rule by plug-in evaluation of the criterion; theory gives an error propagation result for locally Hölder-stable criteria and sharper regret bounds under margin conditions.
AI.result: The framework outperforms direct criterion-specific methods in multiple settings and is evaluated on the ACTG175 HIV trial comparing antiretroviral regimens.
AI.conclusion: A single distributional pipeline unifies treatment rule learning across risk criteria, including hard-to-optimize ones, with regret controlled by first-stage distribution estimation error.

title: When and How SignSGD Outperforms SGD: A Functional Scaling Law Perspective
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 as a spotlight paper
summary: We study how the sign operator interacts with gradient noise to shape the learning dynamics and scaling behavior of sign-based optimizers. In power-law kernel regression with diagonal features, we establish a functional scaling law (FSL) for SignSGD under general learning rate schedules. The FSL describes the learning dynamics through two processes: signal learning and noise forgetting. The key mechanism is noise-induced preconditioning: gradient noise smooths the sign operator, inducing an effective preconditioned SGD. Noise-curvature alignment enables this preconditioning to transform the effective Hessian from $\mathbf{H}$ to $\mathbf{H}^{1/2}$. The resulting dynamics exhibit faster signal learning but slower noise forgetting than SGD. This tradeoff yields a regime-dependent comparison with SGD: (i) SignSGD achieves improved data efficiency in the hard-task regime; (ii) both optimizers achieve the same data efficiency in the easy-task regime, but SignSGD maintains this efficiency at larger batch sizes, requiring fewer optimization steps for a fixed data budget. Power-law kernel regression experiments support the proposed mechanism and predicted scaling behavior. LLM pre-training experiments further suggest that the SignSGD FSL better captures the batch-size dependence of loss dynamics for sign-based optimizers than the original SGD FSL.

AI.tldr: Analyses SignSGD in power-law kernel regression and derives a functional scaling law showing that gradient noise makes sign-based updates act as preconditioned SGD, giving faster signal learning but slower noise forgetting than SGD.
AI.motivation: The learning dynamics and scaling behaviour of sign-based optimizers, and when they outperform SGD, are not well understood, and existing SGD scaling laws do not capture the batch-size dependence of sign methods.
AI.method: In power-law kernel regression with diagonal features, the authors establish a functional scaling law (FSL) for SignSGD under general learning rate schedules, describing signal learning and noise forgetting; the mechanism is noise-induced preconditioning, in which noise-curvature alignment transforms the effective Hessian from H to H^1/2.
AI.result: SignSGD achieves improved data efficiency in the hard-task regime; in the easy-task regime both optimizers have the same data efficiency, but SignSGD maintains it at larger batch sizes, needing fewer steps for a fixed data budget. Kernel regression experiments and LLM pre-training experiments support the mechanism, with the SignSGD FSL capturing batch-size dependence better than the SGD FSL.
AI.conclusion: Sign-based optimization is advantageous in hard tasks and at large batch sizes, and the noise-induced preconditioning explains the regime-dependent comparison with SGD.

title: Stochastic Kernel Mode Decomposition: Information, Uncertainty, and Conditional Regime Inference
summary: When do mode energies preserve regime information as measurement quality changes? Stochastic Kernel Mode Decomposition (sKMD) fits joint regime laws on signed KMD mode coordinates and transfers the reference mode posterior to regime probabilities and conditional reconstructions. For centered Gaussian regimes with independently varying known noise variances, fixed coordinate energies retain the full regime posterior precisely when all classes share their cross-covariances and class variances can differ only at isolated vertices of the covariance graph. We extend the characterization to nonzero means and show that freely varying correlated noise forces a fixed linear log-odds decoder to retain the full quadratic feature span even for two distinct centered regimes. At fixed quality, a three-regime example has no sufficient two-energy basis. Its smallest Bayes log-loss gap over bases of condition number at most $\kappa$ has sharp order $\kappa^{-1}$. Exact Bayes energy posteriors supply numerical gap estimates for specified bases. Additional bounds relate feature compression, independently learned mode spans and sensor-noise error to log loss. Two controlled experiments with 64 independent panels each show that signed information can improve prediction over energy summaries, while integration gives small gains over strong signed controls and depends on how the competing point rule is calibrated and how accurately observation noise is measured.

AI.tldr: Introduces stochastic Kernel Mode Decomposition (sKMD), which maps signed KMD mode coordinates to regime probabilities, and characterizes when fixed energy summaries retain the full regime information.
AI.motivation: It is unclear when mode energies preserve regime information as measurement quality changes, and whether signed mode coordinates carry more information than energy summaries.
AI.method: sKMD fits joint regime laws on signed mode coordinates and transfers the reference mode posterior to regime probabilities and conditional reconstructions; the analysis covers centered Gaussian regimes with known varying noise variances, nonzero means and correlated noise, and includes bounds relating feature compression, learned mode spans and sensor-noise error to log loss.
AI.result: For centered Gaussian regimes, fixed coordinate energies retain the full regime posterior exactly when classes share cross-covariances and class variances differ only at isolated vertices of the covariance graph; freely varying correlated noise forces a linear log-odds decoder to keep the full quadratic feature span; a three-regime example has no sufficient two-energy basis, with a smallest Bayes log-loss gap of sharp order kappa^-1. Two controlled experiments with 64 panels each show that signed information can improve prediction over energy summaries, while integration gives small gains over strong signed controls.
AI.conclusion: Signed mode information can help prediction, but the benefit over strong controls is small and depends on how the competing rule is calibrated and how accurately observation noise is measured.

title: Prevalence Bounds for Edited Watermarked Text: Power Envelopes and Calibration Sensitivity
comment: 31 pages, 3 figures, 8 tables. Code and results: this https URL
summary: Watermark detectors decide whether one document came from a watermarked language model. Auditors often need a different number: the share of a corpus that did. We study this share for Gumbel-max and green-list (KGW) watermarks when every document may have been edited by an unknown amount. Without restrictions on the edits, the upper end of the identified set is 1. Combining a known least-favourable next-token distribution with a sequential coupling, we derive a power envelope indexed by three budgets: a retention floor, an entropy budget, and a budget for in-place substitutions, which for Gumbel-max make edited positions look less watermarked than human text. The envelope gives an identified set that is sharp for the alternatives it dominates, finite-sample bounds on the realized share of a fixed corpus with either the exact null or a null calibrated on an independent human sample, and confidence sequences for streams. In Gumbel-max simulations where the envelope binds, the bounds cover, and the threshold that maximizes the gap between envelope and null is generally as tight as twelve thresholds. On text from OPT-1.3B and Qwen3-1.7B, 12,000 fresh human documents scored under three keys show no robust departure from the exact null, and all bounds covered in resampling trials from finite pools of documents with random edits, substitutions and paraphrases; at a share of 0.2 the exact-null bound is about [0.14,0.38]. These results are fragile in two ways we make precise. LLM-paraphrased KGW pools fall below the envelope, yet at 2000 documents the bounds still covered in these trials. A simulated null error of 0.01, comparable to the largest deviation we observed at our thresholds, is likewise harmless at 2000 documents but breaks exact-null coverage at 100,000; a null calibrated on an independent human sample keeps coverage there, but needs a large reference sample to stay narrow.

AI.tldr: Derives power envelopes and finite-sample bounds on the share of a corpus that is watermarked under Gumbel-max and KGW schemes when documents may be edited by an unknown amount, and tests the bounds on OPT-1.3B and Qwen3-1.7B text.
AI.motivation: Auditors need the fraction of a corpus generated by a watermarked model, but without restrictions on edits the upper end of the identified set is 1, so informative bounds require assumptions on the edits.
AI.method: Combining a least-favourable next-token distribution with a sequential coupling, the authors derive a power envelope indexed by a retention floor, an entropy budget and a budget for in-place substitutions, giving an identified set, finite-sample bounds under an exact or calibrated null, and confidence sequences for streams.
AI.result: In Gumbel-max simulations where the envelope binds, the bounds cover and the best threshold is about as tight as twelve thresholds. On OPT-1.3B and Qwen3-1.7B text with 12,000 human documents, there is no robust departure from the exact null, and bounds covered in resampling trials with edits, substitutions and paraphrases; at a share of 0.2 the exact-null bound is about [0.14, 0.38]. LLM-paraphrased KGW pools fall below the envelope, yet bounds still covered at 2000 documents; a simulated null error of 0.01 is harmless at 2000 documents but breaks exact-null coverage at 100,000.
AI.conclusion: Corpus-level watermark prevalence can be bounded under edits, but the bounds are sensitive to null calibration at large sample sizes, and a null calibrated on an independent human sample keeps coverage but needs a large reference sample to stay narrow.

title: Quantifying structural stability of transparent models for general insurance pricing
summary: The short duration of general insurance contracts leads to rapid distributional shifts in the data, warranting regular model updates. This process may yield a post-update model that differs considerably from the pre-update model in both predictions and structure. Structural stability is upstream of predictive stability, yet existing structural stability metrics are mostly restricted to simple decision trees. Thus, we first introduce the notion of functional transparency, characterising models with a prediction function that can be expressed as a sum of univariate functions for main effects and bivariate functions for pairwise interactions. Then, we propose the Mean Squared Shape function distance, a metric to quantify the structural stability of functionally transparent models, which are particularly relevant in actuarial science. Using three public auto insurance datasets, we present a benchmark study to demonstrate the usefulness of our metric in identifying a stable and accurate transparent model. Generalised linear models with centred numerical covariates are stable, and explainable boosting machines (EBMs) offer a compromise between stability and performance. We also find that stabilisation strategies, such as sequential modelling and fixed hyperparameters, can substantially improve stability for both EBM and XGBoost models, with negligible impact on performance.

AI.tldr: Introduces functional transparency and a Mean Squared Shape function distance to quantify the structural stability of transparent insurance pricing models across updates, and benchmarks GLMs, EBMs and XGBoost on three public auto insurance datasets.
AI.motivation: Frequent model updates in general insurance can change a model's structure as well as its predictions, but existing structural stability metrics are mostly restricted to simple decision trees.
AI.method: Functionally transparent models are defined as sums of univariate main-effect functions and bivariate pairwise-interaction functions; the authors propose the Mean Squared Shape function distance and benchmark it on three public auto insurance datasets, including sequential modelling and fixed hyperparameters as stabilisation strategies.
AI.result: GLMs with centred numerical covariates are stable; explainable boosting machines offer a compromise between stability and performance; stabilisation strategies substantially improve stability for both EBM and XGBoost with negligible impact on performance.
AI.conclusion: The metric can identify stable and accurate transparent models, and simple stabilisation strategies can improve stability without sacrificing performance.

title: Katz Kernel Based Stratification of Breast Cancer Patients
summary: The integration of mechanistic signaling networks into clinical research has become a cornerstone of precision oncology. By capturing the complex biochemical interactions within a cell, these networks provide a functional map of disease progression that goes beyond simple genomic mutations. Consequently, the development of specific signaling models of patients has significant relevance, allowing for a more granular representation of individual disease profiles. In this setting, there is a growing need for robust methodologies capable of comparing graph based pathway structures to identify similarities and differences across patient cohorts. Such comparisons are essential for the identification of clinically meaningful subgroups, and the discovery of novel biomarkers. Standard graph kernels, while mathematically rigorous, often remain too generic for this purpose. They frequently fail to capture features specific to gene signaling networks, resulting in suboptimal clustering performance. In this paper, we present a domain specific graph kernel designed for mechanistic signaling networks. Unlike generic approaches, our method explicitly incorporates biological constraints and gene interaction patterns into the kernel formulation, enabling a more accurate characterization of both topological structure and functional behavior. We assess its performance on breast cancer datasets, focusing on its ability to support disease subtyping. Our results suggest that our approach can effectively contribute to patient stratification.

AI.tldr: Presents a domain-specific graph kernel for mechanistic signalling networks that encodes biological constraints and gene interaction patterns, and applies it to stratify breast cancer patients by disease subtype.
AI.motivation: Generic graph kernels are too generic for gene signalling networks and yield suboptimal clustering for patient stratification.
AI.method: The kernel explicitly incorporates biological constraints and gene interaction patterns into its formulation to characterize both the topological structure and the functional behaviour of patient-specific signalling networks.
AI.result: The abstract reports that the approach can effectively contribute to patient stratification on breast cancer datasets focused on disease subtyping; no specific numerical results are stated in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Domain-informed graph kernels may support identifying clinically meaningful patient subgroups and biomarkers.

title: Thompson Sampling using Prior-fitted Diffusion Transformers
summary: Thompson sampling is natural randomized strategy for optimizing unknown functions in a black-box manner. In continuous global optimization, Thompson sampling has largely been restricted to Gaussian process priors, as these are essentially the only class for which computing the posterior distribution has been tractable in practice. In this work, we introduce \emph{prior-fitted diffusion transformers}, which are diffusion models that perform Thompson sampling in-context at inference time, after being pre-trained using the prior-fitted network paradigm. To apply these models, we develop a set of practical non-Gaussian priors for general black-box functions---including those that have characteristics that cannot be achieved under Gaussianity, such as priors over unimodal functions. We also quantify the tradeoff between model size and the number of pre-training iterations, and show that these models follow scaling laws akin to those observed in transformers defined over other modalities. Across a set of global optimization benchmarks, we show that prior-fitted diffusion transformers with non-Gaussian priors can achieve improved performance compared to traditional pipelines built on Gaussian processes.

AI.tldr: Introduces prior-fitted diffusion transformers that perform Thompson sampling in context for black-box global optimization, pre-trained with non-Gaussian priors, and reports better performance than Gaussian-process pipelines on optimization benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Thompson sampling for continuous optimization has been mostly limited to Gaussian process priors, as those are essentially the only class with tractable posteriors in practice.
AI.method: Diffusion models are pre-trained with the prior-fitted network paradigm to perform Thompson sampling in context at inference time; the authors design practical non-Gaussian priors for general black-box functions, including priors over unimodal functions, and study the trade-off between model size and pre-training iterations.
AI.result: The models follow scaling laws similar to those observed for transformers in other modalities, and on a set of global optimization benchmarks prior-fitted diffusion transformers with non-Gaussian priors achieve improved performance over traditional Gaussian-process pipelines.
AI.conclusion: Pre-trained in-context samplers with non-Gaussian priors are a viable alternative to Gaussian-process Thompson sampling for black-box optimization.

title: Code as Explanations: Executable and Verifiable LLM Explanations
comment: 30 pages, 11 figures, 3 tables, The Fortieth Annual Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
summary: As large language models (LLMs) increasingly make consequential decisions and solve problems alongside humans, we must understand how models arrive at their conclusions. Understanding how an LLM behaves requires observing it across multiple inputs, yet free-text explanations such as chain-of-thought (CoT) are generated per instance and cannot be easily verified on new inputs. We propose {code explanations to address the mismatch in how LLM explanations are generated versus how they are evaluated: a program explains LLM behavior across a dataset of inputs, and its execution enables automatic verification. We define Consistency metric that measures the fraction of inputs on which the program reproduces the LLM's outputs, and use it to evaluate and select candidate programs. Across three open-source code-capable LLMs and eight tasks, we find that LLMs can produce highly consistent code explanations in several settings. Code explanations are also 6$\times$ to 100$\times$ shorter than CoT, and better align with model behavior in 9 out of 24 settings. However, consistency is significantly lower on tasks with more complex linguistic components, where generated programs reproduce model outputs no more frequently than an uninformative explanation baseline, and these programs often rely on longer hard-coded patterns. In experiments with Claude Opus 5.5, providing the model with consistency feedback and code execution improves explanation consistency across tasks, but consistency remains significantly lower on more complex tasks. Our findings establish executable code as a novel, verifiable, and compact approach to explaining LLM behavior and highlight verification feedback as a promising direction for improving explanation consistency. The code for this paper is at this https URL.

AI.tldr: Proposes code explanations: a program that explains an LLM's behaviour across a dataset of inputs and can be executed to verify it, with a Consistency metric measuring how often the program reproduces the model's outputs.
AI.motivation: Free-text explanations such as chain-of-thought are generated per instance and cannot be easily verified on new inputs, while understanding model behaviour requires observing it across many inputs.
AI.method: The authors define a Consistency metric as the fraction of inputs on which the program reproduces the LLM's outputs, use it to evaluate and select candidate programs, and test three open-source code-capable LLMs on eight tasks; they also test Claude Opus 5.5 with consistency feedback and code execution.
AI.result: Highly consistent code explanations arise in several settings and are 6x to 100x shorter than CoT; they align better with model behaviour in 9 of 24 settings. Consistency is significantly lower on tasks with more complex linguistic components, where programs do no better than an uninformative baseline. Feedback and code execution improve consistency across tasks, but consistency remains significantly lower on the more complex tasks.
AI.conclusion: Executable code is a verifiable and compact way to explain LLM behaviour, and verification feedback is a promising direction, though complex tasks remain hard.

title: Characterizing Local Breadth in Language Generation
summary: Large language models sharpen the validity--breadth trade-off: a generator should avoid hallucinations without collapsing onto a narrow set of valid outputs. We study generation from positive examples of an unknown target in the Kleinberg--Mullainathan model, with arbitrary, possibly adversarial order and no distributional or computational assumptions. Breadth is measured by lower Banach density, which rules out arbitrarily large sparse holes, unlike prefix-based lower asymptotic density. 1. Exact optima in one dimension: For each target $K$ in a countable family, we characterize its optimal lower Banach density $b(K)$ via equivalent combinatorial and topological formulations. One eventually valid generator attains all $b(K)$ simultaneously. Every $\alpha\in[0,1/2]$ occurs as $b(K)$ in some countable family; finite Cantor--Bendixson point rank guarantees $b(K)=1/2$, even without a uniform rank bound. 2. Unavoidable trade-offs in higher dimensions: For $d\ge2$, there need not be a single best generator: optimizing density for one target may worsen the guarantee for another. An explicit family quantifies this intrinsically multi-objective trade-off. 3. Complete characterization of density profiles: We characterize the full region of simultaneously achievable guarantees, with equivalent combinatorial and topological formulations, after excluding geometrically degenerate rectangles. Every prescribed product $\prod_i[0,\alpha_i]$, $\alpha_i\in[0,1/2]$ can occur as an exact achievable region for some language collection. 4. Near-half guarantees and the sharp endpoint: Under a near-logarithmic nondegeneracy condition, one generator achieves filtered density at least $1/2-\varepsilon$ at all finite-point-rank targets, for every $\varepsilon>0$, improving the previous polylogarithmic threshold. The exact $1/2$ endpoint can fail even for a rank-zero singleton family.

AI.tldr: Characterizes the optimal lower Banach density of generators in the Kleinberg-Mullainathan language generation model, giving exact one-dimensional optima, unavoidable multi-objective trade-offs in higher dimensions, and a near-1/2 guarantee under a nondegeneracy condition.
AI.motivation: LLMs face a validity-breadth trade-off, and prefix-based density notions can miss arbitrarily large sparse holes, so a finer breadth measure is needed.
AI.method: Breadth is measured by lower Banach density; the authors give combinatorial and topological characterizations of the optimal density b(K) for countable families in one dimension, analyze multi-target trade-offs for dimension d at least 2, and characterize the full achievable region of density profiles.
AI.result: In one dimension one eventually valid generator attains all b(K) simultaneously, and every alpha in [0,1/2] occurs as some b(K); finite Cantor-Bendixson point rank guarantees b(K)=1/2. For d at least 2 there need not be a single best generator, and every product of intervals [0, alpha_i] with alpha_i in [0,1/2] is achievable as an exact region. Under a near-logarithmic nondegeneracy condition, one generator achieves filtered density at least 1/2 minus epsilon for finite-point-rank targets; the exact 1/2 endpoint can fail even for a rank-zero singleton family.
AI.conclusion: The validity-breadth trade-off has exact characterizations in one dimension, while in higher dimensions it is intrinsically multi-objective, and the exact breadth endpoint of one half is not always attainable.

title: Almost Optimal Lower Bounds under Almost ETH for Approximating Euclidean k-means
summary: In the Euclidean $k$-means problem, we are given a set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, and the goal is to find $k$ representative points in space so as to minimize the sum of the squared distances from each point to its closest representative. Algorithmically, de la Vega, Karpinski, Kenyon, and Rabani [STOC'03] and Kumar, Sabharwal, and Sen [JACM'10] obtain a $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation for high-dimensional Euclidean $k$-means in time $2^{(k/\varepsilon)^{O(1)}} \cdot dn^{O(1)}$, which was subsequently improved to $2^{\tilde{O}(k/\varepsilon)} + O(ndk)$ by Feldman, Monemizadeh, and Sohler [SoCG'07]. On the lower-bound side, a recent work of Cohen-Addad, Karthik, Saulpic, and Schwiegelshohn [SoCG'26] proposed the Exponential Time for Expanders Hypothesis (XXH), which asserts exponential-time hardness for $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximating Vertex Cover on vertex expanders, and used it to prove nearly matching running time lower bound whenever $k=\tilde{\omega}(1/\varepsilon)$. We observe that XXH does not hold in the parameter regime needed for the above result, and show how to repair their reduction under a more standard assumption. More precisely, we show that assuming the Almost Exponential Time Hypothesis for 3-SAT (Almost ETH), for every constant $\beta\in(0,1)$, Euclidean $k$-means in $\mathbb{R}^d$ has no $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm running in time $2^{(k/\varepsilon)^{1-\beta}}\text{poly}(n,d)$, whenever $k=\tilde{\omega}(1/\varepsilon)$. By modifying the construction, we also obtain a similar result for approximating the Euclidean $k$-median problem.

AI.tldr: Shows under Almost ETH that Euclidean k-means and k-median have no (1+epsilon)-approximation running in time 2^((k/epsilon)^(1-beta)) poly(n,d) when k is tilde-omega(1/epsilon), repairing a prior reduction that relied on an assumption the authors show fails in that regime.
AI.motivation: A prior lower bound used the Exponential Time for Expanders Hypothesis, which the authors observe does not hold in the parameter regime needed, leaving the matching lower bound unsupported.
AI.method: The authors replace that assumption with Almost ETH for 3-SAT and modify the construction so that it also yields a similar result for Euclidean k-median.
AI.result: For every constant beta in (0,1), Euclidean k-means in R^d has no (1+epsilon)-approximation running in time 2^((k/epsilon)^(1-beta)) poly(n,d) whenever k is tilde-omega(1/epsilon), and a similar result holds for k-median.
AI.conclusion: The conditional lower bound under a more standard hypothesis complements the known algorithms for approximating Euclidean k-means and k-median.

title: Understanding the Asymptotic Transience of Q-Learning via Distributional Expansion
summary: Q-learning has been empirically observed to exhibit substantial transient error. This transient remains uncaptured by the leading Gaussian limit because the central-limit normalization removes the smaller-scale displacement generated by the initial nonlinear evolution. On the other hand, worst-case finite-sample guarantees, while accounting for transient effects, can obscure the mechanisms responsible for the error on a particular problem instance. We develop a finer asymptotic analysis that gives an asymptotically exact characterization of this transient for a fixed instance. Specifically, for synchronous Q-learning in finite discounted Markov decision processes, we separate the last-iterate error into an optimal-policy temporal-difference (TD) component and a nonnegative displacement caused by maximization. The centered TD component has Gaussian fluctuations at scale $n^{-1/2}$, whereas the maximization transient is of order $n^{-1}$ and converges almost surely, after rescaling by $n$, to a random limit. This limit represents the propagated effect of maximization errors generated before the greedy policy stabilizes. We combine this characterization with an Edgeworth expansion of the TD component to identify the corrections to its Gaussian approximation, separating the effects of initialization, non-Gaussian TD fluctuations, and maximization. The results reveal how transient errors arise for individual Q-learning instances and how their effects persist below the central-limit scale.

AI.tldr: Gives an asymptotically exact, instance-specific characterization of the last-iterate error of synchronous Q-learning, splitting it into a Gaussian TD component of scale n^-1/2 and a maximization transient of order n^-1.
AI.motivation: Q-learning shows substantial transient error that the Gaussian central-limit limit misses, and worst-case finite-sample bounds obscure the mechanisms behind the error for a particular instance.
AI.method: For synchronous Q-learning in finite discounted MDPs, the last-iterate error is separated into an optimal-policy TD component and a nonnegative displacement caused by maximization; an Edgeworth expansion of the TD component identifies corrections to its Gaussian approximation.
AI.result: The centered TD component has Gaussian fluctuations at scale n^-1/2; the maximization transient is of order n^-1 and, after rescaling by n, converges almost surely to a random limit representing the propagated effect of maximization errors made before the greedy policy stabilizes.
AI.conclusion: Transient errors arise from initialization, non-Gaussian TD fluctuations and maximization, and these effects persist below the central-limit scale.

title: Common-DAG Support from Targeted Covariance Changes under Confounding
summary: Targeted covariance changes couple structural rows through a common directed acyclic graph. We study the graph support determined by these experiments when structural errors may be correlated. A positive-gap four-node family has a shortcut identified by common acyclicity. A response indegree of at most two additionally gives unique complete support and two compatible coefficient matrices. The same experiments admit a stable feedback model with the shortcut absent. The result extends to connected graphs with repeated branching and merging. Finite response-column alternatives yield exact bounded-parent compatibility decisions through Horn propagation and partial-target completion. Certified ancestry then supplies an observed-ancestor covariance restriction. Gaussian regression and Fieller inversion reduce inference to a scalar confidence set, and quadratic elimination retains the shared nuisance coefficients with finite-sample edge-error control. In 2048 Gaussian conditions, the scalar procedure reports 127/128 positive edges at gap 1/4 and 524288 observations per cell. Its decisions agree with the joint outer-polynomial reference on the same inputs in all 2022 qualified conditions, with zero reports in 512 null conditions. Exact 16-, 32- and 64-node evaluations verify support and target-coverage conclusions. A root-target characterization connects the identifying information to intervention design.

AI.tldr: Shows that targeted covariance changes identify the common DAG support of a structural model with correlated errors under stated conditions, and gives finite-sample edge inference via Gaussian regression and Fieller inversion.
