AI.motivation: Targeted covariance interventions couple structural equations through a shared DAG, but when errors may be correlated the graph support determined by these experiments must be established, and a shortcut identification argument is needed.
AI.method: The authors analyze positive-gap four-node families and graphs with response indegree at most two, obtain unique complete support and compatible coefficient matrices, and give exact bounded-parent compatibility decisions via Horn propagation; certified ancestry supplies covariance restrictions, and inference reduces to a scalar confidence set via Gaussian regression and Fieller inversion, with quadratic elimination for shared nuisance coefficients.
AI.result: In 2048 Gaussian conditions the scalar procedure reports 127 of 128 positive edges at gap 1/4 with 524288 observations per cell; its decisions agree with the joint outer-polynomial reference in all 2022 qualified conditions, with zero reports in 512 null conditions. Exact evaluations on 16, 32 and 64 nodes verify support and target-coverage conclusions.
AI.conclusion: Targeted covariance experiments can recover the graph support under correlated errors, and the scalar procedure agrees with the joint reference on every qualified condition.

title: Winter wheat improves soil carbon sequestration with reduced gains in warmer climates
comment: 19 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Published in Environmental Research Letters. Georgios Giannarakis and Vasileios Sitokonstantinou contributed equally to this work
summary: Sustainable agricultural intensification requires a precise understanding of how land use decisions influence soil organic carbon (SOC) sequestration under varying environmental conditions. We apply causal machine learning to evaluate the heterogeneous impact of winter wheat-based rotations on SOC at the field-level across Lithuania. Using a nationwide dataset collected over five years (2018-2022), including crop types, management practices, soil properties, and environmental conditions, we estimate how the effects of winter wheat-based rotation vary across space and climate. Our results indicate that winter wheat generally enhances SOC levels, but its effectiveness is modulated by climate. Cooler regions experience higher SOC gains, whereas warmer regions show diminished or even negative effects. Future climate projections suggest that the potential for winter wheat carbon sequestration may decline under high-emission scenarios. These findings highlight the importance of localized agricultural strategies that account for climate variability to maximize SOC sequestration and ensure long-term soil sustainability.

AI.tldr: Uses causal machine learning on a nationwide Lithuanian dataset to show that winter wheat rotations generally raise soil organic carbon, with smaller or negative effects in warmer climates.
AI.motivation: Sustainable agricultural intensification needs a precise understanding of how land-use decisions affect soil organic carbon under varying environmental conditions.
AI.method: The authors apply causal machine learning to five years (2018-2022) of field-level data including crop types, management practices, soil properties and environmental conditions to estimate how the effect of winter wheat-based rotations varies across space and climate; they also consider future climate projections.
AI.result: Winter wheat generally enhances soil organic carbon, with higher gains in cooler regions and diminished or even negative effects in warmer regions; under high-emission scenarios the sequestration potential may decline.
AI.conclusion: Localized agricultural strategies that account for climate variability are needed to maximize soil organic carbon sequestration and long-term soil sustainability.

title: Sharp Covering-Number Bounds for Feedforward ReLU Networks via Parameter Symmetries
summary: In neural networks, distinct parameter configurations often realize the same input--output mapping, indicating that nominal parameter counts can overstate functional complexity. In this paper, we characterize the parameter-space symmetries of ReLU and Leaky ReLU networks across fully connected, convolutional, and residual architectures. We prove that every quasianalytic parameter map preserving the network function is a composition of positive channel scaling and channel permutation. By quotienting out both symmetries, we derive uniform covering-number upper bounds in which positive scaling reduces the complexity exponent from the total parameter count $S$ to $S-H$ (with $H$ denoting the number of scalable channels) and permutation symmetry divides the bound by the factorial count $G$ of channel permutations. We establish matching lower bounds showing that the exponent $S-H$ is sharp in general and that the divisor $G$ is attained for one-hidden-layer and generically identifiable networks. We further extend these results to general continuous piecewise-linear activated networks. Finally, we apply our covering-number bounds to derive statistical risk guarantees for empirical risk minimization and capacity control beyond i.i.d.\ settings, and show how the underlying symmetries help explain weight rebalancing in function approximation and flat directions in empirical risk optimization.

AI.tldr: Proves that the parameter symmetries of ReLU and Leaky ReLU networks are compositions of positive channel scaling and channel permutation, and derives covering-number bounds in which these symmetries reduce complexity, with matching lower bounds.
AI.motivation: Distinct parameter configurations realize the same function, so nominal parameter counts overstate functional complexity, and capacity bounds should account for these symmetries.
AI.method: The authors characterize quasianalytic parameter maps that preserve the network function, quotient out positive scaling and permutation symmetries, and derive uniform covering-number bounds; they extend the results to general continuous piecewise-linear activations and apply them to risk guarantees.
AI.result: Positive scaling reduces the complexity exponent from the total parameter count S to S-H, with H the number of scalable channels, and permutation divides the bound by the factorial count G of channel permutations. Lower bounds show the exponent S-H is sharp in general and G is attained for one-hidden-layer and generically identifiable networks.
AI.conclusion: Accounting for parameter symmetries yields sharp covering-number bounds, which give statistical risk guarantees beyond i.i.d. settings and help explain weight rebalancing and flat directions in empirical risk optimization.

title: Non-normal Limits and Joint Calibration of Cross-fitted Heterogeneity Tests
summary: Cross-fitting is used to test whether a ranking learned in a randomized experiment separates units that benefit from treatment from those that do not: each fold is ranked by a model fitted to the other folds, and the standardized difference in estimated effects between units ranked high and low is compared with a normal distribution. Under the null hypothesis of no heterogeneity the ranking is determined by noise, and because each fold helps to rank the others the fold estimates are dependent. We show that this dependence changes the shape of the null distribution, not just its variance. For least squares on one covariate the limit is bimodal for two folds and skewed for many, no variance correction restores the level, and the model is a counterexample to a published central limit theorem. With many covariates the limit approaches normality, but its variance stays inflated. Removing the non-normal component of the statistic removes its power, so we keep the statistic and change its reference distribution: joint calibration simulates together the moments that choose the rankings and those that evaluate them and applies the same selection to the draws; it has asymptotically exact level and requires no refitting. Applications to clinical and marketing trials, together with random treatment reassignments on their covariates, demonstrate that the standard test substantially inflates Type I error and can produce spurious rejections that joint calibration avoids.

AI.tldr: Shows that the null distribution of cross-fitted heterogeneity tests is non-normal and inflated, and proposes joint calibration, which simulates the ranking and evaluation moments together, to obtain asymptotically exact level without refitting.
AI.motivation: Cross-fitted tests of whether a learned ranking separates treatment-benefiting units are compared with a normal distribution, but dependence across folds changes the shape of the null distribution, and a published CLT is a counterexample.
AI.method: For least squares on one covariate the limit is bimodal for two folds and skewed for many; the authors keep the statistic, which has power, and change its reference distribution: joint calibration simulates the moments that choose the rankings and those that evaluate them, and applies the same selection to the draws.
AI.result: With many covariates the limit approaches normality but its variance stays inflated, and no variance correction restores the level in the one-covariate case. Joint calibration has asymptotically exact level and requires no refitting. In clinical and marketing trials, and with random treatment reassignments, the standard test substantially inflates Type I error and can produce spurious rejections that joint calibration avoids.
AI.conclusion: The standard reference distribution is unreliable for cross-fitted heterogeneity tests, and joint calibration gives valid inference.

title: Sharp Gaussian approximation for Polyak--Ruppert averaged linear stochastic approximation
summary: We study how quickly the normalized Polyak--Ruppert average approaches its Gaussian limit in linear stochastic approximation with bounded i.i.d.\ coefficients. For step sizes decaying as $k^{-\gamma}$, with $1/2\le\gamma<1$, we prove an upper bound of order $n^{\gamma-1}$ on the approximation error over convex sets in fixed dimension. A matching lower bound holds for every fixed model. The fastest rate in this range is $n^{-1/2}$, attained at $\gamma=1/2$. We also obtain an $O(n^{-1/2})$ bound on the error of the recursive multiplier bootstrap procedure.

AI.tldr: Proves that the normalized Polyak-Ruppert average of linear stochastic approximation approaches its Gaussian limit at rate n^(gamma-1) over convex sets, with a matching lower bound, so n^-1/2 is the fastest rate, attained at gamma = 1/2.
AI.motivation: The speed at which the Polyak-Ruppert average approaches its Gaussian limit over convex sets matters for valid inference, and the rate for step sizes decaying as k^(-gamma) had not been sharply characterized.
AI.method: For bounded i.i.d. coefficients and step sizes k^(-gamma) with 1/2 at most gamma less than 1, the authors bound the Gaussian approximation error over convex sets in fixed dimension, prove a matching lower bound for every fixed model, and analyse a recursive multiplier bootstrap procedure.
AI.result: The approximation error is of order n^(gamma-1), and the lower bound shows this is sharp; the fastest rate in this range is n^-1/2, attained at gamma = 1/2. The recursive multiplier bootstrap has error O(n^-1/2).
AI.conclusion: The Gaussian approximation for the averaged iterate is sharp, and the bootstrap achieves the optimal n^-1/2 rate.

title: FADO: Learning Causal Explanations with Prior-Fitted Networks
summary: In regression and classification tasks with tabular datasets, most of the literature on explanation in ML (e.g. SHAP, permutation importance) has focused on predictive attribution: does feature $X_i$ help predict outcome $Y$? At its heart, predictive attribution captures correlation, not causation. We instead ask a causal question: would manipulating feature $X_i$ change outcome $Y$? We define a natural quantity to answer this question, the feature intervention effect: $\Delta_i = E[Y\mid do(X_i=+1)]-E[Y\mid do(X_i=-1)]$. In general, estimating this quantity from observational data alone would entail strong causal assumptions. We propose FADO (Feature-wise Amortized Do-Operators), an amortized inference method using prior-fitted networks trained on synthetic tabular datasets generated by structural causal models. During training, the synthetic data-generating process is known, so we can compute ground-truth intervention effects $\Delta_i$, and train a model to predict them at test time from a purely observational tabular dataset. As we demonstrate through extensive experiments, our new causal explainability method is easy to train and provides better explanations under a range of settings for which standard predictive attribution fails, including proxy variables, confounders, colliders, and placebos. We evaluate it on real, synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets, with and without hidden confounders, and compare it to existing predictive attribution methods and state-of-the-art causal inference methods.

AI.tldr: Proposes FADO, an amortized method that uses prior-fitted networks trained on synthetic data from structural causal models to predict feature intervention effects from observational tabular data.
AI.motivation: Predictive attributions such as SHAP capture correlation rather than causation, and estimating the effect of manipulating a feature from observational data normally requires strong causal assumptions.
AI.method: The feature intervention effect is Delta_i = E[Y | do(X_i=+1)] - E[Y | do(X_i=-1)]; during training on synthetic datasets from structural causal models the ground-truth effects are known, and a prior-fitted network is trained to predict them from a purely observational test dataset.
AI.result: Across extensive experiments, FADO provides better explanations than standard predictive attribution in settings with proxy variables, confounders, colliders and placebos, and is evaluated on real, synthetic and semi-synthetic datasets with and without hidden confounders against predictive attribution methods and state-of-the-art causal inference methods.
AI.conclusion: Amortized causal explanation trained on synthetic structural causal models is a practical alternative to predictive attribution for feature-level causal questions.

title: Sampling the Funnel: A Comprehensive Survey of Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for Hierarchical Bayesian Inference
summary: Hierarchical models are central to applied Bayesian statistics, yet the variance structures they depend on can produce posterior geometries that remain difficult to explore even with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC), a designation now covering a large and increasingly heterogeneous family of algorithms. This survey uses Generalized HMC as an organizing framework to describe the many variants of HMC, their methodological and computational properties, and their empirical consequences. Varying the trajectory length, the degree of momentum refreshment, and the presence of a Metropolis correction recovers several familiar Hamiltonian and Langevin samplers as special cases. Three further, largely independent directions account for much of the remaining literature: modifying the metric, as in Riemannian HMC; modifying the Hamiltonian used by the acceptance test, as in modified or shadow HMC; and modifying the numerical integrator, as in multi-stage splitting schemes. We review these variants alongside the procedures used to tune and diagnose them, with particular attention to the effective sample size, whose standard estimators assume a reversibility that generalized and modified samplers lack, and ignore the importance weights that modified Hamiltonians introduce. We close with the open problems these methods face for hierarchical models, taking joint longitudinal and time-to-event models as the motivating example.

AI.tldr: Surveys Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for hierarchical Bayesian models through a Generalized HMC framework that unifies many variants, and reviews their tuning and diagnostics, with attention to effective sample size for non-reversible and modified samplers.
AI.motivation: Hierarchical models produce posterior geometries that are hard for HMC to explore, and the growing family of HMC variants is heterogeneous and lacks a common organizing view.
AI.method: Generalized HMC organizes variants by trajectory length, momentum refreshment and the presence of a Metropolis correction, recovering several Hamiltonian and Langevin samplers; the survey then reviews metric modification (Riemannian HMC), Hamiltonian modification (modified or shadow HMC) and integrator modification (multi-stage splitting), along with tuning and diagnostic procedures.
AI.result: The survey notes that standard effective sample size estimators assume a reversibility that generalized and modified samplers lack, and ignore the importance weights introduced by modified Hamiltonians; it closes with open problems for hierarchical models, using joint longitudinal and time-to-event models as the motivating example.
AI.conclusion: Diagnostics such as effective sample size need revision for generalized and modified HMC samplers, and several problems remain open for hierarchical models.

title: Conformal prediction for censored life history data
summary: We consider individual prediction of general summaries of a multistate trajectory, such as time alive out of hospital or time spent in remission. Right censoring complicates calibration because these outcomes may be only partially observed. We develop a conformal prediction approach for scalar and vector summaries over a fixed clinical horizon supported by follow-up. For each candidate region, we define the coverage determining time as the earliest time at which the observed history establishes whether the outcome lies in the region, even if the outcome itself is still unknown. We weight observed coverage decisions by the inverse probability of remaining uncensored to that time and augment the estimator with conditional coverage probabilities for unresolved histories. For a fixed region, the coverage estimator is doubly robust with respect to the censoring and conditional coverage models and attains the semiparametric efficiency bound when both are consistent at suitable rates. For the calibrated region, we derive a finite-sample lower bound on the coverage probability and establish asymptotic validity if either model is correct. In simulations, using partial histories yields narrower prediction intervals at comparable coverage. We illustrate joint prediction of days in and out of hospital in the HF-ACTION trial and prediction of relapse-free time in the German Breast Cancer Study Group cohort.

AI.tldr: Develops a conformal prediction method for individual prediction of multistate trajectory summaries, such as time alive out of hospital, under right censoring, using inverse-probability-of-censoring weighting with a doubly robust augmentation.
AI.motivation: Right censoring means outcomes such as time alive out of hospital may be only partly observed, which complicates calibration of prediction regions.
AI.method: For each candidate region the authors define a coverage determining time, the earliest time at which the observed history settles whether the outcome lies in the region; coverage decisions are weighted by the inverse probability of remaining uncensored and augmented with conditional coverage probabilities for unresolved histories.
AI.result: For a fixed region the coverage estimator is doubly robust for the censoring and conditional coverage models and attains the semiparametric efficiency bound when both are consistent at suitable rates; the calibrated region has a finite-sample coverage lower bound and is asymptotically valid if either model is correct. In simulations partial histories yield narrower intervals at comparable coverage; the method is illustrated on the HF-ACTION trial and the German Breast Cancer Study Group cohort.
AI.conclusion: The approach gives valid prediction regions for censored multistate outcomes, and using partial histories makes them narrower at comparable coverage.

title: From Link Prediction to Linear Community Detection: A Finite-Sample Guarantee for Graph Pretraining
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 47 pages, 8 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Link prediction (LP) is a standard pretraining objective for graph neural networks (GNNs): hide edges, train an encoder-decoder to predict them, and reuse the node embeddings for downstream node tasks. Despite its empirical success, there is little quantitative theory explaining why an edge-level objective should produce embeddings that are linearly useful for node classification. We study this question in the finite-sample stochastic block model (SBM). For any bounded GNN encoder paired with a symmetric bilinear decoder, we prove a conditional reduction: small population held-out LP excess risk implies small community-classification error for a transductive linear classifier on the learned embeddings. The bound decomposes into an optimization residual, an architectural approximation residual, and explicit statistical terms of order $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{d/n})$ in bounded dense regimes. We further give a constructive few-label classifier: nearest-centroid classification under the positive semidefinite quadratic form $G = W Z^\top Z W$, whose label error is coupled to LP quality. The framework is architecture-agnostic through the approximation residual, and we instantiate this residual as $O(\log n / n)$ for a graph isomorphism network (GIN) with spectral positional encoding and a bilinear decoder. Synthetic SBM experiments validate the theorem chain from LP risk to score error to classification error, and show when the worst-case constants become conservative.

AI.tldr: Gives a finite-sample theory for graph link prediction pretraining in the stochastic block model, showing that small held-out link prediction risk implies small community classification error for a linear classifier on the learned embeddings.
AI.motivation: Link prediction is a standard GNN pretraining objective, but there is little quantitative theory for why an edge-level objective should yield embeddings that are linearly useful for node classification.
AI.method: For any bounded GNN encoder with a symmetric bilinear decoder, the authors prove a conditional reduction bounding community classification error by an optimization residual, an architectural approximation residual and statistical terms of order tilde-O(sqrt(d/n)); they also give a nearest-centroid few-label classifier under the quadratic form G = W Z^T Z W and instantiate the approximation residual for a GIN with spectral positional encoding.
AI.result: The approximation residual is O(log n / n) for the GIN with spectral positional encoding and bilinear decoder; synthetic SBM experiments validate the chain from link prediction risk to score error to classification error and show when the worst-case constants are conservative.
AI.conclusion: Link prediction risk controls downstream linear community classification in the SBM, and the worst-case constants may be conservative in practice.

title: A Latent Semiparametric Mixture Model for Robust Heterogeneity Learning in High Dimensions
summary: Learning heterogeneity from high-dimensional data has become a fundamental task across many data-driven fields. Cluster analysis is a widely used unsupervised tool for this purpose, and many existing methods have been adapted to high-dimensional settings through sparsity constraints. In contrast to algorithmic approaches, model-based clustering offers clean theoretical guaranties and computational simplicity, but can be restrictive in practice due to its reliance on specific parametric distributions. We propose a novel latent semiparametric mixture model for clustering, in which the observed data follow a Gaussian mixture after latent coordinate-wise monotone transformations. Furthermore, assuming a sparse optimal clustering rule in the latent space, we develop a new method, CESME, tailored for high-dimensional clustering. By allowing unspecified transformations, our framework becomes substantially more flexible and robust than traditional model-based approaches. The clustering error of CESME is shown to approach the optimal clustering error at a rate matching that obtained when the true transformations are known. Extensive simulations and real data analysis confirm that CESME outperforms a broad range of existing high-dimensional clustering methods, including those designed for single-cell RNA sequencing data. The online supplementary file contains technical proofs, additional discussions, and more numerical results.

AI.tldr: Proposes CESME, a high-dimensional clustering method for a latent semiparametric Gaussian mixture in which unknown coordinate-wise monotone transformations map the observed data to a Gaussian mixture.
AI.motivation: Model-based clustering is theoretically clean but restrictive because of its reliance on specific parametric distributions, while algorithmic high-dimensional methods lack that structure.
AI.method: The observed data follow a Gaussian mixture after latent coordinate-wise monotone transformations; assuming a sparse optimal clustering rule in the latent space, CESME is developed for high-dimensional clustering without specifying the transformations.
AI.result: The clustering error of CESME approaches the optimal clustering error at a rate matching that obtained when the true transformations are known; simulations and real data analysis show it outperforms a broad range of high-dimensional clustering methods, including those designed for single-cell RNA sequencing data.
AI.conclusion: The latent semiparametric mixture gives a flexible and robust clustering framework that retains near-oracle theoretical performance.

title: Training Calibrated Conditional Generative Models with a Sample-Only Coverage Loss
summary: Conditional generative models have become the tool of choice for sampling posteriors in scientific inverse problems, where we seek to sample images or signals conditioned on a set of indirect and noisy measurements. Yet they are often overconfident, which is a critical failure in scientific applications where accurate uncertainty quantification is essential. Existing regularizers fall short in complementary ways: differentiable coverage objectives require the model's density and do not identify the posterior, while strictly proper scoring rules such as the energy score need only samples but do not directly enforce coverage. We close this gap by introducing a differentiable loss function based on the expected coverage probability, estimated from samples alone. It applies to any conditional generative model, with no need for tractable densities or architectural changes. We prove that it is a strict divergence, vanishing if and only if the model equals the true posterior. On simulation-based inference benchmarks, it matches a density-based coverage loss without evaluating the density. On high-dimensional imaging inverse problems, it yields better-calibrated posteriors than scoring-rule regularizers, with little change in the reconstruction quality of point estimates.

AI.tldr: Introduces a differentiable loss that estimates expected coverage probability from samples alone, to train calibrated conditional generative models without densities, and proves it is a strict divergence.
AI.motivation: Conditional generative models are often overconfident in scientific inverse problems; existing coverage objectives need densities, while scoring rules such as the energy score do not directly enforce coverage.
AI.method: The authors define a differentiable sample-only coverage loss based on expected coverage probability; it applies to any conditional generative model without architectural changes, and the paper proves it vanishes if and only if the model equals the true posterior.
AI.result: On simulation-based inference benchmarks it matches a density-based coverage loss without evaluating the density; on high-dimensional imaging inverse problems it yields better-calibrated posteriors than scoring-rule regularizers, with little change in the reconstruction quality of point estimates.
AI.conclusion: Sample-based coverage regularization can improve posterior calibration for generative models in scientific inverse problems without sacrificing point reconstruction quality.

title: Characterizing the Edge of Stability in Variational Training Without Priors
summary: Variational approaches in deep learning promise to deliver improved uncertainty quantification and out-of-distribution generalization by inferring a distribution over weights, regularized by a divergence to a chosen prior. However, prior elicitation presents a significant challenge in deep learning, resulting in the common practice of significantly downweighting the regularization term in the variational objective. Recently, it was proposed to train solely via the expected loss by relying on implicit regularization from the optimizer, rather than explicit regularization from the divergence to the prior. While this approach largely sidesteps the issue of prior elicitation, current theory lacks an understanding of how key optimization hyperparameters impact the implicit regularization. Here, we theoretically and empirically demonstrate that larger learning rates and fewer parameter samples lead to flatter minima of the loss landscape, which are known to generalize better. We show that training on the expected loss operates at a modified edge of stability, characterized by the signal-to-noise ratio of the gradient estimates and the number of Monte Carlo samples. Experiments on out-of-distribution benchmark datasets confirm the practical significance of the theoretical results.

AI.tldr: Shows theoretically and empirically that training on the expected loss without an explicit prior yields implicit regularization whose flatness depends on learning rate and the number of Monte Carlo samples, operating at a modified edge of stability.
AI.motivation: Variational deep learning needs a prior, which is hard to elicit, and common practice downweights the KL term; a recent approach trains on the expected loss alone, but the effect of optimization hyperparameters on its implicit regularization was not understood.
AI.method: The authors analyse training on the expected loss, relating the implicit regularization to the signal-to-noise ratio of the gradient estimates and the number of Monte Carlo samples, and test on out-of-distribution benchmarks.
AI.result: Larger learning rates and fewer parameter samples lead to flatter minima, which are known to generalize better; training operates at a modified edge of stability characterized by gradient SNR and the number of Monte Carlo samples. Experiments on out-of-distribution benchmarks confirm the practical significance of the theory.
AI.conclusion: Optimization hyperparameters control the implicit regularization of expected-loss variational training, so they should be chosen with this effect in mind.

title: Improved Elastic Weight Consolidation as an Optimization Constraint for Continual Learning
comment: 22 pages, 7 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) is a widely used regularization-based technique for continual learning, protecting performance on old tasks with a quadratic penalty whose empirical Fisher is usually justified through probabilistic curvature. We instead introduce Continual Learning as an Optimization Constraint (CLOC): new training must preserve chosen functionals of learned behavior. EWC's empirical Fisher is exactly the first-order form of this constraint when the preserved functional is each sample's loss. This derivation exposes a flaw: EWC implicitly weights each sample by the scale of its loss gradient, so well-fitted samples lose importance. EWC-DR observed this failure in classification; CLOC identifies its general cause. Improved Elastic Weight Consolidation (IEWC) penalizes output changes according to the first-order approximation of each old sample's loss level set, removing the weighting for any differentiable loss and output geometry, and prevents corrupt samples from dominating the importance matrix. Across classification, segmentation, language, forecasting, and diffusion, IEWC variants match or improve on EWC and outperform EWC-DR. In a held-out evaluation with validation-selected hyperparameters, uniform IEWC improves ImageNet-R accuracy over matched EWC by 2.00 percentage points (95% CI 0.93-3.07).

AI.tldr: Proposes Continual Learning as an Optimization Constraint (CLOC) and Improved EWC (IEWC), which penalizes output changes via a first-order approximation of each old sample's loss level set, removing EWC's loss-scale weighting.
AI.motivation: EWC's empirical Fisher penalty implicitly weights each sample by the scale of its loss gradient, so well-fitted samples lose importance; EWC-DR observed this failure in classification without identifying its general cause.
AI.method: CLOC treats preservation of chosen functionals of learned behaviour as a constraint; EWC's empirical Fisher is the first-order form of this constraint when the functional is each sample's loss; IEWC penalizes output changes according to the first-order approximation of each old sample's loss level set, and prevents corrupt samples from dominating the importance matrix.
AI.result: Across classification, segmentation, language, forecasting and diffusion, IEWC variants match or improve on EWC and outperform EWC-DR; in a held-out evaluation with validation-selected hyperparameters, uniform IEWC improves ImageNet-R accuracy over matched EWC by 2.00 percentage points (95% CI 0.93 to 3.07).
AI.conclusion: Viewing EWC as an optimization constraint explains its weighting flaw, and the level-set-based IEWC removes it across tasks and losses.

title: Your PID Is Already a Neural Network: Learning Its Gains with Only Three Weights and No Teacher
comment: 18 pages main text plus appendices, 17 figures. Code: this https URL
summary: A discrete PID controller is exactly a recurrent neural network, a classical state-space fact: a fixed linear memory of the running integral and the last error, read out by three trainable weights that map one-to-one to the PID gains. Networks with bounded hidden states, such as LSTMs of any width, only approximate it. Trained only on a one-step physical cost (the expected cost of one transition from a fixed state distribution), with no demonstrations, teacher controller, or known gains, the network solves a strongly convex least-squares problem, so gradient descent converges from any initialization to the unique one-step optimal PID gains; the limit network is that PID, with the same action on every error sequence. Partitioned regression then shows what extra capacity buys. Orthogonal residual features keep these gains and improve on the PID if and only if they correlate with the part of the optimal action outside the PID span. On a nonlinear second-order example the gap is 5.88% of the optimal PID cost, and 4.00% against PID with a bias; no controller can improve on PID by more on this objective. A residual started at a tuned PID begins exactly at that PID; at the one-step optimal PID, a fixed-feature residual's first gradient step lowers the cost if and only if its features can improve on the PID. Experiments confirm the realization, recovery, and gap results to numerical precision. On held-out plants of three families, under a protocol frozen before the test data existed, a residual warm-started at a heavily tuned PID and trained with it lowers the long-horizon cost by 3.5%, 3.5%, and 1.9%, with family-wise 95% bounds excluding zero, also under distribution shift; a post hoc comparison with the PID tuned alone suggests that most of it comes from the recurrent part in two families. The primary endpoint, a gain of at least 5% from a generic PID start, is not met in any family.

AI.tldr: Shows that a discrete PID controller is exactly a recurrent network with three trainable weights, that learning its gains from a one-step physical cost recovers the unique one-step optimal PID, and that a residual on top gives a 1.9 to 3.5 percent long-horizon gain on held-out plants, short of the 5 percent primary endpoint.
AI.motivation: Neural controllers with bounded hidden states, such as LSTMs, only approximate a PID, and it is unclear what extra capacity beyond a PID actually buys on physical control tasks.
AI.method: With a one-step cost and no demonstrations, the network solves a strongly convex least-squares problem whose gradient descent converges to the unique one-step optimal PID gains; partitioned regression tests orthogonal residual features, and a residual warm-started at a heavily tuned PID is trained and evaluated on held-out plants of three families under a protocol frozen before the test data existed.
AI.result: The residual lowers long-horizon cost by 3.5%, 3.5% and 1.9% across the three families, with family-wise 95% bounds excluding zero, also under distribution shift; a post hoc comparison suggests most of the gain comes from the recurrent part in two families. On a nonlinear second-order example the gap to the optimal controller is 5.88% of optimal PID cost (4.00% against PID with a bias). The primary endpoint, a gain of at least 5% from a generic PID start, is not met in any family.
AI.conclusion: A PID is the exact optimum for the one-step cost in this setting, and residual capacity helps only modestly, below the pre-specified 5% target.

title: A Matching Lower Bound for Online Smooth Calibration
summary: We study smooth calibration error in sequential binary prediction, which measures how far a sequence of probabilistic forecasts is from being calibrated and, unlike the classical expected calibration error, is robust to small perturbations of the forecasts. Against adaptive adversaries, the minimax smooth calibration error is known to lie between $\Omega(T^{1/3})$ and $O(\sqrt{T})$ (Qiao and Zheng, 2024), where $T$ is the number of rounds. In this paper, we close this gap by constructing a new adversary whose outcome mean moves with the forecaster's cumulative residual. This design makes compensating for past residuals costly, and forces every forecaster to incur an expected smooth calibration error of $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$. This lower bound matches the known upper bound up to universal constants, and further implies $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$ lower bounds for calibration distance and lower calibration distance. Overall, our results settle the minimax rates of these calibration measures in sequential prediction. The proof ideas are partially developed by GPT-6 Astra under the authors' guidance.

AI.tldr: Proves a matching Omega(sqrt(T)) lower bound on the minimax smooth calibration error in sequential binary prediction against adaptive adversaries, closing the gap to the known O(sqrt(T)) upper bound.
AI.motivation: The minimax smooth calibration error was known only to lie between Omega(T^(1/3)) and O(sqrt(T)), leaving the rate unresolved.
AI.method: The authors construct a new adversary whose outcome mean moves with the forecaster's cumulative residual, making it costly to compensate for past residuals and forcing any forecaster to incur expected smooth calibration error of Omega(sqrt(T)).
AI.result: The lower bound matches the known upper bound up to universal constants and implies Omega(sqrt(T)) lower bounds for calibration distance and lower calibration distance, settling the minimax rates of these calibration measures.
AI.conclusion: The minimax rate of smooth calibration error, and of the related calibration measures, is sqrt(T); the proof ideas were partially developed by GPT-6 Astra under the authors' guidance.

title: Gradient Flows over Convex Bodies for Learning Optimal Regularizers
summary: We consider the question of describing gradient flows over the collection of convex bodies. This is motivated by foundational questions arising in inverse problems. Suppose we wish to solve an ill-posed inverse problem using regularization techniques. Can we learn an optimal choice of a convex regularizer directly from prior data? Given a numerical algorithm that computes such an optimal regularizer, is there a principled manner for describing the evolution of its iterates? The objective of this paper is to lay the foundation towards answering these questions. To this end, we consider a criterion of an optimal regularizer based on seeking a convex body that minimizes the expected gauge evaluation with respect to a prior data distribution subject to a volume constraint. The formulation is initially nonconvex, but admits hidden convexity by passing to its polar. We characterize the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions that certify global optimality. We also analyze the $L^2$-gradient flow as well as a minimizing movement scheme with the Hausdorff penalty. Our results show that the objective gap decays exponentially along the gradient flow and we obtain dimension-dependent rates for both the objective gap and distance to the optimal body for the Hausdorff scheme. Finally, we apply the KKT conditions to identify explicit optimal convex bodies. For data where the optimal nonconvex regularizer is the $\ell_p$-quasinorm, $p \in (0,1)$, the optimal convex regularizer is the volume-normalized $\ell_1$-ball. For data described by paired basis atoms, the optimal convex regularizer is the polar of a shifted zonotope.

AI.tldr: Studies gradient flows over convex bodies to learn optimal convex regularizers from prior data, showing hidden convexity via the polar, exponential objective decay along the L2 gradient flow, and explicit optimal bodies for lp-quasinorm and paired-atom data.
AI.motivation: Ill-posed inverse problems need regularizers, and it is unclear whether an optimal convex regularizer can be learned from prior data or how the iterates of a numerical algorithm for it evolve.
AI.method: The authors minimize the expected gauge over a prior distribution subject to a volume constraint; the nonconvex problem becomes convex in the polar, they characterize the KKT conditions for global optimality, and they analyse the L2 gradient flow and a minimizing movement scheme with a Hausdorff penalty.
AI.result: The objective gap decays exponentially along the gradient flow, and dimension-dependent rates are obtained for the objective gap and the distance to the optimal body for the Hausdorff scheme. For data whose optimal nonconvex regularizer is the lp quasinorm with p in (0,1), the optimal convex regularizer is the volume-normalized l1 ball; for paired basis atoms it is the polar of a shifted zonotope.
AI.conclusion: Optimal convex regularizers can be identified explicitly in some cases, and the flows give a principled description of how they evolve.

title: Fréchet Oblique Forest for Non-Euclidean Regression
summary: We propose Fréchet oblique forests (FOF) for non-Euclidean regression with predictors and responses in metric spaces. An Alexandrov inner-product score defines directional splits in metric predictor spaces and recovers ordinary oblique splits for Euclidean predictors. Candidate splits are evaluated through pairwise response distances, avoiding repeated Fréchet mean computations during split search. Forest predictions minimize a weighted Fréchet criterion obtained by averaging leaf weights across trees. For compatible tree rules, we establish integrated consistency and polynomial risk bounds under explicit approximation and entropy conditions. Simulations with matrices, distributions, spherical data and mixed predictors, together with an application to taxi-flow networks, demonstrate competitive predictive performance.

AI.tldr: Proposes Frechet oblique forests for regression with predictors and responses in metric spaces, using an Alexandrov inner-product score for directional splits and a weighted Frechet criterion for predictions, with consistency and risk bounds.
AI.motivation: Regression with non-Euclidean predictors and responses needs tree splits that work in metric spaces without repeated Frechet mean computations during split search.
AI.method: An Alexandrov inner-product score defines directional splits in metric predictor spaces and reduces to ordinary oblique splits for Euclidean predictors; candidate splits are evaluated through pairwise response distances, and forest predictions minimize a weighted Frechet criterion obtained by averaging leaf weights across trees.
AI.result: For compatible tree rules the authors establish integrated consistency and polynomial risk bounds under explicit approximation and entropy conditions; simulations with matrices, distributions, spherical data and mixed predictors, and an application to taxi-flow networks, show competitive predictive performance.
AI.conclusion: The forest extends oblique regression trees to metric-space data with theoretical guarantees and competitive empirical performance.

title: A Sensitivity Framework for Assessing External Validity
summary: Assessing the external validity of experimental results is a pervasive challenge in causal inference as internally valid findings need not generalize beyond sites in which the experiments were conducted. Since the number of sites is often smaller than the number of site-level variables that moderate causal effects, we develop a partial identification framework that lets practitioners assess external validity under a wide range of assumptions that allow extrapolation across site-level variables. Our optimization-driven approach can accommodate any affine family of parameter restrictions, such as interaction terms being dominated by direct effects (the "effect hierarchy principle"). Since standard estimating-equation arguments do not apply in our setting---underspecified parameter directions responsible for partial identification make the covariance matrix singular---we develop a novel debiasing approach for estimands given by constrained optimization problems, giving rise to semiparametrically efficient estimators for our flexible partial identification bounds. We illustrate our approach on multi-site microcredit experiments harmonized by Meager (2019), whose lending environments differ widely in interest rates, loan sizes, and promotion. Holding out one country at a time, we construct external-validity intervals for the held-out country from the remaining source sites and show how our framework connects different extrapolation assumptions to concrete partial identification bounds.

AI.tldr: Develops a partial identification framework for assessing the external validity of experimental results across sites when there are more site-level moderators than sites, with semiparametrically efficient estimators obtained by a debiasing approach.
AI.motivation: Experimental effects may not generalize beyond the study sites, and the number of sites is often smaller than the number of moderating site-level variables, so point identification is not feasible.
AI.method: The optimization-driven framework accommodates any affine family of parameter restrictions, such as the effect hierarchy principle; because standard estimating-equation arguments fail when the covariance matrix is singular, the authors develop a debiasing approach for estimands defined by constrained optimization problems.
AI.result: The framework is illustrated on multi-site microcredit experiments, holding out one country at a time to construct external-validity intervals from the remaining sites, and it connects different extrapolation assumptions to concrete partial identification bounds.
AI.conclusion: The framework gives practical external-validity intervals under explicit extrapolation assumptions, with efficient estimation of the bounds.

title: Recursive State-Augmented Language Models: Persistent Latent-State Adaptation of Pretrained Language Models
summary: Language models rely on finite token contexts, limiting access to earlier interactions. We introduce Recursive State-Augmented Language Models (Recursive SALM), a framework in which a persistent latent state evolves with each observation and generates adaptations of a pretrained language model. A modular read-transition-write architecture separates observation encoding, latent dynamics, and predictor adaptation. We develop deterministic and stochastic formulations. The experiments evaluate only deterministic SALM with frozen GPT-2 small and exclude earlier evidence from its decoder context. On a four-turn hypothesis-inference task, latent-gated LoRA reaches 89.1% accuracy, comparable to 88.0% for a trained full-context LoRA baseline, with earlier evidence available solely through a 64-dimensional state. Zeroing or shuffling the state substantially reduces accuracy. In a two-turn task with codewords unseen in training, several interfaces improve candidate ranking over chance, but rarely generate the exact codeword under the evaluated training schedule. These experiments show that persistent latent-conditioned adaptation can support sequential inference when earlier evidence is absent from the decoder context.

AI.tldr: Introduces Recursive SALM, in which a persistent 64-dimensional latent state evolves with each observation and generates adaptations of a frozen GPT-2 small, allowing sequential inference without earlier evidence in the decoder context.
AI.motivation: Language models are limited to finite token contexts, which restricts their access to earlier interactions.
AI.method: A modular read-transition-write architecture separates observation encoding, latent dynamics and predictor adaptation; the experiments evaluate only the deterministic variant with frozen GPT-2 small, using latent-gated LoRA and excluding earlier evidence from the decoder context.
AI.result: On a four-turn hypothesis-inference task latent-gated LoRA reaches 89.1% accuracy, comparable to 88.0% for a trained full-context LoRA baseline; zeroing or shuffling the state substantially reduces accuracy. On a two-turn task with unseen codewords, several interfaces improve candidate ranking over chance but rarely generate the exact codeword under the training schedule.
AI.conclusion: Persistent latent-conditioned adaptation can support sequential inference when earlier evidence is absent from the decoder context, though exact generation of unseen codewords remains rare.

title: Posterior contraction rates for banded approximations of Gaussian processes
summary: Gaussian process regression models are widely used in modern statistics and machine learning due to their flexibility, interpretability, built-in uncertainty quantification, and strong theoretical foundations. However, training Gaussian processes (GPs) has a computational cost of $O(n^3)$, while the memory and prediction costs are also $O(n^2)$. For large datasets commonly encountered in practice, this becomes infeasible and necessitates the use of approximate posterior methods. In this work, we propose a class of approximations based on sparse covariance matrices, where the kernel matrix is sparsified according to the spatial proximity of the design points. We analyze the accuracy of the resulting approximate posterior distribution and show that the proposed approach preserves optimal statistical inference properties, provided that the dependencies among a sufficient number of neighboring points for each feature are retained. We derive explicit sufficient and necessary conditions on the number of neighbors required in a general setting and apply these results to standard kernels, including the squared exponential and Matérn kernels. Our theoretical findings are supported by numerical experiments.

AI.tldr: Proves posterior contraction for Gaussian process regression with sparse banded covariance approximations built from spatial neighbours, showing optimal inference when enough neighbours are retained, with explicit neighbour conditions for squared exponential and Matern kernels.
AI.motivation: Exact GP training costs O(n^3), and memory and prediction costs are O(n^2), which is infeasible for large datasets, so approximate posteriors with guarantees are needed.
AI.method: The kernel matrix is sparsified according to the spatial proximity of the design points; the authors analyse the accuracy of the resulting approximate posterior and derive explicit sufficient and necessary conditions on the number of neighbours, applied to squared exponential and Matern kernels.
AI.result: The approach preserves optimal statistical inference properties provided the dependencies among a sufficient number of neighbouring points for each feature are retained; numerical experiments support the theoretical findings.
AI.conclusion: Sparse neighbour-based covariance approximations can keep optimal posterior contraction for GP regression, provided enough neighbours are kept.
